generation: Deep convolutional neural networks have had a major impact on segmentation tasks, especially in the field of medical images. However, the problem of domain shift and the problem of corrupted labels, which are common problems in medical images, has a very bad effect on the performance of deep convolutional neural networks in practice. In this paper, we propose a new cross-denoising framework using two peer networks to overcome the problem of domain shift and corrupted labels by a peer review strategy. Specifically, we have one mentor network and one reviewer network. In this way, the two networks are supervised by each other, and to deal with the problem of corrupted labels, a loss function is introduced to encourage the network to find the most important locality and to filter the error in the noise-contaminated label. To further reduce the accumulated error, we have introduced a class imbalanced learning mechanism, which selects the most likely answer in each class to achieve a balance. The experiment on the REFUGE and Drishti-GS datasets shows that the proposed method has better performance than the existing method.

In recent years, deep neural network (DNN)-based edge detection has made great progress. However, although the DNN-based edge detection method is better than the previous method, it is more complicated. This is mainly because the DNN-based edge detection method adopts the neural network structure that has been designed for high-level computer vision tasks, such as image segmentation and object recognition. However, the task of edge detection is relatively local and simple, and the over-complicated network structure and many parameters may not be needed. Therefore, we propose a method that is based on the previous method and is good at detecting edges. The proposed method mainly includes three parts: feature extraction, input enhancement, and feature concatenation, which roughly correspond to the gradient, low-pass filter, and image concatenation in the previous method. This can greatly reduce the complexity and improve the performance of edge prediction. Compared with the recent Bi-Directional Cascade Neural Network (BDCN2), the accuracy of the proposed TIN2 is higher, and the network is smaller.

IMAGE SEGMENTATION is a fundamental task in image processing and in computer vision. In the last few decades, a number of segmentation methods have been developed for various applications. Among these methods, the N-cut method has been extensively applied because of its good performance. The N-cut method is formulated as an energy minimization problem with respect to a predefined graph. Consequently, the segmentation results of the N-cut method are highly dependent on the predefined similarity measure on the graph, and since this measure is usually given by the users, this leads to some unfavorable segmentation results. In this paper, we propose a novel N-cut method that integrates an adaptive similarity measure with spatial regularization. The proposed method combines the Parzen–Rosenblatt sliding window method, the non–local entropy, the N-cut energy, and a phase–field regularizer in a variational framework. The proposed method finds a more favorable similarity measure than the N-cut method by an adaptive procedure. We give a mathematical interpretation of the proposed similarity measure from various perspectives, such as statistical theory and convex optimization. In addition, the phase field regularizer guarantees robust performance in the presence of noise and corrects the similarity measure by spatial prior knowledge. The well–posedness and existence of the minimizer of the proposed method are proved. In the experiments, we show that our method outperforms other methods, such as the N-cut method and the Chan–Vese model.

We deal with the problem of image-on-text segmentation. It is a problem at the intersection of natural-language processing and image-processing. We are given an input image and an expression which designates an object in the image, and our problem is to find the object in the image to which the sentence refers. To this end, we propose a convolutional LSTM neural network to solve the problem. Our model is composed of an encoder and a decoder, where the convolutional LSTM neural network is used in both the encoder and the decoder to capture spatial and temporal information. The encoder extracts features from both text and image of each word in the sentence, and the decoder focuses on the words in the sentence which are the most informative by using the attention mechanism. The decoder then generates the final segmentation map by combining the features from multiple levels of the encoder. We verify the effectiveness of our model on four difficult data sets.

A considerable amount of deep learning has become available in the Machine Learning field. The challenging tasks of object detection, localization, recognition and segmentation in a given scene have been addressed successfully with the help of deep neural networks of different types such as convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, adversarial networks, autoencoders, etc. Several studies have been carried out for the detection and recognition of objects in images. This paper is devoted to the various deep learning techniques of image segmentation. The main purpose of this paper is to give a good understanding of the major techniques which have largely contributed to the image segmentation domain. Starting with some of the basic approaches of image segmentation, this paper continues to explain the impact of deep learning on the image segmentation field. Thereafter, all the major image segmentation methods are classified logically and dedicated to the unique contribution of each of them. By the end of the paper, the reader should be able to visualize the inner workings of the process more easily.

Convolutional Neural Networks have been used in various ways for the study of two-dimensional images in medicine. But in practice, most of the images are in three dimensions. This has led to the development of three-dimensional convolutional neural networks, which can extract the spatial information more advantageously. But the limitations of the memory on the GPU means that state-of-the-art methods are limited to processing a subvolume or a small area, which prevents the introduction of a more extensive context. In this paper, we propose a new technique for fast and efficient semantic segmentation of 3D images. The HDC method is based on a rotation and a spatial downshuffling operation, followed by a conventional 3D convolution. The advantages of this method are that it reduces the memory requirements for the subsequent subvolume processing, but still retains the full information in the input. The results of extensive experiments on hip T1 and T2 images show that the proposed method is effective.

America has a very big railway system. In 2006, the standard gauge length of the American railroads was 145,669 miles. Keeping such a large system and removing all the dangers such as poor track stability and poor drainage resulting from the degradation of the ballast takes a lot of labor. In the past, the only way to determine the degradation of the ballast was to obtain an index called the Fouling Index by taking samples and sieving them. This laboratory work is very time consuming and tedious. But with the recent developments in the field of computer vision, it is possible to develop a new method of ballast inspection, which can replace the old mechanical method. The new method analyzes the image of the ballast and, based on image segmentation, obtains ballast regions. By comparing the regions and their corresponding FI values, this method obtains a new index that has the best fit with the FI. This paper will explain the details of how the new method works.

Semantic image segmentation is one of the most challenging tasks in computer vision. In this paper, we propose a very dense convolutional network, which is composed of three parts: one-to-one decomposition, multiple upsampling, and prediction of the highest level. We use multiple steps of upsampling, the feature map of the pooling layer and its corresponding unpooling layer. Then we output multiple intermediate layers, each intermediate layer is generated by upsampling from unpooling. Finally, these intermediate layers are combined into the final layer, and the convolutional network has a strong advantage in the ability to combine and reuse the features. Our training method also adds a soft cost to the pre-layer and the final layer, and when the loss is propagated backwards, the soft cost has a significant impact on the cost. We test our model on three popular datasets, CamVid, Pascal VOC and ADE20K. We achieve the best performance on CamVid. On Pascal VOC and ADE20K, our model has a significant improvement.

Active contour models, based on partial differential equations, have been successfully used in image segmentation, but the study of their geometric formulation on arbitrary geometric graphs is still in its infancy. In this paper we introduce geometric approximations of the gradient and curvature that are used in the geodesic active contour model. We prove the convergence in probability of our gradient approximation to the true gradient value, and we prove an asymptotic upper bound for the error of this approximation for the class of random geometric graphs. Two different approximations for curvature are also presented, and they are proved to converge in probability in the class of random geometric graphs. We propose neighborhood filtering on graphs to improve the accuracy of the previous approximations, and we define two variants of Gaussian smoothing on graphs, which include normalization in order to deal with the nonuniformity of the graphs. The effectiveness of our active contour framework on graphs is demonstrated in the segmentation of regular images and geographical data defined on arbitrary geometric graphs.

As already mentioned, region-based methods have proven useful for improving the segmentation accuracy of neuronal structures in EM images. Most of these methods rely on a scoring function to determine the merging of regions. These scoring functions are usually learned by supervised learning with large amounts of ground-truth data, which are expensive to obtain. We propose a semi-supervised learning approach that reduces this need. By using a tree-based structure for region merging, we develop a differentiable unsupervised loss that forces the learned function to make consistent predictions. We then propose a Bayesian model that combines the supervised and unsupervised information for probabilistic learning. Experimental results on three EM image data sets show that, with only a small subset of the ground-truth data, 3-7% of the total amount, our method can achieve performance very close to the best fully supervised method using the full ground truth.

We extend the generalized comparison principle for the Monge-Ampère equation due to Rauch and Taylor (Rocky Mountain Journal of Mathematics, Vol. 7, No. 2, April 1977) to nonconvex domains. We prove that, from the generalized comparison principle, there are upper and lower bounds on the solutions of the Monge-Ampère equation with a variable right-hand side. In particular, it is shown that, because of the relationship between the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations and the Monge-Ampère equation, the pressure on a bounded domain cannot be made to vanish in Omega unless p is equal to zero (for all time). At any time t greater than zero, there is a solution z in Omega such that delta p(z,t) = 0.

We report the synthesis and the anisotropic properties of URhIn,5Li. High quality single crystals have been grown in an indium bath. The sample exhibits a second-order phase transition from a ferromagnetic to an antiferromagnetic state at T-N = 98 K. The transition is field-independent up to 9 T. The increase of the resistivity with j along the [100], [110], and [001] tetragonal axes is consistent with the induction of spin density waves with a gap that first opens in the 001 direction. The magnetic susceptibility m, = M/H, is strongly anisotropic. Above T = 200 K, m, follows the Curie-Weiss law with the effective moment mu_eff = 3.71 mu B / m U and the Weiss temperature t_w = -900 K and t_w = -500 K for mu_p oriented in the [100] and [001] directions, respectively. The characteristic Kondo temperature T-K for URhIn,5Li is T_K = 125 K.

We study the problem of allocating n independent flexible tasks to m processors that arises in large-scale parallel computations. For monotonic tasks, the best known result is a $sim3$ approximation of the makespans by a $32$-approximation scheme with time and space complexities proportional to n and $sim2$, where $sim$ is small. We present a new way of modeling the speedup of tasks: for a task T_j, the speedup of the task is linear when the number of assigned tasks is small (up to a certain critical number silon_j), and it is monotone when p=silon_j, and it is monotone when p=silon_j, where k_j is an upper bound indicating an unacceptable delay in dividing the task among too many machines. The generality of this model is proved to lie between the monotonic and linear speedup models. For any positive number $det geq 5$ let u be a positive integer such that $2u geq lceilsqrt2 rceil$, and we propose a new approximation scheme for the makespans of these tasks: $1 theta(det)  (1+epsilon)$-approximation scheme, where the makespans are asymmetric with respect to p, and $u  lceil rceil-1$. As a by-product, we also propose a theta(det)-approximation scheme for the problem of maximizing the throughput of the system with a deadline.

The A_infty T-system, also known as the Octahedron recurrence, is a dynamical recurrence relation, and is characterized by a mutation in a free cluster algebra (Kedem 2008, Kedem and Di Francesco 2009). We define the T-system with principal coefficients from the cluster algebraic point of view, and provide combinatorial solutions to any valid initial condition in terms of partition functions of perfect matches, non-intersecting paths and graphs. This provides a solution to the system for other coefficient choices as well, including Speyer's Octahedron recurrence (2007), the generalized Lambda-determinant (Di Francesco 2013) and higher order pentagrams (Schwartz 1992, Ovsienko et al. 2010, Glick 2011, Gekhtman et al. 2014).

A revised collection of the number of sunspot groups is presented. This collection is based on the work of Hoyt and Schatten (Sol. Phys. 179, 189, 1998). There are mainly two main changes: the elimination of many observations from the Maunder minimum (MM) and the addition of a few long series. Several minor corrections are also given. In addition, we have recalculated the percentage of active days during the MM on the basis of this new collection as a reliable indicator of solar activity. In this way, the level of solar activity obtained in this work is higher than that obtained from the original Hoyt and Schatten data. However, it remains compatible with a solar grand minimum. The new collection is also available in digital form.

With a new task, the Entity Segmentation (ES), which aims to segment all the visual entities of an image without considering the semantic category labels, we show that it has many practical applications, particularly in the image manipulation and image processing applications where the quality of the segmentation mask is crucial and where the category labels are of lesser importance. In this case, all the semantically meaningful segments are equally treated as categoryless entities and there is no more distinction between things and stuff. On this unified representation, we introduce a new ES framework with two novel masking layers to obtain high quality masks. Our experiments show that both our new task and our new framework have important advantages over existing methods. For instance, in ES, it is easy to merge different datasets without the need to resolve the labeling disagreements and any model trained on one dataset can transfer extremely well to other datasets with unknown domains. We have released our code to the public under the name of dv-lab-research/Entity.

Tensor networks are powerful models for tensors, and they have been widely used to model quantum many-body systems. Recently, supervised learning has been tried with tensor networks, but mainly for tasks like image classification. In this work, we propose a novel formulation of tensor networks for supervised image segmentation that allows them to operate on high-resolution medical images. We use a tensor network with a symmetric, non-overlapping patch of the input image to predict the output, obtaining a tensor-based, pixel-wise classification rule in a high-dimensional feature space. The proposed method is end-to-end trained with backpropagation. We implemented it as a strided tensor network to reduce the dimension of the weights. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated on two publicly available medical image data sets and compared to several other baselines. The evaluation shows that the strided tensor network can achieve competitive performance with a convolutional network, using less memory. Based on these experiments, we discuss the possibility of using fully linear models for image classification tasks.

The task of image segmentation is necessarily accompanied by noise due to the uncertainties as to the exact location of the boundaries between the anatomical structures. We argue that this information can be derived at no extra cost from the expert annotations, and when included in the training of neural networks it may allow a better calibration of probabilistic predictions and the real uncertainty. The concept of label smoothing (LS), where the neural network is trained on a “blurred” version of the ground truth labels, has been shown to be effective in adjusting the output predictions. But since LS is blind to the local structure of the image, it can produce over-smoothed and under-confidenced predictions even in the case of a genuinely unambiguous input. In this paper we propose spatially varying label smoothing (SVLS), a “soft labeling” technique which takes local structure into account. This technique is ideally suited to the incorporation of inter-annotator differences when multiple annotations are available. The proposed method has been tested on four different clinical image segmentation tasks of varying complexity, with different modalities, number of classes, and single and multiple expert annotations. The results demonstrate that despite its simplicity SVLS yields superior boundary predictions with improved calibration of uncertainty and model calibration.

Supervised semantic segmentation usually assumes that the input and the training data have the same logical structure. However, the domain mismatch between the training and unseen data leads to a significant performance degradation. Accurate pixel-level labeling for images in different domains is a tedious and difficult task, especially for histopathology images. In this paper, we propose a dual adaptive pyramid network (DAPNet) for histopathology glandular tissue segmentation. The proposed network addresses the domain adaptation problem at two levels: at the image level, we consider the color and style differences between the two domains; at the feature level, we consider the differences in the spatial structure between the two domains. The two components of the DAPNet are trained by two separate classifiers that use adversarial training. We evaluate our proposed method on two datasets with different stains, H&E and DAB-H, and show the effectiveness of the DAPNet. Finally, we compare our method with other state-of-the-art methods.

The quality of images taken in outdoor environments is hampered by bad weather, including fog, dust and atmospheric scattering of particles. This problem brings difficulties to high-level computer vision tasks such as image segmentation and object detection. However, previous studies on dehazing suffer from both high computational complexity and damage to the original image, such as oversaturation and halos. This paper proposes a new image dehazing method based on a mathematical model of haze optical properties and regularized optimization. In particular, we convert the non-convex, bilinear problem of estimating the unknown haze-free image and atmospheric transmittance to a convex, linear problem by estimating the atmospheric light constant. The method is accelerated using a multilevel Haar wavelet transform. The optimization is performed on the low-frequency subbands of the original image, which greatly reduces the dimension of the original image and makes the method suitable for real-time applications. Experimental results show that our method outperforms previous dehazing methods both in terms of quality and efficiency. For implementation details, the source code is available at github.com/jiaxihe/Dehazing-Source.

Multi-atlas image segmentation is one of the most widely used image segmentation methods in biomedical applications. There are two major difficulties in this category of methods, namely, atlas selection and label fusion. In this paper, we propose a novel method of multi-atlas image segmentation that adopts deep learning to solve these two problems. Deep Fusion Net (DFN) is a deep architecture that combines a feature extraction network and a non-local patch-based label fusion network. The network parameters are learned by end-to-end learning to learn deep features that can be used in the NL-PLF framework. Besides, deep features are used as the similarity measure for atlas selection. Testing on two public MR datasets of the heart, SATA-13 and LV-09, we obtain a high average Dice metric of 0.83 on the SATA-13 data and 0.95 on the LV-09 data for the epicardium. The method is compared favorably with the automatic left ventricle segmentation methods. The CAP-MIMIC-S3T data set in the MICCAI-2013 SATA challenge is also tested. The ADM value of 0.815 ranks the highest, at the time of writing.

One of the problems in the successful implementation of neural networks is the quality of annotated images. Annotators can classify images differently, often in such a way that they do not coincide exactly, or even more extreme, they contradict each other. Consequently, the annotations are noisy and, consequently, the prediction is not correct. To overcome this problem in the task of segmenting computed tomography (CT) images, we propose a filtering algorithm for annotated images. It consists of three stages: scoring annotators, which assigns higher scores to better annotators; scoring nodules, which assigns higher scores to nodules affirmed by good annotators; merging nodules, which combines annotations according to the nodule confidence. The proposed filter can be used for many different tasks, such as, for example, the two- or multiclass semantic segmentation, or with minor changes, classification and regression, where several annotators mark one image.

This is an important question in the field of image segmentation. Compared with the general text segmentation, the slicing of the slicing region is much more important in portrait segmentation. However, this problem has not been well studied in the past. This paper proposes a deep neural network method based on the principle of bounding region convolution. The neural network method introduces three new techniques: First, an individual bounding-sensitive kernel is proposed, which is based on the elongation of the contour, and assigns the border pixel with multiple class labels; Second, a global bounding-sensitive kernel is used as a prior, which further restricts the shape of the extracted region. Third, the bounding-sensitive attribute classifier is trained with the bounding-sensitive neural network to embed semantic information in the border. In the experiments, the bounding-sensitive neural network was evaluated on the largest public portrait segmentation dataset, namely, the pfcn-k8 dataset, and also on the four popular image segmentation datasets, namely, the Cocoa-Stuff, the Pascal-Voc, and the Pascal-Stuff-Pascal datasets. The method has higher performance than the state-of-the-art in all the datasets, especially on the border area.

- A new deep convolutional neural network based on group-orthogonal convolution. Using privileged information to enhance the diversity of a single network, we introduce a group-orthogonal convolutional neural network (GOCNN). We use the classification of images as an example, and use the information in the image annotations as the privileged information in the training process. Experiments on two famous datasets - ImageNet and Pascal VOC - have demonstrated the strong generalization ability of our proposed GoCNN. In the ImageNet test, GoCNN improves the performance of the state-of-the-art ResNet-152 by a total of 1.2%, while only using privileged information on 10 images, thereby proving the efficacy of the privileged information.

This paper proposes several novel methods for object saliency detection based on the powerful convolutional neural network. In our approach, the gradients of the input image are used to reduce the cost function of the class-object saliency of the image, and the gradients of the pixel can be efficiently calculated by the back-propagation method. Then the error between the image modified by the gradients and the original image is obtained. Our methods are extremely efficient (with a single GPU, processing 20 to 40 images per second). Object saliency can also be used as a visual object for image segmentation. In our experiments, we have successfully extracted object saliency maps from two types of experiments: the Pascal VOC-09 test and the Microsoft COCO test, and our methods outperform many existing methods, especially in difficult images with complex backgrounds, highly variable objects, and multiple objects, as well as very small objects.

In this article we present a general solution to multi-object tracking using superpositional measurements. Measurements which are functions of the sum of the contributions of the objects present in the area of observation are called superpositional measurements. We have based our modeling on the Random Finite Set in order to obtain a joint estimation of the number of objects and their trajectories. This leads to a labelled version of Mahler's multi-object Bayesian filter. However, a direct implementation of this filter using the sequential Monte Carlo method is not possible, due to the difficulty of generating samples in high-dimensional spaces. We propose an efficient, multi-object sampling strategy based on the Superpositional Approximate Cumulative Probing-Hypothesis-Derivative (SA-CPHD) filter, the labeled Bernoulli and Vo-Vo distributions, and the multi-Bernoulli distribution. The applicability of the proposed method has been verified by simulation in a difficult case of simultaneous and close-range target tracking by a pulsed Radar.

In 2005, for example, it was demonstrated by Kent, Hardy and Hardy that there are methods for generating keys from light that can be proved secure even if one makes a mistake about quantum mechanics or special relativity. The latter is precisely based on the non-local behavior of some quantum systems combined with the no-signal assumption of special relativity. This means that the security of the protocol is completely independent of the operation of the devices of the authentic parties, and the fact that they can operate on any (quantum) device. Unfortunately, the protocol proposed by Barrett, Hardy and Hardy is completely vulnerable to errors in the quantum channel. Moreover, even in the absence of errors, it is not very efficient; its efficiency is Theta(1/epsilon) if the attacker has at most epsilon information about the key, even if only one key bit is generated. In principle, this problem can be solved by amplification of no-signal, or special-relativity, secrecy. But we show that such amplification is not possible for the most important non-locality, and for the application of arbitrary hash functions.

A one-component reaction-diffusion equation with a bistable nonlinearity and a non-local, space-fractional, Riesz-Feller type diffusion operator is considered. We prove the existence, uniqueness (up to translations) and stability of a travelling wave solution connecting two homogeneous stable equilibrium points. Our results generalise and extend classical results on travelling waves. This generalisation to Riesz-Feller type diffusion operators requires a number of technical steps. The main ideas are based on an integral representation for Riesz-Feller type operators, a comparison principle, regularity theory for space-fractional diffusion equations and a control of the far-field.

At Re = 5186, the incompressible channel flow exhibits several characteristics of the wall-bounded turbulent flows at high Re. The mean velocity displays a logarithmic distribution with the von Karman constant, kappa, equal to 0.384  0.0004 and a logarithmic distribution for the asymmetrical variance, although not for the symmetrical one. There is a clear separation between the large outer scales and the small inner ones. The one-dimensional spectra of the streamwise and spanwise velocities in the intermediate region show a kappa-1 dependence for small values of kappa and also, as has been reported in previous experiments, a bimodal structure with local peaks near the kappa-1 range.

In crystallised semiconductors, the movement of the charge carriers is described by the distinction between instantaneous and average velocity, the latter related to quasi-momentum in a periodic potential. It is shown that the average, not the instantaneous, velocity of the carrier is employed in the theory of transport and the optical properties of the carrier. The effective mass of the carriers is discussed and it is demonstrated that, contrary to the effective mass, in the form of acceleration, employed in textbooks, the effective mass, as the product of the carrier’s velocity and quasi-momentum, is a more convenient physical quantity. Other advantages are that the mass is scalar for the energy band k which is not parabola, while the mass of the carrier is not scalar. An important application of the mass is discussed. The two-band model of $hp bm k$ is introduced as the simplest case of the band structure in which the periodicity of the lattice potential is preserved. It is pointed out that this model, applicable to the description of narrow band gap semiconductors (including zero-gap graphene), strongly resembles the special theory of relativity. Examples of this “semi-relativistic” analogy are given. This presentation has a scientific and didactical aspect.

A strong directional infrared radiation at 1367 and 5230 nm is generated in a sparsely excited Rb vapor. The central infrared radiation generated by spontaneously amplified radiation from the 5D–6P transition has a strong component both backward and forward, with a characteristic spectrum and position. Near-infrared radiation with a diffraction limit at 1367 nm, produced only in the forward direction, is produced by a parametric mixing of waves on the ring-like path 5P–5D–6P–6P–5S–5P transition. This strongly non-degenerate mixing involves one external and two internal optical fields. Similarities between mixing of waves in the blue and near-infrared are shown.

Constructed families of stationary solutions of the Einstein-Vlasov system with spherical symmetry, parametrized by the value of the central redshift, are shown to be very well approximated by a stationary solution of the Vlasov-Poisson system, i.e. by a stationary solution of the Vlasov-Poisson system, and the limiting behaviour is analyzed in terms of a physical parameter, depending on the individual solutions. In the same spirit as the authors of a recent work, this result is used to study the stability of these states at small redshift, as one can see in their recent work, that the second derivative of the mass about such a state is positive definite for a certain class of states.

A theoretical study of the differences between the HCG reflectors for TM and TE polarizations, including various grating parameters and properties of HCGs, is presented. It is shown that the TM HCG reflectors have much thicker gratings and shorter periods than the TE HCG reflectors. This difference arises from the different boundary conditions for the electric field in the two polarizations. Due to this difference, the evanescent fields of the TM HCGs are much shorter in the low-refractive-index media around the gratings. This allows a very short effective cavity length of a VCSEL, which is necessary for ultrafast operation of a VCSEL and MEMS tunable VCSEL. This understanding of the polarization dependences of the HCGs is very important for the design of various devices with the HCG reflectors.

The field of view (FOV) of a convolutional neural network is directly related to its performance. It has been widely recognized that elongated convolutions can effectively solve the problem of high FOV, but it takes longer for general-purpose hardware and dedicated hardware to perform elongated convolutions compared with simple convolutions. In this paper, a network structure is proposed—namely, a C-shaped elongated convolution, with a cascaded and separable structure—and a dedicated hardware architecture is proposed to efficiently handle C-shaped elongated convolutions. A C-shaped convolution network consists of multiple cascaded $2  2$ elongated convolutions, which can replace the existing $3  3$ elongated convolutions, without affecting the accuracy of inference. Two applications—face detection and image segmentation—have been tested on the general-purpose hardware and the proposed hardware. Face detection with the proposed network achieves higher accuracy than the previous work, with only 47% of the filter weights in the elongated convolution layer of the context. Moreover, the proposed hardware can accelerate the elongated convolution calculation; the proposed hardware is $2.78$ times faster than the existing hardware when the FOV is $3 3$.

This paper proposes a framework to combine different graphs of high classification power and nonlinearity for natural image segmentation. The proposed framework combines the adjacency-graphs and the kernel spectral clustering-based graphs (KSC-graphs) using a new concept of multi-scale superpixels, which are classified based on their proximity, that is, their sparse sub-space-preserving representation, which is obtained from the sparse sub-space clustering. Using this representation, a KSC-graph is then constructed to explore the nonlinearity of the superpixels. Then, the adjacency-graph at each scale is built, which is further used to update the KSC-graph at the superpixels. Finally, the fusion graph is built to obtain the final image segmentation result. The experiments on the Cambridge and Berkeley datasets show that the framework is more effective than existing methods. The code is available at github.com/yangzhangcst/AF-graph.

This paper presents an efficient labeling procedure and its application to the real-time semantic segmentation of the environment with a narrow-beam swept-frequency, continuous-wave (Frequency Modulated Continuous-Wave) scanning-radiometry system. It is recommended to use this technology over the other standard means of spatial environment characterization, because it operates at a greater range and is much more tolerant of atmospheric conditions. The training procedure is based on a publicly available and state-of-the-art natural image segmentation system and, in contrast to previous approaches, enables the generation of rich labels for the incoming data stream by integrating four image and two LiDAR data streams. Furthermore, the radial losses are computed by accumulating the LiDAR returns along a pose-chain in front of and behind the current position of the vehicle. Finally, the network is presented with multi-channel inputs from the incoming scans of the environment.

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in various fields such as medical image segmentation, but they have long been subject to the criticism that they are a black box. As there is no general theory for the design of deep neural networks, it is difficult to understand, analyze, and improve them. Previously, it was proposed to combine deep architectures with traditional methods. Deep neural networks constructed in this way have the advantage of using the original known operator, which makes it possible to decrease the number of parameters and improve interpretability. However, they are not necessarily able to obtain the state-of-the-art performance for all applications. In this paper, we propose a method for analyzing deep neural networks using known operators. The basic idea is to substitute each layer with an appropriate component and to achieve the same results. This method is evaluated on a high-performance U-Net for retinal vessel segmentation. We progressively converted the network into known components, and a combination of a retrained guide filter and a retrained Frangi filter achieved the same AUC value as U-Net (0.974 vs. 0.972, respectively), with a remarkable decrease in the number of parameters (111,536 vs. 9,575). The layers that are retrained can be mapped to the original interpretation, and they can be analyzed using known signal processing methods.

In this paper we describe a new mobile network, MobileNetV2, which improves the state of the art in mobile models for various tasks and data sizes. We also show how to apply mobile networks efficiently to object detection in a novel framework called SSDLite, and we introduce a way to build semantic segmentation models for mobile networks by reducing DeepLabv3 into Mobile DeepLabv3. MobileNetV2 is based on an inverted residual structure, in which the input and output of the residual are represented by thin layers, in contrast to the standard residual models which use the expanded representations in the input and output. Moreover, we show that it is important to keep the nonlinearities out of the narrow layers to retain the encoding power. We show that this improves performance and provide an intuition for this choice. Finally, our design decouples the input and output domains from the capacity of the mapping, which is useful for further analysis. We evaluate the performance of our method on ImageNet classification, COCO object detection, and VOC image semantic segmentation.

The unsupervised learning is one of the most difficult problems of today's computer vision, but at the same time it has a great practical value, because large unlabelled videos are cheaply available and easily collected. In this paper we discuss the problem of detecting the principal objects in images. We train a deep student network to predict the output of a teacher deep network, which can automatically learn the principal objects from the given videos or large image collections. This approach differs from the existing methods of object recognition by means of unsupervised learning: the unsupervised learning phase takes place during the training phase, and then, at test time, we simply use the usual forward propagation along the student path. This approach has the advantage that the possibilities of generalization are wider during the training phase, and the speed of testing is higher. The unsupervised learning method can go through several generations of student-teacher training. Thus, a number of student networks, trained in the first generation, are simultaneously built by the teacher network in the next generation. In experiments, the proposed method achieved the best results in three current data sets, which were tested on object detection in a video, unsupervised image segmentation and saliency detection. The testing speed of the proposed system is one to two orders of magnitude faster than in the case of existing unsupervised methods.

For the challenging task of semantic image segmentation, the most effective models have generally combined the structured modeling abilities of conditional random fields (CRFs) with the feature extraction power of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). In more recent work, however, the use of CRFs as a post-processing has become less popular. We think that this is mainly due to the slow training and inference speed of CRFs, and the difficulty in learning their internal parameters. To address both these issues, we propose to rewrite the inference rules for the CRF in terms of convolutions, which can be implemented efficiently on GPUs. This method speeds up both the inference and training speeds by a factor of more than 100. All internal parameters can now be learned easily by gradient descent. To facilitate further CRF research, we make our implementation publicly available at https://github.com/MarvinTeichmann/ConvCRF.

Intro: Cardiac MRI-derived mass and function measurements, such as end-systolic volume (ESV), end-diastolic volume (EDV), ejection fraction (EF), stroke volume (SV), and ventricular mass (VM), are clinically well established. Due to the complexity of the human heart, image segmentation is a difficult and time-consuming process. The goal of this study is to introduce -net (n, n-), a deep-learning based, fully automatic, and high-quality endocardial and epicardial contour extraction approach based on a deep neural network, for the extraction of the aforementioned cardiac functions. Methods: A set of 253 manually annotated cases were used to train the network, and then it was evaluated on four multicenter datasets with a total of over 1,000 cases. For LV EF, the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) is 98, 91, and 87 (95) for the first, second, and third, respectively, and for the RV EF, the corresponding ICCs are 98, 91, and 87 (95) for the respective datasets. For a left LV ejection fraction, the corresponding ICCs are 98, 91, and 92 (95) and for a right ventricular ejection fraction, 96 and 87 (95). For LV VM, the corresponding ICCs are 96 and 94 (90) and for the RV VM, 83 and 82 (55). -net shows state-of-the-art performance as measured by the dice coefficient. Conclusion: The present study proposes a simple adjustment procedure to handle the different strategies of the study. The approach yields high-quality biventricular mass and function estimates in the anatomically complex right ventricle. By applying a simple adjustment procedure, the system is flexible enough to be able to operate on new data without extensive training.

Since its discovery in 2006, deep learning (DL) has become an increasingly important subject of research, surpassing in a large number of areas such as object recognition, image segmentation, speech recognition, and machine translation. Nowadays, machine health monitoring is becoming popular because of the popularity of data-driven methods in the modern factory system. As sensors are more and more widely deployed, their connection to the Internet is also growing, and DL can provide a set of useful tools to process and analyze big machinery data. This paper mainly summarizes the current research of deep learning in machine health monitoring, and briefly introduces the techniques of deep learning. After a brief introduction to the technology of deep learning, the main types of DL used in the health monitoring of machinery are mainly self-encoders, restricted Boltzmann machines and its derivatives. Deep belief networks and deep Boltzmann machines, convolutional neural networks, and recurrent neural networks are reviewed. At last, the new trend of DL-based health monitoring of machinery was discussed.

We examine log-supermodular models on binaries, which are probabilistic models with negative log-densities which are submodular. These models give probabilistic interpretations of certain well-known combinatorial optimization problems, such as image segmentation. In this paper we are interested in the most general problem of estimation of the parameters of the log-supermodular models from known upper bounds of the intractable log-partition function. We show that a bound based on separable optimization on the underlying submodular polytope is always less than a bound based on perturb-and-cope. Then, in order to estimate the unknown parameters, using the fact that our approximation of the log-partition function is an expectation of our own randomization, we employ a subgradient method to minimize the lower bound of the log-likelihood. This also extends to conditional maximum likelihood estimation. We illustrate our results in a series of experiments on binary image denoising, where we illustrate the ability of probabilistic models to learn with missing data.

Object detection is a major challenge in computer vision. The underlying problem is how to effectively model the saliency of objects using the prior knowledge of objects from experience. In this paper, we propose a deep learning multi-task saliency model based on a fully-convolutional network with a universal input (the whole raw image) and a universal output (the whole saliency map). The proposed method, in principle, can directly encode the underlying prior information of saliency. Then, through a multi-task learning method, it can explore the intrinsic relationship between the detection of the highlight and the semantic segmentation of the picture. It is also possible to capture the semantic information of highlights at different scales by using fully-convolutional layers, and to explore the relationship between saliency and saliency through feature sharing. Finally, a non-linear regression model based on the graph Laplacian is used to improve the accuracy of saliency detection. The experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.

Superpixel segmentation is an increasingly common approach in computer vision. In practice, an object can either be represented by many finely gridded segments or can be encapsulated in the surrounding area of coarser superpixels, and so a hierarchical superpixel is useful in applications that require different degrees of image detail, depending on the objects to be segmented. Unfortunately, there is no real-time method for producing superpixels with different scales of detail. Here we present a simple and effective approach, Super-Hierarchy (SH). It is as accurate as the state-of-the-art method and, with an accuracy improvement of one to two orders of magnitude, it can be used directly with the latest efficient edge-detection methods, such as structured forest edges, thereby improving accuracy even further. The proposed method has been tested in a large number of computer-vision experiments.

We present MBIS (Multivariate Bayesian Image Segmentation), a clustering tool based on the mixture of multivariate normal distributions. MBIS features multi-channel bias field correction using a B-spline model. The second novel aspect of MBIS is the inclusion of a graph-cuts optimization method for the anisotropic stationary HMM random field. Along with MBIS, we also provide an evaluation framework that consists of three different experiments performed on a multi-view sequence of images. We first check the accuracy of the clustering and the bias field estimation. In the cross-comparison, MBIS is able to beat the widely used MOSS in all three experiments. The second experiment evaluates the stability of the results on two image sequences from a rescan study on 21 subjects. The multivariate clustering is more stable than its univariate counterpart on T1-weighted images. Finally, we show in the third experiment how MBIS is used to investigate tissue volume changes with age in 584 healthy subjects. This last result is important because the multivariate segmentation provides robust results without requiring any prior knowledge.

A new family of mixture models for hyper-cubic components are presented by generalizing the multivariate asymmetric Laplace density. The components are a mixture of scaled and shifted asymmetric Laplace densities. The component densities have two distinctive features: they contain a multivariate weighting function and the marginal distributions are also asymmetric Laplace. The mixtures of scaled and shifted asymmetric Laplace densities are used in clustering applications, but they can also be used in supervised and semi-supervised learning. The maximum likelihood estimator is used for estimating the unknown parameters and the Bayesian information criterion is used for model selection. We use both simulated and real data to illustrate the approach and to illustrate in some cases the hyper-cubic structure of the components.

Let A be a dimorphism algebra and Z its center. It is well known that if A is abelian, then A and Z are noetherian and A is a finitely generated Z-module. Now we will prove the converse. That is, if A is not abelian, as are almost all dimorphism algebras, then A and Z are not noetherian, and A is an infinitely generated Z-module. Z, though not noetherian, is generically noetherian. We also prove that the reduced center is the coordinate ring of a Gorenstein algebra with the strange property that it contains exactly one “deformed” point of positive geometric dimension. As a tool in our proof, we will introduce the concepts of the Higgsing algebra and the mesonic chiral ring from quiver gauge theory.

Let M be an n-dimensional Riemannian manifold, g a conformal metric, and h a smooth function defined on M with a critical point $xi$ of the form $h(xi)=0$, and satisfying a suitable flatness condition. We are interested in finding metrics of the form g_lambda=u_lambdafrac4[4n-2]g for which the scalar curvature is prescribed by h_lambda=h_lambda, where lambda is a small constant. In the positive case, that is, when the scalar curvature is strictly positive, we find a family of metrics of the form $g_lambda$, for which $u_lambda$ is a blunderbuss at $xi$ and goes to zero as lambda goes to zero. In the general case, if we further assume that there exists a nondegenerate conformal metric $g_0=u_0frac4n-2g$, with $u_0>0$, then there exists a bounded family of conformal metrics $g_0,lambda=u_0frac4n-2g$, for which $u_0=u_0$ as lambda goes to zero. This gives us a second family of bubbly metrics $g_lambda$ for which $u_lambda$ is a blunderbuss at $xi$, and goes to zero away from $xi$ as lambda goes to zero. This shows, in particular, that the problem has more than one solution.

The Kasner metrics are one of the simplest solutions of the Einstein equations. They are used here to examine the conformal method for finding solutions of the Einstein constraint equations. After describing the construction of the CMC slices of the Kasner space-time, we focus on the CMC slices of the smaller family of flat Kasner spaces. We then proceed to describe the construction of certain U–n–1 symmetric slices even in the far from CMC regime. In the conformal data set generating these slices we find that most of the data produce only the flat Kasner space-time, but that there are also far from CMC data which produce one-parameter families of slices. These families are analogous to well known CMC families, but they are different in several important respects, the most important of which is that unlike the CMC case, the condition for generating these families is not readily recognizable in the data. In view of this difficulty, we propose modifications of the conformal method based on conformally transforming mean curvature.

This paper deals with the initial value problem for a problem of the Cahn-Hilliard-Darcy system with a mass source, S, which is concerned with the growth of tumours. In the first place, we prove the existence of weak solutions in the plane, and of local solutions in the plane and in three dimensions. We then investigate the behaviour of the solutions when the dimension is two. We prove the existence of the strong solution, and show that it defines a closed dynamical system. We also prove the existence of the minimum pullback attractor for a translated and bound mass source S. Finally, if we assume that S is an asymptotically free source, we prove that all the weak and strong solutions converge to a unique stationary solution as t goes to infinity. An estimate on the convergence is also given.

Analysis of graphs has recently become very important in many areas of application. It poses many special problems in the areas of: (1) software complexity, (2) data complexity, (3) confidentiality, (4) mathematical complexity, (5) theoretical analysis, (6) serial speed, (7) parallel speed. The implementation of graph algorithms by means of matrix-based methods offers a series of interesting solutions to these problems. The GraphBLAS standard (www.istc-bigdata.org/graphblas) is being developed to enable the use of the full potential of matrix-based graph algorithms in the most widespread areas of application. The GraphBLAS standard mathematically defines a core set of graph operations, and it can be used to implement a wide range of graph algorithms in a wide range of programming environments. This paper introduces GraphBLAS and explains how it can be used to address many of the problems that graph analysis presents.

The dynamics of the Warsaw Stock Exchange crash was studied by the use of minimal spanning tree networks. We found that during its development the network of the WSE changed from a (hierarchical) power-law MST network, which represents the WSE’s stable state before the recent worldwide financial crisis, to a supertree-like (or super-hub) MST network of the market, which is decorated with a hierarchy of trees (and which could be an intermediate, unstable state of the market), and finally that this topology has a transitional form to a power-law MST network with many supertrees and hubs. This structure and topology could possibly represent the WSE after the worldwide financial crash and could be considered as a secondary shock. Our results could serve as an empirical basis for a future theory of the dynamic structural and topological phase transitions on financial markets.

However, in the majority of cases, the training images are not available to the domain of the input. Generally speaking, most of the domain adaptation techniques require access to the images of both the source and target domains. In the medical field, this is a very frequent DA case, where, for example, the source and target images could come from different clinical sites. In this paper, we introduce a source-free domain adaptation for image segmentation. The formulation is based on the minimization of the label-free entropy loss over the target data, which we guide with a domain-invariant prior on the desired regions. We propose to estimate this prior from the anatomical knowledge of the analyzed structure. Then, we show that the combination of the KL divergence and the entropy loss provides a very interesting connection between the mutual information of the target image and the predictions of the adapted model. We illustrate the efficiency of our prior-guided entropy minimization on different cases of domain adaptation with a variety of images, such as spine, heart and brain. Our method provides comparable results to several state-of-the-art methods, despite access to much less information, as we do not use the source images during the adaptation. Unlike the current methods, we use a single network, contrary to the famous adversarial methods, which are not applicable to the source-free case. Our method can be easily adapted to many different segmentation tasks and the code is publicly available on Github:

The minimal path is a well-known and powerful tool for boundary detection and image segmentation, both because of its global optimum and well-established numerical methods, such as the fast marching method. In this paper we present a flexible and interactive image segmentation model, based on the Partial Differential Equations, which is based on the idea of image feature enhancement with spatially homogeneous edge maps. The introduction of region-based homogeneity into the metric is one of the main contributions of this paper. We also propose a way to build a simple closed contour as the union of two disjoint open curves. The results of the experiments show that the proposed model indeed outperforms previous minimal path-based image segmentation approaches.

That deep learning is purely a data-driven approach has its merits and demerits. Given sufficient data, it will learn the most suitable model for a given problem; but in most cases this is not the case. Then either the model has to be learned from a small amount of data, or it is taken as a pre-trained model for some other task and then fine-tuned. Both cases may be suboptimal and limit the generalizability of the model. Inspired by this, we are working on a method for informing deep learning models for spatial image analysis to increase their performance when the amount of training data is small or when they are used on tasks other than those on which they were trained. Our specific motivation is to exploit the fact that there are some basic rules for how things are distributed on the earth’s surface, and these rules do not vary substantially from place to place. On the basis of this, we develop a novel method for convolutional neural networks for feature extraction based on geostatistical analysis of Getis-Ord functions. Our method significantly improves the generalizability of a model when it is used on aerial image segmentation.

In this paper, we examine the problem of reducing the discrepancies between multiple domains, called multi-source domain adaptation, and under the target shift assumption: in each domain, the goal is to solve a classification problem with the same output classes, but the proportion of classes is not the same. This problem is ignored in most of the domain adaptation works, but it is a crucial problem in practical applications and we show that its influence on the success of the adaptation is theoretically proven. To solve this problem, we design a method based on Optimal Transport, which has been successfully used in learning domains. Our method is based on the learning of the probabilities of the target class at the unlabeled points, and the coupling of the probabilities of the different domains. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data related to the problem of segmenting satellite images demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over the state-of-the-art.

The brain extraction is a first step in all the brain studies. Here we study the problem of skull removing and we present the CompNets, a neural network designed to accurately extract the brain from T1-weighted MR images, both normal and pathological. The proposed network is designed in the framework of encoder-decoder networks and has two paths to extract features of both brain and its complementary component outside the brain. The complementary path extracts features from the non-brain region and provides a robust solution for brain extraction from images with pathologies that are not contained in the training set. We show the effectiveness of our networks on the OASIS dataset and show that they are superior to state-of-the-art results under a two-fold cross-validation setting. We also show the robustness of our networks by evaluating them on images with introduced pathologies and by showing that they are invariant to unexplored brain pathologies. In addition, our complementary network design is general and can be easily extended to other image segmentation problems with improved generalization.

Semantic image segmentation is an essential component of modern autonomous driving systems, because a precise understanding of the surrounding environment is crucial for navigation and behavior planning. Today's state-of-the-art semantic image segmentation methods rely on pre-trained neural networks that were originally developed for whole-image classification. While these networks perform well for object recognition (i.e., what is visible in the image), they are less effective for semantic segmentation. They lack a good grasp of localization (i.e., where exactly something is located). Therefore, additional processing steps are required to obtain a pixel-accurate, full-resolution semantic segmentation mask. To alleviate this problem, we propose a new neural network architecture that combines strong performance on localization with the well-known accuracy of object recognition. We introduce two distinct incoming information streams into our network. One of them contains a wealth of information at the pixel level, which allows for precise detection of the segmentation boundaries. The other of these two streams is filtered down by a sequence of pooling operations to yield only the most robust features for recognition. Both streams are integrated at the pixel level using residuals. Without any additional processing and without any pre-training, our method obtains a score of 71.8 % on the Cityscapes dataset.

HUMAN SEGMENTATION in images captured in natural settings is a significant open problem, due to the presence of complex backgrounds, articulation, varying body proportions, and partial views. In this work, we propose class-specific segmentation models, which use a large database of human shapes. The main contributions of our method are as follows: (1) a sub-modular energy model combining class-specic structural constraints and data-driven shape priors, and (2) a data-driven class-specifc fusion method, which uses a large training set of human exemplars (100,000 in our experiments) to construct the shape prior on-the-fly, at arbitrary angles, with oblique parts. Lastly, (3) in our experiments, we show substantial improvement over the state of the art on two challenging datasets: H3D and MPII, where we added our own ground-truth annotated human figures, with 20 per cent improvements on first-ranked hypothesis estimates, with an order of magnitude smaller hypothesis set size.

We consider spherically symmetric, stationary d-dimensional composites, consisting of a boson star and a global monopole, minimally or non-minimally coupled to a general-relativistic gravitational field. In the case of a non-minimally coupled configuration, Marunovic and Murkovic have shown that such d-stars are gravitationally compact enough to possibly resemble black holes. We have performed a numerical investigation of this model, which has revealed a number of new and unexpected properties. In particular, by focusing on families of d-stars, which can be parameterized by the central amplitude of the boson field, we have found in both the minimally and non-minimally coupled cases that one or more shells of bosonic matter can appear at large distances from the center of mass. In parameter space, these shells appear at some critical value of the central amplitude. In some cases, the radius of the shells seems to be infinite, and the radius in the vicinity of the critical amplitude is observed to obey a universal scaling law. We derive this scaling from the dynamics and the asymptotic behavior of the fields.

If the quality of the memory of the quantum states is high, it is easy to perform a powerful computation or a transmission of information. The storage capacity of a system with high depolarization is strongly degraded by the asymmetric noise in a certain environment. In this paper, we demonstrate that the noise-contaminated trapped ion memory can be improved a lot by introducing the error-correction by teleportation between two coding schemes that are read out on two registering qubits in the same trap. However, the complexity of the error-correction scheme is usually considerable, but we show that our protocol can be realized by a single global entangling phase-shift gate with an extremely low fidelity. It takes advantage of the fact that the errors of this gate are also dominated by dephasing. As a result, we show that for realistic parameters our memory can have an error rate two orders of magnitude smaller than that of the physical qubits. This is a way of improving the performance of the memory in trapped ions where the use of the non-depolarizing qubits is not possible.

“Then suddenly Ulf leaps up and lunges towards me. “Ulf lives at Farraway Hall, where hundreds of endangered beasts are protected by the RSPCB (Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Beasts). When the founder of the society, Professor Farraway, died, he bequeathed his fortune and estate to the RSPCB. But his son, Baron Marackai, believes he has a rightful claim to his father’s will and has made it his life’s work to get his revenge. At Farraway Hall, an inspector called Inspector Black, intruded into the nursery and told them he was investigating the murder of a baby dragon. He thought the murderer had shot the baby dragon to lure the mother into a trap. The murderer’s intention was to erect a bloody cage of horrors, where the dragon and a pair of endangered beasts would fight each other to the death in front of a public audience. But Ulf saw through Inspector Black’s facade. He believed he had too much inside information about the dragon-killer’s intentions to be an innocent enquirer. Inspector Black has his own agenda, and it is up to Ulf to expose it.

The central plot is that of a man who dreams of talking with Venus about love, but Venus is in furs. The narrator tells his dreams to his friend Severin, who suggests to him to read the Memoirs of a Supersensual Man in order to cure him of his desire for cruel women. In this Memoirs we read how a man named Severin von Kusiemsky, in love with a woman, Wanda von Dunajew, asks her to be his slave and enables her to make him suffer ever more shameful treatment. Initially, Wanda does not understand and does not agree with him, but later, being pampered by Severin, she finds the advantages of such treatment attractive and enthusiastically agrees, although at the same time she is angry with Severin for letting her. Severin and Wanda go to Florence. Severin describes the feelings that he experiences during these experiences as supersensuality. On the way, he takes the Russian servant's name of Gregory and becomes her slave. In Florence, Wanda brutally treats him as her slave and gets him dominated by three African women. The crisis of their relationship came when Wanda met a man to whom she wanted to be submissive, a Byronic hero, Alexei Papadopoulos. At the end of the book, Severin, humiliated by his new lover, loses the desire to submit. He says about her:

The story begins in 1996, on the day Kamila receives her diploma. That is the day the first of the “Wild Geese”* of the new ruling of the emirates of the khans, and of the oppressors, the “Taliban”, arrive in Kabul, the capital of Afghanistan, and of the Sidiqi family. They will later, under the Koran, allow women to be forbidden from leaving their homes, or from working in the mines, or from working anywhere, or from entering the military, or from a life of piety. Father and brothers do not escape the persecution, and soon have to flee the city. Unable to teach and desperate to help the family, Kamila masters the art of dressmaking and gives the knowledge to her little sisters. She takes them with her to the bazaars to find business, and their little workshop to their best clients, the shopkeepers of the shops where she will make her dresses. Immediately the workshop expands, and she sees the opportunity to help women in her environment. Together with her sisters, she opens a school in her house to teach the women to sew, and to give them work once they have been taught. In this way she manages to employ about a hundred women, and yet avoid the eyes of the tyrants.

Jutthunvaa’ is called the Bird Girl. She and Daagoo (Snowgrouse) belong to different clans of the Gwich’in, one of the Athabascan tribes. The two young people long to be free. So they both roam the land, each on his own. Their parents disapprove of such aimless wanderings. Then one day Jutthunvaa’ and Daagoo meet in the wilds. Their paths diverge from that time on. Daagoo is persuaded to go with the hunters of his clan on a hunt. When the hunt is over Daagoo finds that his father and the hunters with whom he has gone hunting have been killed. The killers, Daagoo surmises, are invaders from the north, the Inupiats, called by the Gwich’in Cheekwais. So he takes the women, old people and children away from danger. Daagoo practices hunting with the boys in their new camp. Daagoo has seen his dream fulfilled. The clan leaves the frozen country and moves southwards. Meanwhile, the parents of the Bird Girl are determined to marry her off. She escapes, resolutely, for she does not want to become pregnant. The Bird Girl would like to fight her own battles. She hunts down a caribou. The clan finds a safe haven in a remote cave, but there is no caribou meat. Then the Bird Girl is captured by a Cheekwai and taken northwards. As a slave she has to submit to the will of her captor. When her baby is born she has to give him up to be brought up by a Cheekwai woman. In the summers that follow the three brothers of the Bird Girl keep searching for her. But during one of their search parties in the north the Cheekwais kill them. When the Cheekwais with the help of the two boys who are their captives play with the heads of the brothers, the Bird Girl seeks revenge. At night she blocks up the smoke vents of the Cheekwai huts and everyone in the Cheekwai camp suffocates, even her own son, who had turned his back on his mother. The Bird Girl returns to her own people. Daagoo has found a wife in the Land of the Sun and they have children. Eventually Daagoo is forced to leave his wife and children and returns to his clan. When the clans of Daagoo and the Bird Girl are on the point of rejoining forces, they again meet.

Edward Malone, a journalist on the Daily Chronicle, seeks an adventure and some danger so as to win the heart of the woman he loves, Gladys Hungerton. He is sent to see Professor George Edward Challenger, who has attacked four or five journalists, to ascertain whether the stories he has told of his visit to South America are true. After attacking Malone, Challenger makes known his discovery of the prehistoric creatures he has discovered in South America. Afraid of being ridiculed, he invites Malone to join him on a journey to prove his discovery, together with Professor Summerlee, another expert who is qualified to examine the evidence, and Lord John Roxton, an adventurer who has knowledge of the Amazon and has, a few years before the action of the book, helped to destroy the robber barons who keep slaves in South America. They make their way to the plateau with the help of native guides who are superstitiously frightened by the place. One of these Indians, Gomez, is the brother of a man whom Roxton has killed in South America. When the expedition arrives on the plateau, Gomez destroys the bridge and so the travellers are trapped. Zambo, their devoted black servant, stays at the camp, but cannot prevent the Indians from leaving. They decide to explore the lost world and, in a marsh, are attacked by flying creatures, and Roxton finds some blue clay which excites his curiosity. Challenger, Summerlee and Roxton are then taken prisoner by a tribe of ape-men. In the ape-men’s village, the travellers discover that a tribe of human beings, calling themselves Accalas, live on the other side of the plateau and are in conflict with the ape-men, whom the Accalas call ‘Dogas’. Roxton manages to escape and, with Malone’s help, leads the rescue. The professors, together with some others, are rescued from the village of the ape-men, and taken to the human tribe, who then help to defeat the ape-men and take over the plateau. After the Accalas have seen the power of the guns they want to keep the travellers on the plateau. They do eventually find a way through to the other side, and meet up with Zambo and a large rescue party. When they return to England, they present their reports, with Edward’s drawings, to the public. Challenger, however, has arranged to show a live pterodactyl as proof of his discovery, but it escapes and is lost to sight in the Atlantic. Afterwards, the four men dine together and Roxton reveals why the blue clay was so interesting to him: it contains diamonds, worth £200,000 which they can share between them. Challenger is planning to set up his own museum, Summerlee wants to study fossils in his retirement and Roxton is determined to return to the lost world. Malone returns to find that Gladys has married a clerk and so has nothing to expect from him.

Each of the three original adventures is a dungeon crawl. The player characters face giants of three different kinds, ranging from “Giants, of the rock, ice, and fire,” which is the basic “evil giant” subtype in the original D&D rules. The adventure begins with a prologue that explains how giants of various kinds raid the lands inhabited by humans. They are hunted and persecuted by the humans, who hire the player characters to punish the evil giants. The party is told they have to defeat the giants or they will be executed. They are given weapons, horses, a guide, and a map showing the location of the giants. They are also told that the giants are led by a sly giant chief named Nowra who loves to set ambushes, and that a mysterious force is holding these giants together. The player characters are allowed to keep any treasure they find, but they are ordered to return immediately and report on the “sinister hand” behind the alliance. The majority of the adventure takes place in two locations: the top-level fortress and the dungeon beneath. The adventure starts one of two ways. If the players have finished The Cave of the Fire Giant Chief, they are transported from the Magic Crystal to the Glacial Cleft by the magic of the teleport spell. They already know they are in search of the cause behind the enmity of the giants. If they are starting with The Glacial Cleft of the Frost Giant Jarl, the nobles of the lands have hired them to destroy the frost giants. In both cases, they easily find a secret, hidden cave for their base of operations. As in The Cave of the Fire Giant Chief, the majority of the adventure takes place in two locations: the upper fortress, which is a cave, and the lower dungeon, which is a series of natural caves. In the upper fortress are ice caves, a barracks, and a domed ice castle. These are home to yetis, frost giants, ogres, and ice wolves. In the lower dungeon are caves for the servants, a prison, and a meeting hall for the chief, the ogre, and his emissaries. The prison holds a beautiful storm giantess. In the dungeon are polar bears, the lord’s pet. After the players defeat the lord, they can pull a massive iron lever and teleport to the cave of Snurre, the fire giant king. If this is a continuation of the first two adventures, the players know they are looking for the source of the giants’ enmity. If they are starting with this adventure, they are enlisted by nobles to destroy the fire giants. This adventure is twice as long as the previous two; it is sixteen pages long instead of eight. The first two adventures were set in a single level, but the fire giant’s fortress has three. The fire giants live in a scorching, smoky place of rock, but the characters can easily find a secret, hidden base from which they can attack the giants. The leader of the fire giants is King Snurre Ironbelly, and his cave is made of natural lava caverns. On the upper (outermost) level are the queen’s rooms, the barracks, and the kennels. In this area the players will find fire giants, gnolls, and hell hounds. On the lower level, which is made of natural obsidian caves, are areas of spiritual significance to the fire giants. There is a hall for dead fire giant kings and a place of worship. There are also drow clerics here, which is where the players will learn that the drow are the real masters of the fire giants and are led by the drow cleric Eclavdra, a powerful and dangerous drow sorceress. The third level is a natural dungeon, containing a treasure room guarded by a red dragon. There are also more fire giants and drow; to destroy the fire giants, the players must penetrate deeply into the active volcano where they live. If the DM so desires, a tunnel leads into the earth, deep into the realm of the drow. This makes the adventure continue into the final, next adventure, The Descent Into the Underdark.

Palmer LaRue lived in a little town called Waymer, where they have an annual custom of letting pigeons out of crates and shooting them with shotguns to raise money for a public playground. Ten-year-old boys learn how to pick up the wounded birds that are not dead yet and put them out of their misery. Palmer refuses to take part in such a terrible festival. However, he is forced by his schoolmates, Henry, Mutto and Beans, to agree with them so that they will think he is a regular boy. Then he hides a pigeon named Nipper, who was in the way, from his classmates. On the day of the pigeon shooting, Palmer is very nervous, because he let Dorothy take Nipper. During the shooting, Nipper is wounded, and one of Palmer’s friends brings him back to the field so that the gunman can finish him off. In the middle of the shooting, Palmer picks up Nipper and carries him away. Then Palmer realizes that he might have changed the custom of the town when he hears a little boy telling his father that he wants a pigeon for a pet.

In her own house, problems had arisen. Her mother Rose had started an affair with Jacques, but she asked Camilla to keep it a secret, but Rafferty, her father, begged her to tell the truth. This left Camilla divided between her two parents, and she came to see that they were imperfect people. In order to resolve this conflict, she drew closer to Frank, her friend, who was older than her. He understood the pain she was suffering and helped her to bear up. Frank insisted that she should find herself outside her family, that she should define herself in herself. They shared their ideas about life, religion, philosophy, and were beginning to form a love affair, but the conflict within the families was increasing. Frank’s parents finally separated and he had to leave his mother’s house and go with his father. Camilla’s parents decided to try to patch up their marriage by going on a long holiday together. Unfortunately, while her parents were away, she was to be sent to a boarding school in Switzerland. Despite the grief of losing Frank, she was able to bear the separation and prepare herself for the change in her life.

The book is highly critical of Richard Fuld, Henry Paulson and the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, which in the year 1999 repealed a part of the Glass-Steagall Act of 1933. The book also tells of the author's development from selling pork chops at U. Mass. to teaching himself the required stock-broker material and finally passing the GS exam, and how he eventually developed the site convertbond.com which he sold to Morgan Stanley. While he was at Morgan, he was offered a position as a vice president at Lehman Brothers. Richard Fuld is described as a smug, solitary and ruthless boss with a short temper and a way of throwing tantrums.
