Richard Fuld is sarcastically called "his majesty", "a god", and "a spiritual leader". The author believes that the American government should have saved Lehman Brothers and that Richard Fuld's erroneous expectation that the American government would save the company after his meeting with Henry Paulson in the spring of 2008 was the reason he kept on playing with unnecessary risks and refused a late August offer from the Korea Development Bank for $ 18.

The groundswell is characterized by a number of tactics that guide companies in using social technology strategically and effectively. In other words, businesses should listen to their customers to find out what the market is looking for in their products. And in order to do this, they have to find out if their customers use social media and how they use it. Instead of advertising to the customer, the marketing department must find a way to speak with the customer about their experience with the product and their feeling about the brand. The easiest way to do this is by participating in social media. Enthusiastic customers are part of the groundswell, and the companies can identify and reward these customers by creating virtual communities and social platforms where they can connect with the brand and share their experiences. And they can use the enthusiasm of their employees as well by creating an internal platform that they can use to connect with the brand—sometimes called an enterprise social network.

A white man was arrested by the New York police after he was found standing over the victim of a robbery at Grand Central Station in midtown Manhattan. After answering the police with some unusual responses, he was taken to Bellevue Hospital for a psychiatric examination. Although not physically ill, he had an unusual delusion: that he was from the planet K-PAX in the constellation Lyra. The patient, who called himself “prot” (intentionally lower case to emphasize the triviality of a single life in the cosmic context), was subsequently moved to the Manhattan Psychiatric Institute (MPI), where he was examined by Dr. Gene Brewer. With the help of a telepathic journalist named Giselle, Dr. Brewer determined that Prot was merely the alter ego of Robert Porter, who had lost his wife and child and had later killed the murderer of his family. When Prot left for his home planet, Robert Porter went into a catatonic state; Bess (another patient whom Prot had promised to take with him) disappeared, as did a trunk containing souvenirs he had collected. Prot promised to return in about five years’ time.

In L'Ankou, Ororea asks Spirou and Fantasio to join her for a magic conference in Brittany. When they arrive, they encounter a savage called Ankou, who objects to the building of a uranium-thermal plant on his land. They protect Ororea from a violent attack, but the villains manage to escape. On arrival at the hotel, we learn that Kata Itoh is one of the invited magicians, along with the telepath Al-Kazar, the hypnotist monk Cappuchino and the telekinetic Retros Athana. Together, they are currently working on a magic trick involving teleportation. Fantasio is chosen as a guinea pig for the first experiment, but is abducted by the villains. Ankou reappears, and warns Spirou and his friends not to do anything to the kidnappers. They threaten to give them the fantastic new invention from the uranium-thermal plant in exchange for Fantasio. Kata agrees not to tell his friends, and together the magicians go and steal the new invention. Meanwhile, Fantasio manages to escape, and along with Spirou and Ororea, alerts the police. The villains are arrested, but the stolen invention threatens to explode. Luckily, Spirou manages to alert the magicians in time, and Kata manages to make the invention vanish. This action means that the uranium-thermal plant is shut down. Ankou is thus grateful to Spirou and his friends. So what will they do?

Rosalie is a widow of fifty. Her youthfulness has been completely spoilt by the ‘organic phenomena of the time of life’, or ‘menopause’, as we would call it. She lives with her grown-up daughter and adolescent son, both of whom are a source of perpetual conflict between her and the “old age” that has ‘let itself go’. They engage a young American tutor to help with her son’s education. Rosalie finds herself strangely attracted to him and soon becomes infatuated with him. Her abstemious daughter, who has disapproved of her more-or-less socialising mother in the past, takes an even stronger line now. Then, as if by a miracle, Rosalie’s menopause goes away. Instead of declining vitality and sexual arousal, she is in a state of heightened arousal, and her periods have returned. Rosalie plans a family trip and announces her feelings and her availability to the young man. They arrange to meet at a castle on the Rhine, the Schloss Benrath, but this does not come to pass. She is found dead in her bed, her blood clotting in the uterus, and the surgeons take the opportunity of speculating about the cause of her new youthfulness. The cancerous tumour is obviously the result of the cancer itself; but one doctor wonders if her new desire for love and her altered, erotic personality might have excited the ovaries, and thereby hastened the cancer.

Byrd Starr longs to go to the Queen's Academy to earn her teacher's certificate. But her elders, for the sake of convention, refuse her the privilege. She is offered the chance to go to Shrewsbury High School, with her friends, but there are two conditions. One is that she will board with her Aunt Ruth. The other is the more difficult for her. No word is to be written by her while she is at the high school. At first she refuses the offer, for she can't conceive of a life without writing. But her cousin Jimmy changes the condition. She must not write anything of fiction. This seems not so severe to her, and yet it proves a most excellent discipline for her future. Although she has a collision with her Aunt Ruth and Evelyn Blake, the school poet, she begins to develop her talent for story telling. And by a series of adventures she gets material for stories and poems, and her story of the "woman who spanked the king" is successful. And as time goes on she begins to think of romance, too, and a love affair begins between her and Ted Kent, but it breaks up owing to misunderstanding and the interference of Mrs. Kent. She refuses a suit from Percy Miller and continues her long-standing friendship with Dean Priest. At the end of the story, she is a successful young author, but she does not go away to New York with the eminent authoress, Janet Royal.

The Hardy Boys go to France on vacation. When they meet the 'Grey Man' in New York, they hear of an investigation he has entrusted to him in connection with a secret society in France. The GREY MAN forbids them to take part in the enterprise, because of their youth and the dangers of the enterprise. But the HARDY BOYS secretly and stealthily get into the thick of the investigation, and they are soon in France, disguised as gun-runners, and dressed in the punk fashion. They soon get in touch with a firm called RENYARD & CO., who are in the business of dealing in arms and other contraband articles. They are nearly killed in an accident, but are rescued by a certain DENISE, who manages to make her escape with them. The book has an interesting plot, and everyone seems to betray everyone else, the firm of RENYARD & CO., the lady of the name of DENISE, and many other persons. The HARDY BOYS are also in the clutches of the Sûreté, the French secret police. But they escape, after a desperate struggle with all parties, and just when the book is coming to its end, they are pursued by the Chairman of the Board of Directors of the firm of RENYARD & CO. They are pursued for a long time and the dangers are intense, when the lady, DENISE, saves their skins. And the mystery is solved. The HARDY BOYS return to the U. S. A.

This is a novel which follows the events in Dragonsbright and The Dolphin's Bell. It describes the present condition of the dolphins brought by the colonists. It is set after the events of All the Weyrs of Pern, and carries further the historical thread of the Pern sagas, while at the same time assimilates further the science fiction aspects of the history of Pern. The plot concerns itself mainly with two young characters, and relates the birth of the Dolphin-Crafts Hall and the first of the Dolphineers. Readis, the son of the Lord of Paradise, falls into the sea and is rescued by a "shipfish" from drowning. After this he develops an interest in the'shipfish', and so does T'lion, a young dragon rider from Gadareth's Weyr, who is also saved by a "shipfish." The two young men become friends, and, each in his own way, defy his family, his hold and his Weyr, in order to sustain their friendship for the "shipfish" and to prove the intelligence and speaking ability of the creatures. While many of the characters in the Pern books are struggling to put an end to the Thread, Readis, T'lion and others are struggling to establish a new era of co-operation between human and dolphin.

While he was still at Temple College, Claude had tried to convince his parents that he would receive a better education at the State University. But his parents had refused to listen to him, and Claude remained at Temple College. One day, however, after a school sports meeting, he had met the Erlich family, and had soon learned to love music, and free discussion and thinking. His university studies and his friendship with the Erlichs were both abruptly interrupted when his father decided to buy another farm and Claude was obliged to leave university and take over part of the family business. On the farm, Claude married his childhood friend, Enid Royce. But the dream of a happy marriage was destroyed when he found out that Enid was more interested in socialism and the missionary work of the Christian Faith than in loving and praising him. Having decided to accompany her sister, who had gone as a missionary to China, Claude returned to the family farm. The outbreak of World War I made his parents think the world was ending, and he joined the army. Claude thought that he had finally found a goal in life, which was beyond the boredom of farming and marriage, and he enjoyed the new responsibilities and freedom. Despite the terrible disease of influenza and the hardships of the battlefield, Claude had never felt more important than he did now. In the face of an overwhelming German attack, he had finally decided that he had to fight.

Blair Mallory is the owner of a fitness club called Great Bodies. She got the money to open it from the settlement with her first husband Jason, whom she had caught giving her underage sister Jenni a kiss during a family party. Jason had ambitions to run for Congress, and, as a way of avenging herself, she took a photograph of the kiss. Knowing the photograph would bring him down, he settled for her, and it’s with this money that she opens her gym. But then she notices that one of her clients, Nicole, is copying her every move. She begins to do her hair the way Blair does it, to dress the way Blair dresses, even to buy the same car. And it’s not just her; almost all the women in the gym dislike her, because she hogs the equipment, makes the others feel bad and is constantly flirting with the married men. After several complaints, she sits her down and tells her her membership will not be renewed for another year. Nicole gets very angry and threatens to sue her. As she’s leaving the gym one day, the last to leave, she sees Nicole waiting in the car park and is afraid for her life, so she runs out of the gym and to her car, where she makes a call to the police. At that moment she hears a gunshot, and instinctively throws herself to the ground, burying her mobile phone under the car so that she can’t call for help. She tries to stay quiet so that Nicole won’t realize that she hasn’t shot at her, but she can’t stay quiet for long and runs back into the gym. She makes it into the gym without being shot and, rushing to her office, she calls the police. They arrive, and she explains what’s happened, and they tell her that Nicole did not kill her, because she’d been murdered. Suddenly she hears her ex-lover, Wyatt Bloodsworth, calling to her. He’s a police lieutenant, and he’s come here because he heard about the case on the radio. Then, bringing back memories of the three times he’d dated her, he begins to question her and assures her that she’s not a suspect. She’s so upset she’s in need of some peace, and so she rents a flat near the beach. She spends a day on the beach and falls asleep, waking up with someone’s arms around her. Suddenly she realizes that it’s Wyatt. He carries her back to her flat and is very angry when he tells her he found her from her credit card bills. Suddenly she remembers her love for him. She agrees that they can try again and start their relationship over again. The next day, they go back to the city and the gym, where her car is waiting for her. As she tries to get in, she feels a burning pain in her arm and falls to the ground. Then she sees another car drive off, and she realizes she’s been shot. Then Wyatt hurries to the police station to report the crime and call an ambulance. They take her to the hospital, where they tell her she’ll be all right; the bullet had just missed her heart. That night she goes to see Wyatt, and together they work out that the murderer of Nicole was a man called Dwyane Bailey. They bring him to the police station, and he admits to the murder, but not to having shot at Blair. The next day, she’s driving when she approaches a red light. She hits the brakes, but the pedal moves up and she has to put the car in park. The brakes have been cut and she crashes into the intersection. She’s taken to the hospital, where they tell her she’ll be all right but bruised. Then, while they’re at his house, he receives a phone call: Dwyane’s alibi is working. Then they have to think again about who the murderer could be. The next day, when she’s feeling better, Wyatt gives her a small velvet box. He kneels before her and proposes. They get ready to go to the police station. She spends the whole day in his office making a list of suspects. Then Jason comes rushing in and says that all the detectives have been called to a certain location, but he can’t say where. Then she is alone in the office when she recognizes someone, Jason. He pulls a gun and tells her to shut up. , he’s not capable of murder. Then Jason tells her that it was his new wife, Debra, who shot at her in the car park. He tells her she had told him, and then he’d been afraid she might get caught and ruin his career. He’d then decided to murder her himself by cutting the brake lines. When that didn’t work, he’d feigned a crime and sent the police out of the station so he could murder her. Then Debra comes in. She had followed Jason. Jason thinks she’s in love with him, but then she hears that Jason is here to murder her, and she’s pleased. She also decides that this is a good moment to take the gun from Jason, and she kicks it out of his hand. The SWAT team then arrives and arrests Jason and Debra. Then Blair and Wyatt are together for the first time.

Major Malich, then Captain, is leading a special team in the city of some unknown country, probably somewhere in Iran or Afghanistan, where he used the Persian language, when they were attacked. They returned fire and saved the city, with only one civilian killed, where Captain Malich was rewarded for the promotion to Major. In the department of the Pentojny in Washington, Major Malich drafted plans for sabotaging the American defenses, without realizing that they fell into the wrong hands. They are planning to enter Washington under the sea, where they will sneak in and then attack the White House with rockets, with an informant on the location of the President. Malich and Major Conklin, who have taken up the arms themselves, are confronted with this attack, and although they kill one of the men holding the rocket launcher, the second shoots and hits the south wall of the west wing of the White House, killing the President, the Secretary of Defense and several others. But later it is revealed that the vice president had been killed when a refuse truck backed up to his car. Malich, who had prepared the plans and was at the scene, is accused of the assassination. While Malich is interrogated in the Pentojna, Conklin is invited to participate in a right-wing coup to replace the present government. After a meeting, he describes it on the air and withdraws to New Jersey to Malich. The next morning, they decide to drive the rented automobile to the scene of the attack. There, the insurrection is led by high-tech robots that fire at all uniformed people. They save a police team in New York, go to New Jersey by foot through the Holland Tunnel, where they fight the mechanized troops with the help of the National Guard, where two F-16 fighters hit New York Harbor, one of which hits the dress of the Statue of Liberty. In New Jersey, Malich and Conklin are looking for Malich's wife, who used to work for an Idaho congressman, now the President of the United States according to the heir. When Malich's wife calls, the new president calls Malich, Conklin and his former fellow employees to save the United States. Malich is ordered to retrieve his old op-report from the Pentojna. In this Pentojna, the new President's trusted secretary eljezna betrays him and shoots him in the eye, before the security guards could respond. The fugitives are then chased by the same mechanized troops and speed-machines. Apache attack helicopters sent by the new president finally drive them away. In the meantime, the new national security adviser, Averell Torrent, one of Malich's former professors, sends a team of former special forces soldiers to find out about the organization responsible for the death of Malich and the subversion of the United States of America. They find their way to the Progressive Restoration in Washington's mountain embassy. They attack and arrest the leader. After the defeat of the Progressive Restoration, Torrent is elected president with the support of the Republican and Democratic parties. The president-elect does not want to wait for the next election, so he immediately leaves the presidency to let Torrent take over. When Malich's wife Cecily learns of the fact that Torrent was a former professor and a long-term professor at the University of Bohemia, and that many of the leaders of the insurrection were his students, she suspects that Torrent instigated the whole conflict to get to power. Reeve's notes show Torrent's obsession with the transition from the Roman Republic to the Roman Empire and the belief that the United States is going through this transition. The book ends with Cecily and Conklin, to whom she revealed her suspicions, wondering if this is actually true. Torrent does not have any use of power. The novel was designed for further development.

“A most respectable firm of publicity men called Pyms” (shades of S. H. Bensons, where Dorothy Sayers worked) have come to Lord Peter Wimsey with a mysterious piece of correspondence. One of their copy-writers, Victor Dean, had been killed in a fall from the iron spiral staircase, but had left a half-written letter to the firm’s directors suggesting that there were dark doings afoot. Under the pseudonym ‘Death Bredon’ (actually his middle name) Lord Peter Wimsey sets to work at the firm. He takes over Victor Dean’s office, studies his methods, and starts to write himself, all the while investigating the staff. He discovers a talent for publicity, and soon turns out a very successful piece of business. He also begins to study Victor Dean’s social life. His colleagues were members of the ‘DeMommerie set’, the company of the socialite Dame de Momerie, most of them heavy cocaine addicts. He meets de Momerie’s husband, Major Milligan, who seems to be the cocaine supplier to the set. He is also involved in a major drug ring, which Inspector Parker, Lord Peter Wimsey’s friend and brother-in-law, is investigating. Milligan, hearing that Victor Dean worked at Pyms, makes a wild guess and assumes that Victor Dean is the man in the firm’s employ who is involved in the drug ring. The implication is that someone else at Pyms is involved as well, which might explain the letter to the firm’s directors. He is playing a variety of roles: by day he is Bredon, a distant cousin who is forced to work for his living; in the evenings he is himself. At other times, however, he dresses up as a masked harlequin and by various bold tricks attracts the attentions of Dame de Momerie, thereby annoying Major Milligan. One evening, having been drinking in a pub, Hector Puncheon, a junior reporter on a newspaper, finds a packet of cocaine in his pocket. He had been a hapless bystander in a cocaine operation, but there is no further evidence of anything of the sort at the pub. On the evidence of this, it appears that the gang meets at a different place every week. Wimsey continues to investigate at Pyms and learns that one of the senior copy-writers, Tallboy, seems to be making large cash payments. Later, one of the group, a man called Michael Mountjoy, falls under a moving train. His dead body, as Wimsey observes, is riddled with cash and has no employment or other assets. His effects include a telephone directory with many of the telephone numbers marked out. The marked-out telephone numbers include the one from the pub where Hector Puncheon had picked up the cocaine. Other clues come to light: an amulet in Dean’s office, a large stone on the stairs, and a catapult belonging to ‘Ginger Joe’, the office boy, whom Bredon enlists in the investigation. At last Wimsey solves the mystery. On a Friday morning, one of Pyms’s major clients publishes a large advertisement in a national newspaper. It is given to the paper some days before publication and the first letter of the headline indicates the name of the pub that will be the focus of that week’s activities. A few days before, Tallboy sends a wire to the group containing the letter. A final clue is provided on a company outing, during a cricket match between Pyms and Brotherhood, a soft-drink manufacturer and one of Pyms’s clients. Most of the players are of middle-age and rather slovenly. Wimsey, prompted by a ball that grazes his elbow, goes on to show his former prowess, winning the game for Pyms, which reveals his secret. Just as Wimsey’s real identity is about to be discovered, he is arrested by the police, led by Sergeant Tony Parker, for the murder of Dean de Momerie. The police want to be in on the next run. With Mountjoy’s telephone directory, all they need is the letter of the week, and this is provided by the office boy, ‘Ginger Joe’. As the bogus Bredon is in jail, the real Lord Peter shows his face around London, and the plot is successfully carried out, although Victor Dean’s death is still unsolved. That night, Tallboy comes to Wimsey’s house and confesses to the murder. A mixture of innocent infatuation and the lure of easy money enticed him into a business that soon had him in its clutches. Eventually, he was discovered and Dean started to blackmail him. Taking advantage of a chance to kill him, Tallboy loaded the catapult that Joe was making with a bullet intended for a guinea-pig, and on the staircase shot him dead. He sees no way out and suggests that his only option is suicide to save his family the disgrace of his arrest and conviction. Wimsey peers out of the window and suggests an alternative. All that Tallboy has to do is to go home and not look back. Both men know that the killers of Victor Dean are lying in wait.

He had already met and befriended Valthor, a soldier from the lost city of Athne, where he had freed a group of Shiftas, Tarzan was now captured by the beautiful but insane Nemo, Queen of the neighboring kingdom of the city of gold, Onthar. Tarzan was forced to fight the most powerful man of the city, Phobeg, in the arena. The second scene, when Tarzan was forced to fight a lion, began with Tarzan running away from the lion Belthar, which was hunting him down to kill him. He thought at first that he could escape from the lion, whose speed is limited to a hundred meters. But this one was chosen for endurance and Tarzan had to turn to face him, knowing that, without a knife, he could only delay the inevitable. Fortunately, his ally, Jad-bal-ja, whom he had raised from a lion cub, comes to his aid, kills Belthar and saves Tarzan. Nemo, believing that her life was linked to that of her beast, commits suicide. Unlike most of the lost cities in the books, which were only visited once, the cities of Cathne and Athne were later mentioned in Tarzan the Magnificent, the only other lost city that was mentioned more than once being Opar.

Late in the 21st century, the human species seems to be well situated. The earth is at peace, and self-replicating machines are already at our service, reproducing themselves, building huge wonders. Artificial spheres dot the system, and the Valkyrie is carrying interstellar explorers at near-light speed. All seems to be well. And then, from the cold, dark void of space, swarms of clumsy little cylinders, rocks the size of boulders, flying at the speed of light, they destroy a few atoms of iron at a time, with the power of several large nuclear bombs. They are impossible to detect, impossible to stop. Humankind is almost exterminated by this atrocious bombardment. (To read a discussion of these rockets and an excerpt from this story, see Atomic rockets: a story of radiation.) A few stragglers desperately try to escape the alien mopping-up fleet. They hide in the sun's atmosphere, inside asteroids, beneath the crust of moons, in ice rings, in the depths of interstellar space. But most of them are tracked down and massacred. The last man and woman on earth are caught as specimens for a zoo. In the belly of an alien starship, a squid explains to them the cold calculation of their execution. When we learned to travel at c, we could wreak vengeance on them, because we had learned to wreak vengeance on them. The attack was not personal. Mankind was just too dangerous to have around.

Sassinak and her family live on a newly colonized planet. The end of the year of production is celebrated, and all the products of the colony are to be shipped out to other worlds. But the ship never comes, and the planet is invaded by pirates. The colonists put up a defense against the greater firepower, number, and skill of the pirates. Sassinak watches the death of her parents and siblings, and then is taken to the prison planet as a slave. At the prison planet, she is sold as a slave to the pirates. But she is advised by a slave who was once in the Fleet, named Abe. He teaches her discipline and imprints a secret on her mind, which will be revealed when she meets a Space Force officer. She is sold again, because her skills have improved enough to be used as a navigator on a pirate ship. This ship is captured by the Space Force, and they rescue her and decipher the secret, whereupon they attack the prison planet and free all the slaves. Abe adopts Sassinak, and she begins a quest to go to the Academy, where all officers are trained. After finishing her studies at the Academy, she has a ship and a star, but she has always wanted to hunt pirates with her stars and her ship. On graduation day, Abe takes her out to dinner, but she sees him murdered. So she is left alone for the first time, with no family, even though he had adopted her. She is an orphan again.

Mrs. Nesta Ford, in her London hotel room, admits to Lord Mountry that she hopes to go with him on a proposed yachting excursion, though her ex-husband has got full custody of the child. Mountry leaves, and Mrs. Ford finds her son Ogden with her, whom she has led away from her husband’s house. She gives her son a reward, but then the latter’s secretary, Mr. Minnick, arrives and wants to find out why he has come. Cynthia tries to bribe his colleague, Mrs. Sheridan, but she doesn’t budge. After they have gone, Nesta reveals to her the origin of Ogden’s nickname, the ‘Little Nugget’, and how he was several times rescued from gangsters by her husband, a detective. Nesta is ready to engage an expert, but her fiancé, Peter Burns, a very wealthy man, offers to become a tutor at Ogden’s new school. The reader learns how he, then aged between 21 and 25, had a great love for Miss Adele Blake, the daughter of an impoverished painter. Though he was initially dismissive of her, they got engaged, but soon after the death of her father she ran off and married another man. This was a great blow to Burns, who, after a period abroad, had been very self-centred and headstrong, and had taken up with the odious Miss Drassilis largely out of pity. When she comes to see him the day after his proposal, she persuades him to help her out with her plans. He soon makes friends with the headmaster of Sanstead, the school where Mr. Ford intends to send Ogden. Burns is appointed classics master at Sanstead, where he soon makes the boys’ acquaintance, and is also welcomed by the elegant and engaging Mr. White, the butler. The next day, Ogden arrives, and the surprised Mr. Abney asks Burns to do something about his tawdry language and smoking. But Burns quickly sees that it would take a lot of scheming to get the boy out of the school. That same day, at the local inn, Burns notices an American man, who looks suspect, and White the butler is seen chasing him with a gun. It transpires that the man is from the Pinkerton Detective Agency and that he has been engaged by Mr. Ford to keep an eye on his son. The next day a friendly American, who says he is a friend of Mr. Ford’s, visits the school, and immediately afterwards leaves after a tour of the school. When the next day comes, Burns is strolling in the grounds when he hears Ogden scream, and a man collides with him and falls to the ground. An excited crowd gathers to discuss this, and the man who had broken into Ogden’s room, when Mrs. Sheridan arrives to see Mr. Abney; and Burns soon sees that she is his former fiancee, Adele. They are initially awkward with each other, but make up. Burns also meets the American in the village, who is Buck MacGinnis, Ogden’s former abductor, who takes Burns for his rival, Sam “the Velvet” Fisher. Burns asks White about the two men and learns that, while Buck is a scoundrel, Fisher is a clever man with a dangerously slick manner. Seeing Adele again, Burns sees that his love for her is as strong as ever. And then MacGinnis and his gang hold up the masters at gunpoint, and Burns is caught up in the search for Ogden; but Burns manages to escape by climbing out of the window of the study. He is shot at, but manages to hide in a thicket. There he sees Buck MacGinnis and manages to catch him and fend off the rest of the gang. Ogden is still missing, as is another boy, a friend of his. The schoolmaster, Mr. Abney, tells Burns to go to London and search for the runaway boys, while he and Adele discuss what to do about Ogden. It transpires that Burns has given Ogden enough money to get to London, where he will leave the boy with his valet, whose name is John White. Burns flies to London, and, as he is being pursued by Fisher, he sees that White saw him give Ogden the money and the instructions to Burns. White then tells Burns that he was “the Velvet” Sam Fisher, who had asked Burns to join him in the presumed abduction. Burns is in a terrible panic, and when he reaches his lodgings he finds that Ogden has not arrived there. Fisher arrives after Burns, but on hearing that Ogden was enjoying London, he immediately leaves. The next day Burns finds Ogden, staying with his mother, and takes him back to school, while Fisher threatens to reveal Burns’s actions if his true identity is made public. Then, the next day, after being reminded of their engagement, Burns tells her that he is not in love with her. He takes Ogden to the schoolroom and has him locked in. The term is coming to an end, but the new schoolmaster, Mr. Ford, is unable to take Ogden home for several days, so Mr. Abney asks Burns to stay on to watch over Ogden with Audrey and the butler. Fisher, however, gives away the plan to return Ogden to his mother, and Burns leaves in disgust, but then goes back and tells her about Fisher. She is not pleased, and he notices that MacGinnis is also back in the vicinity. He drives Fisher away and takes charge of Ogden himself, though still without the support of Audrey. Fisher returns with MacGinnis and offers Burns a second chance, which he declines. The telephone wires are cut and they have to wait in the loft of the school stables. Ogden, after tiring of his running away, surrenders to Burns, who consoles the tearful and frightened young woman. Some days later, they confess their love to each other, but she insisted that he must go back to her. They part, and a moment later, the schoolmistress and Nessa Ford arrive. He tells her that Mr. Ogden has found his mother, and that he is afraid of her. After convincing Mr. Ford that Fisher is a suitable chaperone for Ogden, he is able to leave with his wife. And he goes to the carriage.

Paris, France is a memoir, written in a “stream of consciousness” style. It has been interpreted as Gertrude Stein’s personal vision of France and the French people. She notices them eating, drinking, crossing the street, going about their daily lives without deviating from their “Frenchness.” The word “French” quickly becomes a way of being, a state of existence. A noun and an adjective. Throughout the book, the idea of being French in France is conveyed to the reader with a straightforward, cocksure, matter-of-fact tone. For this reason, some critics feel the book was not written as a totally accurate account of the French culture. Throughout the book, Stein frequently mentions the importance of style, independence, logic, tradition, and civilization as the foundations of being French, a Frenchness that cannot be broken, regardless of one’s actual nationality. She describes the state of France in the context of past wars and the possibility of wars to come, the effect that war will have on the French state of being and the actual and ideal French reactions to war. Stein casually relates anecdotes she deems appropriate to the topics at hand, and each anecdote connects with other anecdotes, which are then connected to the whole, forming a picture of France. However, while she goes off on tangents of her own thoughts and personal life, she always comes back to the driving theme of the book, identifying the French traits and paying tribute to England and France.

According to Kesey’s introduction, the book was inspired by an article which appeared in the Associated Press on 31 October, 1864. It was titled: “Dr. Charles Oswald Loach, discoverer of the ‘Secret Cave of the Ancient Americans,’ Causes Archaeological Controversy.” The whole of the rest of the book is devoted to this character, Charles Oswald Loach, a theosophist who discovered a secret cave, to which he testified in the State Senate. Set in the thirties, Loach is portrayed as a convicted murderer (he killed a photographer in order to protect the secret of his discovery) who is set free from San Quentin, under the supervision of a priest, in order to lead a new expedition to the lost cave. This leads to the following comically misadventures: * a priest, Father Paul, an archaeologist, Dr. Jocelyn Crane, Loach’s brother, a museum curator, the publisher Rodney Makai, the ‘Blavatskian’ Makai sisters, the African-American driver Ned, Juke and Boyle, two World War I veterans suffering from mustard-gas poisoning, all go to Utah to find the cave, where Loach claims it is.

“Didier Sand is a fifteen-year-old boy working as a sailor on the schooner Pilgrim. Its crew are whalers who, every year, sail to New Zealand in the midst of a commercial whaling fleet. The hunt this year was poor, and as the crew prepares to return, the wife of the owner of the whaling firm, Mrs. Weldon, her five-year-old son, Jack, and her cousin Benedict, an entomologist, ask to be taken to San Francisco. On the way, they save five castaways from a shipwreck, with a dog that came along with them (Tom, Acteon, Austin, Bat, Nan, Hercule, and Dingo, the dog). Near the end of the voyage, they spot a sperm whale, and the crew, hoping to get something out of this poor season, agree to go after it. Captain Hull, who is reluctant, lets Didier take charge of the ship. But the chase is botched, and the whole crew is killed. Now Didier, with no other experienced sailor to help him, has to sail the ship with the five castaways, who want to go back to South America. But the cook, Negro, who thinks they are all lost, tricks him by destroying a compass and a speedometer, and finally, after making sure the others are dead, leads them to the African coast.

The Hardys are in peril when they agree to help their Greek pen pal, Evangelos Pandropolos, to search for an ancient Greek helmet. It was used in a film made by the uncle of Evangelos, a silent film called Persian Glory, and then the film was lost. At Hunt College, where he, Frank, Joe, and Chet Morton are taking a summer course in filmmaking, they encounter the menacing character of Leon Saffel, who is making things worse and worse. It seems that the villains want to stop Mr. Hardy's investigations into a crime syndicate, but they are also looking for the helmet, which according to Evangelos's millionaire uncle may have been Agamemnon's. Meanwhile, the clues lead the Hardys to the California coast, and then to Greece, where the murderous gang is waiting for them on Corfu.

The book is the story of a relationship between a fantasist, Henry Kent, who attacks solitary rich women, and an old novelist, Daisy Langrishe, who is already in her third marriage and has just bought a cottage. He soon falls in love with her, and begins to win her confidence. First, he offers to become her gardener, and, despite her reluctance, she accepts; then, during a trip abroad, an accident to which she is injured, he begins to correspond with her. This correspondence begins quite naturally, but as he feels her interest in him, he begins to tell her a series of extraordinary stories about his life, in order to arouse her sympathy. When Daisy returns home, and is soon indispensible to her, thanks to a fall she has had, they become lovers. But the family and friends of Daisy, who have discovered the circumstances of their relationship, begin to be very suspicious of him. The fact is that they fear that the information they have on his past may be too late to save Daisy from harm.

In Molly Moon Stops the World, the reader is shown that Molly is now having a happy life, thanks to the money she has made in New York. She is putting this money aside for her orphanage. At the beginning of the story Davina Nuttel, a famous child actress and Molly’s rival, is abducted by Primo Cell, a shrewd and very rich businessman. When Lucy Logan hears of this she calls Molly to her side, because she suspects that Primo has kidnapped Davina and is also hypnotizing famous film stars and singers to perform in his advertisements. Also, she is running for president of the United States. Molly travels to Los Angeles and finds that the diamond she wears around her neck has some special powers. She also discovers that it is possible to hypnotize someone permanently if one stops time during the hypnosis. Molly gets help from Sinclair, Primo’s stepson, and his personal yogi, Forest. She also finds out that she is the child of Lucy and Primo. He is the father of her baby, Cornelius. Molly is now really determined to save Davina. The story ends with Cornelius thinking that he is a lamb, thanks to Molly’s selfless devotion and the help of the diamond.

Princess of Gossip tells the story of Avery Johnson, a fourteen-year-old high school freshman who has just moved from Ohio to southern California. She finds herself mistaken for the assistant of a pop star on Myspace and receives an invitation to a tinsel-town party, where she snaps a photo of a young star and her secret new boyfriend. Having too much juicy gossip to keep to herself, she creates a blog called the Princess of Gossip and posts her find. Overnight, she becomes a media darling. She is sent the most fabulous designer dresses, gets to know the stars, and is in on all the big news. Then she shows up at school wearing the most fabulous designer clothes, and the most popular girl in school is jealous. Then Beckett, the spoiled, star-struck son of a designer, sees her wearing one of his father’s creations and invites her to his house for dinner. The true identity of the Princess of Gossip remains a secret, but when the paparazzi catch Avery and Beckett on a date, Cecilia is even more envious. Only one girl can be the new “it” girl at school. Can the Princess of Gossip keep her crown?

The Swallows, the Amazons, and the Ds are on a sailing trip with Captain Flint to the Hebrides. While the elders clean up the boat to return it to the owner, the younger ones visit the interior, and they see on an island of a loch an interesting bird, which is a bit confusing. There is some question about whether it is a great northern diver, which is not known to nest in the British Isles, or a black-breasted diver. The expert, Mr. Jemmerling, is a mortal enemy of birds because he collects birds’ eggs and keeps birds’ skins. So they are trying to protect the birds while acquiring photographic evidence of the nest. But there is a misunderstanding with the Scots of the area, who speak mostly Gaelic. Because the plot is more exciting and violent than usual, with the egg collector trying to kill the great northern diver, it has been considered by some as one of the metafictional novels of the series, stories made up by the children themselves.

The House of the Wolfings is a romantic reconstruction of the life of the Germanic Gothic tribes, written in a poetic form, in an archaic style, and containing much poetry. The work is based on Morris’s own idealistic view of his subject, but it is also informed by what was actually known of his tribe’s customs and language at the time. He represents them as simple and hardworking, but galvanized into a heroic struggle to protect their families and liberty against the coming of the imperial Romans. Morris’s Goths inhabit a region called the Mark, situated on a river in the forest of Mirkwood, and divided into Upper Mark, Middle Mark, and Lower Mark. They worship their gods, Odin and Tyr, with the sacrifice of horses, and rely on soothsayers, who foretell the future and provide information about the tribe’s enemies. From among the Mark’s people, two War Dukes are chosen, one from each of the Houses of the Wolfings and the Houses of the Laxings. The leader of the Wolfings is Thiodolf, a man of enigma, perhaps divine, and whose influence is threatened by his possession of a magnificent, dwarf-made, ill-omened chain-mail shirt. He is supported by his lover, the Wood Sun, and their daughter, the Hall Sun, who are related to the gods.

Kira Landon, fifteen, has a very ordinary life—until one night her friends persuaded her to go under hypnosis. And she tells of a past she’d never known, remembering her mother carrying her along war-scarred streets in a foreign language. Her best friend, Lorna, is pushing her to find out more—but before they can do so, Mrs. Landon disappears. Then a strange woman appears at the Landons’ door, saying she’s Aunt Memory. Aunt Memory takes Kira to the mysterious land of Crythe, where the citizens are trained from childhood to remember everything that happens to them. Soon Kira discovers that not only is her mother a prisoner in Crythe, but that many people there are not who they say they are. Aunt Memory is her mother, while the woman who calls herself Aunt Memory is really Rona Cummins, a former enemy of her parents, who is determined to uncover her parents’ secrets. As she is pushed ever harder to betray her parents’ trust, Kira must find a way to save herself, her mother, and her best friend—and her parents’ memories.

“The Daughter of Fortune” is the sequel to this novel and deals with the adventures of Aurora Del Valle, granddaughter of Eliza Sommers (Hija de la Fortuna). This daughter of Rachel Louise Sommers (Eliza’s daughter with Tao Chien) and Matias Rodrguez de Santa Cruz (son of Paulina del Valle and Feliciano Rodriguez de Santa Cruz)—a child who, though she can remember only the first five years of her life—has frequent nightmares of black pyjamas surrounding her and losing hold of the hand of someone she loves. She is a child of mystery, as her father never recognized her until the end of his life, when he died of syphilis. When Rachel Louise died, her maternal grandparents raised her, until the death of Tao Chien. After this, Eliza asks Paulina to keep the child, while she travels to China to bury Tao Chien. Paulina asks Eliza to agree that she must cut off all contact with the child, so as not to become too fond of her and later have her taken away. Consequently, Paulina conceals the child’s true origins. But when she talks to her father, Matias, he gives her the real story. In this first part, the author also describes the War of the Pacific, in which Severo Del Valle is a soldier. This war is depicted as very cruel, as can be seen from the scene in which Severo loses his leg to gangrene. In the second part, we see how Aurora grows up. She is given a photgraphic education and becomes a great artist. The family moves from San Francisco to Chile, where Frederic Williams marries Paulina so that he can enjoy the respect of society there. He is thought to be a true lord, and nobody knows his humble origins. Also, we see how Paulina del Valle starts up several new businesses, such as the production of French wine and the importation of Swiss cheese. The Del Valle family travels to Europe, where Paulina undergoes an operation for a tumour. The operation is a success, and she returns to full health. Even though she is more than seventy years old, she does not show any signs of weakness. She uses her mind to overcome her body and to continue ruling the family as a strong matriarch. This part of the novel focuses on the life of the child, Aurora. After growing up, Aurora becomes a photographer and marries Diego Domnguez. She then leaves him and takes a lover, Dr Ivan Radovic, and their affair is explained in the epilogue. Lastly, we learn the true story of Tao Chien’s death.

Kin-Fo is a very wealthy man, and has no lack of property. He is very bored, and when the news comes that his big business in America, a bank, is going to fail, he decides to die. He buys a life insurance policy for two hundred thousand dollars, which covers accidents, death in battle, and suicide. He is going to die by opium and poison, when he changes his mind. He says that he doesn’t want to die without a thrill, and that he’s going to have his old teacher Wang the Philosopher kill him. Wang is not in his house, so he sets out on a journey with two escorts sent by the insurance company and his scheming servant Sun. Finally he receives a letter from Wang, who can’t stand the idea of killing a friend, and has decided to kill himself, leaving the task of killing Kin-Fo to a former friend, a bandit. He and his servant Sun try to find the bandit and buy his life. The boat they are on is captured, and they make it ashore in their life jackets, and blindfolded by the bandit, they are taken back to Kin-Fo’s home, where his old friends are waiting for him. He finally marries the girl of his dreams and is very happy.

The principal character is Eddy Carbone, a poor Italian-American who lives with his wife Beatrice and his orphan niece, Catherine. The play begins with Eddy's being kind and a little fond of her, and his tenderness increases as it progresses. His sentiments are put into sharper relief by the arrival from Italy of Beatrice's two cousins, Marco and Rodolpho. They have entered the country illegally, and have hoped to escape from starvation and unemployment by coming to America. Marco is exceptionally strong and a bull in the eyes of Eddy's friends; he also has a family of four in Italy, a wife and three sons, one of whom has TB. Rodolpho is a rather ugly man, in his late twenties, a blond, with light complexion, a rogue, a good singer (especially Paper-doll), a dressmaker, and a good cook. Catherine soon falls in love with him. After three weeks have passed, and Catherine and Rodolpho are in secret relations, Eddy sets about pointing out his defects to Catherine and Beatrice. He complains that he is not "the real man," and also sings and cooks and makes dresses, which embarrasses him. When Catherine resolves to marry Rodolpho, Eddy becomes desperate and asks his lawyer, Alfieri (the narrator), to help him. He is told, however, that he will not be able to have any legal help unless he denounces the two men before the authorities. In view of his earlier statement that it is an honor to shelter them, Eddy refuses to do so. He continues to slander Rodolpho, and ends by offering to teach him to box. However, he takes the opportunity to hit him. In retaliation, Marco sets a chair on the floor, tells Eddy to lift it with one hand by the foot, and, when Eddy fails to do so, raises it above his head with one hand. This shows his superior strength and that he will keep an eye on Rodolpho and hold him back from Eddy, should Eddy ever do anything against him. After he has found Rodolpho with Catherine in the bedroom, Eddy goes to see Alfieri again, who tells him that the only way to get rid of the situation is to call the Immigration Bureau. The consequences of this are fatal. He returns home to learn that Catherine is betrothed to Rodolpho, and also to learn from Beatrice that two more fugitives have arrived in the meantime. Suddenly the immigration authorities appear and arrest the four men, but before they can be led out, Marco runs from the group, "strikes" into the room, and spits in Eddy's face. Eddy screams out and follows Marco out into the street, raging at him for the insult, not noticing that the crowd is turning against him, as it becomes evident that he is the traitor, for Marco accuses Eddy of having killed his children. He then promises to acquit Eddy if the fugitives are not sent back to Sicily, as the Sicilians are accustomed to do, and is released. In the last scene, Eddy is shown to be furious at his own misconduct, and he does not come to the wedding. He does not respond to the call of peace that is made to him by Rodolpho, and he will not leave the house when he learns that Marco is coming. The scene ends with a fight between Eddy and Marco, before the crowd of his family and friends. Eddy brings a knife to bear upon Marco, who turns it upon Eddy and kills him. It is not known whether Marco intended to stab Eddy, and the scene does not tell. Eddy dies, calling out to Beatrice.

From the usual realistic crime, the story of The Last Hero is a mixture of Science-Fiction and espionage. It begins, an indefinite time after the events of Enter the Saint, with the narrative of the action of the Saint who, by a ruse, destroys an assassin who was about to kill a visiting prince, causing the Saint to become the object of national enthusiasm, and the Government offers him a full pardon and a post as a crime-control agent. The latter politely declines, preferring to remain a secret agent unknown to all but a few. This decision was to change in the story “The Impossible Crime” (later included in the book Alias the Saint) and also in the novel She Was a Lady. For three months the Saint proceeds to work so secretly that he is thought to have disappeared. On the sidelines, he is able to listen to his friend the journalist, who tells him of the possibility of a fresh war in Europe, in spite of Templar’s assurance that after the events of the First World War, there would not be another such war for “hundreds of years.” Then on a country outing with his adventurer-girl, the Saint finds himself at a Government experiment-station where an incredible weapon is being tested, a Cloud-Electron, which produces a vapor which, when it comes in contact with anything, turns it to ashes. Templar and Holm are just about to leave when they meet an enormous man, a monster called Marius, a cruel tycoon, who has his own nefarious designs on the weapon. Templar escapes and decides that he and his men must steal the Cloud-Electron before the Government – or any other Government – can use it against the people, and that the weapon must not fall into Marius’ hands. In addition, in order to prevent any similar weapon ever being produced again, he plans to abduct the inventor of the weapon and, if necessary, kill him. Templar is shocked to find that Marius has seized the girl. He begins to lose patience, and even, with no knowledge of the secret of the identity of the mysterious character who has entered the scene, he realizes that the future is not propitious. Templar sees that the end of the secret agent’s career is at hand, and that he will have to leave the country, and with his gang if they wish to follow him. But he must first succeed in persuading the inventor of the Cloud-Electron to give up his invention, and when the latter insists that he will not, that he is perhaps mad, Templar is forced to see that the man must die in order to save millions of people. But before he can kill the inventor, Marius and his gang attack the Saint’s stronghold. During the fighting, one of Templar’s men, Norman Kent, completes the task by killing the inventor; having realized that anyone who did that would be hanged for murder, he is determined to take the responsibility on himself. Having first of all taken the inventor’s notes and calculations, he is at once arrested by Marius and the Prince, and it is not until they compel him to hand them over that he confesses to having killed the man. Some time later, when Templar and his men have left the country, Marius reveals that Kent had in fact secreted the papers to Simon before they left. The novel ends with Marius shooting Kent dead as the latter stands in front of a window to stop the latter shooting out. It was published in 1927, fifteen years before the invention of the atom bomb and nine years before the outbreak of the Second World War, but The Last Hero seems to contain a prophecy of both events. Only once is the Cloud-Electron actually used, and then only by the inventor whom Templar and Holm had witnessed at work. Marius reveals to Templar that his men have destroyed the machine, and it is not known what Templar has done with the inventor’s papers. The Last Hero was the first of a trilogy. The storyline, especially the role played by Norman Kent, was continued in the sequel, The Knight Templar (published in 1930) and taking place three months after the end of The Last Hero. Then, after a number of short stories and a full-length novel, in 1932, the trilogy was completed with The Escape. In this novel, Holm fades into the background somewhat, though she reappears in the short story, The Holy Terror, published in 1941. The tone of this book is more romantic and tragic than in most of the novels in the series. In most of them, the reader can expect to see Templar facing a series of mortal dangers and terrible dangers, and always surviving, living on to fight again in the next book and the next. In the present book, by contrast, the hero is in fact the ill-fated Norman Kent, who has a hopeless but nobly felt love for the fair Patricia Holm. In this book, Kent rather than Templar is the main hero, at least in the latter half of the book, and is clearly the ‘last hero’ of the title. Of this novel, Caroline Whitehead and George Macleod wrote: A knight-errant of modern times, Norman Kent lives and dies by the rules of chivalry. He loves Patricia Holm, who, like Dulcinea, is unaware of his love. He is devoted to his noble liegeman, Simon Templar. Like Sir Gawain in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Kent takes on his master’s perilous tasks; not only those that threaten life and limb, but those that could inflict dishonour on his master, and on his reputation as a Templar. He is willing to bear the lash for King Arthur, and to bear the lash without hesitation for Simon Templar.

The play is set in the seventeenth century, during the Thirty Years’ War in Europe. The recruiting officer and sergeant are introduced, both complaining of the difficulty of recruiting men to go to war. A woman called Mother Courage enters with a cart, which she uses to supply the soldiers, and thus to profit from the war. She has three children, Eiliv, Kattrin, and Swiss Cheese. One of the children is missing. The sergeant negotiates with Mother Courage, while the recruiting officer takes Eiliv away. A year later, Mother Courage has an argument with a Protestant general’s cook over a hen, while Eiliv is praised by the general for killing peasants and stealing their cattle. Eiliv and his mother sing ‘The Fisherwoman and the Soldier’. Mother Courage scolds her son for the risks he takes that might get him killed, and slaps him. Three years later, Swiss Cheese is a soldier’s paymaster. A whore called Yvette Pottier sings ‘The Song of Fraternization’. Mother Courage uses the song to warn Kattrin against becoming too involved with soldiers. Just before the Catholic army arrive, the cook and the chaplain deliver a message from Eiliv. Swiss Cheese hides the regiment’s money from the invaders. Mother Courage and her daughters hurriedly exchange their badges of the Protestant army for those of the Catholics. Then Swiss Cheese is captured by the Catholics when he tries to return the pay box to his general. Mother Courage has to sell her cart to get money to try to pay off the soldiers and rescue her son. She takes too long negotiating the amount of money needed to keep herself, the chaplain, and Kattrin alive, and so Swiss Cheese is shot eleven times and killed. If she acknowledges the body, she could be killed, so she refuses to see it and it is thrown into a pit. Then Mother Courage, waiting outside the general’s tent to lodge a complaint, sings ‘The Song of Great Surrender’ to a young soldier who is also waiting for the general. The soldier is annoyed that he hasn’t been paid, and wants to complain too. But Mother Courage is convinced that she can’t complain either, and decides not to. When Catholic General Tilly dies, Mother Courage asks the chaplain whether the war will go on. The chaplain suggests that Mother Courage should marry him, but she refuses. Mother Courage finds Kattrin terribly disfigured after she is raped by the chaplain while collecting more supplies. Sometime later, Mother Courage starts following the Protestant army again. Then two peasants wake her up, to sell her supplies, and to tell her that peace has been declared. The cook turns up, and tries to cause an argument between Mother Courage and the chaplain. Mother Courage leaves for the town just as Eiliv enters, dragging the unconscious body of his mother. And so the cook and Mother Courage start their own little business. When the war begins again, they start collecting food for the army. But then, in the seventeenth year of the war, food and money run out, and the cannons run out. Mother Courage and the cook, with the young soldier from the beginning of the war, are now called to try to collect money and food for the army. It is a very small inn, and when Mother Courage refuses to leave Kattrin there, the cook goes off with her. Then the Catholic army attacks the small Protestant town of Halle, when Mother Courage is not in the town, on business. Kattrin is woken by a hunting party of Catholics who are taking peasants with them. Kattrin snatches a drum from the cart, climbs up on the roof and bangs it, to try to wake the people up. Though the soldiers shoot her, she manages to wake the town. In the morning, Mother Courage sings to her daughter’s corpse, has the peasants bury her and hitches herself up to the cart. She has no more children and her supplies are almost gone.

In the early eighties, Liza goes to many auditions at the insistence of her mother, Peppy, who dresses her in strapless evening gowns, makes her wear thick makeup, and binds her in false eyelashes. The novel is an account of her life, which continues to humiliate her as she and her family, after having set up a restaurant in Marin, go on with their pathetic existence, humiliating themselves in every way. In the first half of the book she has to perform in a dilapidated fire station, which is both theater and home, she is bullied at school, and even raped. In the second half she is a girl of many moods, at first she goes in for punk and takes on the image of the girl in the music clip of the artist known as the Plasmatics, Wendy O. Williams. In the end she ends up in a relationship with a drug dealer, even becomes a drug addict during a stay at Elf House, a group of hippies, according to the author, who were terribly obsessed with elves and spoke “Quenya, the high elven language of J.R. Tolkien, from Lord of the Rings.” Then, working for Centaur Productions, which publishes “slash” novels, she turns herself into a sex phone star and a star of the Las Vegas stage, thus creating a new definition of success that is connected with the theatrical aspirations that her mother once had.

Anne began to keep a diary on June 14, 1942, two days after her thirteenth birthday, and twenty-two days before she and her family went into hiding. They went to the attic of the building in which her father had his office, where a secret wall was put up. Four months later, Mrs. van Pels’s dentist, Frédéric Pfeffer, also joined them. In the published version, the names have been changed, so that Mrs. van Pels is called Mrs. van Daan and Frédéric Pfeffer is called Mr. Dussel. In this way, with the help of a circle of trusted people of Mr. Frank’s, they lived in hiding for two years and one month, until they were betrayed in August 1944, when they were deported to concentration camps. Of the eight, only Mr. Frank survived. Anne died of typhus in Bergen-Belsen in the early days of March, about two weeks before the liberation by the British army in April.

The novel begins with the devastation of a planet that has been overrun by an experimental warship. Thence we follow the two main characters, one of whom, having been recruited by the Sutherlin Alliance, sworn to the destruction of the Alcon Empire, begins his career as a member of the Imperial Devil Squadron. The other recruit, having served for some time in this squadron, then resigned, in order to become a mercenary and a bounty hunter, is similarly recruited by the Sutherlin Alliance. Both are among the best fighters in the galaxy. The Empire, however, learns of the presence of the Sutherlins and brings in its star-destroying warship. A few days before its deployment, the two men learn of the ship's existence and of its intended target, and contrive to destroy it and its considerable escort. The novel's chief concern is with the attachment and the need for belonging. Both of the main characters have to struggle with this: the elder one to remain aloof, heedless of the needs of others; the younger one to forge a bond, wishing not to be the victim of a cruel war.

L. H. Fitzwilliam finds himself on a train going to London in the same compartment with a pleasant old lady, Miss Pinkerton, who, though apparently demented, reminds him of his aunt. She speaks to him of the recent deaths, which have taken place under a pretence of accidents, in her home village of Wychwood. The local police are apparently at a loss to find out the murderer, but she knows his identity by the expression on his face, just before he strikes. Since he has turned his attention to the village doctor, she is on her way to Scotland Yard to identify the murderer and save the doctor. Unfortunately, she does not tell him who the murderer is. The next day he learns that Miss Pinkerton was killed in an accident before she could reach Scotland Yard. He is not very suspicious at first, but the death of the doctor does surprise him. He goes to the village, posing as a researcher of folklore, and starts searching for the murderer. Soon, four main suspects present themselves: an unnerving antiques dealer, a bitter lawyer, a smug doctor and a new peer, a show-off, who is about to marry a pretty young woman.

Kazuko Yoshiyama, a junior high-school student, is cleaning the science laboratory with her classmates, the students Kazuo Fukamachi and Goro Asakura, when she is overcome by a lavender scent, and faints. During the next three days, strange events occur around Kazuko, and her house burns down, and she is transported back twenty-four hours. She tells Kazuo and Goro of her experiences, and they are not too convinced until she has accurately predicted an earthquake and fire. Their teacher, Fukushima, the science teacher, says that she is able to “teleport” and “leap forward in time.” To find out how to use this power, she must teleport four days back. Finally, her determination brings her back to the day when she was transported to the laboratory and met her classmates. However, she meets a strange man who looks exactly like Kazuo. He is actually a man from the future, the traveler Ken Sogoh, and he has come to the present time by accident. After he has been with her for a month, Kazuko falls in love with him. He leaves, and everyone forgets about him, except Kazuko. She does remember vaguely that he promised to return whenever she smelled lavender.

Algarve renews the assaults in the south of Unkerlat towards the Mamming Hills, from which Unkerlat gets its cinnabar, and which leads to the great Battle of Sulingen. More and more refugees from the Isle of Krakum begin to appear at Zuwayza, which is overrun with them; others escape from a caravan at Valmiera and are taken captive by Skarnu and his comrades, who have blown up the convoy to hinder the Algarvians; others are set free by a raid of Lagorza’s men on a camp at Valmiera. Leofsig is killed by Sidroc, who has joined the Plegmunds’ brigade. In the west of Unkerlat, Ishtar and his company, in a raid on a camp, are led to partake of a goat-stew, and are subsequently purified by their captain. In the Land of the Ice People, the Algarvians kill a group of kaunians in the hope of destroying the magic of the lagoans by killing kaunians, but the ice people’s magic destroys the Algarvians instead, and they are forced to withdraw from Unkerlat altogether, and leave it to the Lagoan. The Algarvians are beginning to feel weary of their battles, and are beginning to rely on Sibians, Forthwegians, and, more and more, unreliable Yaninanians, to fight their battles against Unkerlat. The Battle of Sulingen is won by the Unkerlatians, and Trasone dies in the battle in the last scene of the book. Algarve begins to lose the war. The Naantali expedition begins; Kuusamo’s men take Obuda.

This is the first of the Second Sons trilogy. It takes place in the fantastical world of Ranadon, where there is no night. Two suns revolve around the earth and bathe it in constant radiance. This is said to be the work of the Goddess, a benevolent but sometimes harsh deity, who is believed in by most people. The lore is that long ago the second sun mysteriously disappeared, and this brought about the age of shadow. Then, at the behest of the self-appointed High Priestess of the Shadow-dancers, the Lion of Senet, a powerful and pious man named Antonov, sacrificed his infant son Gunta, and then the suns were restored. It is after a volcanic eruption, and an earthquake, that Duke Dirk Provin of Elcast saves a shipwrecked seaman from certain death. While he is healing, it is discovered that he is the exiled King of Dhevyn, Johan Thorn, who was defeated by Antonov during the Age of Shadow and is now the most wanted man in all of Ranadon. Soon the news of the rescue reaches the Lion of Senet himself, and the apprentice doctor is forced to understand that his own world has been slowly turning upside down.

The gunsmith Cornish McManus, who was inspired by a fine piece of maple-wood, made this rifle in 1768. The barrel,.40 caliber, 42 inches long, is shorter than the usual barrel of the day, the rifling more severe, a turn in one and a half yards, and the butt is less cut back than usual to increase its accuracy. On the completion of the gun, the Canadian finds it a most accurate instrument, able to shoot three balls at once into the same hole, at a distance of thirty-five yards. Nevertheless, owing to lack of money and a contract for marriage, he is compelled to sell the rifle to a certain John Byam, who carries it into battle against the redcoats. The gun was handed down to the succeeding generations, was lost, rediscovered, and sold as an antique, and ended by residing on the mantle of a mechanic. On Christmas Eve, 1824, the owner, as he was cleaning his fireplace, lights a brand, and the rifle goes off by accident. The ball passes through a window and hits a little boy in the next room, who was putting a candle into his Christmas tree. The book ends with Harv throwing the gun into the river, whence it is recovered by another person.

“‘Subbies’ live in the outskirts of Silverdale, a large fictitious town. ‘Chippies’ live in the town centre. The children of the ‘subbies’ love to go chipping (that is, visiting the dance halls of Rawhampton). They are prone to drugs and violence. The government has introduced a series of TV advertisements warning of the dangers of chipping. Zoe’s friend Tabitha is the daughter of a very rich builder and she takes her friends, Ned, Larry and Joanne, chipping. Ned takes them to the Blue Moon dance hall where Daz also happens to be. They have to say that they are going to visit Zoe’s cousin in the next suburb and they have to show their identification cards to the bouncers. Zoe and Daz are attracted to each other as soon as they see each other, although at first Zoe thinks it is the ’lobotomizer’, a drink containing coke, rum and ‘a couple of other things’. “ She is so embarrassed that she is smiling and Daz thinks she likes him. Finally he shouts to her loudly and his shouting coincides with a break in the music. The policeman intervenes and a chippie throws a chair which is deflected by the shoulder of Ned. Daz comes to their rescue, takes Ned by the arm and tells them all to run for their lives.

When his mother, Kerry, disappears, young Carl and his brother Harley are sent to live with their aunt Beryl, who lives at Wattle Beach. While there, Carl works on a tugboat belonging to an old friend of his grandfather. Young Carl doesn’t know that his grandfather was involved in an accident that killed the skipper’s eight-year-old son, Graham. At first, Carl keeps his emotions hidden and doesn’t reveal his concerns about his mother’s disappearance or his worry about his brother Harley, who is in and out of juvenile detention. But during the course of the novel, he gradually begins to trust people and gradually shares his feelings with them. In the end, it is revealed that when trying to get home to her children, Sarah, Harley and Carl, Kerry was killed in a bus accident. When the news of his mother’s death reaches him, his aunt Beryl has already left to go off with her lover, Bruce. Since he has nowhere else to go, Joy Duncan takes him to live with her at Wiseman’s Cove with his brother Harley, who is already living there and considers them his family.

The events of the second novel left the Alignment exposed and evicted from the United States Government, an ancient celestial globe in the possession of the Pentagon, an earthly one in the possession of the Vatican, and Conrad still in search of Atlantis. But when Conrad stumbles upon the wreckage of a German submersible that has on board a powerful Atlantean explosive device that uses water as its oxidizing agent, he is prevented by a Russian oil magnate and member of the Alignment, Roman “Midas” Midasovitch, who leads him into further conflicts with the Alignment. In the meantime, Serena Seghetti has penetrated the Alignment and is exposing its remaining members to the world. She is merely transporting both globes to the Grand Master’s castle in order to use them to indict their leaders in the forthcoming “Summit Meeting”—the first secret meeting of the Alignment in centuries—when Conrad shows up to ruin her plans, then sacrifices his own life to protect her and to reveal the Alignment’s plans for Armageddon. When the novel ends, both are supposedly dead, having failed to stop a controlled explosion beneath Jerusalem that was to set off a holy war. But it is revealed that they have lived on, away from the Alignment, the governments, and the Church which has so long held them in thrall.

A writer of Western novels, Roberta (Bobbi) Anderson, happens to come across a metal object in the woods outside the small town of Haven, Maine, which turns out to be the hull of an ancient, submerged alien spaceship. When the hull is disturbed, it emits an invisible, odorless gas which, in the atmosphere, transforms people into beings similar to the ones who inhabited the spaceship, but who possess a limited intelligence which gives them genius in some respects, but which does not give them philosophical or moral insights. The gas causes violent behavior in some people, like Becka Paulson, who kills her adulterous husband by rewiring their television set, and disappearances, like that of David Brown, whose older brother, Hilly, teleports him to another planet, which the Havenites call Altair IV. The principal character is a poet, a friend of Bobbi, James Eric Gardner (Gard), a good man with a liberal social outlook, who is insensible to the effects of the spaceship because of a steel plate in his head as a result of a childhood accident. Gard is also an alcoholic prone to drunkenness, and to rages of violence which lead to long blackouts. His relationship with Bobbi deteriorates as the novel proceeds. She is almost wholly taken over by the desire to “become one” with the spaceship, but Gard increasingly sees her health deteriorate and her mind become more and more clouded. * This book contains many metaphors for the dangers of drug abuse, which was King’s own preoccupation at the time, as well as for the dangers of atomic power and radiation (which may be seen in the physical transformations of the townspeople), for uncontrolled technological development, and for the corruption of power. The whole of the governing bodies of the town are depicted as corrupt and totalitarian, and Gard is finally persuaded by Bobbi to enter the spaceship. That day he has a chance to kill her, and decides to use the same gun that State Trooper “Monster” Dugan had used to shoot her in her field. But Bobbi, who has been able to trance-out while taking Valium, immediately sends out a psychic APB, and the whole town rushes to her house to kill Gard. Benefactor Ev Hillman, grandfather of David and Hilly, helps Gard to escape into the woods (which are soon set on fire by one of the aliens’ “toys”), in return for using the “new and improved” computers, and the small amount of “becoming” he has experienced to save David. Gard then enters the spaceship and, with the last of his strength, telepathically propels it into space, thus killing almost all of the transformed townspeople but preventing the aliens’ deadly threat from spreading into the wider world. At the end of the novel, representatives of the CIA, the FBI, and “The Establishment” arrive at Haven and take away some of the survivors and some of the devices that the aliens had invented, while almost a quarter of the remaining inhabitants are killed. Finally, we find David safe in Hilly’s hospital room. The title of the book is taken from a children’s rhyme. King claims that he invented the second verse, but that he had heard the first one as a child.

The main character is Tashi, an African woman, a secondary character in the novel The Color Purple. Now in the United States, she comes from Olinka, a country where female genital mutilation is practiced. After marrying an American, Adam, she flees Olinka, which is at war. Tashi chooses to go back to Olinka to be circumcised because she is torn between two cultures, Olinka and Western. Instead of feeling freed by this childless status, she worries about it. She wants to honor her Olinkan roots and submits to the operation in her adolescence, although it is usually applied to young girls. Later, Tashi sees many psychiatrists, for she goes mad because of the shock of the mutilation, before she finds the courage to act. The novel is told by various characters, who are all the characters. It is a question of what it means to have one's gender culturally determined, and it is emphasized that torture is not culture.

The narrator is a writer who works as a fact-checker for a highbrow magazine, probably Harper's or the New Yorker (where the author once worked as a fact-checker), but for which he once hoped to write. By night he is a cocaine-addicted party animal, who goes to a club called Heartbreak, where he usually has to bury himself. His wife Amanda has recently left him, and he tries to ignore it by not telling anyone that she has gone. He hopes she may come back someday, but ends up by searching for her at a fashion show. His lusting after every possession of hers in the house, every model photograph, every nightclub where she may have been, even the mannequin that looks like her, brings him to the point of almost being fired by his whimsical boss. This novel was the basis of the movie Bright Lights, My City, also written by Jay McInerney. In 1999 the novel was the basis of an off-Broadway musical by the New York Theatre Workshop, written by Paul Scott Goodman, directed by Michael Grief, with orchestrations and musical direction by Richard Barone.

The Warlock, whose true name is both unknown and incomprehensible, is a great magician of more than two hundred years of age. He notices that when he stays too long in the same place, his power diminishes and returns only when he goes away. This causes him to construct a machine (now called the Warlock's Wheel) consisting of a metallic disk enchanted to spin forever. This ends up using up all the mana in the area, and the result is a failure of magic in that place. This explains the Warlock's fears that mana is a finite resource and that the magicians were to some extent responsible for it, since it was their magic that nations used to enforce their will, both in the home and abroad. The widespread failure of magic in the Warlock's time led to a new search for a new source of magic (the moon), resulting in the events that are told in this book. It is revealed (in The Magic May Return) that mana was originally carried to Earth and the other bodies in the solar system by the solar wind, and was replenished slowly over time. However, sometime in the recent past (about a few thousand years ago) an ancient god created an invisible barrier between the Earth and the sun, which prevents the solar wind from carrying mana to the Earth and thus eventually causes a failure of magic.
