The matter was settled without a trial, and Evans’ name was added to the list of producers. At the Golden Globes, Mr. Evans, who was cited as one of the winners, slipped past a security guard and got his picture taken with Mr. DiCaprio, Mr. Scorsese, Mr. Mann and Mr. King. And it was on that occasion that the AMPAS put a limit on the number of producers who could share in an award. In the case of Shakespeare in Love, which won in 1999, the producers who took home awards were five. The producers’ branch of the AMPAS met on Wednesday to decide who was to be nominated for The Aviator and Million-Dollar Baby. The Academy will meet in Los Angeles on February 27 to present the Academy awards. It will be the first time that the Chinese actress Ziyi Zhang, star of Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, Hero and The House of Flying Daggers, will appear as a presenter.

An inexpensive horror film produced by the director of the "Evil Dead," Sam Raimi, has topped the North American box office. Boogeyman, the story of a man returning to the place of his childhood to confront his repressed memories, has taken $19,500,000 (including $195,000 in the first three days of its opening). Last week's number one, the Robert De Niro thriller Hide and Seek, fell to fourth place. New arrivals included the comedy The Wedding Date, starring Debra Messing of "Will & Grace" in second place, the comedy Are We There Yet? in third, and the film with three Oscar nominations, Million-Dollar Baby, in fifth. Other contenders for the Academy Award, including The Aviator and Sideways, continued to draw large audiences. The Aviator, which has taken $70,000,000 to date, and Sideways, with its more limited release, have taken $46,000,000 and $24,800,000. “I think that it's one of those films where people are influenced more by the trailer than by reviews,” Sony Pictures head of distribution Rory Bruer said. In general, the box office took a strong showing, despite the fact that the weekend was also the Super Bowl weekend, when cinema attendances usually fall. This year the top 12 films took $91,000,000, compared to the Super Bowl weekend in 2004 when the top 12 films took $73,400,000.

The veteran Spaniard Conchita Marn beat the Italian Roberta Vinci at the tennis tournament in Doha. Then he won the match 5-7, 6-0, 6-2 and thus entered the second round against the French Open champion Anastasia Myskina. The fifth-seeded Schnyder also had to fight hard, he also had to fight to the end with the Chinese Na Li. Slovakia's Daniela Hantuchová beat the Bulgarian Magdalena Maleeva 4-6, 6-4, 6-3 and entered the second round against the Russian Elena Bovin. The veteran Marna was initially in trouble with Vinci, and even after the Italian made a two-game break in the third and eleventh games, the game of Vinci began to crumble and Marna was victorious with strong forehands. In the other matches of the day, Japanese Ai Sugiyama defeated the Australian Samantha Stosur 6-2, 6-2. Nicole Pratt beat the Tunisian Selim Sfar 7-5, 6-2 and entered the second round against the compatriot Alicia Molik.

A musicologist in America has restored to light a hitherto unknown music by Johann Sebastian Bach. The work, entitled “Wedding Cantata,” was composed in 1728 for the marriage of the daughter of a German customs officer, and had been inexplicably lost for more than seventy years. Joshua Rifkin, a composer and a leading interpreter of Bach, has reconstructed the missing instrumental parts. He admitted that he had at first been reluctant to recreate the lost cantata. “Maybe a fragment should stay a fragment,” he said. “But then I thought of paleontologists who, from a single bone, are able to reconstruct a whole skeleton of a sauropod. The cantata is my sauropod.” The eight pages of music, sung in German, consist of seven arias for soprano and alto, lasting between twenty-five and twenty-seven minutes. The accompanying parts are entirely lost, except for two numbers, a duet and an aria, that were culled from other works of Bach. Rifkin likened the task to solving a musical Rubik’s Cube. “I could not reconstruct the music that Bach wrote, but I could show people what his music might have been like.” “It sounds like Bach,” he said. “But the listener can’t tell which part is Bach’s and which is mine.”

“Charlie Bell, the uncompromising former president of the hamburger firm of fast food, has died of cancer, at the age of forty-four. Last May, a month after his appointment, he had been notified of colorectal cancer and in November he resigned from his post in order to fight his illness. Starting as a 15-year-old part-time employee, Bell had quickly risen through the ranks, becoming the youngest store manager in Australia at the age of 19. A spirited and successful worker, he was credited with reviving the company's sales. He is survived by a wife and a daughter. “While we mourn his death, I ask you to keep Charlie's family in your thoughts and prayers,” Chief James Skinner said in a statement. “And remember that, despite his short time on earth, he was the man who always stayed in the center of his love for his family and for the firm. Bell, who had run the Australian franchise of the firm during the 1990s, was transferred to the United States in 1999 to run Asian, African and Middle Eastern affairs. He was appointed to run Europe in 2001, when he was named chief operating officer and president in 2002. After the sudden death of his predecessor, Jim Cantalupo, in April last year, Bell took over as chief executive, choosing to focus on improving the performance of existing restaurants rather than on rapid expansion. He had promised not to let the company "drown in the chaff" and, according to Reuters, once told analysts that he would squirt water down the throats of competitors if they were drowning. Bell had overseen the creation of the advertising campaign "I love it", and had been the brainchild of the introduction of the popular "McCafe", which is now the most successful coffee shop brand in Australia and New Zealand. Co-workers said that Bell was proud of his humble beginnings and that he liked to serve as a cashier or clean the tables when he visited restaurants.

After the Dutch champions, the legendary coach, the inventor of Total football, had a strong impact on the field. The 77-year-old Rinus Michels was called the "general" in the Netherlands and led the Netherlands to the final in 1974, where they lost 2-1 to Germany. The following year, however, he led the Netherlands to the European title in the final against the Soviet Union: 2-0. Michels played for Ajax and coached the club to four national titles between 1965 and 1971 and the European Cup in 1971. The Dutch team of the seventies, with Johan Cruyff and Johan Neeskens, was built on the total football of the Dutchmen, based on the cooperation of the team and the individual flair of each player. Cruyff was the driving force behind the flexible, attacking game of the players, who switched from defense to attack freely and were allowed to use the imagination. The severe coach also worked for Barcelona, where he won the Spanish title in 1974, for Cologne and for Bayer Leverkusen. Michels, named the best coach of the century by FIFA in 1999, played five times for the Dutch national team as a rough defender. Dutch Sports Minister Clemens van Dorp said: "Along with Cruyff, he made Dutch football big."

Two of the most senior officials in one of the biggest Chinese commercial banks are said to have disappeared, and it is alleged that they are responsible for a financial fraud worth up to $120 million. The bank is the Bank of China in Harbin, the South China Morning Post reported. The case has sparked a series of reactions from foreign investors, and will make them doubt whether China's big four banks can be listed in the United States. The government sees the listing of Chinese banks abroad as an important reform. Bank of China is one of the two big banks that can be listed abroad. The other is China Construction Bank. They both received a $45 billion bailout from the central government in 2003, in order to prepare for their listing abroad. However, a recent report in the China Economic Observer said the two banks might have changed their plans to list in New York, because of the costs of meeting the tighter regulations since the Enron scandal. The Bank of China is China's biggest foreign-exchange bank, and the China Construction Bank has the most domestic deposits. The two banks have reported about $200 billion in bad debts, but according to estimates from Chinese banking experts, the real figures are much higher. Efforts to tighten lending controls and to weed out frauds at the banks have revealed a series of scandals involving bank officials and cronies. The most notorious of these was the case of Wang Xuebing, former president of Bank of China in New York, who was sentenced to 12 years in prison in 2003. He had left Bank of China to become the head of the China Construction Bank when the case broke. And last month, the manager of a China Construction Bank branch was sentenced to life in prison for an embezzlement case. The banks used to act as cashiers for state-owned enterprises, and did not check on their creditworthiness. Even after the market reforms, the banks have tried to become more professional, but the connections between them and local governments remain strong. They continue to be able to offer huge loans to local governments and enterprises. Nevertheless, the banks' performance remains poor, and two problems remain: one is their policy of lending to the most profitable enterprises. The second is the policy of not allowing bankruptcies, because the enterprises employ so many people. Another problem is that some of the smaller banks have borrowed heavily from these inefficient state-owned companies, without carrying out the proper credit checks. This is what is behind the huge bad debts at some smaller banks. Another major financial company, China Life, was forced to suspend its Hong Kong listing plans in July, after its parent company reported accounting irregularities.

Two major American corporations have started advertising campaigns to "clear the record" about their products and their behavior. The world's largest retail chain Wal-Mart bought over 100 full-page ads in major newspapers to refute criticisms of its compensation, benefits and career policy. Eli Lilly and Company, a pharmaceutical manufacturer, will counter the rumors that have been going around for a while about the drug Prozac. Wal-Mart, which had initially published an open letter to the public in the Wall Street Journal, then bought in newspapers such as the Washington Post, the New York Times, The Washington Post and the Wall Street Journal, a statement saying: “There are a lot of urban legends going around these days about Wal-Mart, but the facts are the facts.” “Wal-Mart is good for consumers, good for communities and good for the US economy,” it said in a statement. In the advertisements and in a new Web site, the company announced that it would create more than 10,000 jobs in the US in 2005. The average salary at Wal-Mart is almost double the minimum wage of $ 5.15 an hour, and employees are offered health insurance, life insurance, shares and a retirement plan, the company said. Unions have long argued that Wal-Mart pays its employees less than its competitors and gives them fewer benefits. In California, the company is fighting a local opposition to the opening of new stores in cities where they are accused of driving out local competitors, and the state legislature is examining allegations that the company uses the health insurance for employees. “I think it will be difficult for them to overcome people's beliefs,” said Save Our Community leader Larry Bevington. Wal-Mart is also facing two lawsuits - one alleging discrimination against women and the other - discrimination against black employees. Meanwhile, Eli Lilly and Company is buying ads in 12 newspapers to explain the facts about its antidepressant drug Prozac. The move follows an article in the British Medical Journal, which said that some documents from the company were missing, which could link the drug to suicide and violence. In a statement, entitled "An open letter from the company's president Sidney Taurel," the company said that the article continues to "needlessly scare" the patients taking Prozac. "It's just wrong to suggest that the data on Prozac was missing or that important research data about the benefits and possible side effects of the drug were not available to doctors and government regulators," it added. The article is "false and misleading", Breier said, because the data in question was actually prepared by the Food and Drug Administration and presented at a meeting of the FDA in 1991. Subsequently, the FDA scientific advisors agreed that the data were flawed and that there was no increased risk of suicide.

By the increase in the stock of Skis Rossignol, the world's leading ski maker, stock speculation that the company might be bought by the American surf-cloth manufacturer Quiksilver. According to the Spanish financial press, the Boix-Vives family, which owns the ski maker, is considering a bid from Quiksilver. According to experts, other sporting goods companies may also want to have a closer look at the skimaker, which could lead to an auction which would drive up the value of the sale. The shares of Rossignol rose to 17.70 and fell back to 16.60, up 7.8%. Speculation that European sporting goods companies, whose foreign revenues have been hurt by the falling dollar, are increasingly attractive, according to experts. Firms like Quiksilver could reduce their distribution costs by selling Rossignol's skis in their own stores, experts say. The Boix-Vives family is said to have spent the past two years examining the possibility of selling Rossignol, which also makes golf equipment, snowboards and athletic clothing.

SANDRA HOWARD, Michael’s ex-retailing agent wife, is to play a prominent part in the Conservative election campaign. She will be campaigning on her own in key seats, and will accompany her husband on his helicopter whirls across the country. The day will begin with a press conference at the Conservatives’ headquarters in London, and Mr. Howard will have daily news conferences there, said Liam Fox, one of the co-chairmen of the Conservative Party. ‘We want Michael to be as accessible as possible,’ said Mr. Fox, adding that the Conservatives were not afraid of scrutiny. Tony Blair too has declared his intention to talk to as many people as possible during the campaign. But his aides deny that Mr. Blair intends to hold daily news conferences. Mr. Fox said this showed the Prime Minister was hiding from the scrutiny of London journalists. The Liberal Democrats are also to hold daily news conferences with Charles Kennedy. On Mrs. Howard’s role, Mr. Fox said: ‘She’s already been campaigning with Michael on a number of occasions, and on her own for short periods. ‘That’s how it’s going to be. It’s worked well so far.’ Mrs. Howard made her first speech at the Conservative Party’s autumn conference at Bournemouth last October, and spoke about a drug counselling charity, Addaction, which she supports. Mrs. Howard has also appeared with her husband on several chat shows. On This Morning, she said she often criticised her husband for not showing the real side of him.

UK aid to the Asian disaster victims will not divert resources from Africa, Prime Minister Tony Blair has promised. Speaking on the BBC's Breakfast with Frost program, he said that the money for the Asian disaster would not "clash" with the money the United Kingdom wanted to spend on Africa. When asked if he had not lost faith in God in the disaster, he said: I haven't lost my faith in anything. He added that he would give new figures to the House of Commons on Monday about British casualties in the disaster. Foreign Secretary Jack Straw said on Friday that about 440 Britons had been killed or were missing, and he said that the figures had not changed much since then, and that this must be a sign that the figures are starting to drop. But we can't be sure. It's a hugely difficult task to get accurate figures. Every country is struggling with it. The original £50 million set aside by the Department for International Development is now largely allocated. But until the World Bank has finished its evaluation, the precise amount of aid cannot be determined, he said. In the next few weeks, it will be clearer what the reconstruction costs will be. But Africa, where every month a "tsunami of preventable deaths" is reported in poverty, conflict and disease, will not be forgotten. As Britain prepares to take over the G8 presidency, the African agenda has taken on a greater significance, he said. Now for the first time, a plan has been devised that not only covers debt and development, but also the governance of African countries and conflict resolution. A lot of the problems in Africa are due to conflict, and these too are preventable if the right conditions are in place.

Intel claims it has invented a silicon-based laser, which should speed up communications. Intel scientists have solved a problem that has prevented silicon from being used to produce and amplify the light of a laser. This breakthrough should make it easier to link data-processing equipment to data-communication equipment. The Intel team claims that products based on the discovery could be available by the end of the decade. Dr Mario Paniccia, who directs the photonics technology lab, and colleagues Dr Haisheng Rong, Richard Jones, Ansheng Liu, Oded Cohen, Dani Hak and Alexander Fang have now published their work in the journal Nature. As it stands, says Dr Paniccia, equipment that amplifies the light that travels down a fibre-optic cable is expensive because it uses exotic materials such as gallium arsenide. Telecommunications companies and chip-makers would prefer to use silicon because it is cheap and there have been advances in the technology for making it on a large scale. But so far, despite work on making some components for directing light, silicon has not been able to produce and amplify the light pulses that carry data over long distances. However, silicon is a better amplification material for light pulses than the type used in fibre-optic cables. This is because of the crystalline structure of the silicon used in chips. It means that when a pulse of light travels through it, some of the photons collide with the atoms in the material, knocking them out of their orbits. This, explains Dr Paniccia, creates a cloud of free floating electrons, which absorbs the light. But the Intel team has now found a way to collect these errant free-floating electrons, making silicon a material that can both produce and amplify the light of a pulsed laser. The advantage is that the light can be tuned over a very wide range of frequencies, using relatively cheap optical filters. Until now, only a very narrow range of frequencies has been possible in silicon-based light sources. The result could be a more direct connection between the fibre-optic cables that carry data in the form of light pulses, and the silicon-based chip that processes the information. The team's work is one of several steps that need to be taken if silicon is to be used to carry and process data in the form of light pulses, Dr Paniccia says. "It's the first proof that it's possible," he says.

Once a large enough number of people have accepted digital TV, DVDs and digital VCRs, the next revolution in television is on its way to our living rooms. High-definition (Hd) is regarded in many circles in the media and technology industry as the greatest development in the history of the color tv. HD is, so to speak, four times better than tv quality. And yet, there is genuine concern that the public is not being properly informed about HD in shops and on the high street. Thousands of flat-screen tvs, both liquid-crystal displays, plasma screens and DLP projection tvs have already been sold as "hd", even though they are not able to play high-definition. Britain is the biggest display market in Europe, according to John Binks, managing director of the GfK group, which monitors the global markets. And yet he added that only 1.3% of flat-screen tvs sold in the UK are capable of receiving high-definition. There are currently 74 different products sold as "hd" but not with high-definition capacity, according to Alexander Oudendijk, senior vice president of the satellite company Astra. Although they are excellent quality, they do not all have the necessary adapter (the DVI or the HDMI plug, high-definition multimedia jack, with which the receivers can receive the high-resolution digital signals). The problem partly comes from the lack of training and understanding of the staff in shops, according to experts who have gathered at the second European High-Definition (Hd) summit at BAFTA in London this week. "We must prevent the public from being confused. We have to learn a lot about the product," said Mr. Binks. Industry representatives said they were faced with a challenge to communicate the right information to the audience. Eventually, this audience will be everyone. The BBC is currently developing plans to make all its programs in hd by 2010. He is already making preparations to turn off the analogue signal in some places, and is filming with hd cameras. Sky is planning to sell its first generation receivers for Christmas, and these receivers will be personal-recording receivers like the Sky+ receivers. But for high-definition to really work, the receiver must be connected to a tv that is capable of displaying the much higher resolution images of hd. By 2010 it is estimated that one in five British households will have a tv or other screen that can display hd. But for the moment, it all seems very confusing for the audience, which has only recently begun to deal with "digital". So all the major actors in the industry, including the producers of the flat screens, the satellite operators and the producers, formed a High-Definition Forum in 2004 to be sure that everyone communicates with each other. A significant part of the forum is concerned with the development of industry standards and content protection. The producers are also working on ways to make it easier for the audience to know what they are buying. From next month, all devices that have the right connections and resolution will have a "hd-ready" label. This also means that they can handle both analog and digital signals, and so comply with the minimum requirements of the industry. The label is seen as a very good thing by the industry, but it is only the beginning. "There is still no sign of it on many products on the shelves," said David Mercer, an industry consultant. Mr. Oudendijk says it is impossible to get more than this out of the manufacturers at the moment. "There will probably be some disappointed customers in the next few months," he said. The European Broadcasting Union is now testing hd formats, so that it can be prepared for even better formats later. As it also sees it as its task to ensure that the audience is informed about the formats and which devices support them. "We think that consumers buying expensive screens need to know that it's worth their money," said Phil Laven, the EBU's head of technology. The tv producers would like the audience to have at least a 42-inch tv, so they get "real high-definition" from it, but also say that smaller screens will do. The sharp decline in the prices of hd-ready screens may also make it possible to buy. Prices fall by about 20 percent each year, say the industry experts. Last year the prices of lcd screens fell by 43 percent in Europe, according to Mr. Oudendijk.

For a thousand pounds, it was said, the American wolfhound, which is able to make more than a hundred-fold jump. Michelle Paver’s Wolf Brother is the first of a series of six novels. Fox bought the film rights for $ 400,000, and they’ve been passed to Ridley Scott’s production company, Scott Free. The director said he was thrilled with the project. Wolf Brother is an enchanting book, he said. Michelle Paver, a former lawyer who lives in London and is currently studying biochemistry at Oxford, began writing the book in the eighties. As an established author of romantic novels, she turned her work-in-progress into a children’s book. It was published in 2004, and Paver earned $ 5 million, the highest advance ever paid for a first novel for children. Wolf Brother tells the story of a twelve-year-old hunter who lives in the woods. After his father is killed, he becomes a friend with a young wolf and begins a great and terrible mission to rid the wood of an evil power. Paver is now writing the second part of the series. “Michelle Paver lives and breathes the world she writes about,” said the author’s spokesman. “I’ve told her about the film deal, but at the moment she’s writing the second book and her head is six hundred years in the future, deep in the primordial forest.”

The BBC has chosen the 2,000m Olympic victory by Kelly Holmes as the best TV moment of the year. The eight hundred-metre gold medal took precedence over favourites from drama, comedy and documentary programmes. Natasha Kaplinsky's victory in Strictly Come Dancing was the entertainment favourite, while a breast-feeding scene from Little Britain took the comedy prize. The best of the year's entertainment, drama and comedy moments will be aired on BBC One at 2000 on Wednesday. The double Olympic champion, Kelly Holmes, won the best sporting moment of the year, beating Maria Sharapova's win at Wimbledon and Matthew Pinsent's Olympic victory in the rowing. The sight of the royal correspondent, Jennie Bond, with dozens of rats crawling over her on I'm a Celebrity, won the prize for entertainment factual moment. BBC current affairs programme This World was favourite in the documentary category for a report by Michael Buerk on his return to Ethiopia after covering the famine there twenty years ago. The best moment in the soap, Eastenders, was the scene where Dot Watts told Den Watts that she was ill.

Young readers have voted Fergus Crane, a tale of a boy taken on an adventure by a flying horse, the winner of two Smarties Book Prizes. Fergus Crane by Paul Stewart and Chris Riddell was the best book in the six-to-eight-year-old age group and also came first in the prize voted for by after-school book clubs. Biscuit Bear by Mini Grey was voted best for children under five. The children voted for the winners from a shortlist of seven books chosen by a panel of adults. The award, which is in its 20th year, is billed as the UK's biggest children's book prize. Fergus Crane has text by Paul Stewart and illustrations by Chris Riddell, who also worked together on The Edge Chronicles. Julia Eccleshare, chair of the adult judging panel, said children's books had never been in such a strong position. The prize was "respected because the final decision is made by the most demanding of all judges - the children themselves. This year the young judges chose from an exceptionally strong and diverse shortlist that reflects the very best of children's books at the moment." Previous winners have included J K Rowling, Jacqueline Wilson and Dick King-Smith.

Sales of cards by Damien Hirst and Tracey Emin sold out in hours on the first day of the Royal Academy of Arts Secrets sale, in which the identity of the artist is kept secret until the work has been sold and the signature is found on the back. “There are some big names left like Mario Testino,” said Sue Bradburn, Royal College of Art. All postcards are sold for £35 and the sale closes at 6 p.m. on Saturday. Bradburn said there had been a long line at the start, but it had now diminished. She said the buyers who had bought famous cards had been among the first and had sifted through each card carefully. “They probably knew what they were looking for. The exhibition has been on display since 19 November. Ken Loach, fashion designer Hussein Chalayan and Blur guitarist Graham Coxon are among the artists who have made cards for the sale. Some of the participating artists are students or recent graduates from the Royal College of Art and other top art schools. The money raised from the sale will be used for the Royal College of Art’s Fine Art Fund, which gives grants and scholarships to students. The famous Secrets sale has been held for ten years.

The avalanche of losses that the Asian floods and the resulting landslide has caused to Asian governments and to international agencies has shaken their hearts. James Wolfensohn, the president of the World Bank, says his organization is “only beginning to understand the magnitude of the disaster and its economic consequences.” At least 25,000 people have been killed in this catastrophe. Millions of people have been left homeless, millions of businesses and other industries have been destroyed. Economists believe that several of the ten countries that were affected by the giant wave will see their economies slow down. In Sri Lanka, the figure may be as high as one percent of annual growth. The figure for Thailand is much lower, at 0.1 percent. The governments of these countries, to stimulate the economy, will probably reduce taxes and increase government spending. “In view of the enormous human displacement, the government may be forced to ease fiscal policy considerably,” the chief economist of the Societe Generale told AFP. The economic consequences of this disaster will certainly be enormous, but not enough to make the Asian region deviate from its growth momentum in 2005, he says. “The main thing is that this is a human disaster.” India's economy, however, is likely to slow down less, because the affected areas are still some of the least developed. The Indian giant, which has grown quite strongly in the past year, will be under pressure to ensure clean drinking water and to arrange for hygiene to prevent the spread of diseases. Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, who in a statement put the figure of damage at $ 500 million, which is most likely to increase. The fishing and real estate industries will also be affected by the impact of Sunday's magnitude 9 earthquake, which sent a giant wave from Malaysia to Africa. Malaysia said that more than 1,000 fishermen were swept away and that damage to the industry was “significant”. The speed of reconstruction will be the key to containing the disaster. In three months we should be able to repair 70 percent of the damage in the three worst-affected provinces, said Juthamas Siriwan, the director-general of the tourist office. - but that does not mean that Sri Lanka's tourist industry will be quick to recover. World Travel and Tourism Council, which represents 40,000 tourist companies, says that the industry creates employment for 19 million people in the South-East Asian region.

MTV has been attacked by American indecency campaigners for its "endless sleaze": the Parents Television Council, which monitors violence and sexuality on American television, says MTV is "a cesspool of immorality." This organization is in the forefront of a frantic campaign to clean up American television. The PTC is convinced that MTV, which is mainly aimed at young people, is a threat to their families. The PTC spent 171 hours over a period of seven days watching MTV, which featured its Spring Break programmes. The PTC recorded three thousand five hundred and fifty-six instances of sexual activity or nakedness and two thousand eight hundred and eighty-one references to sexual activity. President of the PTC, Brent Bozell, a prominent conservative activist, said that MTV is "simply selling sexually explicit material to children." "Compared with normal, broadcasting-industry-classified sex, slang, and violence, MTV contains more of all of them, and its programmes are aimed at children as young as twelve. There is no doubt that television affects the attitudes and perceptions of young people, and MTV is consciously aiming its sleaze at millions of innocent children." It was the breast-baring incident of pop star Janet Jackson at the Super Bowl last year that led to the PTC's investigation, which was prompted by the breast-baring incident on CBS, the parent company of MTV. MTV spokeswoman Jeannie Kedas said that the company uses the same standards as broadcasters and reflects the culture and the interests of its audience. "We find it unfair and wrong to label MTV as irresponsible," she said. "And we think it underestimates the intelligence and sophistication of young people." She added that MTV won an award in 2004 for its programme Fight for Your Rights, which dealt with issues such as sexual health and tolerance.

Chepkemei is sure that she is fit to compete in the next edition of the Great Edinburgh International Cross Country. Previously, it was doubtful if she would be able to recover from the marathon battle with Paula Radcliffe in New York, but she has now confirmed that she is ready for the upcoming race, where she is competing with world cross-country champion Benita Johnson. “Susan will add to the strength of the whole field,” said the race director, Matthew Turnbull. Three years ago, when the Great Edinburgh Cross Country was held in Newcastle, Chepkemei won the race, which was run over a six-kilometre course. The next year, Tirunesh Dibaba, winner of the previous race on Tyneside, will be defending her title. On January 15, in Edinburgh, the European cross-country champion, Britain's Hayley Yelling, will also be there, as will the in-form Scottish athlete, Kathy But-ler.

Jackie Stallone, mother of the famous actor Sylvester, has become the first star to be evicted from the Big Brother. She and John McCririck had to go through the voting on Friday, and of those who voted, 67% preferred to keep the pundit. Afterwards, Stallone, who was 71 years old, said: "I'm totally depressed, I need a holiday. It was a hell. I've lost about five pounds in the last two weeks." But she was pleased to have reconciled with the actress Brigitte Nielsen, her former daughter-in-law. She also appeared on a live broadcast from the fourth-night tv program on Monday in order to surprise Nielsen. She was the hottest favourite to be evicted first, with odds of 7/4 to go out first, but McCririck had earned himself enemies with his uninhibited views about women. The spokesman for Ladbrokes, Warren Lush, said: "It may be that we underestimated the strength of the anti-McCririck brigade, but it's so difficult to call, there are people who either love him or hate him, there is no middle ground." The former Happy Mondays dancer Bez is favourite with odds of 7/4 to win the competition, with the singer Kenzie from the Blazin' Squad in second place at 7/2. "Bez has won over the public, and is the man to beat. He's always in control and never takes things too seriously," said Lush. But on Friday morning, 15 activists from the Fathers 4 Justice campaign group were arrested when they threw fireworks at the Big Brother house at about three o'clock in the morning. After feminist activist Germaine Greer walked out of the show on Wednesday because of the producers' "bullying tactics", the program has been attracting an average audience of four million per night.

The United Kingdom has 529 quangos, supported by billions of pounds of public money, many of which are ineffective and duplicate each other's work, says a report. Author of The Essential Guide to British Quangos, Dan Lewis, said at least 111 of the appointed institutions had been created since the Labour government took office in 1997, and that a limit should be set on the number of such bodies that can be set up by each department. The Conservatives and Liberal Democrats welcomed the report, saying that it underpinned their policy of abolishing unwanted and unnecessary quangos and downsizing the rest. A Conservative government, he said, would abolish 162 quangos in a drive for more efficient and accountable government. Meanwhile, Liberal Democrat spokesman Ed Davey said that instead of the bonfire of quangos promised by the New Labour government, there had been an explosion. He said that under both Conservative and Labour governments, unaccountable institutions had mushroomed. The Liberal Democrats, he said, would abolish many of them, merge others and make sure that those that remained were properly accountable. Labour was not available for comment. The new report follows the government-commissioned Gershon report, which last year called for the public sector to be stripped of many of its unaccountable bodies. Mr Lewis said he wanted a public inquiry into the regional development agencies, which receive £1.8bn a year, saying the money was "apparently wasted on ineffective and duplicated work". Also, he said, a statutory limit of five years should be set on the life of any body with executive powers. He also listed what he called the "nine most useless quangos" - the British Potato Council, the Milk Development Council, the Energy Saving Trust, the Agricultural Wages Board, the Wines Board, the Westminster Foundation for Democracy, the Football Licensing Authority, Investors in People and the Economic and Social Research Council. The existence of the British Potato Council, which employs 60 people and was set up in 1997, he said, was "strange". And he said the £80m spent annually on the Energy Saving Trust, which promotes the use of renewable energy, could be better spent on installing boiler jackets in eight million homes. The Economist reported that the trust employs only 10 people. He said: "If a football club can afford to pay £27m for a footballer, why should the taxpayer, many of whom do not even follow the sport, be forced to subsidise the Football Licensing Authority to the tune of over £1m a year?" The report is published by the Efficiency in Government Unit, a joint venture between the Centre for Policy Studies and the Economic and Social Research Council. Before setting up a new public body, it says, ministers should consider whether a similar function could be carried out by an existing charity or other private organisation.

Former Northern Ireland minister Sir Nicholas Scott has died in a London hospice, his family has announced. He was 71 years old and had been Conservative Member of Parliament for the London borough of Kensington and Chelsea. Sir Nicholas had been a minister in the Department of Northern Ireland under Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher in the period from 1981 to 1987. As Northern Ireland minister, he had been responsible for education and later for security, where he managed to survive the mass escape of the IRA from the Maze prison in the year of 1983. As a result of his work on education, he had come in for some criticism, especially over the issue of school closures. He also presided over the merger of the New University of Ulster and the Ulster Polytechnic, which created the University of Ulster. He was a strong supporter of the Anglo-Irish Agreement and was regarded with respect in both government circles in Dublin and in the SDLP. He was, however, viewed with suspicion by some unionists, who gave him the title of 'Minister for Discord'. After leaving the Department of Northern Ireland in a ministerial reshuffle, he became a minister for disabilities in the UK government. Sir Nicholas's successor as MP for the London borough of Kensington and Chelsea was the outspoken Alan Clark, who had been deselected from the party by his own constituency in December 1996. His deselection was preceded by a series of scandals, including the fact that, during a Conservative Party meeting in Bournemouth, the police found him unconscious in the street and brought him back to his hotel. Sir Nicholas explained that he had taken a combination of strong painkillers and a small amount of alcohol and that it was bad for his health. After his deselection, he bitterly complained that, despite support from some Cabinet ministers and Conservative MPs, the local party was 'determined to get rid of me'. Sir Nicholas's colourful career also included an argument with his daughter Victoria, on the question of disability rights. He admitted misleading Parliament when he denied that his department had deliberately wrecked the UK Disabilities Bill in the year of 1994. Activists on behalf of the disabled roundly criticized his attitude and, worse still, joined the call for his resignation. He left his ministerial post two months later and was a member of the opposition benches.

Russian oil company Yukos has been sentenced to stand before a court in the United States on Thursday, in its continuing fight for survival. The company has been broken up by the Russian government, which is demanding payment of the debt of $27 billion (about £15 billion). The company has filed for bankruptcy in the United States in the hope that it will be able to use international bankruptcy law to prevent the forced sale of its principal oil-production division, Yuganskneftegas. The division was, however, sold for $ 9 billion to state-owned oil company Rosneft, but only after the state auctioneer failed to put the tender to a vote. Yukos’s lawyers say the sale was illegal under US bankruptcy law. The company and its main shareholders have vowed to attack any company that buys its assets by every legal means. The company is demanding $ 20 billion in damages on the grounds that Yuganskneftegas was sold for less than its market value. At the hearing on Thursday, Judge Letitia Clark is to hear a number of motions, including one from the German bank Deutsche Bank, which was one of six banks that was prohibited from providing financing to Gazprom, the Russian state-owned oil company, which had been expected to win the auction for Yuganskneftegas. Meanwhile, the bank, which is also acting as an adviser to Gazprom, has asked the court to review the decision of the bankruptcy court. This would remove the uncertainty that surrounds the bankruptcy case and clear up the bank’s position, according to the bank’s shareholders. The bank’s shareholders are sceptical about Yukos’s prospects in court. It has been repeatedly pointed out that the Russian government, and in particular the head of the Russian judiciary, Vladimir Putin, have rejected the notion that the United States has any jurisdiction over Yukos or its legal disputes. In addition, the company has very little property in the United States. Yukos, however, has been able to score a number of small victories, and is bullish about its prospects in court. “Do we have any influence over what is happening? Yes, we do,” says Yukos spokesman Mike Lake. “The legal risks are very real,” says the Moscow-based Credit Suisse First Boston analyst Vadim Mitroshin. The head of Yukos, Mikhail Khodorkovsky, is in jail. He is being investigated on charges of fraud and tax evasion.

The rainy season, the increase in material costs, and the sluggish economy of the European Union have combined to limit the growth of Swiss food and beverage group Nestlé. Sales fell by 1.4% to 87 billion francs (about 77 billion dollars or 49 billion pounds) in 2004, and ice cream and mineral water were hit. However, the company was helped by its American and Chinese branches. It has decided to increase its dividend by 11% after paying off part of its debt. Nestlé blamed the high franc against the dollar, the sale of some branches, and difficult trading conditions in Europe. As for ice cream, which in 2003 was very much in fashion, the poor weather in the summer “profoundly” hampered demand. Also, the sale of mineral water suffered, but chocolate, coffee, frozen products and pet food fared better. The company nevertheless reported “excellent” results in North America, where it had outperformed the market. It also achieved “excellent” results in Asia and Africa despite the effects of high oil prices and political unrest. But its operating profit was still down slightly on the previous year, despite the fact that it had been able to increase its profit margins. As well as increasing its dividend, the company is also buying back shares worth a billion francs (about eight hundred million dollars or 475 million pounds). It is forecasting organic growth of around 5% in 2005, but is warning of continuing competition. There is still uncertainty about the future of Perrier, the famous French mineral water which Nestlé owns. The French branch has long been in dispute with the unions over the level of productivity, and this has led Nestlé to consider selling it.

A group of MPs, anxious to bring Tony Blair under pressure over reform of the Lords, have produced a detailed report which lays down a detailed plan for change. The draft bill suggests a smaller second chamber in which two-thirds of the members are elected. Parliament and the Lords have failed to agree on any reforms since 1999, when 600 hereditary peers were deprived of their seats. The group claims it can win support for the removal of the remaining 92 hereditary peers. The government has put off any further attempt to remove them because it feels it would be unsuccessful after the recent defeat in the Lords. There have been suggestions that the Labour manifesto will contain proposals for reforming the powers of the second chamber. But the all-party group, which includes Conservatives Ken Clarke and Sir George Young, and Labour’s Robin Cook and Tony Wright, and Liberal Democrat Paul Tyler, is confident its plan will win support from a large majority of the House. And they list as supporters of the proposals former Conservative leader William Hague and former Labour leader Neil Kinnock. The group argues that a majority of the public and a majority of MPs support the idea of an elected second chamber. Its plan suggests the Lords be renamed the Second Chamber of Parliament and its members the Second Chamber of Parliament. The membership of the chamber would consist of 385 members, of whom 270 would be elected and 87 would be appointed by the prime minister. Their term of office would be between 12 and 14 years. Mr Cook said that elections for the chamber could be held on the same day as elections for MPs. He said: “Over the last year, we have heard a number of senior politicians saying that we must have more democracy. “And what could be more democratic than choosing the people who sit in the second chamber of our parliament?” The group believes the pressure is mounting for change and the government’s current position is untenable. It wants all three parties to commit themselves to an elected second chamber in their election manifestos. Mr Clarke said the reform of the Lords was “a matter of fundamental concern for the whole health of our political system”. And Mr Tyler said the prime minister’s view that there was no general agreement on the future of the Lords was not tenable. The group’s proposals, he said, were a “show of force” by those pushing for change. The Elect the Lords Campaign said the plans were an important contribution to the debate. “We consider the draft Bill sufficiently detailed to allow proper parliamentary scrutiny,” said spokesman Peter Facey. “In the absence of any other clear proposals, the government should now allow this to take place.”

Bill Conti’s job as music director of the Oscars is not for the faint-hearted. It is the most plate-spinning job there is, and this year is the 17th time that Conti has directed the orchestra. “The most thrilling part for a musician is the live performance,” he says. “All your peers, everyone in the film industry is in the auditorium. All the important people. It is of course a televised event, but we always think of it as something more.” The orchestra strikes up over 110 times during the course of an average Oscars evening. As well as playing for the arrivals and departures of presenters and winners, they have to play for the breaks and entertain the live audience. “It is a very busy night, and there is a certain amount of preparation required, music preparation, orchestrating, planning and rehearsing before the event.” But much of this preparation is for pieces that will never be used. “We don’t know who will win. And many of the things we prepare will never be used.” “When they say ‘and the winner is’, we have five different pieces prepared, and they say the name, and we play the right one straight away.” The orchestra also gets called on to play when the winners, who have been instructed to be brief, go on for too long with their acceptance speeches. The decision to drown out the star with music, and kill them off with music, comes to the orchestra through Conti’s earpiece from the director’s box. “I don’t like it, but it’s not my decision,” he says. “As soon as the director says ‘music’, the orchestra plays and we get a long shot of the auditorium.” “Usually you don’t see the star whose mic has just been cut, but they’re usually just 10 feet from me, and they look at me as if I’m the one who did them in.” On some occasions, stars have taken it upon themselves to give the music director a heads-up before they begin to speak. “When Julia Roberts won for best actress, she told me to stand down, because she had so much to say,” he says. The composer won the Oscar for best original score in 1983 for his work on The Right Stuff. He also received nominations in the category of original song in 1976 for his song ‘Gonna Fly Now’ from the film Rocky, and in 1981 for the title track of the Bond film For Your Eyes Only. “People who have spent their lives in front of the camera or performing, get a bit star-struck, as it were,” he says. “But it’s a wonderful thing to win, and they’re just on top of the world, and they’ve just won the biggest award they can ever win, and they’re not in control, or they want to thank everyone they’ve ever met.” It’s hard for Conti to see these stars as ‘outsiders’, because it’s he who keeps them in line, and keeps the ceremony moving. But behind the scenes, he has to deal with a dazzling array of technology. “There’s a big script and a lot of monitors, and then there are the sound desks, which have to be kept going at all times. “I have an earpiece in one ear and another in the other, and I can hear different things in each of them at different times. I also have to communicate with the director.” “I have a foot pedal to control the sound,” he explains. During his first year as music director in 1977, the orchestra informed him that they could smell smoke. “I started shouting and abusing the director,” Conti recalls. “I said, ‘We’re not going to die for this show. Either you do something, or I’m going to come up with 60 musicians and we’ll leave.’ ‘No, Bill, don’t do anything,’ they said. So, imagine, these wonderful musicians, in their evening clothes, and they’re playing, and then firemen come in with their helmets and axes, and they crawl among us and try to find out what the smell is. And it was just a smell of the new paint burning on the music stands.” No one was hurt, but Conti still finds the story funny. After the ceremony, he and his family attend the Governors Ball, “where I have a drink and look back at the show.” “I’m not one for going too wild. I go home and I unwind. It takes me about a day.”

British economic future will be at the center of the election campaign, said Chancellor Gordon Brown, who spoke after a last cabinet meeting at number 10 before the expected election announcement. He said the voters would realize that the stable economy and the good development had been established under the Prime Minister and would continue under his watch. Meanwhile, the Conservatives have presented their plans for fighting the culture of "snap" and the Liberal Democrats have explained their plans to replace the local tax. Earlier, the Archbishop of Canterbury had written to all three parties, asking them not to take advantage of voters' fears in the election campaign. He said they should rather focus on the environment, development, arms trade, family policy and criminal justice. The shadow foreign minister, Michael Ancram, said the Conservatives had run a very positive campaign. "I think he should carefully consider what Jack Straw said about Michael Howard," he said. Straw said of the Conservative leader: "He is intelligent, articulate and tactical, but he is not wise. He lacks strategy and judgment, and his hasty character too often gets the better of him. " The Foreign Secretary later said on the BBC: "It is no surprise that Michael Howard reacted so strongly to Jack Straw's criticism of his opponent. " The Liberal Democrat chairman, Matthew Taylor, said the voters were already tired of the negative campaigns and the environment, especially, would be in the foreground. The new focus on the economy for the government came the same day as a new report from the Institute for Fiscal Studies was presented in which it said that incomes had fallen for the first time in more than a decade. This was partly due to what it called the Chancellor's tax-raising budget in 2002. The Treasury dismissed the report as "complete nonsense". The chief election strategist for the Labor Party, Alan Milburn, said that the apparent fall in the average income was due to the self-employed having suffered from the world's falling fortunes. Since 1997, the average take-home pay had risen by twenty percent in real terms, excluding the self-employed, he said on BBC Radio 4's "Today" program. The Chancellor also rejected the figures and said that the "average family" was much better off under Labor.

A preliminary report from the German company, which suffered heavy losses in the previous year, shows a profit of 400 million francs. The operating result was 380 million, ten times higher than in the previous year. The German company had been damaged in the year 2003 by the onset of the Iraqi war and the scare caused by the SARS epidemic, and was further hampered by its catering company in the United States. The company also suffered from the bankruptcy of a number of European and American air companies. The board of the company recommends a dividend of 30 francs per share for the year 2004. The shareholders received no dividend in 2003. The company will report on its full financial year on March 23rd.

Profits in the EMI Music company fell over 16 percent, after a warning on profit after disappointing sales and the delay of two new albums. The company warned that sales of music will fall by 8 or 9 percent during the current year, while profits are expected to fall by about 15 percent. They blamed the poor sales since Christmas and the delays in the release of new albums by Coldplay and Gorillaz. At noon on Monday, EMI shares had fallen 16.2 percent to 236.25 pence. "It's a lower than expected January, especially re-orders," the company said. Its sales, "in constant currency," are expected to be 8 or 9 percent lower than in the previous year. Profits are expected to be about 138 million pounds. Alain Levy, the head of EMI Music, said it was disappointing, but added that he was optimistic about the development of the industry. "The physical music market is showing signs of stabilization in many parts of the world, while digital music, in all its forms, is continuing to develop quickly," he said. Mr. Levy commented on the delay of the albums by Coldplay and Gorillaz, saying that "the creation and marketing of music is not a precise process and cannot always be coincident with the reporting periods." "While the rescheduling of the albums and the current softness are disappointing, it does not change my view that the world's recording industry is improving," he said. Paul Richards, an analyst at Numis Securities, said the market was focused on the decline in music sales rather than the rescheduling of the albums. "It's very unusual to see this much of a downward adjustment just because of the rescheduling of the albums," he said.

Fishing could be prosecuted under the plan to restrict cruelty to animals, a parliamentary committee has warned. Vague wording in the draft Animals Bill could leave fishermen and fishermen open to prosecution, although this was not the intention, the environment select committee said. The members said they were 'concerned' that the government had not consulted them on its plans for animal welfare. The plan aimed to improve and modernise animal welfare legislation, and intends to protect kept animals and companion animals by creating a duty of care. The committee said the draft bill should be a 'cast-iron guarantee' that any regulation of animal industries, such as pet fairs and game bird rearing, would be consulted. In addition to preserving the current offences of cruel treatment of animals, the bill also creates a new offence of 'animal neglect' by owners who fail to protect animals in their care. The bill also provides for animal welfare officers to intervene to prevent harm to an animal, and to outlaw the'mutilation' of animals, unless it is proved to be in the best interests of the animal. The environment committee made 101 recommendations after hearing from 51 individuals and organisations. One was to amend the bill to ensure that fishing was not encouraged, even if the cases failed. The committee agreed that commercial fishing and sport fishing should not be covered by the draft bill and support the government's intention to exempt fishing as an activity. However, the committee said that fishing should not be allowed to suffer if it failed. The committee also said that some of the rights of animals were lessened by the bill, for example, the abandonment of animals, which would be'substantially reduced'. The committee recommended that the government consider redrafting the provisions for prosecuting cruelty offences. As it stands, the draft bill would not make it possible to prosecute certain acts of cruelty that should be prosecuted, such as causing unnecessary suffering to an animal through neglect or causing unnecessary mental suffering. Chair of the committee Michael Jack said: "Any change in the law affecting animals always arouses strong emotions and public interest. The bill is no exception." "My committee welcomes the fact that a different approach to animal welfare is now emerging, which does not just wait for a problem to arise, but which enables action to be taken to protect animals before irreversible suffering occurs. " But he said the bill "had a very 'in-progress' feel to it and urged the government to ensure that it was 'ironclad' in law that the obligation to consult was part of any new legislation that affected pet fairs, circuses or game bird farms. " "The government must do its best to improve the first draft before the bill is presented to parliament.

Liberal Democrats have announced plans to build 100,000 new ‘affordable’ houses on publicly owned land. This would enable people to buy a part of a house, using a co-ownership scheme, thus enabling them to enter the property market. And they would also encourage the conversion of existing buildings, thus protecting the countryside. This is the latest campaigning issue, because the IPSOS survey found that 9 out of 10 people had no hope of buying a house in the UK. The Tories want to extend the right to buy and Labour has already announced that it would help first-time buyers. The Liberal Democrats want to enable people to buy a part of a house, usually worth five per cent of the building cost. The idea is that they will buy the building but not the land, which is already owned by the state or by local councils. The cost of the house would be around 30 per cent of their monthly salary. When they moved, they could sell their share and benefit from any increase in property prices. Mr Kennedy said that ‘co-ownership’ would give people the opportunity to gradually build up an interest in a home, paying only as much as they can afford. The local golden share scheme, tried by the Liberal Democrats in South Shropshire, would be extended to other areas. The idea is that local councils would be able to negotiate with property companies to own a share of about one per cent in any new property development. They would then be able to sell the houses at the cost of building them to local people who the council has decided need local houses. The Liberal Democrats say their help for first-time buyers would cost nothing extra. But they want to change the tax on renovating old buildings, which they say is too expensive. The Conservatives say that the proposal means a new tax of up to £11,000 on every new house. “This is typical Liberal hypocrisy. They pretend they want to help first-time buyers, but the small print in their policies shows they are going to put even more people out of the market.” And Mr Kennedy’s opponents say that he is ‘just being Liberal.’ He said that the Conservatives’ main proposal was to extend the right to buy to a million more people. Labour had already announced that it would allow 300,000 more people to buy a part of their council house or a housing association home. But, he said, the Liberal Democrats had not given any figures. He asked whether the Liberal Democrats would match the Labour Party’s £42 billion programme for building and renovating council houses by 2010.

As the study of the research company Preventon has shown, older people and women are increasingly taking charge of protecting the family's home computer against malicious attacks on the Internet. The number of women who bought protection programs for their PCs from viruses, trojans and worms increased by 11.2 per cent from 2002 to 2004. There is a certain probability that 40% of the purchasers of home-based protection programs are retirees. However, more retirees (53 per cent) are buying the protection programs than retirees (39 per cent). The study shows a change in the character and the demography of the users of the Internet and the increased awareness of the dangers that the high-speed and unlimited connection to the Internet poses to the surfer. The study predicts that by 2005, 40 percent of the buyers of home-based protection programs will be women, and by 2007, if the trend continues, women may even become the main purchasers. "I think that older people are more diligent about protecting their PCs, because they are more careful and would like to have insurance if something goes wrong," said a woman over 60 who took part in the study. In the past 10 years, it has been mostly young men, a cliché of Internet users, who have been the main users, said Paul Goosens, director of Preventon, as reported by the BBC. But the Internet service provider must take on more responsibility for informing users of the dangers of the Internet before they go on-line, especially when they are new to high-speed connections. The security programs should also be easy to use, have a simple interface and instructions written in non-technical language, said Mr. Goosens. The nature of the threat is also changing and is no longer limited to e-mail viruses alone. The alleged problems with rogue dialers, spy- and other similar programs that are secretly installed on the PC, have also increased the awareness of the need to use not only an anti-virus program but also a combination of anti-virus, a fire wall and spy-removing programs. If you don't have any protection, you can get these programs by simply surfing the Internet. 30,000 people per day are enlisted by so-called “security” programs that spread both spam and malicious code, a Symantec study showed last year. Viruses that have been designed to infect millions of people, a new form of prank by programmers, are becoming less common, according to Internet security experts. It is more common to see malicious programs designed to make direct money for gangs of criminals, often based in Eastern Europe, rather than those that have been created to show off the hacker's skills or to cause a nuisance. This study shows that more people are taking this criminal threat to the Internet more seriously, because, said Mr. Goosens, the press is now much more aware of the danger. "The elderly are being sensitized by the press, and they are asking the right questions," he said. The worst are young people who think that because they use a known Internet provider, they are safe from these attacks. An unprotected Internet connection can be infected in minutes. By the end of this year, it is estimated that about 30 percent of households in the UK will have a high-speed connection. The connection to the Internet over a high-speed connection exceeded the traditional analogue modem in July last year, according to figures from the National Statistics Institute.

High-speed Internet connections in Britain are more popular than ever. BT reports that more people subscribed to its broad-band service during the last quarter than at any other time. The 600,000 connections brought the total number of people who have signed up for broadband service with BT to 3.1 million. Nationally, more than 5 million people are browsing the Web at high speed. Britain now ranks among the highest users of high-speed Internet connections in Europe. The increase is reflected in figures compiled by the government’s media regulator, Ofcom, which show that Britain has now overtaken Germany in the number of people using high-speed Internet connections. The 5 million figure in Britain equates to a rate of 7.5 connections per hundred inhabitants, compared with 6.7 in Germany and 15.8 in the Netherlands. BT’s figures include customers who get their service directly from BT as well as from the many companies that resell BT’s service under their own name. In part, the upsurge in the numbers is due to BT’s expanding the range of ADSL connections, the most widely used form of broadband in Britain, beyond a distance of three miles. The standard speed for ADSL connections is 512 Kbps, though higher speeds are available. “This breakthrough caused an explosion in orders, as we suddenly found ourselves able to satisfy the pent-up demand that existed in many areas,” said Paul Reynolds, the head of BT’s wholesale division, which supplies phone lines for other companies to resell. The retail division, which sells its service under its own name, also had a good quarter, bringing in about a third of the new subscribers, a slight increase over the previous three months. Despite the good news on the growth of high-speed connections, figures from Ofcom indicate that BT faces increasing competition and decreasing influence in other areas. However, BT’s share of the market is shrinking as well. In the past year, rival companies such as NTL and Cable and Wireless have announced that they are investing millions of pounds in equipment to allow them to operate the phone lines into customers’ homes. At the end of September, more than 4.2 million lines were using services such as One.Tel and Talk Talk that use non-BT networks to deliver the phone service to customers from the local phone exchange. At the end of the same period, more than 300 companies were offering CPS services, and BT’s share of the market had fallen to 55.4%.

The international world of bloggers is to lend support to two Iranian bloggers. The one-month-old Committee to Protect Bloggers is asking that on February 22, “Day of Mojtaba and Arash,” they dedicate their blogs to the same cause. Both Arash Sigarchi and Mojtaba Saminejad are sitting in prison in Iran. Blogging is a form of free expression, and for some time the regime has been clamping down on influential voices. “I hope this day will make people think,” said Curt Hopkins, director of the committee, in an interview with the BBC. The committee has drawn up a list of possible actions that bloggers can take, including writing to the Iranian embassy. For its first campaign, the committee has declared Tuesday “Free Mojtaba and Arash Day” and is calling on the “blogging universe” to raise awareness about Mojtaba and Arash as well as other “cyber-dissidents.” “If you have a blog, you could at least post ‘Free Mojtaba and Arash Day’ on it,” Hopkins said. “That would make the slogan appear on the screen a total of 71,000 times. It’s not much, but it would shine a light on the situation.” “And if you don’t have a blog, you could set one up, it takes only about thirty seconds.” Technorati, a search engine that indexes blogs, now says it is following 6 million of them, with more than 12,000 new ones being created every day. According to a report from the Pew Research Center, a new blog is started every five minutes and forty-four seconds. The Committee to Protect Bloggers was founded by American Curt Hopkins, who was a former flight attendant who was fired from a major American airline after she ran a blog critical of the company. She is now a deputy director of the committee and has also initiated a petition, the International Bill of Rights for Bloggers, that is intended to protect the freedom of speech of bloggers. Although the Committee to Protect Bloggers is not the only group devoted to human rights issues, it does aim to be the centre for organizing and supporting bloggers’ freedom of speech. On Tuesday, the committee is holding its first international meeting, and, despite its lack of time in existence, is intending to launch a new campaign every month. “Blogging is in a funny place; depending on your view it can be construed as one thing or another,” said Hopkins. “There are some who are trying to be like journalists, and others like me are just publishing their opinions. But they have no official status and are in the cold.” The problem is that bloggers are not only concerned about the situation in countries where it is forbidden to publish certain views. A growing number of cases in which high-profile cases of people being fired for posting anonymous comments on their personal blogs has been increasing the debate over the status of blogs in general. “It’s a very confused situation,” Hopkins said. “It’s such a new way of doing business, that the reaction will be a repression.” But it is precisely the courts that will ultimately determine the rights and responsibilities, and in his view that is all part of the “messiness” of the situation. “If you don’t already have a policy for dealing with employees who have a blog, you will tomorrow,” said Hopkins. “Everyone is doing it – stay-at-home mothers, liberals, conservatives. There are many companies out there that offer you a simple, instant service that will allow you to publish your own personal page.” “And that’s the main difference – you don’t even need your own computer.”

Using your home computer you can help to solve the world's hardest problems. The World Community Grid, which is launched this week, is a distributed grid computing project that uses spare computing power to test solutions to these problems. By pooling these spare computing resources over the Internet, the World Community Grid is creating a virtual supercomputer. It follows the success of other distributed grid computing projects that have used the idle computing power of millions of home computers. One of the most successful of these projects was SETI@home, which used spare processing power to analyse radio signals for signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. Anyone can donate the spare processing power of their home computers by downloading a special screensaver from the World Community Grid's website. The screensaver automatically receives a piece of the work and returns to the grid when it has finished. The first World Community Grid project to be launched is the Human Proteome Folding Project, which aims to discover how the human body's proteins fold. An international scientific advisory board will review applications from leading academic, public sector and not-for-profit organisations. The board will oversee up to six projects a year. Members include the UN Development Program and the World Health Organization. Their ambition is to inspire others to look beyond the technological limitations that have hitherto prevented progress on some of the world's most intractable problems. IBM has donated the hardware, software and technical skills to build the basic grid computing platform. Working with the United Devices organisation, IBM previously created the Smallpox Research Grid, which linked more than two million people in 226 countries to accelerate the analysis of 35 million drug molecules in the search for a cure for smallpox.

The Berlinale, which will open on Thursday with the historical film Man to Man, is to be devoted to a new European cinema. Of the 21 films in competition for the Golden and Silver Bears, more than half are from Europe, France in particular. Director Dieter Kosslick calls it a "new sense of European cinema." "The Europeans have an unbelievable success streak," he told the Reuters news agency. "Not that there are no good American films," he continued, "only that there are more good European films." But he denied that the wide-ranging opposition to the war in Iraq had turned audiences against American films. "There is no anti-Americanism," he said. This year's festival will present 350 films, while another 300 will be shown at the European film market. More than a dozen movie stars are due to attend, including Will Smith, Kevin Spacey and Keanu Reeves. Kosslick said many more would have attended if the Oscars had not been moved to February 27. But he said he hoped the festival would be able to be held in January next year to avoid a clash. The 61st Berlinale will run until February 20.

A spruce tree, whose branches are connected by wires to the wireless terminals, has been unveiled at the Tate Gallery in London. The Christmas tree, which is adorned with broken dishes and light bulbs, will receive text messages through the Bluetooth system. The sculptor Richard Wentworth, who has designed the tree, will then read these messages to the public. This is the seventeenth year in which the gallery invites an artist to decorate its Christmas tree. Among the previous artists to dress it, in 2002 there was the naughty and thorny Tracey Emin. The tree, a Norway spruce, is located in the vestibule. The adornments, very few light bulbs, were thrown around its branches. The plates adorning the branches will be sold for charity, to the benefit of the ArtWorks charity for children. Wentworth worked as an assistant to Henry Moore in the late sixties. His reputation as a sculptor has been increasing since the eighties, and he has been one of the most influential teachers in the last two decades. He also took pictures of the everyday, of subjects such as a cigarette pack under the crooked leg of a table.

The American rap star 50 Cent is the first to place three songs in the Top Five of the same week. His record ‘Candy Store’ remained on the number one spot, and ‘Disco Inferno’ climbed one spot from six to five. His other song with rap protégé The Game, ‘How We Do It’, is still number four in the United States but is now no longer in the Top Ten in Britain. The pair have been at odds for some time and in recent times The Game was sacked from the G-Unit rap collective after the rapper accused him of disloyalty. Since his explosive appearance in 2003, 50 Cent has had only three singles reach the British Top Five, and his album ‘Get Rich Or Die Tryin’ was just not quite good enough to reach number one. But in the United States he topped the end-of-year album and hip-hop charts. His new protégé The Game’s debut album stayed on the number one spot for five weeks in a row, while 50 Cent’s second album ‘The Massacre’ came out in the United States last week. In May this year, the R&B singer Usher scored a chart first by achieving three songs simultaneously in the Top Ten of the American Top Five, something only ever achieved by the Bee Gees and the Beatles. These hit records were taken from his album ‘Confessions’ which stayed on the American charts for a remarkable eight weeks.

An MEP in the European Parliament, Robert Kilroy Silk, was splattered with a pail of dung in Manchester. The Ukip politician was arriving at a BBC radio show when the attacker rushed out from behind a bush. Fellow M.P. Ruth Kelly was also splattered. Kilroy Silk said the man, who later vanished, had told him he was doing it “in the name of Islam”. Kilroy Silk had already been sacked from his BBC One show in January for a comment in which he called all Arabs “suicide bombers” and “limb-cutter-offers” to women. The Muslim community protested. The attack took place on Friday at the entrance to the High School for Girls in Manchester, where the radio programme Any Questions was being recorded. The police were called, but the man had vanished by the time they arrived. They are now treating the attack as an assault. Kilroy Silk, after being given a change of clothes, managed to appear on the show. He later told reporters that he was very angry and would press charges against the man if he was caught. He said the man had shouted: “You have insulted my religion and I am doing this in the name of Islam.” “I was totally covered, it went through my clothes and stank to high heaven. It went inside the car and covered Ruth Kelly as well.” A BBC spokesman said: The attack was “totally unprovoked and disgusting”. The police added that others in the vicinity had also been spattered with the foul-smelling substance. They took witness statements but so far no arrests have been made. Police said the man had escaped towards the Wilmslow Road after the attack, and that he had previously been seen driving a red Vauxhall Corsa. He is described as white, aged about thirty to forty, with a reddish beard. The police are appealing for any witnesses to come forward. Kilroy Silk, a Ukip M.P. for the East Midlands, quit the Ukip whip in the European Parliament in October. At the time he said he wanted to become leader of the party. He said he still hoped to become leader by Christmas. “I think that is sufficient time to put in the necessary preparations for a leadership election... in time for us to be in a position to contest the next general election.” A spokesman for Ukip said it would not be possible for there to be a leadership election before March.
And now, with all our hearts, I answer you, "I do." I do love you, and will love you until I die; my love, I tell you, is for ever.

He spoke of Burns. The coarse men crowded round to hear his praises of a man whose heart was made of manly, simple stuff, as simple as their own. And when he read, they leaned forward, absorbing with wet mouths and ears his stream-like verses, which never made thee untrue to your humble tears. Slowly there was a dawn of tenderness and tenderness on the faces, hardened and brown, as if they were able to see in him, the man who read, the presence of the bard. It was a sight for sin and injustice And slave tyranny, for faith in high humanity. I thought that these men would carry away from that night, at least, reminders of their former lives, and something of a nobler reverence for beauty and truth and love. God scatters love on every side, He spreads it free of cost among his children, and always hearts lie wide open Where some flakes can fall. There is no wind that does not sow seeds of a more true and open life, Which in unexpected things will become a deed of the soul And beauty fills the path. We find in these souls wild seedlings of a higher birth, Which in the poet's warm heart produce flowers that smell of the earth.
