In all hearts are found These promises of a wider bliss, Which bloom into unfading hopes at such sunny hours. And thus, in the poor and ill-educated, Great deeds and feelings are cradled, Which cast shadows on the golden schooling of ancient Greece and Rome. You, mighty soul of mankind, Where you are, in the low and in the high, With your sky-wide arch ringing, Your expanse of joy extends Over infinity! All thoughts that build the age begin Deep down in the primitive soul, And rise up from the many slowly to one who understands everything: In his wide brain, the deep feeling That struggled on the many tongues swells into a tide of thought, which then surges over the weak thrones of wrongdoing. Every thought begins in feeling – the great base is hampered in the countless mass, and in thought it stands immobile, like a pyramid. No one is wrong to believe that every hope that rises and widens in the world's heart is the consequence of a well-ordered drive from the great heart of God. , but in common souls hope is only vague and undefined, Until from the poet's tongue the message breaks Through fear and pride to the lives of his own. Never did the poetic life seem so full of heaven to me, as when I saw how it could break through the pride and fear to the lives of the most crude men. It may be glorious to write Thoughts that can gladden the two or three High souls, like the distant stars that are visible Once in a century; but it is much better to say One simple word, which every now and then can awaken the free nature in the weak and beleaguered people, and write a serious poem or verse, which seeks not to earn the praise of art, but which gives a clearer faith and self-esteem to the ignorant heart. This may be forgotten in its own time, but it is a crown that will never fail to be worn by those who live and speak forever.

Seeing you through the trees you planted, I cut down the hardest wood for my fires. I use the empty nests you kept like a crazy librarian to kindle my fire. The birds have all left for the south. And your elitist and liberal metaphors, which I find plagiarisms and clichés, like the trees you so zealously protect, are only another source of energy for woodchucks and beavers like me, who need to express a little anguish from time to time. ... Poet, green is no longer just the color of envy; it is the color of your gods. And as I know what to expect, I am prepared to take on your own mediocre examples and allegories. Poet, by going into the wilderness, embracing trees and bunnies, you have not been able to silence the unholy and blasphemous gossiper who denigrates everything you do as politics. And though I am only a reader, you should know that I am not a believer in search of a cause. — Sheridan, Thomas, August 18, 1842.

“An enigma is an animal,” said the hurried, harried schoolboy. “And an animal that is divided against itself cannot stand. And a colossus is a man who believes that he has too many wives. What harm is there in that?” O the boundless fertility of poetry is equaled by its endless, inexhaustible freshness, as in the discovery of America and of poetry. From this it is clear that truth is not narrow and straight, but infinite. All roads lead to Rome, and to poetry, and to verse, dear verse, and the aforesaid aforesaid and the aft thereof and the aforesaid and the reversible and the reverting are all of the same typography. Hence a poet must be a little nave, and an infant, for unless a man be like a child, he shall not enter into the kingdom of poetry. Hence a poet must be able to become a tiger, like William Blake, a waltz-party, like Rilke. Hence he must be everything, in order to be free, a pavement and a monument to every situation possible or actual, the cuckold, the cuckoo, the conqueror, and the fool. It is to him that the zookeeper and the hyena cry in the zoo: “Good morning! Take off your hat, King of the Beasts! And sit down, please!” And a poet must seek to be anonymous. He must die a little death every morning. Bones. He must swallow his toad and study his spit as Baudelaire studied Jeanne Duval’s charogne. He must be, or become, Keats and Renoir and Keats in Renoir, Mozart in the person of Figaro, Edgar Allan Poe as Ophelia, overwhelmed and drowning in the perpetual river, and Keats as Mimi, Camille, and an elderly gourmet. As Baudelaire refused Madame Sabatier when she invited him with the fair hair, For Jeanne Duval was more than enough for him, although she cuckolded him with errand boys, lackeys, and waiters. Reality was Jeanne Duval.) A poet must be Casanova and Saint Anthony, Adonis, Nero, Hippolytus, Heathcliff, and Phèdre, Genghis Khan, Genghis Cohen, and Gandhi the courtesan, Sir Peregrine, and Disraeli’s Messiah. He would have worn the horns of existence, He would have perceived them by looking in the mirror, He would have needed them as a moose needs a hayrack, Above his heavy head and with his smoky eyes, He would have seen the meaning of the hat rack, Above the mirror, in the dark anteroom. For a poet must become nothing but poetry, He must be nothing but a poem when he writes, until he is as absent-minded as the dead, as unconscious as the nymphs of Lethe, and as lobotomized. (“That fat grass that rots on Lethe’s bank.”)

- When I was a young man on the farm, that's twenty years ago, I have a friend who lives near me, named Jean-Baptiste Trudeau. Often, when we're alone, we talk about it. Bateese gets it in the end that he's too much educated to make a farmer's tenant, he's better off with the state, 7 And so, one summer evening, we're driving the cows, and he told me all the beez-ness of it, as you're hearin' me now. - Me, me, me, me, me, you know, me, me, me, me, me, me, me, we stifle the fact that it's boring and that we don't go for the jam, 12 Without going on to another place and making some money. I say to him: - What are you spik-in' like dat? you're gone crazy. 22 There are people in the state who are more clever than you, 23 And even if you make l'argent, you spend it like a Yankee, and not like a countryman. 25 - For me, Bateese! i tell you this, I am very satisfied, 26 because the best of men doesn't live too long tam, ba gosh, one day he dies, 27 And what if you have a good trotter horse and a nice Canadian woman, 28 With a plate of plaintee de maison pour manger – What else you want, my friend? 31 - You see! that it's been fifteen years or more since Bateese left, 34 that I found myself at the River-Loup, a fine, fine winter day, 35 and the fast train would come thar! 36 But as soon as it came, it would stop, and a great fellow would jump off the car, that was boss by a nigger man. - He's in first class, he's got a new suit on, with a long mustache sticking out on the upper side of his nose, 38 A nice gold watch chain, a nice box, a long, long overcoat, 40 With a beaver hat, and a red tie on his throat - 41 I'm saying: - Hey Bateese, hey! how are you doing, my old man! he's saying: - Forgiv-ing me, my friend, I don't know you. - I'm saying: - She is ver-y curis-t'ing, you're Bateese Trudeau, who grew up at the same place as me, fifteen years ago? he's saying: - My friends must be told, ma name is not Bateese Trudeau any more, but John B. Waterhole! - He says: - Hole on the water is a funny name for a man who is called Trudeau. To celebrate the trip, he was invited to join us at the Hotel du Canada, where he was treated like a big fellow, but he can't take white wine, he says it's a little strong for a man who's come out of the central waterfall, and tobacco Canada, Goddamn, he won't smoke it at all! - he smokes big pile of them, he doesn't care about money! - He is a big shit, but when he wakes up, he forgets everything in his head, I mean it, all winter, when we have a soirée, it's a great business, Bateese Trudeau, dit Waterhole, he's de boss man, - you bet he had big times, but when spring came again, he bought a first-class ticket to go back to the State. You remember when the hard times came to Les État-Uni-ons, and the plebes were leaving to stay on their own soil? I'm going to La Rivière-du-Loup again, to unload my two t'ree carts of hay, and also to make a little visit. The freight train is just arriving, only ten hours late, she's never carry a passe-gou-se, dat's what they always say, - I see the poor man on the char cab-in, he's got a small suitcase, my God! I almost took a fit, it was him, he was Bateese! Ak, Napoleon, that's the truth, Bateese, I hope you know, he's your old man, Bateese Trudeau, I'm just coming from the State to see ma familee again, I get on the Central Fall, I'm not going back there. I'm taking Bateese with me, once more, to the Hotel du Canada, - and he's happy to drink some good white whine! Démon, he's hung-ry! I see de w'ole beez-nesse mese - Monte, he's hung-ry! - I watch de hole damned beez-nesse messe - Mon Dieu! he's hung-ry! - Madame Charette keeps the whole place a-fi-ree, because Bateese keeps stuffing himself, du pain doré, de potat-e-pie, and de 'nother thing be there. - But when Bateese gets him out, they'll go anywhere they like. It don't take long for the news 'Bateese's come from the State' to spread, and pretty soon they've got a big crowd, the village is making a big fuss, then de ole man says: 'Bateese, are you here to stay?' and Bateese he's crying like a big baby, 'Bâ j'eux rester ici.' - 'Bah j'eux voir le State agan, an' I don't care.' - 'Correct,' Maxime says right off, 'I'll get you a farm, bâ j'eux go to the mill.' - 'Bâ j'eux come wi' me on de shop, I fix you up, bâ j'eux - And then you'll be ready to go home and see ma familee.' - Then de ole man an' Bateese come back from the shop, Bateese's lost his North-eastern clothes, he's dressin' like a Canadian, with sauvage boots, fléché cinturon, frock coat wi' capuchon, and a French longsword, he's like a Frenchman. - I see Bateese the other day, he's on his daddy's farm. He says: 'I don't care about the State, mon cher Napoleon, he's Kebec for me, Hooraw for Canada.'

I met with sleep who embraced me and kissed me on the brain. The eye of the sleeper, shifting to light, turned on me like the moon. I was flying at the speed of thought with my friend and crashing into dream and the high sky. I fled from the earth and climbed naked up to the sky. I came to a second level far away from the stars. There, I wept with another, an apparition, our eyes from our mothers on the heights of trees. “My father’s globe strikes its center and sings. ” “And this land where we walk was also your father’s land.” “But this is where the angelic bands move. Sweet are the father’s faces on their wings.” “These are but dreamers. A breath and they fade. ” My mother’s-eyed elbow faded, and, chasing the angels, I was lost on the cloud shore to the last dark buried one. I blew the dreamers to their bed where they still sleep unaware of their ghost. Then all the matter of the living air was raised to a voice, and, climbing on words, I spelled my vision with my hand and hair. How light is the sleeping on that agrarian star. How deep is the awakening in the inhabited clouds. There is the hour’s ladder up to the sun, love or loss, to the end, The minutes whose blood monkeys the blood of man. And the old one still climbs in his ghost. My father’s ghost climbs in the rain.

Surpass us with your grace, Obtain us with a miracle cure, Help us with your great invention, Atheists are working on a plan to transform the world; they have abandoned you and your tenets. But you preserve your garden; you properly guard your treasures. As a matter of course, God, you have to intervene. We implore you to vote for us, We know you will grant us full marks, We shall be happy with ten, We shall be in a position to defeat them, They have cut us off from the womb, They have robbed us of five hundred planets, We are wailing in pain, We shall be at the top when you vote for us.

An angel grew bored with heaven and drank from the cup of the golden street. He wore his halo low and his harp silent at his feet; Then the Lord stooped to pity, and gave him a pass to go down to the earth, to mingle with men. He took off his celestial garments, without waiting to hang them up. He took leave of Peter at the golden gate. The sempiternal singers chanted farewell, and the imps, pounding on the red-hot flagstones of hell, raised their heads. Never had such an angel been seen in the world; his eyes like the heavens, his face like Apollo’s, his hair the color of gold. The women adored him; his lips were like Cupid’s bow; but he did not dare to use them, so they all considered him dull. Until finally, one woman came, a marvel of beauty, And whispered to him: “Do you love me? And he replied to this woman: “Yes.” Then she said: “Take me, and embrace me, and kiss me, and hug me.... But he drew back furiously, saying, “It’s wrong, and I know it!” Then she snickered and went on, her eyes full of wit: “You, a man among men, speak like a child. The old order of things has outlived its time; The old Protestant knot has been broken.” Then the Lord feared for his angel and called him back, Because ah, the woman was marvelous, and ah, the angel was tempted! And deep in his hell, the Devil was singing this song: “Old, rotten Protestant morality!”

Memorial Day for the fallen in war. Add now your own grief to theirs, even that of the woman who has left you. Mingle sorrow with sorrow, like history, which merges holiday, sacrifice, and mourning into one day for the easy, convenient recollection. “Behind all this lies great happiness.” The sweet world soaked, like bread, in the milk of the terrible toothless god.... There is no use crying in private and shouting outside. Memorial Day. The bitter mash of salt is dressed up as a little girl in flowers. The streets are closed off by a cordon of flags, to separate the living and the dead. The children, carrying a grief that is not theirs, walk slowly, like stepping on broken glass. The flute-player’s mouth will not open again for many days. The dead soldier floats above the children’s heads, with the floating motion of the dead, with the ancient error of the dead, that water is a place for the living. The flags lose contact with the ground and float away. A shop window is filled with blue and white dresses for pretty girls. And everything is written in three languages: Hebrew, Arabic, and death. A huge, noble animal dies all night under the jasmine, and still it stares. A man who lost his son in the war goes about the streets like a woman with a dead embryo in her womb. “Behind all this lies great happiness.”

Is marriage a kind of forced prostitution? Or a noble institution? Why raise a silly question? There is no doubt that the knot is tied when it is done, after a lot of fight, when you have caught a beautiful creature in your hand, when you have overcome many obstacles and even if you have gone through some adversities? Once the marriage is over, the question of how to begin a new life and when to begin comes to mind. When the initial days of happiness and joy, when we use all kinds of tricks to make our wife happy, when all the vessels start clanking in the trough, when everything that happens now is their responsibility? When we think of how to start a new life, in marriage, in the initial days, when everything is fun and games, when we think of how to please our wife, when we think of how to live without them, how to stay? It's time to see the reality of the situation, when the end of the honeymoon is over, when we have seen the end of our time, when our marital life begins?

Success lies beneath the popular support. If you establish the goodwill of the masses, success is inevitable. If you fail to succeed in the plan, you must heed the expert’s advice. Not to give up, but not to sneer. If your intentions are sincere, you must stand firm, and not yield, even if it means dying. You must not give up, not to sneer, not to be late, for if you succeed, you will reap success. Success is close at hand, why not achieve it? Why not work and fight for peace? Life can be easy, and you can rest at ease.

Joy is an illusory prank; pleasure is but the trivial bauble the donkey follows to the market or the precipice. But crushing suffering, the rock under the tower, the battlement at the summit, the thundering head of the turret – is terrible and real. Thus the insane monk who bores a knife into his chest seems to have conquered the world. The god of the world is the torturer and the madman, but also the only foundation and the only fountain. Whoever resists him eats his own flesh and dies of hunger; whoever hides in the grave to avoid him is dead; whoever flees into the Hindu refuge to escape him is dead; whoever falls in love with the god is washed clean of death wished for and death feared. He has joy, but joy is a trick in the air; he has pleasure, but pleasure is a cheap trick; and he has peace, and that is more solid than suffering. He has overstepped the limits a little, and that will estrange him. He is monstrous, but not in the measure of the god... However, I suppose that few in the world have the energy to hear all the way to the end. But I have told you.

The valiant Geraint, one of the noble knights at Arthur’s court, a tributary of the kingdom of Dewi, had married Enid, the only child of Yniol, and loved her as he loved the sun. And as the sun varies, now at sunrise, now at sunset, now by night, with moon and stars, so Geraint liked Enid to change with the day, in crimson and purple and in gleaming stones. And Enid, ever keen to please her husband’s eyes, who had first loved her in a state of poverty, now in a ruined condition, daily dazzled him with a fresh blaze. The Queen, grateful to Prince Geraint for her kind act, loved her and often helped her deck her up with her own fair hands, as the prettiest person, after her own self, in the whole court. Fellow-women, seeing them together, Geraint was as happy as if he had been alone. But when the rumours began to be spread about Queen Guinevere’s guilty love for Lancelot, though there was no evidence of any kind, nor had the world’s gossip resounded, Geraint believed it and feared that his innocent wife might have been hurt by the sordid nature of their affair. For that reason, he prayed the King to give him permission to go away to defend his borders; and after the King had given him his leave, the Prince and Queen took fifty knights and rode with them to the banks of the Severn. From thence, the Prince never left her side, and in peace, forgetting his promise to the King, forgetting his falcon and hunting, forgetting his tournament and tilt, forgetting his glory and his name, forgetting his princely duties and obligations. Forgetting was a great encumbrance to him. And then the people, when they met In pairs or groups, began to scoff and mock and chaff him As a man whose manhood was done away, and melted down to mere love. She learned this from the people’s eyes; the women who adorned her, desiring to please her, dwelt on his boundless love, and Enid was saddened by it. And day by day she would have told Geraint, but, though she wished to, she could not, out of her mischievous reluctance; and he, seeing her sad, was the more suspicious that her nature had some hidden flaw. which brought all these thoughts to her mind; and when they were sleeping (they lying by each other) the morning sun glared through the uncurtained windows, And warmed the strong warrior in his dreams, And he stirred, and threw back the covers and bared His ruggedly curved throat, His lusty breast, massive and square, And arms, in which the muscles sloped as over a spouting spring. And Enid, waking, stood beside him, And admired him, and said in her heart: “O thou most noble breast and valiant arms, May I be thy cause that men abhor you, and say that all your strength is poured out for love’s sake?” And yet I love thee not less, for his stay here; For I cannot love him and not his name. Far better had I, wet with his blood, hung on his breast his harness, And joined him in the midst of the battle, To watch his mighty hand striking great blows at the tyrants and the wrongdoers. Far better were I laid in the dark earth, Not to hear his noble voice any more, Not to be more folded in his dear arms, And blacked from the glimmer in his eyes, Than that my lord should suffer shame through me. Am I so bold, and can I so stand by, When I see my dear lord wounded in the strife, And bleeding to death before my eyes, And yet dare not to tell him what I think, That men slander him and say all his strength is melted away to mere effeminacy? O me, I fear I am not a good wife.” [76] — And she said this half inwardly, half aloud, And her heart’s passion made her weep, Real tears on his wide naked breast, And these wakened him, and by great misfortune He heard but a little of what she said: “I fear I am not a true wife.” Then he thought, “In spite of all my cares, despite all my pains, For all my pains, poor man, For all my pains, she is unfaithful to me, and I see her Weeping for some jolly knight in Arthur’s hall.” Then though he loved and reverenced her too much To dream she could be guilty of a shameful act, He felt a sudden pang, The kind that makes one, before the fair face of her whom one loves, a lonely wretch. — So he dragged his great-legged frame out of bed, And woked his slumbering squire, and cried, “My charger and her palfrey!” and then he said to her, “I will ride forth into the wilds, For my spurs must still grow, for my height’s not reached yet. And thou, take thou thy worst and basest clothes, And thou shalt come with me.” And Enid asked, amazed: “And what shall I wear?” “I charge thee, ask not, but obey.” Then she remembered a faded silk, A faded mantle and a faded veil, And walked toward a cedar coffer, Where she kept them folded in reverence, With summer’s greenest branches tucked between the folds. She took them and dressed herself in them, Remembering when he came on her aglow in this raiment, And all her foolish apprehensions about the dress, And his journey to her as he himself had told her, And how they came to the court. For it was Whitsuntide, and King Arthur held court at old Caerleon on the Usk. I saw him sitting high in the hall, A forester of the forest of Dean, Wet from the wood, with a tiding of a white hart, Taller than all his fellows, of the day, The king’s sight. Then the good king commanded horns to be sounded, And gave the order to be seen by the hunt. And when the king was asked to ride with the hunt, He was more than happy to go. , and all the court was gone by morning. But Guinevere slept on late, lost in love and dreaming of Lancelot, And forgot about the hunt, But at last she got up and took her horse, And rode to the banks of the Usk, And to the wood; There she stood, on a little knoll, waiting for the hunt. But suddenly she heard a sound of hoofs, for Prince Geraint, who was late, was not wearing his hunting cloak, nor carrying any weapon except a gold-hooped brand. And so he hurried past them, and came galloping up the knoll. A purple scarf, on either end of which hung an apple of the purest gold, Was waving around him as he galloped up to them, looking like a dragonfly, In summer dress and summer silk. Low bowed the deferential Prince, And she, Sweetly and graciously, and with all the grace of womanhood and queenhood, answered him: “Late, late, Prince,” she said, “Late as we are!” “Yes, my dear queen,” he replied, “So late that, like you, I come only to see the chase, Not to join it.” “So wait with me,” she said, “For on this knoll, if anywhere, we might hear the hounds, They often break covert at our feet.” And while they were waiting, listening to the distant hunt, And especially to the baying of Cavall, King Arthur’s hound with the deepest throat, A knight, his lady, and a dwarf, were slowly riding past, with the dwarf trailing behind. The knight had his hood raised, and he showed a young face, With high haughty features. And Guinevere, who had not seen him in the king’s presence, wished to know his name, And sent her maid to ask the dwarf; But the dwarf, who was shrewish, old, and irritable, And reflected all his master’s unhappiness, replied angrily that he did not know it. “So shall I ask it from him himself,” said she. “Nay, by my faith, thou shalt not know it,” cried the dwarf; “Thou art not worthy to ask him.” And when the lady turned her horse towards the knight, He struck him with his whip, and cut his cheek. The Prince’s blood spattered his scarf, Dyed it, and his quick, enraged hand grabbed his hilt as though to slay him, But, because of his noble courage and high-minded spirit, he restrained himself from saying a word of anger at such a monster, and said as he returned, “I will avenge this insult done to your maid, you, O kindly Queen; and I shall pursue this wretched man, who insulted you, noble Queen, With his whip. For though I ride unarmed, I doubt not that I shall find armour at some place or other, either on loan or on pawn, And once I have found it, I shall fight him, and break his pride; And on the third day I shall be here again, to stay, if I fall not in a fight. Good-bye.” “Farewell, fair Prince,” replied the kindly Queen, “in this as in all your journeys, And come back from it safely, in the happiest of spirits, And live to wed her whom you first love; But, before you wed, bring your bride to me, And I, if she be the daughter of a king, Or if she be but a beggar out of a hedge, Will clothe her for her nuptials like the sun.” And Prince Geraint, thinking he heard the horn of the hart at bay, now the call of the hounds on the hunt, now the sound of the distance, Somewhat vexed at the loss of the hunt, some more vexed at the vile occasion, sat still, gazing fixedly at the three. Behold, they emerged from the grove, And climbed the level and fair ridge, And showed themselves against the sky, And vanished. And, here they came, and below him, the great lord beheld a long street of a little town, And on one side, white with a mason’s hand, a fortress rose; and, on the other side, a castle in decay, beyond a bridge that spanned a dry stream. And out of the city and the valley came a noise, As of a great stream of water flowing over a bed of pebbles, Or of rooks singing, at a distance, ere they seek their night-roosts. And they rode on, and entered the fortress, and vanished behind its walls. — “Aye,” thought Geraint, “I have tracked him to his place of rest.” And down the long street, riding wearily, he found all the hostelries full, and every man hammering at his work, and the hot hissing and bustling shriek of the lad who scours his master’s armour. And he asked one of them, “What is the noise in the city?” And he replied, “The sparrow-hawk!” And then, drawing near an old crofter, who, dusty under a dusty sloping beam, was sweating with a sack of wheat, he asked, “What is the hubbub in the city?” And the man answered gruffly, “Eh! the sparrow-hawk!” Then, passing on, by a smith, who, his back bent to his work, was riveting a helmet on his knee, he asked the same question; but the man, not turning round, nor looking at him, said, “Friend, the smith who makes for the sparrow-hawk has little pity for idlers.” Whereat Geraint was in a sudden fury: “May a thousand piplings devour your sparrow-hawk! May wrens, titmouskers, and all winged noughts peck it to death!” The people of your burg deem the hammering of your hammers the buzz of the world? But, what’s that to me? O wretched wrens and sparrows all, Whose piping is of no note save that of sparrow-hawks! Be that not all men here are such as the rest of you are: Speak! if you are not of the kind as the rest, Where can I find rest for my weary days? And arms, arms, arms, to fight my enemy? — Speak!” ‘Twas then that the armourer, all amazed at the sight of so many-hooved knight, who, riding in his purple velvet, came to him and held his helmet in his hand, answered, “Forgive us, sir knight; we have a tourney here to-morrow, And time is short to complete half the work.” ‘Methinks, my lord, we need arms, in truth. Let me have a halter. How I shall find one, I know not; all sorts are in need here. And a harbour? I know not where, in truth, save at my Lord Ynywl’s, o’er the bridge yonder.” Having spoken, he fell to work again. Then, some way, and yet with some displeasure, the Sir Glyndwr rideth o’er the bridge o’er the dry ravine. There sat the hoary-headed earl, In a suit of old-fashioned splendour, as in those days were set on a a jubilee or other; “Whither, fair son?” quoth he. To which Geraint answered, “O lord, I seek a place for the night.” Then said Ynywl, “Enter and take the poorest entertainment of this house, Once so rich, but now so poor, but always open-handed.” ‘ “Thanks, venerable friend,” quoth Geraint, “given that ye will not serve me a supper of sparrows, I will enter, and I will eat With all the zeal of a man who has fasted a day.” Then sighed and smiled the hoary-headed earl, and answered, “My cause is much greater than yours, to curse the robber of hedges, the sparrow-hawk. But in, enter ye, for save you choose it, we will not touch him even in jest.” And then did Geraint ride into the court of the castle, with many a prickly star of thistles his charger trode. He saw that all was ruinous. Yea, a long, grey arch tinseled with fern; And yonder, a mighty rib of a tower, like a rock, had fallen from the cliff, And like a rock was it hung with flower-dappled wildings; And, high above, a spiral of turret steps, smoothed by silent feet, bared the sun, and monstrous stems of ivy clung, with prickly arms, to the grey walls, wherein they sucked the space between the stones and looked like a knot of snakes beneath, and a wood, above. And while he waited in the castle court, the voice of Enid, daughter of Yniol, rang clear through the open windows of the hall, singing, And as the sweet voice of a bird that can sing well-loved by men, When a man in the wilds of the wild, When first comes the liquid note loved by men, Flying over many a windy wave, To Bryn Mawr in April, sings from a copse gemmed with red and green, the man pauses in his discourse with a friend, or in his toil at his task; and so he thought with Geraint, “Aye, by the grace of God, this is the voice that I seek. And so the song that Enid sang was of Fortune and her Wheel, and Enid sang: “Turn, turn thy Wheel, and cast down the proud, Turn thy wild Wheel by Sun, storm, and cloud: Thy Wheel and Thy Wheel we love neither hate.” And with a voice of loveliest twang, she sang the Wheel of Fortune and the man’s heart afresh. “Smile, Fortune, and we smile; We are lords of many lands; Cry, and we smile, we are lords of our hands, For ’tis true, a man is lord of his fate. Turn, turn thy Wheel, above the stars that gaze; Thy Wheel and thou are shadows in the cloud; Thy Wheel and thou and we neither love, nor hate.” By the bird’s song ye may know the nest,” said Yniol; “Enter thou quickly.” Then he entered the hall, Over a heap of new-fallen stones, The hall of the dark-roofed, many-webbed hall, And found an old dame in dark brocade, And near her, like a bloom of vermeil-white, Which light-wing’d the faded sheath of a flower, Moving about, the fair Enid, her daughter. Then Geraint thought, “Here by God’s Rood is the maid for me!” “Enid, the noble knight’s horse stands in the court. Go, take him to the stall and feed him there; Then, buy us flesh and wine in the city; And we will make ourselves as merry as we may. Our wealth is scanty, but our hearts are great.” He said, and the prince, as Enid went by, fain to follow, strode a pace, but Yniol caught his purple scarf and held it, and said, “Thy friend! let us not speak of thee! My house, though ’tis waste, my son, will not suffer her guest to slay.” And Geraint, reverently, in pure politeness, held his tongue. And Enid led his charger to the stall, And followed on her way, crossing the bridge, And, while the prince and the earl still spoke, came in with a youth, who followed with a calash, bearing the goodly welcome, the flesh and wine. And Enid, bearing cakes that cheered, With manchet bread wrapped in her veil, Served the three. And seeing her, so good-natured and helpful, For ever, Geraint yearned to kiss the tender little thumb, Which cut the trencher as she laid it down. And after all had eaten, Geraint, for now wine made summer in his veins, let his eye roam as he glowed in love with Enid, as she labored at her sluttish work, one moment here, the next there about the dusky hall, then all at once he sought the hoary earl, “Good host, good earl, hear my request; This sparrow-hawk, what’s his name?” why, good faith, I won’t have it, “For if he is the knight whom I saw ride in to that new fortress by your town, White from the hands of the mason, then I swear I shall have his name From his own lips. I am Geraint of Devonian, and this morning, when the queen sent her maid to ask his name, His fool of a slave struck her with his whip, and she returned, indignant, to the queen. And then I swore, “That I will find my arms and get his name, and I will be vindicated.” Then cried the earl, “Are you really he, Geraint, a name among men, who stand for noble deeds? And if you know where I might lay hands on arms, or if thou should have them, tell me, for I have sworn That I will break his pride, and have his name, Avenging the queen’s great insult.” I speak not now of vain flattery; for this dear child has often heard me praise your deeds, and oft has asked me to continue, and every time has loved to hear, so sweet are the sounds of great things to noble hearts who see but wrong doing. O, no maid ever had so many suitors, like that maid, whom the first was Lestren, a creature given to drunkenness and uncouthness, who was drunk even when he wooed, but if he is dead, I do not know; for he went into the wilds. The second was the cruel Roper, the bird of prey, my wretched nephew —I dare not let his name slip — who, after the tender feelings that I had for him, would not tolerated, but he, when I turned him down, he became prideful, and since a proud man is often a low one, he sows the lie in the ears of the whole land, and the more so because my purse was open to his eyes, because of my lack of care in the keeping of my people, because of the meagre hospitality of my home. He stirred my own people against me the night before my Enid’s birthday, set fire to my house, deposed me from my earldom by foul and foul deed, and has me held in this ruinous tower, where he no doubt would kill me if his haughty pride did not despise me: And I myself sometimes despise myself: For I have not been so valiant, I have not used my power to any purpose; And now I do not know whether I am very base or very wise, nor whether wise or foolish, if this hawk-brained nephew fights in tomorrow’s tourney, I shall break his pride. But this tourney no man can tilt, unless the woman he loves is there. Well said, true-hearted friend,” said Geraint. “Arms I have, but they are old and rusty, rusty and old, Prince Geraint, And therefore at your wish are they thine. And this, what knights shall there come and lay claim to, That the lady at his side may win this prize, And clash with my mighty nephew thereon; Who, apt at arms and of great stoutness, has ever won this prize for the lady at his side, And has thus won for himself the name of ‘the hawk-brained’. But you, who have no lady, can do no battle.” To which Geraint, with eyes shining, replied, “Thy leave, O noble host, to wield my spear for this dear child, because I have never seen, though I have seen all the glories of our time, Nor could I see in all the world, any one more fair. And if I fall, her name will be unblemished as before; But if I live, may Heaven help me when I do my utmost, That I shall make her my true and faithful wife.” And, though he drew near to avenge the wrong, he looked up and saw no Enid, (who, hearing her own name, had run away), but that old dame, to whom he gently strode, And folded her hand in his, he said: “Mother, a maiden is a tender thing, And best known to her mother who bore her. Go thou to rest, but ere thou rest, tell her, and prove her heart for the Prince.” So spoke the good-hearted earl, and she went to find the maid, half undressed for her rest, With frequent smiles and nods, half disarrayed as to her sleep; and at first she kissed her cheeks, and then laid a hand on each glistening shoulder, And so they parted, and she could not bear to bear her own: Her head sank, falling slowly as the scale falls, As weight is put only grain by grain, Slowly to her gentle breast, with eyes closed, rapt with awe and awe, and reflected on her unworthiness. Then, as the pale and bloodless east began to show, she rose and raised her mother, and both came hand in hand down to the meadow where the jousting was held, And there waited for Yniol and Geraint. Even as he did, his own power was a step too slow. Then he beheld her, and knew, Though she were the prize of all his bodily might, He could not bring himself to push her from the she-bearer. Then Yniol’s rusted arms Were on his princely frame, but his noble bearing shone through them, and errant knights, and damsels, and at length the town came, and set in the ring round the three forks, And set over the three the silver spear and the golden sparrowhawk. On a hand was set Yniol’s nephew’s empty horn, And thence was a herald’s horn that called to the tenacious knight, And said, ‘Advance, and take, as fairest of the fair, The reward of beauty that I’ve won for thee these two years past.’ Yniol’s nephew with his horn blasted loud: ‘Say not, the prize is for a better.’ Then the prince with no more than a breath, “Forbear, there is a better;” And with a little surprise, a thrice as much contempt, the knight turned and beheld the four, and his face Glowed like the heart of a great fire at Yulet, Burning with passion and courage, crying: “Do battle for it, no more!” Then each, as each brought his spear up, would thrust so, that the whole company were filled with wonder, and from the distant walls came a clap as if by ghostly hands. Those two fought twice, and breathed twice, but the dew of their great labor, and the blood Of their strong bodies gushed, to drain their strength. And each of them was even until Yniol’s cry, ‘Remember the dread insult the Queen suffered!’ Which, redoubled Geraint’s might, who smote his blade high, And cracked the helmet through, and bit the bone, And fell him, and set his foot on his chest, And said, ‘What’s thy name?’ To which the prone man made answer, ‘Edyrn son of Nudd!’ And ashamed that I should tell thee so. ‘ And now, Edyrn son of Nudd,’ replied Geraint, ‘Thou shalt do two things, or else thou shalt die.’ , And he adduced his reasons for the law: First, thou shalt ride with the damsel and the dwfn, Ride to the court of King Arthur, and crave pardon for the insult the Queen suffered; thou shalt abide the judgment of her will; next, thou shalt restore their earldom to their kinsfolk. These two things thou shalt do, or shalt die.’ Having risen, he rode to Arthur’s court, And there the Queen forgave him without much ado. For, young as he was, he was prone to change, and loathed his crime as a traitor, and he drew himself slowly out of his old dark life, and he fell in the great battle, fighting for the King. But when the third day, from the hunting-morn, Made a dull splendour in the world, and wings moved in her ivy, Enid, as she lay, her fair head bathed in the faint yellow light, Amidst the dancing shadows of the birds, woke to remember her promise made to Prince Geraint, for he was so intent on setting out on the third day, that he would not leave her till she had given her promise: To ride with him that very day to the court, And there be made known to the Queen, And then be wedded with a great ceremony. Then she glanced at her dress, And wished she had never been in it, for ’twas as like as a leaf on the blight-nest of November, as her own at the time of Geraint’s coming. She looked on, and her awe grew; of the dazzling court, With eyes all gazing at her in her faded silk, And she said softly to her dear heart: ‘This noble prince who won our earldom, So great is he in looks and deeds, My heavens, what a naught I shall have to show!’ Little Guinevere’s fancy, as she lay there, was wandering in the past, And visiting the lovely places she’d known: she recalled how she’d once watched, near that old house, at a pond of golden carp. And one of them, patched and dull and tattered, swam among the brilliant ones. And as she thought about how, once, she’d been able to see, near that old home, a pond of golden carp; and then she remembered how she’d been able to spy, with a faint light, over them, admiring them, so rich did it seem to them, that Edyrn’s men had found them and driven them off, With naught but the jewels they wore, which were sold and bought them bread, she wished to see Edyrn’s men come after them, and that they’d be the ones to take them to the woods, and the Prince found her in the ruins; and then she began to dream she was such a faded one amidst the sun-beaten carp in the pool, And she half-dreamed a comparison of that carp and her own faded self, and the gay court; and she slept on again, and dreamed she was a faded creature among the gold-colored carp. But this was in a king’s garden, and though she was dark in the pool, she knew all was bright: there were birds of sunny plumage, in gilded trellises; and lords and ladies of the great court, discussing things of state, in silver-tinselled hanging raiment; and children of the king in golden clothes, glancing at the doors or playing at the wayside, and children of the king in golden clothes, ran to her: Why not? And one seized her, And she awoke, all clouded with the dreary dream. And her mother was squeezing her tight, to wake her. And in her hand she held a suit of shining clothes, which she laid flat on the bed and said, in triumph: It’s never been worn, I think: Look at it, child, and tell me if you recognize it. And Enid saw, but was confused at first, Could hardly tell it from her foolish dream, But then she knew it, and was glad; And said: ‘Ay, I know them; your gift, That was lost on that ill night; Your gift!’ Then said her mother: “When Yniol went through the town yesterday, he found the stolen goods and our plunder, All scattered through the houses of the town, and he gave order that all that had been ours, should now be ours again. And last night, while you were sweetly talking to your prince, one of them came and put it in my hand, out of love or fear or to ask for our favour, Because we’ve our earldom back again. And last night I wouldn’t tell you, but kept it for a sweet surprise. Is it not a sweet surprise? Did I not wear out my old clothes as you, my child, have yours, And Yniol has his, howsoever he has put up with them. Dear one, he took me from a good house, With rich clothes and fine food, and page and maid, and squire, and seneschal, And the delights of hawk and hound, And all that goes with a noble court. And he brought me to a good house, But since fortune turned from sun to shadow, and through that young traitor, cruel need took us all down, we’ve been given better times. So put on these clothes that better suit Our mended fortunes, a prince’s bride. For though you’ve won the prize of fairest-of-them-all, And I’ve heard him call you fair-of-all, You can’t ever be fairer than when she’s in new clothes.” Time passed and Geraint awoke, and he called for Enid, then rose, her fine maid, then left her maiden’s bed and robed herself, helped by her mother’s keen eye and hand, without a mirror, in the wonderful gown; and then her mother turned her around and said she had never seen her so fair, and compared her to the maid of the old tale whom Gwydion had fashioned out of flowers and sweeter than the lord’s wife, whose love brought Caesar to Britain; but we turned him back, as did we this great Prince when he came to invade us; and welcomed him, too, and not turned him back, but welcomed him with joy. But while the women were rejoicing, Geraint awoke from his slumber in the upper hall and called for Enid; and when Yniol gave him word that this good mother had dressed her in fine garments like a princess, , Enid, feeling all abashed and not knowing why, did not dare to look up at her good mother’s face; but silently, without a word, her mother silently took from her limbs the costly garment and clad her in her ancient suit, and so he descended. No man was more joyful than Geraint to see her thus dressed; and with an all-penetrating glance, as if the way robins watch a farmer’s toil, he made her cheeks flush and her eyelids flutter; then, seeing the mother’s dark brow, he took her in both hands and said sweetly: “O my new mother, be not angered or affronted by my new son’s petition. When I last departed Caerleon, the great Queen, in words that linger to this day, words so sweet and sweet, vowed she would clothe whoever I brought home. She promised me that she would do it.” Beholding one so bright in a dark condition, I vowed that if I should win her, our fair Queen, hers would be the hand that would pierce the clouds from your Enid’s soul; and perhaps I thought, too, that the service would bind them together. How could they fail to love each other? I have another thought: I came to you so suddenly that her gentle presence at the challenge-feast Might well have sufficed as proof that she loved me; but I questioned whether her tenderheartedness, or her easy nature, might not let itself be shaped by your desires for her welfare; or if some false sense in her own mind of my contrasting lustre would not make her dream of court and all its perilous glories; and I thought that if I could prove such power in her, merged with such love for me, that she could, at a word (and no reason given) cast off a adornment dear to women and therefore dearer, or even if it were not new, yet ten times dearer by the power of her forbearing habit, then I felt that I could rest, like a rock in the tides, firmly on her faith. Now, now, I rest, a prophet, certain of my prophecy, That not a shadow of mistrust will ever fall between us. When your child’s hair is done in the joyous look of its new gift, when she is placed beside your hearth and you have on her knees, perhaps, a little creature who shall have learned to speak to you, who shall be in thanks to you.” He spoke, his mother smiled, and half in tears, She drew a cloak, and wrapped it around her, And kissed her, and they rode away.” There was a stone tower, they say, from whose height one could see the fine hills of Somerset, and white sails on the yellow sea; But not to the fine hills or to the yellow sea, Did the fair queen look: not to the yellow sea or the fair hills, but to the valley of the Usk, by the flat meadows, she went and met them at the gate; She embraced her, in the true embrace of a friend, and honored her as the Prince’s bride; And all that week old Caerleon was glad, for by the hands of Dubric, the chief saint, They were wedded with great solemnity. And this was Whitsun last year. But Enid kept the faded silk, Remembering how he first came on her in this garment, and how he loved her in it; And how he told her, And how they came to the thrones of court. , And so today, when he said to her: “Wear your worst and least expensive,” She found it, and she clothed herself in it.

A new beginning, a new task, and the arduous tolerance of an attitude of anger and resentment, a smile that allures and a glance that beguiles, a recompense that transcends human aspiration. No one can attain the perpetual praise, but the soul which descends to the earth of Sayonara filled with the most adorable smiles and bringing eternal respect from the one who sits on the throne. The desk and the pen say nothing, but see all, they recite your gratitude, your labor, your honor, and your work, even though the night is long gone. A blessing of fun, a joke, a happy day, take it all in your hand, and save for one day; a fresh morning for you, with the blessing of a happy day, thank always your boss for it and chant a merry melody to the one you love and are blessed by, save up for a day; freshness in the morning, save for one day, the coolness of a splendid, glad morning. Enjoy all these things with a joyous heart, and lay aside your day, for the morning and evening will be beautiful and serene.

The world and its desires pass away, but whoever does God's works, stays with God, for God is without beginning and without end. (1 John 2:17) So it is with the human life that will pass away in the end. We long for years that can be achieved, and ask for them of the Lord, because there is still something for us in the world. It is the world, and the year begins in January. The month goes by to December every year. But January is special to me because it is the month I want to pray, ask for and call to mind: to thank my parents, especially my mother, that she let me see the first light in her dark womb, thank God for the life given me so far, and let me see this beautiful world at least as it is: to see it until senescence. Grant me so that I can enjoy the whole world without hindrance. To live with my physical and mental health, and always be with my friends and family, until I live on the 23rd of January every year, until the end of my days, and until I come to my end, my will and my prayers, as the world turns, all the time, day by day.

One is on the alert, says an expert, until the last moment. Yesterday’s game between Japan and Belgium: hurrah, the Japanese team has won! They’ll go on to the quarter-finals. But Japan suddenly became passive. Belgium had a player on the bench who was tired. There was a surprise and victory for Belgium. Sylvia Frances Chan: Monday, 2 July, afternoon, West European time: Japan v Belgium, 0-3, Victory for Belgium. If I may say so, the Japanese team should stay on the alert, stay on the lookout, and above all be assertive. They should attack the Belgian goal, and be as aggressive as in World War II. They lost the game because they were passive, as if waiting for the whistle to signal the end. Yes, I watched them, or else I couldn’t write this poem and add these comments as my notes. I have an expression in Dutch: “Op saak en droom, drikke bult”. It is an idiom, so no suitable translation.  Sylvia Frances Chan, Dutch poet, evangelist, world traveller and photographer, 2 July, afternoon, West European time. Victory for the Belgian team.

This is a crime committed every day, and often the scene of the scene. The offender cannot raise his hand and his blood does not fall on the ground; the victim does not raise his hand and the bell does not ring; The victim dies of anguish and sorrow; He will not find a place for his protests; He will have to endure the situation and go into exile; Slander is a weapon that can inflict enormous pain on the victim; No court can help, nor can the jury; The culprits can get away without being caught; He becomes the victim of a strange situation, and his way of judging the world is ill-founded; It is a disgrace to which he cannot make amends; He will regret that he did not follow your advice; He will regret that he did not do yours; If he does not listen to your advice, he may feel sorry; If he does not follow your advice, he may be very annoyed; And it would be good that he does not fight for avenging; If he follows your advice, he will die; There is no solution, and no rescue; He will bleed to death, without a stab; Your property will be destroyed, without a bomb; You are cheated, and robbed; The culprit will escape, and you will be the victim; The character assassination will expose the enemy; The adversary is exposed, the defendant is trapped; They are ostracized, confused and harassed; In both cases, it is a direct and clear death; Death in these two cases is visible, and prominent.

A lamenting song, not a sung: ‘Awake, the Lord, awake,’ The hushed choir sings, or it lulls on. In the twilight of the lighted church, wreaths of evergreens still hang from the aisles, marking the gloom of death. And round the altars, altars, and shrines, a dark glory is cast, the brighter for their somber hues, signs of Him who has passed from the grave into glory. Such were the lights and the music of the mighty resurrection. But when the mighty Cross gleams proudly, the filthy note, ‘Father and King, oh where art thou?’ still seemed to float far on the wind, with the note of ecclesiastical farewell. A greener wreath adorns thy brow, and brighter rays surround thee; Oh, for one hour of prayer like thine, To be pleading in the holy shrine For Britain lost and found! And he whose gentle voice taught us to rejoice in trials, like a faithful dove, who builds again a home beside some ruined abode, and who pours her beloved music over the long-deserted fields, – why comes he not to bear his part, to raise and lead the rejoicing heart? We bless him; he sighs for rest, and heaven accepts the prayer. And let us not grieve for thee in the skies, For after thee shall come a day to rise With thy song to heaven. Yes, thou shalt be there, ever near, To cling with thy love to our hearts.

– sing – sing! Music was given to brighten up the gay, to kindle the love. Souls here, like planets in the heavens, by harmony’s laws alone, are set in motion. Beauty may boast of its eyes and cheeks, but love has wings to its dart from the lips. And she who only feathers her dart with a word, At once sends it home to the heart when she sings. When Love was being rocked by his mother, calmed by the cares of sleep, “Hush! Hush!” Venus said. “No voice but his own can wake him.” Then Love dreamed of music, slumbered all the while, Until from his lips a gentle lullaby escaped. Venus, enchanted, looked on with a smile, as Love awoke to his own sweet song. Sing, sing, music was given to brighten up the gay, to kindle love.

My husband loved me, pity the fool, we met when I was young, when I was very tender, and grateful for his love, he meant everything to me, but we changed, and my love turned into hate. At first, he was very kind, but he grew bored, my aged body, my sagging belly, my wrinkles that took over my face, my once golden complexion, which had vanished in the sands of time. His faithfulness faded, his heart hardened, like my own; I made the dinner, I prepared the lunch, I pleased him as best I could, But he plotted revenge, For the infidelity. He mocked me, he humiliated me, He lied to me, But to the outside world, I was none the wiser, Playing the foolish old woman. He deserved pain and death, To feel what it is like to be betrayed. I logged on, Using my few cyber skills, And managed to snatch a vial of cyanide. Tonight we will have the talk, And I will pretend to forgive him, For my aged body, And my face that has lost its youth, And when the authorities come, They will not know the truth, He will have a heart attack in his bed, His head on his pillow, Dead. His heart, feeling how it feels, To be crushed, The heartless idiot, dead, Gone for good. But the police have arrived: They have discovered what I did, Even though I told a story, I shall now rot in prison, My husband’s body, cold in the ground, And I shall reflect on the hate, Which ruined our marriage.

A bright summer sun shone brightly; emerald-green fields, waving trees, soft breezes; above, the purest blue sky; all around, bright flowers of loveliest hue. Allured the beholder’s eyes. But what were all these charms to me, when one sweet breath of remembrance, gently wafted, When I could think of nothing but a flower, a primrose, Just about to open. Sweet Memory, ever-bright, Always smiling upon me; nature’s loveliest blooms have all their origins in you; Oh, do keep bringing your gifts! And keep the golden crocus, a heavenly flower, The pride of the spring. And linger still, enwrapped in the scent of the lily, The flower of my childhood. And give a little daisy its little smile, And fill the bright goblet of the buttercup With all the old vigor. Always let your dreamy charms still envelop the star of the mountain, The small bell of the heather; never let them fade in the frosty, glittering frost, And never depart from the ice-flowers, when snow and wind coax them. Is childhood a time of divinity? Or is it the splendor of memory that gilds the past? It is not all divine; though pain may have been fleeting, it was sweet while it lasted. Nor is it all your glory, For only our first joys are blessed with the ray of the blessed. No enchanting spell can rekindle later joys, though they have long since vanished.

We waited patiently, and at a quarter to one the whistle sounded. I looked at the others, drew breath. It was nearly time to go. The train drew nearer, and before me it loomed larger than life. It was the first time I had jumped on a coal-train and had got a free load of coal. We ran like lightning, jumped like the oath, climbed up on the roof of the car, and rushed down the line. With all our might we threw down the coal. Then we gathered it up and sold it in the town. The train came every day at a quarter to one; the first time I jumped off it was to be my last. Another true story from my boyhood in Sydney, Nova Scotia. We would jump off the coal-train to make a few cents, a very small gain. When I look back on it now, I see the danger of the game. The gain was not worth all that. A word to the young, stay out of harm’s way. Be honest and loyal. The coal-train was not for me, and it is not for you.

The dark warriors stood around the pyre, with scowls on their knotted brows. No one had to look at the sacrificial stakes and the ropes to know that they were about to perform an ugly, bloody deed. Yet, among those sin-stained men, could anyone have been wicked enough to attack the victim who stood helplessly bound? The girl was slender, fragile and childlike, but with the wise and sweet presence of a woman. O, how lovely that childlike face was! No one, even among the most beautiful European women, could have matched it. Her coral lips had never smiled with a more glorious, lustrous smile. Her eyes had never shone with a more charming light. Despite her helpless plight, she stood majestically and with dignity, a queen, although bound and pinioned. The sight of death, which could have shaken a stronger soul, did not remove the depth of her contempt from her brow, nor the color from her cheek. And yet it was not surprising that such a lofty, graceful air surrounded her, a princess of her own race. She knew that they had come to her to exact revenge for her name and to kill her by fire. But she had learned the hard lessons of childhood. She firmly resolved that no womanly tears, no pathetic weeping would impress her haters. Instead, as befitted her noble lineage and her family’s pride, she would die with her noble and courageous head held high. She prayed: “Hear me, Great One, Protector of my Race, Whom in the Land of Spirits I shall soon see face to face. “ Pour down on my tribe Thy blessings and let them rise to triumph, Above the guileful Iroquois, Thine and our foe. And give me strength to bear every pang with courage great and free, That I may be fit to reign, thy God, with Thee.” Then she was finished with her prayer, and again she assumed the attitude of a crowned queen. Then she turned away with an eye of scorn and an indignant air, and said to them: “Nay, don’t touch me! I’d rather be bitten by a venomous snake! My old father and all my tribe will soon learn with true pride That a child of the Huron race has fallen like their own chieftain’s daughter.” Then, with a laugh of contempt, she pushed aside her dark hair and, like a fawn, she leaped like a fawn on the dreadful funeral pile. And even while these bloody men were putting the torch to her, they were singing of her courage, her proud heart, and her majestic defiance.

So Sister, sing me a song, Sing me to sleep. Some song low and long, Slow as the summer song Of the deep and dumb. Some song long and low, Which creeps to and fro On the shaded borderline Between the soul's night and day Washing “awake” away into “sleep.” Some song low and long, Never so weak or strong As to let me go while it can hold my heart, Without any sigh or pain, Or to hold my heart when it sighs, "No. " A song low and long, As long as the swaying shadow. The shadow swaying to and fro. Through the crowing roosters, And by the swinging clocks, Some weary mother rocking her weary woes. Some song long and low, As low as the world's darkest day. So and so, up and down, Like the rocking of a dreamboat, Low and high, high and low, Now and then, then and now, And when the now is the now and the then is the now And when the low is the high and the high is the low, So and so, So and so. Glide, glide, glide, glide.

It is not surprising that happy people are popular, since all men desire happiness, and laughter spreads happiness. Only a heartless man will not like the sound of laughter; laughter is a happy sound. Only those who are heartless will not like laughter. Laughter is the only happiness in the world. If you are sad, your heart will be sad. Even friends will not come near you. The happy ones gather many friends. Laughter spreads and is heard, a thousand miles away, and the world laughs.

The skies are golden and the plains are bare; death and desolation are everywhere. The last year’s flood is only a pale ribbon on grey-black mud. Salt springs bubble, the mires shiver. This is the lament of the Darling River: I rise in drought from the rains of Queensland. I fill my tributaries again and again. I dam up the billabongs in vain. I make pretty islands and green glades, I turn drought-ravaged hollows into wave-lapping streams. But in vain I try, oh in vain I try to show the sign of the Great Water Giver, to be the word to a people: O, lock up your river! I do not want to be a steaming swamp with the barges of old; I want to be a rippling stream with boats on its waters, with a people’s love and praise, with pretty houses along my lonely paths, with people’s love and praise, with children in bathing suits, and pretty girls in the water. And cool, green groves and gardens for ever— this is the lament of the Darling River. The sky is brass, the bush is bare, death and desolation are everywhere. Thrown high to bleach, or deep in the mud, the bones from last year’s flood lie buried by this year’s flood, and the demons dance in the Never Never to laugh at the rise of the Darling River.

You – beautiful Medusa, your hair driven by the wind, red and flames, swaying on the crag of the mountain – I, too, like a pillar of stone. And your hair is still as flame, above your brow, the sun flares, your thoughts bursting like snakes from your mind – a fiery serpent of red thoughts, and a tiny box camera severs your head from your body. The camera and you, you – mythological, inaccessible, red-haired, a red river – I want to drown in the water of your hair. You have waterfalls over your shoulders, the flaming waves of your hair, tumbling down your hips and thighs and buttocks! My hands like fish swimming all over your body, soaked with the beauty of your hair, touching you, and touching you – the naked truth of you! You – naked and not, you wear the dress your hair weaves for you, you – magical, as if in a half-forgotten fairy tale. You undress, throwing your hair over your shoulders, and I come to you, as if obeying an enchantment, and you wrap me in your hair. Both our nakedness – we, in your hair, covered by your hair, in this refuge of kisses. A fellow poet – well, not really a fellow, because it was not a man – confessed that she, too, was red-haired. This homage to redheads came to me on the basis of this information. Memories and images return to me.

I can see the beauty of my life in a rainbow, and I can laugh and say “Ah,” because there is good reason for such a comparison, for my life is so rich in colors as is the rainbow, with its double row of colors. Burning red lights up my life, burning red, even though my life has been hard at times; it’s easy to find my way in the world – with the help of a little faith, like a ray of sunshine; It’s as if everything is yellow, like a huge lot of autumn flowers; Even though I am living in this recent century, I cannot help looking back, like a flower-colored, autumn-blossoming tree. Sometimes I feel so utterly alone, I’m reduced to weeping, so I may as well see that a rainbow may not be a rainbow, but I still can see its rays.

Then you began to weary of our tears, and with dazzling feet you led Belshazzar’s court in a tinkling dance along the dark street. They came bearing mead, chanting shame. In front of them flew the red flag of lust. And Istar’s music made your mouth move, and you remembered the ignominy of Baal. You could ride in the royal chariot, forgetting our people’s burden. You could sleep in silver beds—for all was bitter and dark in our house. And you could laugh many nights, unaware of my hopeless prayer, until the day when God’s spirit drove you away from Istar’s shrine. Then, beloved of Babylon—by the black Euphrates, near the stony flood—your beauty became more dear to me than my slave’s daily bread and my heart’s blood. We sang of Zion, the place of justice, where peace dwells. We sang: “Hold not your peace... I’ll hold you in my hands.” What were your other sins? Was it not the drinking at Belshazzar’s table? And how you laughed at my tears and spoke of your favorite slave—those who sewed cloth all day and night. You were a holy, humble maiden, tied to our labors. “Your God shall be mine until I sleep with the patriarchs,” you said one night. Forgive me, daughter of Babylon, if this night—when our lover strolls beneath the walls of our hanging gardens—my broken hopes return to me, my memories of your friendship—until I curse your painted eyes and cause your flower-mouth to die.

You, the poems I did not write, you are my children, my lost ones. Born in a stillborn birth, never to be known, never to be brought to the dais. Why has fate been so cruel to you? Blocks are quarried, quarried, broken stones. Where are the fine, flawless marbles, the sculptured, pure stones? Often scattered, crumbling and rotting in the bedrock. Lament, lament, lament for all my lost children. Cheated so often by birth, those of noble lineage. The pain of the lost one strikes a dissonant, shrill note. The ransom has been paid with an excessive price. A body is incomplete, it has lost the ethereal. Lost beyond the reach of the search, the ethereal never to be retrieved. In the night of the unripe day ideas slip away. A journey at the brink of distance becomes painful. Post-mortems are meaningless. Consider the opportunity and the time available. Did we achieve anything worth noting? Thoughts have stayed as a lifeline to those unborn. How toiling, time was used to create with a honed skill. Patience, the older we get, the harder we work. Tools of the highest quality are used. To see that which is of such great potential wasted. Discarded. Fallen. Drifted away. Withered, shrivelled, shriveled and dried up. Precision is lost, vanished into a void. A rebirth has to begin in the new day. The artist has gone away leaving the gates of his heart open. Who will come in to pick up his chisel? (Terence George Craddock, copyright, http://poemhunter.com/terence-george-craddock/)

Frank, thou wilt not live unhappily. Trust not too much in the heaving sea; Thy star, calculated by sure event, look on the gleaming face of the sea. Yet set up your rest here and take your place, And build your fortunes on calm and pleasant fields. Do thou lie still, thou Frank, and make as little noise as its inhabitants, as the untrusting deep, nay, stand firm as if there were a newfound land, fit for colonization. Till terror wakes thy senses and thou shalt see Thyself a fragile game for the wind; And thou tost in thy loose thetis’ cloaks. Frank, what art thou doing to thyself? Be not too sure, thou Frank, of a shore: For even that, since now the wisest know (and that, ow, to Galileo’s judgment) That the paltry shore is every jot as frail, inconstant, shifting as that blot We lay on the sea that sometimes lies under its own bottom. But this eternal wheel of Ixion, strange and oblivious, Never leaves the reeling earth to stand until all things are turned about, till they are Turned back to that ancient confused state they were. Who lovest the golden mean, needs a thorny cobweb, old and broken; a castle where snakes and moths feed on their food-reeds; a toy, we may (true) call a mistress, whose eyes and feathers weigh them all; And cloaks that larks would wrest from him in the sun, Which mock him in the night, when his turn is run. To raise a building so high that envy’s eye will not reach it, nay, not even a thought, thou should build low. Thou wouldst know how such a structure should be raised. For an imperious top can’t fall; And in proud turrets, ’tis the imperial top that won’t fall. Nor doth the lurching storms of the invisible wind shake the bravest, propulsive oak: And that high-soaring mountain-foot He strikes with lightning; The humblest hollow is struck by His lightning. A firm breast withstands all shocks of fate; Fears in the best, hopes in the worser; Heaven forbid that time ever have, as of old, ever thrive in the inverse Spring. Aeolus has his Zephyr and his Boreas, too; It’s a false inferential, soloecism against the aphorisms Fortune has given us to believe That just because it’s bad, it’s bound to be so, Apollo does not always bow; And often, uncrowned by His divine light, With his quiet harp, He wakes the sleeping Nine. Why dost thou despair, Frantz? Great in hope, yet, for thy fate, Fear, too, can’t be too small. Pull in thy sails, though no storm threatens thy ruin. Tell me, pray, what’s the difference, ’twixt a stormy sky and a too-hailable day?

This candid age was only able to tell by itself that it was ingenious. That candid age knew only how to make a man's praise sublime, and it was the highest praise to give than to carry the bays: then the modest ambition only sought to honor itself and worthy people. These virtues have been banished from the city, our civil wars have lost the civic crown. He builds the highest who destroys the most artfully, and who employs his fame against another's. I see the envious caterpillar sitting on the pretty flower of every growing wit. The air is already poisoned by swarms of insects rising up against you: tommies de mots, paper rats, book scorpions, Sons of a stale wit. The bearded censers begin to look like the black congregation at your book, and on each line they cast a reforming eye, stricter than the young priesthood. And when they have read you in vain, you will be accused of being without fault. Some who read your Lucèstaines, will say that you have violated the privileges of the house. Some will say that you are under a restraint, and others that the book prohibits them because they sent their petition by the author. But when the pretty ladies found out that their dearest Lovelace was threatened, the one who thawed the most iced heart, the one who loved the most, and who defended the most, whose hand clumsily grasped the steel brand, whose hand so gently melted the lady's hand, they all, in a mutiny, although they were still undressed, were going to fight for his defense. And one, the prettiest who had ever been seen, thinking that I was also betrayed, my eyes invaded with a woman's spite, (she knew what pain it would cause to lose this sight): "O no, do not make a mistake, I would die for you or for him. " But he, sure of his glory and of his time, climbs above the envy and the aid of me. You will find him surrounded by the beautiful and the brave, his book is loved by them, and by you he is loved.
Equal power carries the struggle on. The seabed of the universe is carried along by a field. The center of gravity is borne along with the rotation of the stars.

Because life is a river of ordinary moments, one moment blending into the next, it is not possible to escape from the fate which dissolves every wave of the river into the ordinary, and I can only wish for a mild and easy well-being as I travel in my small canoe along the ever-flowing current of the everyday. The ordinary, then, is so beautiful that I wonder if it is called that; and yet it is the ordinary, because it is quiet and unnoticed, a man who selects oranges at the market, a woman taking a bath, a child playing in the grass in the back garden, all the people in the street who simply walk along. There is no one who stands above another, this river is perfectly democratic; every thrill and intoxication flows downriver, and later, perhaps, as well as grief and loss, but that seems harder, the void seems to last longer before the water fills it. No one is illustrious for the ordinary, it is unimpressed. The ordinary is the true wife of every man, the true husband of every woman. One returns to it from all journeys, and it is everything that one really needs. It was just as though everything were being separated from everything else. I felt the walls of my “I” beginning to solidify, separating me from everything, like the butterfly that sits on a branch in the sun, waiting for its wings to dry and the chitin to harden after its emergence from the chrysalis, ready then to buzz and die, and I answer the voices, “No, thank you,” and I say to the hands that tug: “No, thank you.” I do not want to be snatched out of the ordinary current to some pinnacle or tower, only to have to climb or fall back down again; I do not want to be so special, I want to run out of thoughts in my head and empty my mental treasury of thoughts and not have any more put in their place, I want to disappear and become that river into which all distinct drops are lost, and then the ocean into which all the rivers flow and die.

All night long, Lyca’s parents walked—through gullies and nooks; they walked tired and downcast. As desarts cried, hoarse with moaning: they spent seven days walking in the desert. For seven nights they slept. In darkness, in shadow, they dreamt of their child, hungry and famished in the wild desart. Her pale apparition wandered through the desert’s dim, shadowy gloom; and in the morning, weak and sickly, she cried out from anguish, with a hollow, pitiful cry. Rising from unrest, the trembling woman ran; with feet heavy with suffering, she could go no further. And her husband, with sad, sobbing arms, bore her along. He carried her in his arms until he reached a resting lion. Turning back, they were in the hands of the beast. He struck them to the ground. Then he turned to them. He scented his prey, but their fears were dispelled when he licked their hands, and stood there in silence. And they looked into his eyes, full of surprise, and they beheld, marvelling: a spirit, clad in gold. A crown on his head; from his temples hung his golden locks. They were struck dumb. Their troubles were dispersed. Follow me, he said, and do not weep for the girl; she is asleep in my mighty palace. And they walked, in the footsteps of the apparition, and they saw their sleeping child, among tiger cubs. Until now, they have lived in a desolate nook, untroubled by the howl of the wolf, nor the growl of the lion.

It seems the church is in a mess; that is nothing new, Every day it sees itself getting smaller, but what to do? Let the children express their opinions. Let wisdom guide them, 1 Tim. 4:11. Be careful that no one confuses them, Prov. 18: 2. They are quick to see when something is new And they show it when they’ve learned To restrain them would be absurd, Matt. 19:14. It could lead to a deep division. What is to stop them from running amok? What makes them well-behaved? The King of kings sees it clearly, So on paper, black on white, 1 Cor. 14:26. He wrote that all the saved must proclaim the truth, the good news of Christ, Mt. 28: 18–20, that all must partake of His salvation, Exod. 18:17–26, that the truth is not just for one. That all can help to hone the plowshares, Prov. 27:17, and dig into the ground, 1 Cor. 9:10. Don’t silence the lips that cry out, not for a moment, Don’t shut off my Spirit, 1 Tim. 5:19, That you, who come to me to seek my face, Grow, expand, develop...

My window shows the fleeting clouds, the spent leaves, the altered sky, the crowds coming and going; the whole world passes by. They don’t waste their measured hours, but men and masters plot and build; I see the towers crowned, and promises kept. And I, if my intent could count on the prediluvian age, the efforts I should have expended would have been accomplished; but now before the crucible glistens with undiscovered gold, the bellows will no longer blow, and the furnace will turn cold. It’s too late now to remedy my helplessness and my cumbersome shame, which renders me, when I am with other people, more powerless than a blind man or a cripple. No, I would not love the city more than my unrequited learning; I would prefer the wilds or the landslide beach. I go up to my windy belvedere To look at the low or levanting sun, I see the city pigeons swirl, I watch the swallows go from the towers to the ground, from the towers to the sky. Then I spot something on the horizon, and I hunger to be there. Then I hate the most any knowledge which gives no promise of success. And I love the houseless shore, and the free and forgiving wilds. Ancient mounds hiding bones, rocks where cliff swallows rest, and stone trees, and silence, and a wide air. There, on a long, level height, I would lie down After sunset, and stare into the yellow, waxen light with long, free gaze, before I die.

swimming away, swimming away, yes swimming through the deep blue sea, nothing but red skies in front, so put on your hat, sun-screen and suntan lotion, feel the wind and the waves moving. Let's go swimming in your mind's ocean. The water so calm and the breeze so sweet No cause for alarm, but you're dead to the world in your sleep, Not a soul in sight, not a worry in the world, just an open sea where you can simply be.

The flower in the glass jam-jar, which had formerly stood in the kitchen, bent to take a place in the light; the wardrobe door opened because I had used it before, and remained kindly open, awaiting its owner. I began to feel miserable as I lay on the pallet listening to the music; miserable, because that is what makes me want to sing. The room was closing in upon me, I awaited the coming of the Divine Creator, I beheld my walls and ceiling in grey paint; they enclosed my room, they enclosed me, as the sky enclosed my garden, I opened my door; the climbing vine was twining round the cottage-post, the leaves at night were still where the day had laid them, the animal heads of the flowers where they had risen to think of the sun. The gracious desire to grow, the gracious desire to exist of the flowers, my ecstasy at being among them, you must seek the sun, too. Will the thought of recording cloud my mind's open eye? My books awaiting me in the place where I have placed them, they are not gone; time has left me its fragments and the quality of its qualities for my use—my words, my texts, my manuscripts, my love. For a moment I was clear, I beheld the emotion at the heart of things, I went out into the garden crying.
