I beheld the red blossoms in the night, the sun is gone, they were already there, grown, caught up in time, awaiting the day, awaiting the sun, which they would not know until it came, but which I would faithfully water in the evening, in a dream, without them knowing how I loved them. I am so lonely in my glory—except them, too, out there; I looked up, there were the red bushes and the flowers which beckoned to me from the window, waiting, love, blind; their leaves also with hope, they too looked up, flat up to the sky to receive it—all creation, the whole flat earth, it would seem, open to receive it. Music descends, as does the long stem of the heavy blossom, because it must, to live, to draw out its last drop of joy. The world knows the love which is in its breast as it is in the heart of the flower, the lonely, suffering world. The Father is merciful. The ceiling is old, the socket has been nailed to it, after the house was built, for the purpose of holding a sconce, and my gramophone now stands on it. The door to the pantry is open, I left it open, it is merciful to be open, should I wish to enter the kitchen. —I remember when I first was married. HP graciously took my cherry, I sat on Provincetown's piers at the age of twenty-three, joyful, full of hope, and the door of the womb was open, I could go in, if I wished. There are sockets in the rooms all over the house, but they are not used. I don't have the money to have them wired. The telephone—it is very sad—it is on the floor—I haven't had the money to have it wired up. I want people to bow to me, when they see me, and say: he has seen the presence of the Creator. And the Creator granted me a touch of His presence to grant my wish, not to rob me of my desire for Him.

“That’s the place for a snark!” the bellman cried, as he carefully landed his crew. He lent a hand to each man as he stepped onto the shore; each one had a finger curled in his hair. “I’ve said it twice: That should inspire the crew. “I’ve said it thrice: Anything I tell you three times is true!” The crew was complete. There was a bootmaker, a hatter, a milliner, a broker, a lawyer to settle their disputes, and a billiard player who might have won more than his share, but a banker was entrusted with their cash. There was also a sailor who sat on the deck or made lace on the bow, and who, the bellman claimed, had saved them many times, though the sailors didn’t know how. One of the men was famous for forgetting things when he boarded: his umbrella, his watch, all his jewels and rings, and the clothes he’d bought for the trip. He had forty-two well-packed boxes with his name on each one; but since he’d failed to inform anyone, he’d left them all on the shore. He could have come in a dozen clothes: He’d worn seven coats and three pairs of boots; but the worst thing was that he had forgotten his name. “He’d answer to any call, even “Bang bang!” or “Bang bang my head!” And especially “Bang bang!”” the bellman exclaimed. And for those who preferred a more memorable name, His friends called him “Shotgun” And his enemies “Toasty.” “He’s ugly, and not too bright,” the bellman would say. “But he has courage. That’s the only thing you can say about Snark.” He’d quarrel with hyenas, mocking them and shaking his head, And he’d walked paw-in-paw with a bear, “Just to keep it happy,” he told them. The bellman was driven to distraction, He came as a baker, but he confessed too late— Which drove the poor bellman half mad— That he could only bake wedding cakes, for which, let me say, They didn’t have the supplies. And the last of the men was an incredible idiot; He had only one idea—but since that one was “Snark,” the bellman had quickly made him his assistant. He’d come as a butcher, but after the ship had sailed for a week, he said solemnly: He could only kill beavers. It was impossible to find a beaver. The bellman’s beaver—there was one—was the only one, The bellman’s very own pet, Whose death would cause a great deal of distress. The beaver, who’d overheard this, said that it couldn’t take it—that Even hunting Snark could not erase the pain of this surprise. It advised the butcher to take his own ship. But the bellman insisted that that would never do With the plans he had already made for the voyage: Navigating was a difficult matter, Even though it was a one-ship affair, And he really could not undertake a second ship. The beaver’s best course was, no doubt, to get A secondhand coat against daggers— As the baker suggested—and then insure its life: the baker offered to sell it, Or to rent it, At very reasonable rates, Two wonderful policies, One for fire and one for hail. But ever since that dreadful day, When the butcher was near, The beaver kept looking away, With no apparent reason.

The blue crow stands on the apple tree stake, he is ignoring the cold wind of this cold morning, and does not even stir his tail. When he turns his head towards me, I look at his eyes without blinking. A week ago, my wife called me over to watch this crow chase a rat into the thick leaves of an orange tree. We watched it up close, and saw the rat digging its claws into an orange, then its face buried in it, then smearing the juice with its paws. After looking at its white belly and open and defenseless position, I suggested that we get our.22 rifle. She asked: “Want to shoot him?” But I didn’t. There are oranges for him, the jays, and us. On the other side of the fence in the neighboring yard, oranges are rotting on the ground. There is a dread in the name “rat”, perhaps a dread that is personal. As a child, hearing the tales of savagery, about how the rat had half-eaten sleeping people and children before they could wake up, I became acquainted with this dread. It was as if this animal, which was alive, had become enormous and powerful from its need to eat human flesh. But I was mistaken. Every night I wake up to a dream of a city, a wonderful, splendid city, and I realize that this city is the very same city that I had thought was lost when I lost the faith that someday I would reach that world. The wind blows, and it dies, swaying the stake-apple tree, which in three months has taken root in the hard clay of our front yard. In a single leap, the crow turns its back on me and takes wing.

All girls at some point have fallen victim to Cinderella's spell. And then, of course, there are dreams and fantasies, But it is by no means always the case that they come true. She envisioned herself with a stepmother and stepdaughters who would abuse her cruelly; But then a fairy godmother appeared and she became the most beautiful girl in the world. In a gorgeous dress, in glass slippers, she rushed out to the ball. She thought the prince would see her and think her the prettiest of them all. And then she would dance with the prince, enchanted, Knowing their love would come true after the kiss they would share. But midnight struck, and the carriage changed back into a pumpkin, But she knew the ending of the fairytale, She knew her dream would not come true. She had no glass slipper, And the shoe no longer fit, And her dream of being the prince's adored, was only a counterfeit. But young girls dream on, not knowing that the prince and the glass slipper are never real.

Sleep flies me like a lover, Too eagerly pursued, Or like a bird in hiding, In some distant forest, Where the thickest boughs shade Her most secret rest. The nets I have laid to catch her, Although they are cunningly made, Only frightened her, And now she dares not be caught. To those who best can get her, She comes ungraciously. She flutters at their pillows; She gives them sweet dreams, The bluish-green of willow leaves, The cool murmuring of brooks, Or vast billows rolling, On which the starlight falls. No enchanting vision Enters my weary eye; No wonderful stories Make night swiftly pass; Only feverish fancies Beset my slumbering mind. The black midnight steeps The slopes and lawns, But I lie still not sleeping, And I draw back the curtains, To see the first hint of my desired dawn. Maybe when the sun rises, When the birds have begun to sing, And I, weary with night’s wakefulness, call out to them to hush their shrill notes, Sweet sleep may have pity on me, And come in at last.

The evil that men do. It’s coming to a town near you, For we, the men, are coming to get you. Tortured beliefs, Living on a knife-edge, A desire for the erotic, A craving so great, it seems unsatisfiable, The basic instinct of man, Has not changed in all this time, Society has tried to suppress, Laws have tried to contain, This world that we live in, Is so full of pain, The worst brought about by men, The act of war. Men push the buttons for your son to die for, But no one ever takes the time to think about what war really means. We read about war, But never stop to think that death is a man’s best friend, And driven to the end, Pushed to the limit, The screams inside a man’s mind can never be heard. Sending him into that darkness, Like a child, Holding his favorite toy, He stares about. His big, blue eyes, Once blue, Now forever set in black. After tasting death, cast down from on high, Dumped back into society after the job is done, And you expect him to be the same? After living the life of a madman...

For weeks and weeks the autumn world stood still, cloaked in the shadow of a smoky haze. The fields were dead, the wind had lost its will, and all the world was silent, over hill and hill, during those withering days. Sixbehind a cloud the grey sun hung, Sevenat night the moon nestled in a cloud; Eighta ghost-fisherman cast his net; Ninea the lake forgot to shriek and whirl, and hushed its noiseless cavern. Else the birds were silent in the smoky woods, except for a jay, or a lonely toad, piping for water, while in the depths of a bog a toad trilled in his dream. On a day like this the tawny sun went down, leaving the heavens bathed in a rosy glow. Red were the fields and dry, parched meadows, Red were the creeks stealing through the bogs. Not a breath of wind. Suddenly it felt like winter was in my veins. I felt a tremble of icy warmth. I woke up and heard the wild vibration of the North Wind.

The Moshuka is a torrent of gentle joy, of shimmering sun and opal skies; of warm midsummer air, light and murmuring, in a thousand, thousand circles, which swing in soft a-folksong that has a sadness in it. As a tiny fern swayed, nearing the brink, a green reflection greeted it. Its touch was so subtle, and the very edge of the boundary of their vision was indistinct, and the fusion of the two was so perfect. A thousand firs, so far, on the hills of brown grass, and old elms, leaning, with moss-covered trunks, a hundred feet above, their semblance mirrored beneath them, and the ripples didn’t even make a shadow. There was a double-edged beauty to it: land, strength, beauty, might – nothing of all that would bend, nor was there anything I could do with it; and then the shadow, ah, all the shadow – to make it or mar it – to dip a paddle in it, and have it, all mine, as long as I live. Oh, it is all a beautiful lake! Oh, my own pathless life! The great ideal, more mine than the real one ever was! For others, fame, and the red flame of love, and gold. For me, the shadows and dreams.

In my first sleep I reached the river, I looked into the limpid water—nothing so pure, frothing, tumbling over the stones; a clean brook, not found in reality; a brook that rolled on forever. A house lay there, by the river, and I had come there, a visitor, about to explore the old gardens and the book-laden rooms, but the car was waiting to carry me away. On its rocky bed, living water writhing in spirals, tumbling straight ahead. There was the car to take me away; we crossed the river, the living water, I couldn’t stay, I had to go back along the path too short, to the waking day. In my second dream I was free, pure and open, by the torrent. I threw into the water a bottle, clear glass, a sphere that rolled and twisted in the whirlpool of the torrent, and caught on the current, my crystal form, joyfully caught on the flashing water.

Some governments execute drug traffickers after they have served a long prison sentence. Their idea of morality is justice; but when it comes to actions, they fall short of their own ideas. If you deliberately take someone’s life, it’s murder, and the death penalty is murder, too. To order the execution of another human being is very callous and heartless. To order the execution of someone’s child after years of incarceration doesn’t make you a good person. Let the guilty ones age out in prison.

And that he was trying to make her happy, You awoke before her, and it all went by in a haze; I sneered at her and put a cigarette in my mouth, and told her that I had been in the south six times, and that I liked the countryside in this part of the country, where life is simple, and technological changes are rare. You said you were no longer a fan of this country, because the city of Atlanta had spread out and was poisoning your life, You resigned yourself to the fact that the dog barks worse than that, but said welcome to Georgia, but said it anyway. I told her I was from Amarillo, that the cops are bad, and the democrats are yellow. You grinned and said: 'They're worse, but they're not as bad as yer,' You added: 'Still, welcome to Georgia.'After coffee we went for a walk in the park, which was quiet and peaceful, and the dogs were not barking. You accepted the compliment of this young man without complaint, but you did close your eyes; he kissed you quite unexpectedly, but you didn't seem to mind, closing your eyes, then kissed her, which surprised her a little, but you didn't mind at all, closing your eyes;

Success is a word that means a lot to a lot of people. To be called a success is to be said to have “made it,” but the question is “made it” in what? By passing a test? By becoming a landlord? By winning the lottery? By marrying the woman of one’s dreams? By marrying the man of one’s dreams? By being in an administrative position? By winning an election? How does one define success? Can one be a success as a pilot or a flight attendant? How would you define the word success? By being a success in business? By being rich? By being a success as a soldier? By being a success as a policeman? What is your definition of success? Are you a success if you’re a writer, a teacher, a minister, a cab driver, a member of parliament, a doctor, a mechanic, a film star, or a director? Are you a success if you’re an architect, a builder, or a banker? Success is in the eye of the beholder. Success is a very subjective thing.

A poem is like a life. A poem that has been destined to make history is itself destined to become history by a mysterious incident, a tragedy which is in many ways the reverse of the poet’s intention. A dear poem, which I had written, has evaporated in the air, and I have no way of rescuing it. I have lost it in my folly, not having copied it in advance. This, my friend, has been the occasion of some bitter questions which are resounding in my mind, hard to answer. My dear, I have resolved to pay for your loss, and I confess that you have left me, but I shall always remember you in the hard disk of my memory. —— O my friend!

What will I write to her this year? Will it be a poem about the childhood I remember? Will it appear in the local papers in December? “If you have a mother still, sir...” and “a tiny bug smiling at her,” and “a boy in Lederhosen?” Yes, memories are never far away, they never fade or die. Something has left a little scar, and like a hiccup comes a sigh. A rose bush patiently waits for life to come to it, and the petals are there for love, and the thorns always stand at its side. Now that she is showing the signs of age, her hand still rests on your heart. She holds life by the hand, and what she is about to do is more science than art. There is a strong thread of love that binds you to your mother, you may know it—your love and her tears. The whelp is slain for human greed; the mother mourns in her despair. The fur will be used to satisfy a need, and no one will ask what becomes of the mother. A child, still young and full of vigor, falls ill and dies; the message is delivered to her in a dream; she wakes up and her nervous humming is still heard. Mothers, let me tell you, my friend, will bear burdens that would crush the strongest of men. And still she will be there when you wake up.

“I was reclining, sleeping like a log. I remember, I cry, and cry with great pain. I rise up from the bed where I was sleeping, so bereft of spirit, that I couldn’t hold my head up. My passsion was so great, that I didn’t even know myself. With me was death, to keep me company. What was more difficult was not that I was dying, but that I was failing to serve the one I was to serve.” —I was serving a lady who wanted me more than I wanted her. She was the cause of my inveterate suffering. That middle of the night, ya que era acerca del da, I got up from my lodging to see if I could get some sleep. I went to where she was living, whom I wanted more than anything, whom I wept for, though she didn’t heed me. And walking about, all dislocated from the anguish I was in, I saw my lady coming toward me, and I declaimed: ‘Si dormis, linda seora, remember with courtesy that you were the cause of my distress. Remedy my great anguish, satisfy my despondency, for if I should have been denied that, I would have lost everything.’ And with my eyes full of tears, I was weeping inconsolably, with sobs erupting all over me, and no one else felt anything like it. Having reached my lodging, as I could see it was getting light, I returned home, sobbing, without joy.

When the foeman of France, with his fiery torch, his cruel sword, his drums blaring, comes to ravage her, I curse him and his plundering host! And what is gained by us assuming the costume of woe? Let’s be merry, and in laughter we can win something from the foe! Oh, many a valiant man is trembling. I (a coward) do not tremble. When Bacchus sends his blessing, comrades, I drown my trepidation in his wine. Come, gather round my humble board, and let the sparkling wassail run down your throats, rejoicing at the thought, as you drink: ‘This much have we won from the foe!’ My creditors so oppressed me, and made my lodgings so constrained, that I was ready to take them to the point of payment; when the news of this invasion came, as you know; I will not pay my debts; lend me some more, and I will keep it from the foe! My mistress is a pretty lascivious lady, who pretends to be terrified by this military noise, but she, that crafty wretch, would love to meet those soldiers! I tell her they are rough and uncouth; but I feel she does not believe me; but never mind, if she is good-natured, I have gained something from the foe! If, comrades, hope has in store no friendly looks for us, let us die rather than greet the foe of France; but, like the swan who sings as it dies, let us go singing away to our end; then our song, as we near death, will be so much won from the foe!

From the banquet room at dinner, after his supper, he sat down to work with more intensity. He examined the box of dried yeast in his hand, and saw that it was well used, but as the packet was cracked into the water, he poured a little of it into a small bowl. He took the yeast, mixed it into the flour, and added it to the dough. He turned the dough out onto a floured worktop, sprinkled baking soda over it, and kneaded lightly (about two minutes). Then he placed it in a large bowl, which he greased with cooking oil, and turned the top to coat it. Cover and let stand in a warm place (about 80 ° F, free from drafts) for one hour, or until doubled in bulk. He poured dry sherry and half a cup of water into a medium-sized saucepan, brought to a boil, and covered, reduced heat, and simmered for twenty-five minutes, or until the chicken was tender. Take the chicken out of the broth, and let it cool. Set aside one cup of broth and let it cool completely. Discard the remaining broth. Then remove the chicken from the bones and cut into small pieces. Stir half a cup of broth with cornstarch, set aside. Heat 2 tsp oil in a medium non-stick skillet over medium heat. Add onion and cook for three minutes, stirring constantly, until tender. Add curry powder, ginger, and garlic and cook for thirty seconds, stirring constantly. Add broth mixture and bring to a boil. Cook for one minute, stirring constantly. Then remove from heat and stir in chicken and salt, set aside. Squeeze down dough and turn out onto a lightly floured worktop. Divide into fourteen equal pieces. Divide one piece of dough at a time (cover remaining dough to keep from drying out) and roll into a four-inch circle. Spoon one and a half tablespoons of chicken filling in the middle of each piece. Fill with a small amount of vegetable filling and close by pinching edges to seal. Cover and let stand for forty-five minutes, or until puffed but not doubled in bulk. Place seam side down, in a greased seven-inch round steamer. Cover with lid and bring one inch of water to a boil in a large pot. Lower steamer into the pot and steam for fifteen minutes. Give a quick rinse and drain well. Note: If you want to bake the buns, preheat oven to 350 ° F. Place seam side down on a baking sheet that has been sprayed with nonstick cooking spray. Then brush with egg and water mixture and bake for 18 minutes. The baking makes the buns crunchier, and steaming makes them more moist and a little sticky.

1 tablespoon butter or oil. Two large leeks, washed and thinly sliced. One pound of sweet potatoes, usually one, and one pound of parsnips, if they are small. 12 teaspoon coarse salt. 14 teaspoon white pepper. Grate on the large side of a grater and place in a large bowl. (If you do not have the patience to grate by hand, you can also use the shredder of a food processor. But put a third of the contents of the bowl into the food-processor with the knife and grind it a few times.) Add salt, pepper, nutmeg, feta, egg, and matzo meal, and mix well. Add the boiled leeks. Pour the oil, enough to fill a saucepan to a depth of 12 inch, in a saucepan - if you don't have another pan, but if you want to work quickly, also use the one you boiled the leeks in - over a medium flame until it gets hot - when you drop a piece of latkes, it should bubble. This, hold out about three tablespoons of the mixture in a round shape (I like to fill a fourth cup and squeeze it in), and then place it in the oil. Flatten it a little to form a small pancake, and do this as many times as you have room in the pan. Do this for five to seven minutes, then turn over and cook on the other side. Latkes are more delicate than normal potato pancakes, especially warm ones, so be gentle. When cooked on the other side, remove and place on a plate lined with brown paper, and arrange as needed. Take out the crumbs that have fallen into the oil now and then and keep them from burning. Or... For those who do not eat immediately, put the cooled latkes in a closed container and spread them out on paper and freeze. When you want to serve them, preheat the oven to 375 degrees, put the latkes on a baking sheet - if you like, put them on a grill above the sheet, for me, this is not necessary - and bake until they turn brown and sizzle for ten to fifteen minutes.

This is a recipe I got from: 8 cups of low-fat, reduced-sodium chicken stock; 2 cups water; 3 and a half pounds boneless, skinless chicken breasts (I used frozen); 1 large yellow onion, quartered; 1 bunch of washed and stemmed fresh coriander; 6 garlic cloves, peeled; 2 whole serrano peppers (stems and seeds removed if desired to reduce heat, see Note); 1 can Ro-tel (crushed tomatoes with green chilies) 1 can tomato sauce; 1 tin (15 ounces) chopped tomatoes. In the large soup pot, heat the chicken broth, the water and the chicken breasts slowly. Then add the onion, coriander, garlic, peppers, Ro-tel and blend them until they are completely mashed. Then, once the chicken is cooked, i.e. no longer pink inside, remove it from the broth and keep it aside. Then pour the spicy mixture from the food processor into the broth and simmer. Add the tomato sauce, the tomato paste, the cumin, salt and pepper and simmer, stirring occasionally. Once the tomato paste has dissolved, in a small bowl or cup, add the cornstarch and stir until completely dissolved. Add the cornstarch-water mixture to the soup and stir until it is boiling. Then, shred the chicken breasts. You can do this with forks (and a helper), but I prefer to use the grater attachment of the food processor. Then I shred three and a half pounds of chicken breasts in two minutes! And turn the heat down to the lowest setting. Add the shredded chicken, then add the tin of corn and cook until heated through. Add the chopped coriander, the chopped tomato, the sour cream and sprinkle some grated cheese on top and serve with corn chips or corn bread. The leftovers are wonderful, the taste develops even more over time. This soup also freezes well. Note: Serrano peppers can be very hot. Two peppers were enough for me. My husband loves it when I use two large or medium peppers. So, you can use the peppers that are appropriate for you.

5 lbs. of ribs, boned or without, 1 sweet onion, chopped, 2 cloves garlic, 2 tsp. chili-powder, 1 tsp. coriander, 1 tsp. cumin, 1 tsp. paprika, hot, piquant, 1 tsp. oregano, 1 tsp. thyme, 1 tsp. paprika, 1 tsp. paprika, pimento-hot (or pimento-hot paprika, smoked), 3 tbsp. mashed pumpkin, 2 mugs of stout beer, 1 mug of espresso coffee, 1 ounce unsweetened chocolate or cocoa, 1 tbsp. cornmeal mixed with 12 cup hot water, 1 28-ounce can tomatoes, 1 15-ounce can black beans, 1 28-ounce can tomato puree, 1 15-ounce can black beans, 1 28-ounce can tomatoes, 1 15-ounce can black beans, 1 28-ounce can of stewed tomatoes, 1 15.5-ounce can black beans, 1 15.5-ounce can black beans, 1 28-ounce can tomatoes, 1 15.5-ounce can black beans, 1 15.5-ounce can smashed beans, 12 ounce salt, 12 tsp. brown sugar, a little hot sauce, jalapeno ring, sour cream, grated cheese, and chopped parsley. The ribs season with salt and pepper. Then put together in a little bowl the chili-powder, coriander, cumin, thyme, oregano, and smoked paprika. Start heating the oil in a large saucepan over medium heat. In this, in several batches if necessary, brown the ribs all over on both sides and transfer them to a large platter. Add the onion to the oil and stir it about. * Cook for about 4 minutes, or until it’s nicely browned, then stir in the garlic and let it cook for about half a minute. Add the tomato paste, the soy sauce, the Maggi seasoning, and the chili-powder and spice mixture. Stir for a minute and pour in one and a half bottles of beer; drink the other one. (You should end up with about 16 to 18 ounces of beer.) Add the coffee, the chocolate, the mashed pumpkin, and the tomatoes. Bring to a boil, stirring from time to time, then add the browned ribs and simmer, covered, in a slow oven, for about three and a half hours, or until the meat is tender. * Stir in the black beans and brown sugar and continue cooking, uncovered, for about 30 minutes, or until the pumpkin is tender. Let the ribs cool until you can handle them. * When they are cool enough to handle, cut the meat from the bones. Use two forks to break up the meat and return it to the sauce. Season with salt to taste. Serve the stew in bowls and garnish with hot sauce, grated cheese, sour cream, sliced jalapeno, and chopped parsley, or any combination you like.

Food: 7 tbsp. rice, 255g of peeled, unpeeled ginger 4 tbsp. water, put the rice in a heavy 4-litre saucepan and add enough water to cover it by 1in. Stir the rice with your hand 8 to 10 times around, then leave it for a minute, and then carefully drain off the milky water. This will remove some of the starch from the rice. Then add the dashi and the ginger, and bring it to a boil over a high heat. Cover the pan halfway, and then lower the heat to a strong simmer. The rice should be cooked in gently bubbling water, without boiling over the sides of the pan, for about 5 minutes. Stir the rice gently so that it doesn’t stick to the bottom of the pan, then lower the heat to a gentle simmer, and continue to simmer for 1 hour, or until the rice is cooked, and the liquid has turned a milky white and thickened slightly. There shouldn’t be much difference between the rice and the liquid. Stir the rice well so that it is evenly dispersed in the liquid. Discard the ginger and spring onion. Taste and add salt, adjusting the amount according to your preference and the type of stock you have used. Then this is a soup base that can be seasoned with various flavourings. This can be made a day in advance, and heated over a medium heat, with a little water to prevent it sticking, or you can leave it in the refrigerator overnight. It may get thick after cooling, so you can dilute it with water. After you have made the soup, don’t boil it, or it may burn.

One table-spoonful of olive oil, one sliced leek (about one big onion), two teaspoonfuls of minced garlic, half a teaspoonful of dry oregano, three-quarters of a teaspoonful of salt, one-quarter of a teaspoonful of red pepper flakes, one-eighth of a teaspoonful of black pepper, a cupful of spinach, thawed, squeezed dry, one skin-less, boneless chicken breast, cut into four pieces, and trimmed of the fat; four medium chicken breasts, cut into four pieces, each with a rib. In a medium-hot frying pan, heat the oil and when it is hot, add the leek, the garlic, the oregano, the salt, the red pepper and the pepper; cook and stir until the leek is limp, about five minutes. Remove from heat and add the spinach, stir until well blended. Add the chicken, cut in half horizontally and rubbed in the salt and the pepper, and then place the bottom of the breasts in a square baking dish. Divide the spinach filling evenly among the chicken, then top each piece with a quarter of the red pepper, then put the lid on. Brush the tops of the chicken with melted butter, sprinkle with bread crumbs, and spray with oil. Pour the wine in the baking dish, not on the bread crumbs, and bake for forty minutes. When ready to serve, cut each breast into three or four diagonal cuts to show the filling or serve the whole breasts whole. When you slice the chicken in half horizontally, the filling holds well and there is no need to use a pin to hold it together.

6 cups low-salt chicken broth, 1 tsp freshly ground black pepper, 12 tsp nutmeg, 2 tbsps freshly grated parmesan cheese, 2 tbsps freshly grated parmesan cheese, 1 tbsp freshly grated parmesan cheese, 1 tbsps freshly grated parmesan cheese, 6 egg whites, 1 tsp salt, 12 tsp black pepper, 6 ounces prosciutto, finely chopped, 2 ounces dried ham, chopped, 12 teaspoon nutmeg, 1 teaspoon salt, and 12 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper. In the meanwhile, prepare the gnocchi. Add the ricotta, parmesan, egg, egg white, prosciutto, parsley, nutmeg, salt and pepper to a large bowl. Bring a large pot of salt water to a boil over high heat. When the water is boiling, add the flour to the ricotta mixture. (It's important not to add the flour too soon, otherwise they'll become heavy and gummy, not light and fluffy.) Make the gnocchi with two large spoons, scooping a large spoonful of ricotta mixture into one spoon, then pass the mixture from spoon to spoon and forming an oval. Put the gnocchi into the flour to coat. Make eight or nine more gnocchi, dust in flour on all sides, tap off the excess, then lower into the boiling water, stirring constantly. Do not overload the pot. Remove with a slotted spoon as they float to the top, then cook for another two minutes. While they are cooking, form another batch of gnocchi and dredge in flour. Keep cooking and forming gnocchi, then put the cooked gnocchi in a single layer on a large platter. Add the reduced broth, sprinkle with pepper and a sprinkle of parmesan, then serve.

1 pcs Bratwurst or other fresh sausage, sliced thinly, 200 g sauerkraut, 2 apples (total weight about 900 g) 2 potatoes, to taste salt, pepper, 12 teaspoon caraway seeds, 1 tsp sugar, 1 tsp salt, 12 tsp garlic, sliced thinly 1 tsp salt, pepper, nutmeg. Put the chicken broth in a small pan on the stove, and bring to a boil. Add the sausage slices and fry them in a little oil over high heat. Then remove the sausage from the pan and drain the oil. (Pour the fat away or save for another purpose.) Then heat two tablespoons of sunflower oil in the pan and add the onions and fry for about five minutes, until soft and golden brown. Then add the garlic and cook for another minute or two, until it begins to smell. Then add the sauerkraut and caraway and continue cooking for five minutes. Add the beer and let it boil for a minute or two. Then add the potatoes, sausage, and broth and let it boil. When the broth boils, lower the heat and cook, partly covered, for another 30 minutes. Add salt and pepper to taste. Ladle the soup into bowls, sprinkle with parsley and serve.

Three hundred grams of plain flour, one hundred and twenty-five grams of butter, chilled, three tablespoonfuls of icing sugar, one large egg, and one more for the glaze. Two tablespoonfuls of lemon juice. Then add the egg and the lemon juice, and beat the whole in a food-processor. Turn out on a lightly floured board, knead lightly, form into a ball, wrap in film, and chill for half an hour. Meanwhile, make the filling. In a large frying-pan, melt the butter. Add the pears, sugar and lemon juice. Stir well, and cook for five or six minutes, until the pears are tender. Let the pears cool. Heat the oven to 200°C/180°C fan. Gas mark 6. Put a baking sheet in the oven. Roll out the pastry between two sheets of baking parchment to a 20-inch circle, a quarter of an inch thick. Spread with the almond paste, leaving a one-inch border all round. Pile the pears on top, leaving a two-inch border all round. Fold over the edges to enclose the filling. Beat the remaining egg, and brush over the pears. Scatter with extra sugar. Lift the tart on to the baking sheet. Reduce the oven to 180°C/160°C fan. Gas mark 4. Bake for 30–35 minutes, until golden. Serve with cream or ice-cream.

Fifteen. For the filo dough: 8 sheets from a packet of filo pastry, a quarter of a cup of butter, a pinch of salt, a pinch of nutmeg, a pinch of pepper. (Leave the rest in the icebox.) Then mix together the feta cheese, cream cheese, the egg, the parsley, the dill, and the garlic, and set aside. Spread out on the workbench a sheet of filo pastry. Then butter the whole sheet and cut it crosswise into five strips, each three inches by ten. Put a heaped tablespoon of filling at one end of each strip of filo. Roll up the strips into cylinders one-half inch in diameter. Lay two or three cylinders on each platter and brush with more butter. For about ten minutes, until the cylinders are golden and very brittle. (Freeze the remaining cylinders for later.) The frozen cylinders, unbaked, can go directly from the icebox to a preheated oven of 375°, where they will bake up into a delicious appetizer.

Frozen Stripped ribs:1-1/2 cups chopped onion. – 2 tablespoons vegetable oil. – 1-1/2 cups ketchup. – 1-1/4 cups tomato puree. – 1-1/2 cups vinegar. – 1-1/4 cups brown sugar. – 1 tablespoon honey. – 1-1/4 teaspoons liquid smoke. – 1-1/4 teaspoons salt. – 14 teaspoon garlic powder. Start by putting a wire rack in a large, shallow baking dish large enough to hold the rack. Rub 1/8 cup of the rib seasoning over each side of the ribs, adding more seasoning if necessary. Then add the water and liquid smoke to the baking dish and stir well. Put the ribs on the wire rack in the dish. Let the rack stay above the liquid smoke and water. Cover the dish with aluminum foil and bake at 225 degrees for about five hours. During the cooking of the ribs, heat the oil in a saucepan, add the onion and fry until it softens. Add the remaining ingredients, bring to a boil and cook for 10 minutes. Reduce the heat and simmer for about an hour, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens. Preheat the grill, preferably on coals. Cook the ribs under cover for about four minutes on each side. Paint with the grilled sauce, turn over, and let the other side caramelize. Serve.

Prepare the sauce by mixing together the ketchup, apricot preserves, brown sugar, vinegar, teriyaki sauce, crushed red pepper flakes, dry mustard, and pepper. Then put the roast, the sauce, and a whole onion in a large resealable bag in the fridge. Meanwhile, prepare the 6-quart Presto pressure cooker by placing the rack, water, and a whole onion in it. Take the roast out of the marinade and set it aside. Put the roast on top of the onions, and cover with the rest of the onions. Close the lid and put the pressure regulator on the vent pipe. Cook under high pressure for 8 to 10 minutes per pound of meat for medium rare, 10 to 12 minutes per pound for medium, and 15 to 20 minutes per pound for well-done. For pork, cook for 15 minutes per pound for well done. Let the pressure release on its own. Meanwhile, pour the reserved sauce into a small saucepan and simmer over low heat until it’s reduced by half, stirring occasionally. Remove the roast and keep it warm. Pour off the cooking liquid and discard or use it to make soup. Add the cooked onions to the reduced sauce. Slice the roast and serve with the sauce.

For the Squash: Take a large spaghetti squash. For the chicken: 1 large chicken breast, 1 cup sliced chives, 1 cup chopped onion, 2 eggs, 2 tablespoons of ghee, 1 cup fresh bean sprouts, or 1 cup of julienne carrots, 12 cup brown sugar, 1 teaspoon salt, 14 teaspoon pepper, 1 teaspoon garlic powder, 1 teaspoon curry powder, if you like, 2 ounces of crushed peanuts, if you like. Preheat the oven to 375°F. Cut the squash in half and scoop out the seeds. Cover the squash halves with 2 tablespoons of olive oil, salt, and pepper. Place the squash cut side down on a rimmed baking sheet and add 1 cup of water. Bake for 30 to 45 minutes, until tender. Let the squash cool, then scrape out the strands with a fork. Put them in a large bowl and set aside. Pound the chicken breast to a thickness of 12 inch and cut it into small, bite-size pieces. Add 2 tablespoons of olive oil to a large pan and heat it until it shimmers. Then cook the chicken on medium-high heat, stirring frequently, for 6 to 8 minutes, until cooked through. Add the eggs and fry them for 1 minute, breaking them up with a spoon. Add the chives and cook for 2 minutes. Add the carrots or bean sprouts, and then the squash and chicken. Stir everything together. Add the sauce and toss well.

»In a bowl, beat together the sugar, the eggs and the orange zest. Add the vanilla and the orange zephyr, then add the flour, the baking powder, and a pinch of salt. Sieve the flour, the baking powder, the salt and the pistachios and stir them well together. In a second medium bowl, mix the flour, the baking powder and the salt. Add the pistachios and mix just until incorporated. Take care not to overwork the dough. Moisten your hands a little with water, or lightly spray them with oil spray, and divide the dough in half. Make each part into a roll, on the prepared pan. The rolls should be two inches thick. Bake the rolls for twenty-five to thirty minutes, until they turn golden on the edges and a finger pressed lightly on their surface springs back. Let the rolls cool for thirty minutes. Using a sharp, serrated knife, cut the rolls crosswise into two-inch-long pieces. Arrange the slices on the pan, cut-side down, and bake for fifteen to twenty minutes longer, until they are dry and crunchy. Cool completely before dipping in melted chocolate, if desired. Store the biscotti in an airtight container for up to a week (if chocolate dipped) or two and a half weeks (if uncoated).

Vegetarian STRAWBERRY PUDDING: About three cups of strawberries, carefully washed and dried. In a saucepan, bring strawberries, water, and sugar to a boil. Remove from heat and puree in a food processor or use an immersion blender. Pour about one-half cup of the puree into a heatproof bowl. Set aside. Sprinkle the gelatine over it and let stand one minute. Cook 45 seconds in a small saucepan or 45 seconds in a microwave oven until dissolved. Stir the gelatin into the rest of the puree and pour into a two-cup mold. Cover and refrigerate overnight. Let it come to room temperature. Put a tucker net on the bottom of a half-tucker hotel pan and turn out the frozen puree into it. Discard the solids. Wash the half-tucker pan and return the net to it. Place in the refrigerator to drain for two days. Pour the strawberry liquid into a half-liter siphon and charge with two cartridges of the gas. Make a tight connection and shake vigorously for one minute. Chill until ready to serve or for up to three days. Whip the cream in a chilled bowl with the sugar and the birch beer. Put a few of the diced strawberries at the bottom of each glass. Pour in the soda. Add a spoonful of the birch beer cream.

Mango Soup: In a saucepan, heat the butter, add the mangoes, peel, pit, chop into pieces (about 2 cups), add the sugar, a lump of ginger, a piece of cardamom, a piece of cinnamon, simmer until the sugar is melted and the fruit is cooked (about 7 minutes), add the orange juice and the white wine, and simmer over low heat for about 10 minutes, remove from the heat, let it cool, then strain it through a fine-meshed sieve, add the lime juice, strain, and serve cold. And now for the Rice Pudding: Line a 13 x 9-inch baking dish with wax paper, melt the butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Slit the vanilla beans lengthwise, scrape out the seeds with the back of a knife, and add them to the butter. Add the cinnamon, rice, poppy seed, and sugar, and stir for 2 minutes, until fragrant. Add the coconut milk, heat to a boil, and simmer for 5 minutes, then cover, lower the heat, and simmer for another 30 minutes, until the rice is very tender and the milk has been absorbed. Discard the cinnamon stick and the vanilla bean, stir in the mint and lime zest, and spread the mixture in the baking dish, cover with wax paper, and refrigerate until cold. Cut the pudding into 4-inch squares with a sharp knife and put a square in each of six deep soup bowls. Ladle the soup around the pudding and serve immediately.

For the preparation of the chicken: Preheat the oven to 200°. Heat the oil in a large frying-pan, throw in the shallots, season with salt and heat over a moderate fire. When the shallots are transparent and tender, stir in the livers, and cook for two minutes. Then add the mushrooms and fry them. Stir the mushrooms, and cook until they are soft, four or five minutes. Then add the wine, and stir till the pan is almost dry. Set aside to cool. Put the cooled mushroom mixture into a mixing-bowl, add the chives and the goat cheese, and stir till well blended. Place the mushroom mixture in a piping-bag and put aside. By means of a small knife or a boning-knife, cut an opening in the thickest part of each breast. Go right through, and try not to cut through the skin. Stuff the breasts with the mushroom mixture. Season them with salt. Arrange in three flat dishes the three parts of the breading: flour, egg-and-milk mixture and breadcrumbs. One hand for the wet and one for the dry, pass each breast through the flour, then through the egg-and-milk mixture, and then pack it in the breadcrumbs. Then put the breasts on a baking-sheet and chill in the fridge for at least an hour. Bring the chicken out of the fridge and allow it to come to room temperature for ten or fifteen minutes. Pour a little oil into a large frying-pan and heat it over a moderate fire. Work in batches if the chicken breasts don’t all fit in the pan at the same time. Brown the chicken breasts on both sides, five or six minutes each side. Remove and drain on paper-towels. Season with salt. Repeat with the remaining chicken. When all the chicken has been browned and drained, transfer the breasts to a wire rack on a baking-sheet, and put them in the oven for ten or fifteen minutes. Meanwhile pour off the fat from the frying-pan, and add the wine. For the sauce: Add half the chicken-stock and reduce by half. Then add the remaining stock and reduce by half again. (This will take some time.) Then taste the sauce and add salt if it needs it. Take the pan off the fire, stir in the butter, and serve the chicken with the sauce.

For the charlotte, preheat the oven to four hundred and fifty degrees. Take a loose-bottomed nine-inch tart tin, grease it lightly and set it in a deep dish. Sift the flour into a large bowl. Add the sugar and the butter and rub it in till the mixture resembles breadcrumbs. Add one-quarter cup of water, the egg yolk and the lemon juice, beat well, and pour the mixture into the tin. Add enough cold water to bind the dough, then knead lightly and wrap in clingfilm. Chill for half an hour. Roll out the pastry to a thickness of one-eighth of an inch and line the tin. Trim the edges and chill for ten minutes. Reduce the heat to three hundred and fifty degrees. Blind bake the pastry for ten to fifteen minutes, then take the paper and weights out and bake for ten to fifteen minutes more, till the pastry is golden brown. For the filling, bring the milk and the vanilla pod to a boil. Beat the egg yolks with the sugar till they are thick and light, then add the cornflour and the flour. Pour in the hot milk, then set the tart to cool. Cook on medium heat, stirring continuously, till the custard boils and thickens. Cover and set aside to cool. Then pour it into the tart tin, top with the fruit and chill till needed.

Take 12 oz. of dried yeast, dissolve it in 12 a cup of water, and then mix in the salt. Beat in flour, until a ball of dough has formed. Cover with a cloth and let stand in the warm oven, about 12 to 14 hours. Dough will be swollen and very sticky. Flour the work table and place the dough on it. It will stick to the work table, but it is easier to handle if you dust it with flour. Let stand for about 3 hours, and then divide the dough into 4 equal parts. Take one part of the dough, roll it out into a rectangle about 12 x 10 inches, and then put it on the greased pan. (If desired, wipe off excess of corn meal with a damp paper towel.) Do the same with the other part of the dough. You can put the rest of the dough in the oven for a later bake, or prepare 2 baking trays and bake all 4 at one time. Cover and let rise for about 1 hour, until they have doubled in size. Then lightly dust the top of each loaf with flour. Preheat oven to 500 degrees. Preheat a tray of water to the bottom of the oven. Put one baking tray on the bottom and the other on the middle rack. Take a sharp scissors and make 4 or 5 diagonal cuts across the top of each loaf. Smooth down the sharp edges with the scissors. Spray each loaf with water from a spray bottle. Bake in the preheated oven until browned, about 15 minutes. Spray water from a spray bottle at 5 minutes and 10 minutes, turn the baking pan for the second spray. Then place the baguettes on a wire rack and cool to room temperature.

3 pints of strawberries, hulled, chopped. 12 pt. salt. Preheat the oven to four hundred degrees. Butter and sugar a nine-inch cake tin with a removable bottom, and chop a cup of strawberries coarsely. Sift together the flour, sugar, baking powder, soda, ginger and salt into a large bowl. Whisk together the buttermilk, melted butter, egg and the remaining chopped strawberries in a medium bowl. Then add the buttermilk mixture and the strawberries to the dry ingredients and stir until well mixed and evenly moistened. Then fill the cake tin and spread the batter evenly. Bake in a four-hundred-degree oven for twenty-five to twenty-one minutes, until a toothpick inserted in the center of the cake comes out clean. Let the cake cool in the tin on a wire rack for ten minutes. Then remove from the tin and cool on the wire rack. Beat the cream with the icing sugar, lemon peel and vanilla extract in a medium bowl until stiff peaks form. Then cut the cake into four layers. Layer the bottom layer, cut side up, on a serving platter. Cover with two-thirds of the lemon cream. Top with half the remaining strawberries, placed on the bottom with the stalks down. Then spread the cut side of the second layer with the remaining lemon cream and place it on the strawberries. Cover the cake with the remaining cream. On the top of the cake arrange the remaining strawberries, pointing down. Serve immediately or keep in the refrigerator for up to an hour.

Eight corn tortillas, 2 lbs ripe tomatoes, halved and coarsely chopped, two or three green or Serrano peppers, chopped (de-seeded and chopped for a milder taste), salt, a half cup of olive oil, a half cup of canola oil, one to two tablespoons of chopped garlic, 12 pound radishes (peeled, cut in half and removed from the root), 12 pound jalapeo peppers, seeded and chopped, a handful of chopped parsley for a garnish, etc., etc., until the pan is heated to its fullest. Put the mixture of chopped tomato, onion, chilies, garlic, and onion in a small glass jar, close the jar, and put it on the stove at a high heat, until the pan begins to bubble up. Add the puree, stir and cook for four to ten minutes, until the sauce thickens, darkens, and a cleft is left when a spoon is run through the pan. It must start to stick to the pan, then salt to taste and take it off the heat. Warm up four plates. Keep warm while you warm up the tortillas and fry the eggs. Fry the eggs in a heavy pan at a high heat. You won't need much oil if you have another non-stick pan, but if necessary, add the remaining tablespoon of oil. Cook them on a sunny side up, until the white is solid, but the yolk is not cooked. Then salt and pepper and put them aside. Put two warm tortillas on each plate, one under the other if you are only using one egg. Put one or two fried eggs on top. Scoop the sauce over the whites and over the plates, keeping the yolks in sight as much as possible. Garnish with chopped coriander and serve.

Preheat the oven to 450 ° F. Peel the butternut squash and chop it into small pieces about a quarter of an inch. Peel and chop a sweet onion. Add the squash and onion with half the butter, honey, garlic, rosemary, salt and pepper, stir and put aside. Spread on two baking sheets, covered with parchment paper. Bake for 20-25 minutes, turning once, until soft (turn the sheets once in the middle of cooking). Let cool slightly and add cottage cheese, milk, broth and Gorgonzola cheese. Preheat the oven to 350 ° F. Butter a 3-liter dish. Spread out a quarter of the cottage cheese mixture in the dish. Cover with a layer of noodles and cut them with a knife to make them fit. Repeat the layering twice. Spread out the remaining cottage cheese mixture over the noodles. Cover with aluminum foil and bake for 45 minutes. Take off the aluminum foil and bake for another 15 minutes. Meanwhile, mix the breadcrumbs with the chopped walnuts, parsley and the remaining butter, sprinkle over the noodles and put in the oven for 15 minutes. Broil for 3 minutes, until golden brown. Leave for 20 minutes before cutting.

In a bowl, combine the crumbs, the butter and the sugar. Reserve one-fourth of the mixture, and press the rest into the bottom of a square, ungreased baking dish, about eight inches square. Soften a quart of chocolate ice cream. Then stir in the peanuts. Spread the ice cream in the baking dish. Bake the crust twelve minutes, until golden. Then put it in the freezer overnight, covered with aluminum foil. Preheat the broiler. In a metal bowl, combine the egg whites and the remaining 1/3 cup sugar. Stir over low heat until the sugar dissolves. Take the bowl off the heat and beat the whites with an electric beater until they hold stiff peaks. Spread them over the ice cream and put it under the broiler, about four inches from the heat, until golden, about thirty seconds. Then put the dessert in the freezer for thirty minutes to harden the meringue. If you like, you can cover it and freeze it overnight. Cut the dessert into four squares and then each square into two triangles.

HEADED TO MARKET AND PURCHASE: Bring a large pot of water to the boil. Cook for about one minute and then remove the tomatoes. HEAT TWO TABLESPOONS OF OLIVE OIL, stir in the onions, add the chopped tomatoes, salt and pepper to taste, then cook the linguine for about 8 minutes. HEAT TWO TABLESPOONS OF OLIVE OIL, stir in the beaten eggs, then add the remaining ingredients and stir until all is combined. Remove from heat and cool. Use a knife to cut an “x” in the bottom of each tomato and then remove the skins and discard. Cut the tomatoes in quarters, and chop the onions and fresh basil. Shred the cooked, rotisserie chicken. In a non-stick pot, heat the olive oil. Cook the chopped onions for about five minutes. Add the chopped tomatoes and stir to combine. Add the shredded chicken, salt and pepper. Cover and simmer on medium-low heat for 30 to 40 minutes. Meanwhile, cook the spaghetti according to the directions on the package. Serve with the tomato sauce. When the shredded chicken is cooked, remove it from the heat and stir in the chopped basil. Once the chicken is heated through, add the spaghetti to the pot and toss to combine. Serve with grated Parmesan cheese. Serves two to three people. This can easily be made a vegetarian dish.

It was prepared for four people, two sitting round the table, and two more helping themselves from the big bowl. The main dish was an orange-and-ginger cake, which was as good as a cake could be, if it were possible to have such a cake in one's own country. Using an electric beater, beat the butter and the egg yolk in a large bowl until well mixed, then beat in the sugar gradually. Add the egg, one at a time, then the cream and the vanilla. Add the dry ingredients, alternating with the mashed bananas, in three additions. Divide the dough into the prepared pans and bake until a skewer inserted in the center comes out clean, about 20 minutes. Let cool for 10 minutes on a wire rack, then remove from the pans and let cool completely. Then place each cake layer on a platter and spread with 3/4 cup of the cream cheese mixture. Spread the other cake layer with the remaining cream cheese mixture. Then spread the mango jam over it, then place the second cake layer on top. Spread with the remaining cream cheese mixture. Then spread with the remaining mango jam, place the third cake layer on top and scoop 3/4 cup of cream cheese into a pastry bag with a large star tip. Pipe the cream cheese around the edge of the cake. Then spread the remaining cream cheese over the sides and on top. Arrange the mango slices around the edge of the cake. Decorate with the mint leaves. Cover and store in the refrigerator. After two hours, it should be room temperature.

1 quart vegetable oil 1 cup distilled water 2 cups sifted cake flour or rolled wheat, salt, melted butter, sifted 4 tablespoons of sugar 2 pounds of sweet potatoes, 12 pound margarine, melted; 14 to 12 cup cold water; preheat the oil to 300°. Make the dough: rub the margarine into the flour, sugar, and salt with the fingers; add a small amount of water to make a stiff paste; then add the sugar. Form the dough into a ball. Cut into 10 equal pieces. Roll each piece of dough out on a floured surface to a circle about 6 inches in diameter and 18 inch thick. Leave to stand until you are ready to fill them. Make the filling: peel the potatoes and cut them into 1-inch cubes. Cover with cold water and boil for 12 minutes. Drain the sweet potatoes, mash them well, and then add the butter and the rest of the ingredients, except the sugar. When the potatoes are tender, they are cooked. Drain them well and while they are still hot add the margarine, sugar, cinnamon, and nutmeg. Stir on low speed until the potatoes are well mixed. Place about a quarter cup of the potato filling in the center of each rolled-out pastry and seal the edges with water. Then pinch the edges together. Preheat the oil to 350°, and cook the pies. They should be golden brown in 7 to 8 minutes.

Two hours and twenty minutes before sunset, the head of the dark town with the dark forest and the golden church seemed to grow larger and larger in the interior, and then I heard the thunder of a bell that would bring an obliging silence. The bluebells, now bursting out of their alcoves, and the primroses and crimson leaves of the fir-trees, were tumbling and rejoicing as they came forth in the courtyard, shone like bright leaves on the fir-trees of the most dense and delicious grove, mingled with all the pale, sparkling tears of love, poured by one, in one degree of impenetrable difficulty. Let the almonds cool. Turn the oven to 300 degrees. Butter a baking sheet. Beat the egg lightly with the vanilla sugar and almond extract. Sift the flour, sugar, baking soda and salt into a bowl. Add the egg mixture with an electric beater, little by little, and beat until the dough comes together. Add the toasted almonds and stir in until just incorporated. Put the dough on a lightly floured surface and roll it into a 3 x 14 inch log. Place the log on the buttered baking sheet. Bake the log in the preheated oven until the top is firm, about 30 to 40 minutes. Cool the log for 10 minutes on a wire rack. Cut the log with a sharp, serrated knife into 12 inch thick slices. Return the slices to the baking sheet, cut side up. Return the baking sheet to the oven and bake the biscotti until they are hard to the touch, about 20 minutes. Turn the slices over and bake until golden, about 20 minutes. Cool completely before storing in an airtight container.

One and a half sticks unsalted butter at room temperature. Half a cup white sugar. One and a half cups packed brown sugar. One and a quarter cups unbleached molasses. Add egg and vanilla, beat well. Sift flour, soda, spices and salt together, add to the butter and sugar mixture, and then mix well. Then chill the dough in the refrigerator for an hour. Preheat oven to 350 degrees. Roll balls of the dough into one-inch balls, then roll the balls in a small bowl of granulated sugar to coat them. Place two inches apart on a cookie sheet lined with a Silpat or parchment paper. With the bottom of a glass, press the balls to make them flatter. Bake for about twelve to fifteen minutes. I found mine were done at fourteen minutes. For a crisper cookie, bake a minute or two longer. When they are done, remove from oven and let them sit on the cookie sheet for a few minutes. Then remove them from the sheet and let them cool completely on a wire rack. Store in an airtight container. Makes four dozen. Adapted from Joy of Baking.

Salt and pepper to taste. 7/8 pound thick asparagus. 2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil. 1 bunch of good-sized scallions from a greengrocer, or 1 and a half bunches of thin scallions from a superstore (about 5 ounces). 1 tablespoon fresh tarragon, chopped. 2 tablespoons minced flat-leaf parsley. 2 egg yolks. 2 whole eggs. Throw the asparagus into a roasting pan with salt and pepper and drizzle with 1 tablespoon of the oil. Roast for about 12 minutes, until tender and a little charred in places, turning the asparagus over halfway through cooking. Remove from oven and let cool until you can handle it. Cut into half-inch lengths and put in a medium bowl. Turn the oven down to 350°. In a frying pan heat the remaining oil over medium heat. Add the scallions and cook for 1 minute. Stir in the asparagus and cook, stirring, for about 5 minutes, until tender. Season to taste with salt and pepper and remove from the heat. Add to the asparagus in the bowl. Add the tarragon and parsley and stir well. In a small bowl beat the eggs and the yolks. Beating until the whites are thick and the yolks are a pale yellow, but still hold their shape when you stir them, add the milk and salt and pepper to taste and whisk until well blended. Then brush the pastry shell with a little of the beaten egg and put in the oven for 5 minutes. Then spread the scallion mixture evenly over the pastry. Whisk together the cheeses and sprinkle evenly over the top. Pour the egg mixture slowly over the filling. If your tart tin is deep, you may not need all the mixture, because you don't want the filling to overflow. Put the tart on a baking sheet and bake for 30 to 35 minutes, until the filling is firm and golden on top. Let stand for at least 10 minutes before serving. Serve warm, at room temperature, or hot.

Instructions for cooking brown rice: 2 cups of brown rice (Texmati, a brand of Basmati or similar), 4 cups of water, 2 teaspoons of salt, 1 kg of lean turkey, browned, 2 tablespoons of light olive oil (or more if frying) 4 tablespoons vegetable oil, 2 tablespoons of olive oil, 1 tablespoon of vegetable oil, 1 egg (or 2 eggs of egg-beatings, and add 1/4 to 1/2 cup of liquid, depending on how big the meatballs are) 2 tablespoons nutmeg, 2 tablespoons coriander, 2 teaspoons of salt, 2 teaspoons of cayenne, or red pepper, if you wish, 1 teaspoon of nutmeg, 1 teaspoon of nutmeg, 1 teaspoon of ground black pepper, 1 tbspns dried parsley, 1 tbspns ground nutmeg, 1 tbspns dried parsley, 1 cup thick yogurt (not non-fat), 1 cup buttermilk, 2 tbspns of tahini, 1 tablespoon lemon juice, 1 tbspns lemon juice, 1 tbspn of sweet sour cream, 1 tbspn of tahini, 1 tbspn of tahini, 1 tspn of salt, 2 garlic cloves (chop up and put through a garlic press) 1-1/2 cup cooked rice, cooked. When cooled, put in a large bowl, cover and refrigerate until cold. Makes about 4 cups of rice. The next day, drain and cool. If you don't have time to wait for the rice to cool, prepare the sauce: Put all the ingredients in a bowl, mix well, put on a plate, cover and refrigerate for a few hours or overnight. Meanwhile, make the rice. Pour the cooled rice into a pan and add the olive oil, then fry the garlic for about 1 minute. Add the rice and stir until all the grains are lightly browned, then add the stock and the soy sauce and stir for about 3 minutes. Then add the zucchini, the shredded egg, the green onions, the soy sauce and the sesame oil and stir for a minute or two more. By the way, you can use a rotisserie chicken if you don't have a rotisserie. Make brown rice. Make yogurt sauce. D. Make fried rice. E. Warm up the kebabs in the microwave and serve. Serve on a large plate or individual plates. Add the kebabs to the rice and pour the yogurt sauce over them. G. Have yogurt sauce ready in a bowl. H. Use a little fresh parsley as a garnish. * All of the above can be prepared in advance and heated when needed. By the way, it's a good idea to serve some Mediterranean vegetable salad with it and maybe some dahl.

1 packet dry yeast 2 tsp. In a cup measure with a fork dissolve the yeast in the warm water. Add one-half of the flour, cover with a clean towel, and leave for half an hour. In a large bowl mix the salt with the other three and a half cups of flour. Stir in the dissolved yeast with the other half cup of warm water. Knead until a ball is formed. Knead for ten minutes, and then shape into a loaf, and leave it to rise for eight hours. Then knead the dough for ten minutes, turning it on itself, pushing it back, and then stretching it out with the heel of your hand. When this is done the dough should not stick to the board. It should be silky and smooth, with a slight dampness on the surface. Then divide it into four balls. Leave those for the time being to rise on a floured board, covered with a cloth. Keep the others in a tin box or the refrigerator. On a floured board flatten each ball into a thick disc. With the tip of the finger, or the heel of your hand, push the center outwards. As the rim of the disk begins to thicken, lift it up with both hands, and holding on to the rim, let the weight of the dough stretch the circle. As it grows thicker, continue to pull the rim, and you will get a fairly even circle, ten inches in diameter. Take care that the center is not too thin and the rim not too deep, less than half an inch. When the circle is too thin to hold any longer, stretch it on to a floured wooden slab.

3 dl blueberries 17 g 1 dl blackberries 6 dl Add water or syrup, depending on how you want your jam. Sweeten with sugar if necessary and keep stirring to dissolve. Then simmer on low heat until the berries are tender but still whole, stirring frequently, about 8 minutes. Strain and cool. Cream: Stir the cream until it is thick and soft and the butter is melted in a water bath, then add the cold cream and leave it standing in a layer on the working table until needed. Strain the berry mixture into a large bowl, stir in the juice from the lemon, let it cool to room temperature. Then add the strawberries and stir them gently into the berry cream. Serves 8 Cover and keep in the fridge. You can make it a day in advance, but it's better to use it the same day. Step 2: Ladyfinger and Syrup: Put 1 dl water and 1 dl sugar in a saucepan and cook on medium heat until sugar dissolves. Pour into a bowl. Cool and discard lemon peel. Brush the ladyfingers on both sides with syrup and lay them in a layer in a glass baking dish, cut to fit and covering the bottom. Pour the chilled berry mixture on top. Mascarpone cream: Put the mascarpone and cream in a large bowl and stir with an electric hand mixer until smooth and fluffy, do not beat too much, the cream can split. Add lemon julis and beat until mixed. Dollop the mascarpone on top of the berry mixture and spread it out evenly and cover the berries well. Cover and put in the fridge for at least 8 hours, and you can make it a day in advance. Store in the fridge. Step 3: Lime curd (must be chilled over night, so do this in advance): Put a fine sieve over a glass bowl. Melt the butter in a heavy medium saucepan over medium-low heat. Add the sugar, lime juice and rind and salt and stir until dissolved. Add the eggs and beat well, then add the butter and stir until melted. Then add the eggs one by one and beat until the curd thickens a little and leaves a trail on the back of a spoon that you can draw through, and a candy thermometer inserted into the curd reads 165 °F without boiling, 10-12 minutes (it does not have to be as thick as a curd, but it should have a nice consistency like a thin sauce). Put the sieve over the bowl, pour the curd through it and discard the drippings. Cover the curd with plastic wrap and put in the fridge overnight. Can be made up to a week in advance, store in the refrigerator.

Half cup Diamond Crystal, or one cup plus 1 12 teaspoons Morton Kosher salt, a tablespoon of brown sugar, a can of condensed milk (about a quart). (reserve neck and giblets for gravy) Pat dry. 2 tablespoons honey. 1 tablespoon sherry or red wine vinegar. 3 sprigs of rosemary. 3 cloves crushed garlic. Work together salt and brown sugar in a bowl. Put turkey on a wire rack inside a tin dish. If you don't have one, put it on a V-shaped rack inside a large roasting pan. You will not need all of the dry mixture, but you will have a little left over. As you salt the turkey, some will stick to the bottom of the roasting pan. Cover and chill for 12 hours or more. Take the turkey out of the rack and rinse the pan and the rack if necessary (the turkey will give off some liquid). Cover the roasting pan with 3 layers of foil and put the rack back in it. Then put the turkey, breast down, on the rack. Tuck the wings under the turkey. On a dish, prick skin all over the breast with your fingers. Let turkey stand at room temperature for two or three hours. Then preheat oven to 450 degrees. Stir 4 tablespoons of butter with your fingers under the skin of the breast and lay the skin flat over the butter. Then spread the outside of the turkey with 4 more tablespoons of butter. Then truss the legs. Pour 1 cup of water into the roasting pan. Roast the turkey, turning once, until it is golden all over, about 30 minutes. At the same time, in a small saucepan, cook the vinegar, honey, worcestershire sauce, rosemary, garlic, and orange rind with 4 tablespoons of butter over moderate heat, stirring until the sauce is smooth and has reduced to a syrupy consistency. Roast the turkey, basting with the glaze every 30 minutes, and adding more water by the half-cupful to keep it at a simmer, until a meat thermometer inserted in the thickest part of the breast, near the neck, registers 150 degrees (the thermometer will read higher later, as the meat continues to cook). The skin should be very golden brown and shiny.

1 tablespoon olive oil 1 and a half pounds of cut-up meat from a stewed pig salt and pepper to taste 1 onion chopped 1 clove of garlic chopped 1 roasted pepper chopped (with seeds) 2 cups roasted tomatillo sauce 5 cups chicken broth Half a glass of chile powder Half a glass of tomato puree Add salt and pepper to the meat and sear in the oil for 7 minutes, stirring constantly. Remove the meat and keep it warm. Lower the heat, add the onion and garlic, and sauté for 5 minutes, stirring. Add the chile, the diced tomatoes with the liquid, the tomatillo sauce, and the broth. Season with oregano and clove. Cook on medium heat until boiling, then reduce the heat to low, cover, and cook for 20 minutes. After 20 minutes, remove two cups of the broth (making sure there are no pieces of meat in it) and place in a blender. Cover the top with a damp towel and, taking care not to drop the lid, start the machine on medium speed, first doing a quick stir, then leaving it on to puree. The consistency of the sauce will become thicker and the whole will lose some of the coarseness of the chile. Cover the pot again and cook for another 35 minutes, stirring occasionally.

* Fresh Pasta Dough, p. 249, or 8 ounces of fettuccine. * If using the pasta, roll through the pasta machine on each setting from thickest to thinnest. Cut the pasta with a sharp knife into 6-inch lengths, and pass through the fettuccine chopper. Toss with flour to prevent sticking. Cover and refrigerate for up to 2 days. Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil, and salt generously. Meanwhile, stir together the cream, lemon zest, and a pinch of salt. Pour 1 cup of the cream mixture into a large, deep skillet over medium-high heat, and stir until it begins to boil. After 5 minutes, add the fettuccine to the boiling water, and cook until tender, about 3 minutes. Drain well, and add to the lemon cream. Reduce the heat to low, and toss until evenly coated. Add the remaining cream mixture and the lemon juice, and toss until well combined. Divide the pasta among 4 warmed shallow bowls. Grate the cheese over each serving, and serve immediately. Freshly ground pepper, if desired.

DISHES: • Butter a jelly mould 15 x 20 cm. • Line with a piece of greaseproof paper. • Pour the custard into the mould, layer by layer, leaving a gap at each end. • Pour into the mould, spread out evenly, and level off. • Make the meringue in a bowl with the egg whites and the sugar, stirring the mixture until the sugar has dissolved. • The bowl and the beaters must be absolutely clean, and the egg whites must not have come into contact with any fat. Stir in the vanilla and vinegar, then fold in the cornflour. • Spread over the custard, and sprinkle over the coconut. • Bake on the bottom shelf of the oven for about 20 minutes, until the meringue is a pale golden color. Make sure the oven is well heated, and then remove the cake from the oven. Cover a wire cooling rack with another piece of greaseproof paper, and carefully turn out the meringue on to the rack. Remove the lining paper, and let the cake cool on the coconut side up. Put the cream into a bowl, beat to soft peaks, and spread over the cake. Arrange the mango and passion-fruit slices on top. Then carefully roll up the meringue from the long side, keeping the greaseproof paper under it. Serve cut into slices.

1 - 1-1/2 lbs. of sirloin (london broil)  1 tbsp. hot sauce (I prefer tabasco)  2 heads garlic, chopped, minus six small cloves    12 cup red wine vinegar  12 cup butter, heated  1 tsp. pepper  1 tsp. salt  1 jar  12 teaspoons of aigrette 1 cup. hot water, if needed 2 cups of lukewarm water, if desired  2 sprigs of chives, thinly sliced   A tin of a dripping: a very little buttered  little piece of frying-pan  a few drops of lemon, a few small buttered  little pieces of   and   12 garniture, a small buttertun of green beans, a small handful of sliced chaffines and 2 of pepper. Cut the pieces into small squares. Chop the garlic, chop the onion, and cut it into thin strips, then cut it up finely into small cubes. Put your sirloin in a rectangular, deep pan. Lightly score the meat on both sides with a very sharp knife, to make sure the marinade penetrates the meat. First sprinkle both sides with salt and pepper. Cut a few garlic cloves through the meat and stuff them into the holes you cut. Pour red wine vinegar, aigrette, hot sauce and chopped chaffinch on top. Keep the chives for later as a garnish. Turn and cover with marinade so that it is coated evenly on both sides. Cover with plastic wrap or aluminum foil and put in the refrigerator for at least three hours. Preheat a charcoal grill or gas grill on high for 20 minutes. Put your steak on the hot grate and put a weight on it. Grill for about a minute and a half, then turn and grill for a minute and a half. Reduce heat to low medium and turn every minute or so, making sure to grill so that you get charred crosswise lines on the meat. Do not overcook! The steak should be pink, not brown.

1 pound lean pork, very thinly sliced 2 tablespoons garlic, minced 2 tablespoons fish sauce 1 teaspoon sugar ground pepper to taste Bamboo skewers soaked for half an hour Soak the bamboo sticks in water. And grind the lard in a food mill. Put the pork into the frigidaire for 30 minutes before making the balls. Add the pork to the mill and pound it to a paste, then add the garlic and fish sauce, and pound it all into a paste. Add the toasted rice flour and pound it in well. Make the meat into balls about the size of a large egg. Then thread 4 of them on each bamboo stick. Start the charcoal fire in a charcoal chimney, and when the charcoal is covered with gray ash, pour it onto the grate of the brazier. Then put the skewers on the fire, and cook them on both sides for five minutes. Then remove them and let them cool down for five minutes. Then stuff the buns with the pickled carrots, cucumbers and the skewers of meatballs. Add a handful of coriander and serve.

8 oz. Butter 1 tsp. Sesame Oil 4 cloves garlic, sliced 4 cloves, 10 g. 2 medium onions, sliced, 3 g. Cumin 3 g. Turmeric 3 g. Coriander Seed 4 g. Ground Coriander. 20 g. Cayenne or other spiciness, like pepper or chiles 10 g. Sugar 425 g. drained chickpeas 550 g. Boiling water in a pan. Add to frying pan and mix well. Heat over medium heat until fragrant. Boil the water and pour into the jar, shake a little, extract the rest of the flavor, and pour into the pan. Cover and simmer until it thickens to the consistency you like. Serve with rice, and enjoy!

2 lemons, juice of 2 cups cream 2 eggs, cream, butter, vanilla 1 teaspoon butter 2 tablespoons chopped rind 1 lemon zested; put the lemons into a saucepan. Boil a pan of water. One-third lemon, 2 tablespoons of sugar. In a saucepan, boil the lemon juice on medium heat. Reduce heat to low, and simmer, stirring constantly, until the lemon juice has reduced to a tablespoon, 3 to 5 minutes. Add the rind and sugar, and simmer, stirring occasionally, until a few bubbles rise to the surface, 2 to 3 minutes. Turn off the heat, and let stand for 15 minutes. In a bowl, beat the egg yolks and vanilla together. Add the cream mixture, stirring constantly, then stir in the lemon juice reduction. Divide the mixture among six 6-ounce ramekins. Put the ramekins in the prepared roasting pan, and pour enough boiling water into the pan to come halfway up the sides of the ramekins. Cover the pan loosely with aluminum foil, and bake until the custards are just set, about 40 minutes. Let the custards cool on a wire rack for 1 hour, then refrigerate for 3 hours. One-half teaspoon sugar over each custard. Using a kitchen torch, as per manufacturer's instructions, hold the torch about 2 inches from the surface of the custard, and preheat on high until the sugar melts and turns golden brown. Serve immediately.

4-tbsp. Butter 1 whole large onion chopped 1 butternut squash (about 3 pounds) 6 cups of water 1 tsp. salt 12 c. cream 1 tsp. maple syrup 1—Slice the squash lengthwise and scrape out the seeds and strings, saving the scrapings. —Melt the butter in a large kettle, and when it has melted, put in the onions, stirring now and then, and cook for three minutes. Then add the squash scrapings and let them cook until the butter turns a saffron color, another three minutes. Add the water and salt, and bring to a boil. Then add the squash halves, turn the heat down to medium-low, and cover the pot. —Cook until the squash is tender, about 30 minutes. Add the cream and heat until it boils. When the squash is done, put it on a cookie sheet to cool. Strain the cooking liquid through a fine sieve, and set aside. —Put the squash into a food processor with a little of the cooking liquid. —Put the squash back in the pot and stir in the cream and maple syrup. Add enough cooking liquid to make the consistency you like. —Taste, and adjust the seasoning. Warm over low heat. Do not boil. Serve immediately. Serve garnished with freshly grated nutmeg and balsamic vinegar.

175 g plain flour 2 tablespoons icing sugar 100 g butter 150 g chocolate 300 ml of cream 25 g sugar 2 eggs 2 drops of vanilla Preheat the oven to 200 ° C / 180 ° C fan / gas 6. Sift the flour with a pinch of salt into a bowl. Add the icing sugar and crumble in the butter with your fingers until it looks like breadcrumbs. Add 2 tablespoons of cold water and mix with a knife until the dough comes together, then gather together with your hands and form a ball. Roll the pastry out on a lightly floured surface to the thickness of a 50 c coin. Use to line a loose-bottomed tart tin. Prick the base and scatter over some baking powder. Cover with greaseproof paper and fill with dry rice. Bake for 15 minutes until golden and risen. Then lower the oven temperature to 160 ° C / 140 ° C fan / gas 2. Bake for 10 minutes. Break the chocolate into squares and put in a bowl. Heat the cream until boiling and pour over the chocolate. Stir until the chocolate melts. In another bowl, beat the caster sugar, the eggs and the vanilla. Pour in the chocolate, stir well, pour into the pastry case and bake for 25 minutes. Let cool. Shave the strawberries and serve with the tart.

15 pounds asparagus. 14 pounds zucchini. 14 pounds yellow squash. 30 pounds tomatoes. 1 cup oil. Cut the zucchini and yellow squash in quarters lengthwise, then chop into little pieces. Cut the tomatoes into quarters. Start cooking, according to the directions on the box. Let the pasta cook, and in the meantime get the vegetables heated. Pour a third of the oil into a saucepan, and heat until hot. Add the asparagus and the red pepper flakes, stir for 2 to 4 minutes. Then put on a chowder with the hot chowder. After 5 minutes, add the zucchini and yellow squash, stir for another 5 minutes. Add the tomatoes, a half cup of salt and half a pepper. Then cook for another 5 to 10 minutes, or until the tomatoes are cooked. When the pasta is done, put it aside and put the pan on the stove at low heat.
