Add the rest of the oil, and if you like it hot, add more red pepper flakes. Then heat the oil until it's warm, put the pasta in the pan and stir frequently. Change the fire to medium-high. Keep an eye on the pasta to make sure it doesn't burn. As the pasta is fried a little, put the vegetables in and stir them well. Then serve and eat.

Two ready-made cakes, 9 or 10 inches in diameter, 3 or 4 cups chocolate icing; to decorate, a packet of chocolate wafer biscuits, a packet of milk chocolate wafer biscuits, some printed papers and three straw-coloured wooden sticks, each a foot long; chocolate balls, chocolate éclairs, chocolate mashmallows; top and tail the cakes with chocolate icing, cutting off the bottom of each cake to help them stand upright. Cover them with cling film and chill in the refrigerator to set. Then apply a coat of chocolate icing, drawing lines for the planking with a palette knife, then chill for at least an hour to set the icing. Use the large wafers for the gunwales, sticking them on with a little icing, and then add the smaller wafers on both sides for cannons. Finally, tie the wooden sticks into knots and stick them in the cake, and then add the decorations. Give it some sundaes, mashmallows, some gold coins, and some root beer barrels, then add some pirates. For safety, put candles in the cannons, but make sure the surface the ship is standing on is not wax-sensitive, as the wax will drip.

For each mole, season the potatoes with a pinch of salt, 1 tablespoon of oil, and a dash of sour salt; heat a half-cup of oil in a large saucepan and sauté the onion in it, stirring it with a pinch of salt. Set the mole aside, sprinkled with the remaining oil, and salt. Then put the potatoes in a medium bowl, add 1 tablespoon of the oil and a pinch of salt, cover with a piece of plastic wrap, and heat on high in a preheated toaster for 3 minutes. Return to the toaster and heat until tender, another two minutes. Let stand. While this is happening, heat a large frying pan on the stove, add the remaining tablespoon of oil, and then heat the oil in it. Add the onion and cook until it softens but does not brown, about 3 minutes. Add the chorizo and cook, stirring often, for 3 to 5 minutes, until it begins to brown. Add the potatoes and cook, stirring, for 3 minutes, until a little browned. Add a handful of spinach and stir it occasionally until it begins to wilt, then add more. Continue until all the spinach is in the pan and continue cooking, stirring, until the spinach is almost cooked, about 3 minutes. Add the sour cream and chiles, if using, and season with salt to taste. Serve with warm corn cakes, queso fresco, coriander, and lime wedges.

5 tbsps. sugar 1 tbsp. lavender 1 litre skimmed milk 12 lb toasted and chopped almonds Spray canola oil 12 ripe figs, chopped 3 tbsp. port wine Take a saucepan and heat the oil. Add the figs, almonds and wine and bring to a boil. Simmer until the syrup thickens slightly and a wooden spoon is held back from the surface, about 8 minutes. Then remove from the heat, add the lavender and stir well. Strain into a bowl, remove the solids and leave to cool. Stir in the milk and sugar, then pour into an ice cream machine and churn. Cover and freeze until firm. Place the ice cream in a plastic container and stir in the almonds. Cover and freeze for an hour or until firm. Pre-heat the oven to 350 degrees. Spray a 23 x 13-inch baking dish with canola oil. Pour 2 tbsps. of honey in the bottom of the dish. Arrange the figs cut-side down and bake at 350 degrees for 20 minutes or until the figs are soft. Turn, add the port and baste the figs with the honey syrup. Bake for 5 minutes more. Then serve the ice cream with the figs and the sauce.

Meringue: 9 egg whites at room temperature 1 tsp cream of tartar 2 cups caster sugar 1 tsp vanilla essence. 1 1/2 cups whipped cream 3 tbsp sour cream. 12 tsp vanilla essence. Preheat the oven to 270°. Take a baking tray and line it with a sheet of baking paper. Wash the bowl and whisk of a standing mixer, or the glass bowl and beater of a hand-held beater, with white vinegar and wipe them dry. Take the egg whites and the cream of tartar and whisk them on a low speed until they begin to froth, for about 2 minutes. Increase the speed and begin to add the sugar, little by little, and beat to a stiff consistency. With so many egg whites this may take a little longer than you think, maybe up to 10 minutes. Don’t overbeat, though – the egg whites must look soft and glossy, not gummy or dry. Add the vanilla essence and beat in. Transfer the meringue to the lined baking tray and spread it out in a smooth layer, right to the edges. If there are dips in the meringue, don’t worry, it’ll look good later. Place the tray in the oven and reduce the heat to 140°C. Bake for about 2 hours, until the meringue is completely cooled and firm. Turn off the oven and leave the meringue in the oven for a further 3 or 4 hours to cool completely. I like to serve it straight from the oven on the tray – you can just put a spoon in the middle and let everyone help themselves. If you’re planning to serve it on a platter, you should probably transfer it before adding the topping. But be careful – meringue can break easily at this stage. It’s best to serve it straight from the tray on the baking paper. In the bowl of a standing mixer, whisk together the cream, sour cream, icing sugar and vanilla bean paste. Then whisk in the cream. Add the cherries and the lemon rind, then spoon the cream over the meringue and serve. Serve with extra lemon rind.

In a large bowl, mix flour, sugar, salt, baking powder, and spices. Preheat oven to 425° F. Brush a cookie sheet with melted butter or put it on a parchment-covered baking sheet. Whisk together egg and pumpkin puree. With a fork, a pastry knife, or a food processor, cut butter into flour mixture until mixture is crumbly and no visible pieces of butter remain. Put aside. In a separate bowl, whisk pumpkin puree, milk, and egg. You are preparing a nice, thick batter. Fold into dry ingredients and form a ball. Roll the dough on a floured surface to about 1 inch thickness. With a large knife or a dough cutter, cut the dough into three equal parts lengthwise, then crosswise into six equal triangles. Place the triangles on the buttered baking sheet. Bake for 14 to 16 minutes, until the tops are golden brown. Let cool on a wire rack. Make a plain glaze. Whisk together 1 cup powdered sugar and 2 tablespoons milk. When the scones are cool, brush them with a plain glaze. While the glaze is drying, prepare the spiced glaze. Whisk all the ingredients together. Pour the glaze on top of each scone and let it dry for at least an hour before serving. Spray bottle or the end of a small whisk.

Preheat oven to 350 °. Spray four eight-inch cake tins with no-stick cooking spray. Prepare two mixes, according to package directions, and pour the mixture equally into the four tins. Frost the cakes with the prepared icing. Bake at 350 ° for 30 minutes, until the cakes pull away from the edges of the pan and a skewer inserted in the center comes out clean. Let cool in the tins on a wire rack for about 15 minutes. Cut the tops flat and even. Once cold, take out one of the layers of the cake and place it on a flat surface. Spread a layer of icing on top, put another cake on top and repeat the operation with the other two layers. Put the cake in the refrigerator for about half an hour. Then frost the top and sides of the cake. Put the leafy licorice all around the cake. On a medium bowl, mix the coconut with 5 or 6 drops of green food coloring, mix well and spread on the top layer of the cake. Arrange the bunnies, the eggs, the sticks and the tinsel as desired.

Stir the butter into the beer and the rest of the ingredients. In a large bowl put the seeds and pour the boiling water over them to soften them. Let them stand about fifteen minutes, then add the molasses, salt, buttermilk, beer and yeast and mix it well together. Finally, knead in the rye flour and mix it well. Cover the bowl with a clean dish-towel or a film of oil and let it stand until it has doubled in size, for about an hour. It must be soft to work with. Add the rest of the flours and mix the dough well, then put the bowl in the refrigerator overnight. Remove the dough from the bowl and divide it between two buttered nine-by-five-inch pans. The dough will be very soft and has to be spooned in. Preheat the oven to 400°. When the dough has doubled in size, make a few holes in it with a skewer or a chopstick dipped in water and pour the melted butter over the top. Bake for about one hour and twenty minutes, until the top is golden and the temperature reaches 205°, check it every half hour, if it is getting too dark, turn the oven down to 320°. Invert the pans on a cooling rack and remove the bread. Wrap it in clean dish towels and let it stand overnight on the racks, preferably twenty-four hours, then store it in plastic bags. Serve in thin slices.

Several days later, we went to an inn, to the establishment of the Sainte-Marie, and drank there with our friends at lunchtime. I found a cold dreadful. Isn’t there a cure for it? This is it: a quarter of an hour before your departure, strain your cold into a glass jar and let it stand for a day. Then take one ounce of it, squeeze it into a bowl and quickly throw it into the pan, so that it retains its form when it hits the water. Then do the same with the rest of the eggs, cook five minutes, and then a lace curtain of yolks. Then if you want the yolks to be firm, cook them for another minute. Finally, with a slotted spoon, take them out of the water, lay them on a paper towel to dry, and cover them with a piece of tinfoil. On each plate, a piece of toast covered with a piece of ham and a cold. Cover each with one or two tablespoons of warm mustard sauce.

Then she gave me the recipe for the poppy-seed bread pudding. It is delicious, and quite rich. But it is good and easy to make. Set the milk in a saucepan with the poppy seeds and let it boil for about three minutes, stirring. Then pour the mixture into a buttered dish, press the bread down gently with a fork, and leave for half an hour to soak up the egg mixture. Then bake in a preheated oven for about forty-five minutes or until the pudding springs back when tapped lightly. Serve hot with vanilla ice cream, French vanilla cool whip, a vanilla sauce or a bourbon sauce. Vanilla sauce: During the time the pudding is baking, mix together in a saucepan a tablespoonful of sugar, a tablespoonful of brown sugar, a tablespoonful of milk and a tablespoonful of margarine. Bring to the boil, then remove from the heat and add a teaspoonful of vanilla. Serve warm over the pudding. Bourbon sauce: a half cup of heavy cream, a half cup of half-and-half, two teaspoons of vanilla extract, a quarter cup of sugar, a tablespoonful of cornstarch, and three tablespoons of bourbon. Serves two. 1. Heat the cream, half-and-half, sugar, and vanilla in a saucepan over high heat, stirring constantly, for three minutes. 2. When bubbles appear on the surface of the cream, stir in the cornstarch dissolved in the bourbon. 3. Then take the pan off the heat and stir until the sauce thickens slightly, then set over low heat and simmer for a minute. Serve hot with the pudding. Or cool and refrigerate in a jar or container. It should be quite thin, not too thick.

1  12 pounds of deer trimmed, a loin of about two inches in thickness, if possible; 12 cup port; 3 strips of orange peel, each three inches long; 1/2 teaspoon coarsely ground black pepper; 1/8 teaspoon allspice; 2 tablespoons olive oil, divided; 1 tablespoon shallot; 1/8 teaspoon garlic; Salt and freshly ground pepper; 2 tablespoons cold butter, divided; 1 tablespoon shallot; 1/8 teaspoon garlic; 12 teaspoon allspice; the juice of half a lemon; 1 bay-leaf; 2 tablespoons flour; 12 cup fresh cream; the juice of one lemon; a cinnamon stick, 12 cup sugar; demigogues; juice of one orange, fruit of a lime; 12 pound sour gooseberries, halved in half; sauce, 1 quart jugful; 1 pint 60 ml. of white wine; 2 tablespoons cold butter, chopped; 14 cup brown sugar; 1 pint 60 ml. of fresh cream; a tablespoon of finely chopped garlic; 12 cup brown sugar; 1 quart of hot beef broth; 1 bay-leaf; 1 teaspoon of mace; 12 cup water; 1 cup cold red wine; 12 cup of veal; brown flour; stir together; then mix in the butter, shallop, garlic and sugar, season with salt and pepper, and put in a bag in the cellar. Tumble the deer overnight, turning once or twice. Take out the deer from the cellar, season all sides with salt and pepper, then add to the juice. Preheat the oven to 180 ° C. After boiling the ointment in the oil, fry the deer on all sides in the hot oil for one to two minutes. Then transfer the pan to the oven for 17 to 20 minutes, depending on the doneness you want. The venison is medium-rare when it registers 125 ° F on an instant-read thermometer. Take out the deer and let it rest for 10 minutes before cutting. Add a tablespoon of butter to the frying pan in which the deer was browned. Heated over medium heat, add the shallot and garlic, and sautéed, stirring constantly, for about 30 seconds, until softened. Add the reserved marinade, sugar and cinnamon, then heat to boiling and boil until reduced by half, about 3 to 4 minutes. This sauce should be syrupy and thick. Add the gooseberries and heat to a low simmer. Cook until the gooseberries have softened and the sauce has reduced and thickened, about five to seven minutes. Add the cream and cook for one more minute, then add the remaining butter and stir to melt. Serve hot with the venison.

In a bowl put the flour, sugar, salt and yeast, then beat for a minute. Sift the flour. Pour the oil and water, and mix well. Clean and dry the worktop, and knead the dough for about ten minutes. Cover and leave to rise in a warm place for about half an hour. Divide the dough into 15 pieces and make round, lemon-size balls. Roll each ball with a rolling pin to get a disk 62mm in diameter and a thickness of 4mm. To make the coconut filling, in a thick-bottomed pan bring the coconut milk, sugar and cinnamon to a boil, and then cool to about 40° C. Add the coconut to the milk mixture, and stir until well blended. Cool completely. Put a heaped teaspoon of the coconut filling in the centre of each disk, and then roll it up. Then shape into an oval. Use a sharp knife to cut the top to make the quills, and place on a greased baking sheet. Porcupine steamed buns are cooked for about ten minutes. Let cool slightly before removing from the steamer and placing on a serving dish. To decorate, use the black marker pen to add eyes, mouth and whiskers to each bun. The way I did it is shown in the photo above. For the whiskers I used coconut husk. Serve slightly warm. Enjoy! For more of my recipes see www.recipsrl.com. http://www.stellarecipe.blogspot.com/ See also http://recipsrl.webs.com

2 cups water 1/3 cup coarse salt 4 unpeeled garlic cloves smashed 3 large sprigs fresh sage 1 teaspoon whole black peppercorns 2 bay leaves, preferably fresh 2 cups iced water 1 5 pound bone-in loin of pork, with the breastbone removed, 1 12 pound tart apples, cored, and cut into 1-inch wedges 4 tablespoons coarsely chopped onions 12 cup chopped celery 1 tablespoon chopped fresh sage 3 cups finely chopped ribs of apple, 3 cups finely chopped sage, 4 tablespoons olive oil, divided 1 1 lb. reconstituted bread crumbs (crusts removed from a French loaf), coarsely ground in a food processor, 1 and 12 cup apple juice, water, and a handful of salt, Pd, and tbsp. Add 2 cups ice water and cool to room temperature. Place the roast in a large zipper-lock bag, put the bag in a pot, and put the bag in the brine; seal. Put in the refrigerator and brine overnight. Remove the roast from the brine and drain. Let the roast rest at room temperature for 1 hour. Preheat oven to 325°. Put the first 4 ingredients on a heavy, 18 x 12 x 1-inch rimmed baking sheet and pour 3 tablespoons oil over. Salt and pepper; toss. Push the vegetables to the side of the baking sheet to make room for the roast. Heat the remaining 1 tablespoon oil in a heavy 10-inch skillet over high heat. Dry the roast and put it in the pan, fat side down. Cook, turning once, until golden, about 6 minutes. Place roast, fat side up, in the center of the baking sheet with the vegetables. Add apple cider to the pan drippings. Boil until reduced to 1 cup, about 15 to 20 minutes. Pour reduced cider over vegetables and roast. Half of the maple syrup-mustard glaze. Roast until a thermometer inserted into the center of the roast reads 140°, brushing every 45 minutes with more glaze, about 2 hours. Then remove the roast from the oven and let it rest on a cutting board for 15 minutes. While the roast is resting, combine the melted butter with the remaining 1 tbsp. mustard in a small bowl. Toss in the bread crumbs and stir until well coated. Salt and pepper to taste. On a small rimmed baking sheet. Increase oven temperature to 375°. Beam for 10 to 12 minutes until golden and crisp. Remove the roast from the oven. Carve the pork into 6 to 8 slices across the grain, but against the grain, each about 12-inch thick. Arrange the pork slices on individual plates. Using a slotted spoon, divide the vegetables among the plates. Pour the juices from the baking sheet into a cup. Cover with the mustard crumbs and serve with the juices. Shake the crumbs to release the juices and put on a buttered baking sheet. Bake in the oven until golden, about 10 minutes.

EXTRACTS: 10 ounces TOMATOES, No. 10 CANS 12 ounces GREEN PEPPER, SWEET, FRESH ONE POUND SUGAR, ICING, 10 lbs. 1 tbsp PEPPER, BLACK, 2 lbs. Preheat the oven to 325°. 1. Add the sugar to the tomatoes, and heat them to a boil. 2. In a skillet, fry the onions and peppers in the lard or perhaps a little lard, and when tender, stir in the flour, and cook for about two minutes. 3. Then add the onions and peppers to the tomatoes, and bring to a boil, stirring constantly. 4. 5. Place 100 hamburgs in the end of each dish. 6. Pour an equal amount of sauce over each hamburg. BAKE FOR 30 MINUTES, OR TILL TENDERS UP. NOTE: 1. In Step 2, use one pound of dry onions. A pound of onions yields 12 ounces of minced onions, and a pound of green peppers yields one pound of minced peppers. 2. In Step 5, remove the fat from the canned hamburgs by letting them stand for five minutes in a pan of hot water. 3. In Step 5, remove the fat from the canned hamburgs by placing the cans, unopened, in hot water for five minutes. 4. Other pans may be used. See the recipe card. SERVING SIZE: Two Patty Pans.

Two small blood oranges (or other thin-skinned oranges, preferably organic) 13 cup olive oil 2 cups of unbleached flour 12 teaspoon baking powder 12 teaspoon salt 4 eggs 12 cup white sugar 1 teaspoon vanilla extract, optionally powdered sugar for sprinkling Pre-heat the oven to 350° F. Butter and flour the cake pan. Wash the oranges well, clean them with soap, rinse them in water and then with fresh water, pat dry, and take off the stem and the tail, and cut off the top and bottom of the orange, so that you have only the flesh. Remove the seeds and cut the orange into large pieces. Put the oranges in the food processor and puree until coarsely chopped. Add the olive oil slowly, pulse the food processor and let it go for a while, then stir the oranges into the eggs, sugar and salt. In a bowl, sift together the flour, baking powder, soda and salt. Beat the eggs well and add the sugar little by little until the mixture is thick and lemony. Add the vanilla and, if desired, the powdered sugar. Into the eggs, stir in a third of the flour and beat well. Then add a third of the orange puree and beat well. Add more flour and orange puree until all is incorporated. It will be a very thick mixture. Pour into the cake pan and bake for 60 minutes or until the cake is golden brown and has risen from the sides of the pan. If you have used a springform pan, remove the sides. If not, let cool for five minutes and then remove from the pan. When the cake is completely cooled, sprinkle with powdered sugar.

1 1/3 cups flour, 6 tablespoons butter, diced 3 tablespoons of sugar plus 1 tsp sugar ; half a teaspoon salt - 3 tablespoons sour cream, 3 tablespoons sour cream - depending on your mood 2 tablespoons of cream or crème fraiche - and, finally, knead the dough until it is smooth and firm. Split the dough in half and roll each half into a slightly flattened ball. Cover with a cloth and leave in the fridge for an hour. Then preheat the oven to 320° F and grease a baking sheet with butter. Having floured the work surface, roll one piece of dough into a thin layer, about 14 inches. Using a round cookie cutter, cut out the biscuits and put them on the greased baking sheet. Do the same with the remaining dough. Then bake for 12 to 15 minutes, until golden, with a slightly charred rim. Put on a grid to cool and store in an airtight container.

6 ear-corns of the tastiest freshest corn, about 6 tablespoonfuls of butter (see above for recipe) Take the husks, and draw them down as far as the end without removing them, remove the silk. Put the corn in a basin or a pan of cold water. Let them soak for two hours or more. Take them out, wipe them, rub the ear with butter, put on a few slices of onion, and cover with the husks. Then make a fire of mesquite, fig, hickory, apple, or similar wood in your furnace, at 225° F. Put in the ear-corns in the furnace, leaving a little space between each one, so that the smoke may circulate. Also a gas fire may be used: Place your wood-chips in a receptacle on the furnace above the flame, and lower the temperature when the smoke begins to rise, to 225° F. It is now a good time to prepare a compound butter, using the recipes above. After the ear-corns have been smoking for about half an hour, put a teaspoonful of the compound butter under each husk, and if you can, put it on the whole of the ear-corn. Then let them smoke another half hour. Repeat this operation in about another half hour.

I have been searching for a hobby and have stumbled upon a hobby that is restoring old guns. It is a hobby that I really want to engage in and I also hope to revive old historic items that I like. A few days ago, while visiting a firearms dealer with my father and grandfather, I stumbled upon a section in the back where they were selling guns for extremely cheap. I asked my grandfather why they were so cheap and he said they were probably only hangers and they weren't in the best condition. I decided to try out this hobby because I like guns and old, antique things, as well as history. I am wondering whether I should make it so that they still shoot and operate in a completely normal way, which is quite dangerous and almost illegal unless I am old enough to have a gun license, or whether I should restore them and take the firing pin out so that they do not shoot any bullets or cartridges, so that I can keep them and have them as a beautiful historical object in my room and in my house, but I do not know which to do as taking out the firing pin might damage or lower the value of the item. I do not know which to choose, but I think I will probably choose to take the firing pin out of the guns so that I can use them as decorations and historical items without worrying about any legal restrictions. Any thoughts or ideas?

I just watched the section of Glee where they scolded Kazuya for that scene where he wasn’t running after Mizuhara and I’m wondering... When I first read the novel, I felt that he was a real pain in the neck, but I thought I understood where all his pranks came from and so I gave him a pass. I know his perversion is a pain, but I think it’s mostly the author trying to be funny but failing. And later, he’s really great. That scene where he tries to make up to Mizuhara for not running after her was actually pretty touching, and there were many more times later on when I really sympathized with him. Am I just a fellow incel who feels sorry for other incels? I was feeling very depressed myself for a while and so I related to Kazuya’s self-esteem problems, especially because it was so encouraging to see him fight for himself out there.

My friend has acid in the stomach. He had a coloscopy and they said he was perfectly well. He ate something, and up it came and he spat it out. He has lost a great deal of weight from it. He has taken all sorts of medicines to cure himself. I told him to go to the doctor, and say to him, if he is perfectly well, why does it happen? The medicines they gave him do not help, and he is losing weight fast and needs to. I am asking this group if anyone has or has had this experience, and whether there is any remedy.

If you have enough money to keep in your bank account to pay all your bills during the month, put them all on automatic payment, even if you don’t, if you have a credit card with enough room, put them on that card and set a monthly payment on your credit card. I cannot tell you how much money I’ve saved on late fees and the effort of dealing with customer service on the phone. Usually, if you ask when you’re setting up automatic payment, they’ll offer some sort of a discount or reduction, so you’ll save even more in the long run. I used to avoid putting bills on automatic payment because I was afraid of overdraft and not having enough to pay them, but I’ve found it’s much easier to keep a little more than I think I’ll need in my account and have them automatically pay because I always end up forgetting to pay them and end up with a huge bill. I don’t have great credit, but I was able to get a secured card and I put some of my bills on it so I don’t have to worry about an overdraft and I set up automatic payments for that as well.

I'm buying a large shipment of floorboards from a Chinese manufacturer through Alibaba, and I'm having it shipped to the U.S. The manufacturer has already paid for the door-to-door delivery but has asked me to give him my business name and tax ID number so that they can send it through customs. I think it's probably my social security number since I don't have a business. I'm not planning to sell the floorboards. We're using them for a house we're building. Is it really wrong to give my social security number? Is there anything else I can do? I've read that if I give them my social security number, they'll put it on the outside of the box so that anyone can see it. The order is large. It's five pallets and weighs about 4,400 pounds.

Hello. I've been reading this sub for a few months and I can relate to many people here. For context, I'm an 18-year-old man trying to leave my parents' house. My mom has been withholding my birth certificate and my food stamp card, and I want to escape from the abuse I've suffered for years. I have no idea how to proceed. My mom was trying to give away my food stamp card and I hope whoever she gives it to will refuse it, but my family's history doesn't seem to support this. I asked my father for my birth certificate, but he says he doesn't have it. Has this happened to anyone else on this subreddit? What measures should I take to keep my personal information safe? Thanks for your help.

I've been on testosterone for almost two years, and I'll have my breast surgery in June. I'm passing as a cis at work, with only four people knowing, I think. I told one of my friends that I was going to have a surgery in June, and he began asking me what surgery. He then asked who else knew about it, and got very angry at the fact that he seemed to be the only one in our area who did not know. However, I feel sorry for him, and I would like to tell him. I have often thought about what it would mean if I told him. I know that he would encourage me in my breast surgery and not ask me too many questions if I had to put a limit on it. He is also a super nice person and I love working with him. I trust him, but I do not trust him enough. I'm afraid that he will start to treat me differently out of respect. I do not want him to treat me differently, I do not want our friendship to change in any way. So I wonder if anyone has had their friends treat them differently after they became transgender?

Hey all, I’m Milo, 25 and transgender. I gave birth to my wonderful child in 2014 at the age of 19, and suckled him for a little while after the birth. I had my womb reconstructed in November, and though I’m not too worried about the hip dysphoria or feminization once I start hormones, I’m wondering if the breast surgery would interfere with my hormones. I’ve heard that taking hormones for six months before the operation will improve the results. My breasts are large and saggy, and they’re more like a U shape than an O. While I was looking up breast surgery I could only find references to small breasts; one site basically implied that I should forget about having surgery until I’d shrunk to a slender figure with A or B cups. Of course, that’s not going to happen, but will I run into medical gatekeeping if I do decide to have the surgery? Would I be put under pressure to just have a reduction rather than a top as well? Am I the only one this happens to?

For most people outside of my world, it is impossible to imagine how difficult it is to refrain from buying make-up. This year I have spent less than $200 on make-up, whereas last year and the year before I spent over $200. My make-up collection is gradually getting smaller, and this is very good. I have a wish that it was my future ghost and that I would be able to see myself in the ball’s eyes.

“I do; I have an audience with a kindly gentleman who says he can tell me all about it, but he has no more time than I have to say the truth of it—and that’s not exactly a lie.” “You may well be right, sir,” I said, “but please do not leave me to suffer this way alone.” I took the liberty of looking at the curiously swollen birthmark on my shin and observing how it was accompanied by ever-increasing tension. Nevertheless, I kept on apologizing to him for disturbing me; I couldn’t stay in the apartment with these unpleasantries unaddressed. I’m sure people are much more sensible than that. Besides, I don’t care about those illnesses, but I’d rather not discuss them with just one person. “Once again, sir, it would be far better if you didn’t care about those things and let me go to my destination,” I said, “you will be most welcome. You may be sure I shall tell all I know to the kindly gentleman I have an audience with.” I turned around to leave, for I was tired of apologizing. But I felt a prick of conscience, I’d rather not discuss these things.

I was told to state in the beginning that I fell like a rag doll on my foot and hurt myself. The ailment in particular was a bruise on the top and sole of my foot, which was very painful. My husband is a doctor, and he agreed that my foot was broken, but he also agreed with the health authorities that it was a fracture of the Lisfranc joint, and needed close observation. I could not thank you enough for the explanation of Lisfranc fractures. X-rays showed that it was indeed a Lisfranc fracture, which required the use of a cast to immobilize it, and the need to be off it for many weeks. Unfortunately, since I have Charcot-Marie neuropathy, this was my good leg. So, I am still lying in bed until I am able to walk on my foot again, if ever. Since my decline in my nervous system has been so swift, I must stay still for the time being. I've been handed the world's worst jackpot of lemons at once. But all in all, I am secure and sound, so life could be worse. Thank you for all your kind thoughts, and for your beautiful advice, which I value highly.

I think when modeling for games, the modifiers and non-destructive approach to working in Blender makes it superior to most 3D packages. However, there is one thing that is essential when working with high-to-low poly, and that is keeping the geometry as simple as possible and being able to modify it without having to tack on a loop every time it goes around a corner. Maya's crease set tool was excellent for this, and I can't understand why someone hasn't released an add-on for this yet, because it would speed up my work enormously. Don't tell me I can do it with vertex groups, because it just doesn't cut it; it gets too cluttered, and the crease values are lost as soon as the model gets complex. Perhaps it's too difficult to code? I would happily fund it. Let me know what you think.

My seventeen-year-old dog died last week, and somehow I sensed the moment of her death without knowing it. I must add that the day before I took psychedelics and couldn’t sleep all night. I wonder if anyone else thinks like this, or if I’m going mad. This is how I’ve learned to think about reality. It does make me anxious, but it makes me concentrate on stringing together good days. There is no present, or at least time moves too fast for us to perceive it. By the time the light catches it, and we understand something, it’s gone. We’re simply stringing together recollections of the past. The best thing is to keep on building a better future, so that you can live with the past you’ve made. Spend as little time as possible in the past, and don’t worry about the memories you have too much, or they’ll get mixed up with the present. Look for information, for nostalgia, for hope—but don’t look at a memory too long, or it’ll get contaminated by the present. Just give it a quick look. Once you’ve learned all there is to learn from the past, don’t go back there again to look for more information. You’ll get it contaminated by your wishes and change it. And above all, don’t let your jerk of a mind dwell too long in the past, or it’ll contaminate your future.

After I had been playing a while with Ji-Woon, I had one nagging gripe. The wound should not wear down at all while the player is running. In order to make up for the lack of healing when the player is running, perhaps the healing time should be reduced slightly while the player is walking. I think this would make the game more lively. Instead of simply running like in Deathsinger, putting the victim between you and the killer, you would be forced to slow down more. If the victim ran away from you, you could at least keep track of him through his wound meter, even if you couldn't strike him directly. If you lose a victim, you could always check the wound meter to see if he's running away or not. Another thing is the final strike. Although it is possible to keep the wound meter from reducing to a single point, if you do, you are forced to stop using your knife, which you may need later. It would be more convenient if you could use the final strike at any time instead of having to wait for the fifteen second interval. In spite of this, Ji-Woon is a great killer for players who want to be a ranged killer who doesn't need to hit the enemy every time.
