SPOILER ALERT: Full Metal Jacket is a 1987 war film set in the Vietnam War, and it’s one of the best films ever made, in my opinion, based on a novel by Gustav Hasford. The script was written by Kubrick, Michael Herr and Gustav Hasford, based on his novel The Long Walk. It won the Academy Award for Best Writing, Adapted Screenplay in 1989, and is one of my favourite war films. I love it to death. There’s a fantastic ensemble cast in this brilliant film by Kubrick, about the Vietnam War and the dehumanizing process that turns people into killers. Matthew Modine as the Joker, Vincent D’Onofrio as the hound dog, Dorian Harewood as the pig, Arliss Howard as the cowboy, and a whole lot more as trainees, all put through hell by a leather-lung drill instructor (Lee Ermey) who doesn’t think much of the wretched wretches he has to supervise. The action is savage, the story is unsparing, the dialogue is laced with a wicked sense of humour, and the film scores a direct hit. The film features two parts, showing the effects of the military mindset and the Vietnam War on American soldiers. A dehumanizing hell-camp turns young boys into trained killers. It’s the late 1960s at Parris Island, South Carolina, a Marine Corps training centre. A new batch of recruits have just been shaved and put through their paces by the sadistic Gunnery Sergeant Hartman (Lee Ermey), who has orders to ‘weed out all non-snappers’. Every trainee is given a nickname, a talkative fellow (Matthew Modine) becomes the Joker, an amiable fellow from Texas is the Cowboy (Arliss Howard), and a six-foot-three-inch, 280-pound dim-witted lad with no ambition or ambition becomes the Gomer Pyle (Vincent D’Onofrio), because he can’t keep up with the slimmer ones on the obstacle course. The first part of the film is a view of the training process that turns recruits into trained killers and sends them off to war in Vietnam, told from the point of view of Private James T. Davis (Matthew Modine), who is on the losing end of a cruel treatment regime inflicted on him by his drill instructor. – and how this young lad is transformed into a bloodthirsty killing machine, blowing Hartman’s head off! And Pyle sits down on the toilet, puts the barrel of his gun in his mouth, and pulls the trigger, killing himself. The second part deals with the war in Vietnam, when the Joker is a war correspondent for the Stars and Stripes newspaper and has to cover the Tet Offensive. His colleagues, photographer Cutter (Kevyn Major Howard) and Joker (Matthew Modine) meet a prostitute (Leanne Hong) and a thief (Nguyen Hue Phong), who steal Cutter’s camera. On their return to base they are assigned to new beats, but the Joker wants to be assigned to the front line to get a good story. Poisoning the land mines is not enough for him, he wants to be on the front line, where he is assigned to a special unit of the “Rapid Fire” snipers. The Joker, Cutter, and the prostitute go with the Joker to the front, and find about twenty dead bodies in a lime pit. This is the best film ever made by Stanely Kubrick about the war in Vietnam, and it is one of the best films ever made about the war in general. The film is superbly shot, with a wonderful, almost claustrophobic feel to the landscape of the country, and the contrast between the demented treatment inflicted on the recruits in the training camp and the contrast between hours of boredom and seconds of terror in the scenes in Vietnam is powerful, and not for everyone, but it is REAL. The film focuses more on the city of Hue, and there is a major battle scene there. The tanks drive through the city, the streets are strewn with corpses, buildings are on fire, and buildings are being blown up. naive M60 machine-gunner “The Butcher’s Boy” (Adam Baldwin) is one of the best characters in the film, and yet he is only an extra. But he is so memorable that he looks like a main character. This, it turns out, is because of the “dual nature of man” as defined by Carl Jung.

First of all, it's an Adam Sandler movie. If you hate Adam Sandler movies, you won't like it. I gave it 8/10 because it was one of the better Adam Sandler movies. The plot and storyline was better than I expected, the character development was quite good as well. There were a few moments when I wanted to hit myself in the face because it was so slapstick funny. Yes, it's highly unrealistic, but if you're looking for realism, what the hell are you looking for? Yes, I know, it's a dumb story about an ugly woman who fucks her a lot, but she played it quite well.

The Grand Illusion is a film about class, which has no hostile attitude towards any class. I know that there are a lot of weak and wussy pictures that "show all sides" and that make you groan with their inconsequential point of view, but that's not what I mean. Those are merely films about class, and I'm rather partial to the "Eat the Rich" films. But the Grand Illusion deals with class without contempt for anyone. The aristocrats, whose world is dying, are tragic figures, involved in a code that is quickly becoming meaningless. The Frenchman, the aristocrat, knows that his time is past, the German, the aristocrat, is aware that his time is passing, and he doesn't agree with the Frenchman, and blames the French Revolution for the Frenchman's mood, but both know that their world will soon be forgotten. And it would have been easy for Renoir, a French communist with proletarian sympathies in the mid-thirties, to demonize these two; but he does not demonize them; he allows them their humanity, and this is the most typical thing in his films, because he is the great humanist of film history. The bourgeois are good people; the world might be in their hands, at least as well as in anyone else's (except for the tendency of nations to war). All the middle and lower-class characters in the film are shown as people, not as stereotypes. But Renoir does not achieve this by destroying all class distinctions in the name of a homogeneous universality. These characters are not only in their class, but they are in their class, and it is clear to the viewer what class they are in. The film is not about the absence of class, but about the oppressive ironies of the class that really exists in the life of the characters. This is an amazing film, in which, in a way, the hero is from the bourgeois-working class, but the upper class is not demonized, and the lower class is not romanticized or despised. And it is all so easy that many (perhaps most) people who have not seen it will think it's a nice but not great film, and it slips away.

In his inexperienced days, young Dewey Cox had a bad accident and cut his brother in half with a knife, which started him on a long, winding road through the most important events in the history of music from the 1950s to the present day. It was wrongly advertised as Judd Apatow's comedy, and though Apatow was co-writer, with his trademark naive, sexual and ironic jokes, The Dewey Cox Story is closer to Christopher Guest's mockumentary style. Like Waiting... and Best in Show, but channeled through the cramped colon of the Naked Gun series. The comedy is played in a completely serious way, and the aim of the satire is so clear, that it will be completely lost on those who haven't really seen "Walk the Line" and who were expecting a "Superbad" rip-off. It's so accurate in its imitation of its inspiration that it even comes out midway with its cadence, almost breaking in the middle of its own, quickly passing over several points in history and the lives of musicians, from the temptation of touring with drugs and seducers to visits to a sick-house and bitter divorces to the most creative periods of life, with all the clichés that you've heard a million times, all in one, under the leadership of John C. Reilly, who's showing off his best voice. A former Chicago nominee, Reilly has a career as a background actor and comedian, with Will Ferrell in "Talladega Nights", and this is his first time in the film. Kristen Wiig, Chris Parnell, Apatow's alumnus Paul Rudd as John Lennon, are joined by others from SNL and the Apatow camp, including Paul Rudd as John Lennon. Mr. Hill and others... and the ever-popular Jonah Hill, surrounded by a slew of funny visual gags and verbal jokes. Then there is a plethora of current pop stars, such as the lead singer of the White Stripes as Elvis and the Pearl Jam's Eddie Vedder, who makes a completely nonsensical and quasi-spiritual speech to Dewey Cox when he is awarded a lifetime achievement award. The heart of "Walk Hard" is the songs, a lot of which you can easily imagine as the hits of that time. It is also fun to listen to the lyrics. Cox's duet with Darlene is particularly funny, and my personal favorite is a parody of Bob Dylan. With the way the writers took so much care and time with their silly, free verse, they managed to write a poem that was both an homage to Bob and a subtle insult to his genius for words. In the end, the whole movie is really smart, incredibly stupid and absurdly clever. It's true that it failed in the first day, but it will surely find its audience in the long run. When he is trying to persuade his wife to believe in his ability to become a great singer, she replies to him: "I believe in you, darling. I just believe you're going to fail." I couldn't have said it better myself, and I'm still laughing.

* SPOILER WARNING *********** I had the pleasure of seeing the film twice in the cinema. The only films I've ever seen with a more engaged audience are The Dark Knight, Spider-Man 1 & 2, X-Men 2 and Rocky. The film is interesting from start to finish. As good as all the actors (and actresses) are, it's Sean Bean who shines. The villain can make or break a film, and he was the best choice for this particular villain. The character's arrogance, intelligence and determination come to the fore. The only problem with the film is that it's rated PG. It should have been rated PG-13. Some overt violence was toned down. Even people who don't swear would drop the f-bomb at the appropriate times. But, as it is, it's still a film that's enjoyable for everyone.

Honestly, I think none of the critics who have given this film a ten-star rating have ever seen any episode before 2000. I went into this film thinking it would probably be good. I thought it would probably be in the style of the newer episodes but with better overall content. If anyone says it was like the “old Simpsons,” they’re kidding themselves. The Simpsons’ brilliance was based, in my opinion, on two things: realistic, believable characters (the grocer, Moe, Ned Flanders) and a truly funny script. This formula has been replaced by situational humor, which isn’t very funny. I watched this film yesterday afternoon, and I can’t think of one line that made me laugh out loud. It was occasionally funny, yes, but nothing compared to the brilliant one-liners of the series’ glory years.

When I saw The King's Speech, I saw many elderly people in the hall, and it occurred to me that some of them were probably alive when George VI made the actual speech to the English nation, which had just declared war on Hitler. The King's Speech is a nice film, but a very adult one, and while it tells a good story, well written, absorbing and believable (except for a few lines here and there), Tom Hooper's film is more driven by character than by plot. The only time he does not stammer is when he curses, something that a new teacher of speech recommends in a scene that is rated R. In a sense, The King's Speech is also a proud moment for Geoffrey Rush. This is his best role, and he and Firth are almost the whole film. Their dialogue is utterly flawless. The King's Speech also has a very strong cast, including Helena Bonham Carter, Michael Gambon, Derek Jacobi and Guy Pearce, who all have a lot to say and contribute to the film, despite a very limited screen time. There is also no doubt that it is one of the best films of the year.

Since the story is about kids who want to go to a concert, it's quite obvious that in the end they'll see the concert. It's a question of whether you enjoy the trip to get there. And I did. Despite its being a teen comedy (which is why there's a puke scene) and some physical comedy that was slightly abrasive, the movie was a lot of fun. Every high school kid can remember the time when they worshiped a band and would give anything to see them live on stage, and this movie captures that feeling perfectly. It also captures the time period perfectly, with the music, the cars, and the fun pop music (I mean, the shoes the girls in the disco wore!) And there were a few surprises and surprises, including the ending, which was very sweet. It's a very well-done high school musical. And although I'm not a fan of Kiss, I can still remember the time when the music was my one and only salvation. 7 out of 10.

Ok, so here's a horror movie that's actually worth watching. I've seen a lot of vampire/zombie films and this one stood out because, even though it sometimes uses some gore, it's not what makes it scary - it's the tension. You don't know what's going to happen next, the mood is eerie and the film gets under your skin like the Alaskan cold, and most horror films end really badly; this one sort of did too, but it had a nice romance.

Did this movie represent a huge improvement over the original Thor movie? No, unfortunately not. But is it another enjoyable, fun super hero movie? Yes, definitely. And if you look at the way director Alan Taylor shot this movie, it’s really not so different from what Branagh did back in 2011. Chris Hemsworth is good as always and Tom Hiddleston is even better than ever as Loki, but unfortunately the villain Malekith, played by Christopher Eccleston, is somewhat of a disappointment, mainly due to the lack of motivation.

APOCALYPSE NOW is not only the best war film ever made but one of the best films ever made, for it won the prestigious Palme d’Or at Cannes and has become a milestone in film history. It was based on Joseph Conrad’s novel Heart of Darkness,* and is not primarily about the Vietnam War, but about war in general, and serves as a profound study of the dark places in the human soul and how war can affect the individual. The film’s plot is quite simple: a US army captain, Benjamin Willard (Martin Sheen), is sent on a dangerous, secret mission to Cambodia to kill a renegade, Colonel Kurtz (Marlon Brando), who has become insane and a deity to the local tribe. This is a plot that even the most casual filmgoer can follow, but the film is not at all shallow, for it is a journey into the madness of hysteria, a study of the dark side of humanity. I could write a whole book analysing this film, so much can be said about it. My own interpretation of the river is that it is not only a journey to find Kurtz, but a descent into madness and a reflection of the characters’ inner journey towards evil, which is achieved through the film’s principal theme of dehumanization. * The journey down the river is reminiscent of Dante’s perilous journey through indescribable hell and abyss. Before reaching Kurtz, there are three major stops on the river, and each of these stops is a reflection of the dehumanization brought on by war, and each stop in the river introduces a new kind of evil. First, in the camp of the Americans, we see how their love of war has deluded them and made them blind to the consequences of their actions. In one scene, the ‘heroic charge’ of the American soldiers, as they march forward in their helicopters to massacre the enemy, Kilgore, to inspire his men and inspire terror in the enemy, is seen using Wagner’s The Ride of the Valkyries to motivate his soldiers and intimidate his enemies. We see that while everyone is inhuman towards the enemy, they still understand that the enemy is innocent. At the second stop on the river, the USO show, we see the loss of all morality and the dehumanization of the innocent. We see the soldiers at this stage dehumanizing everyone but themselves, turning their backs on everyone and becoming so selfish that they are willing to sacrifice anyone for the sake of instant gratification. At the third stop, Do-long Bridge, we see a man who has reached the end of the line and is unable to cope with the horrors of war and has been driven to desperation. He has become completely dehumanized and is beyond redemption. At the fourth stop, Kurtz, only Kurtz and Willard are still sane and at peace, and they are now both searching for the heart of darkness, that ultimate evil which each of us possesses. The soldier who has sounded the charge sees that Kurtz is innocent, but his hatred of Kurtz has blinded him to the reality of the situation, and so he decides to act on his own instinct and kill Kurtz, thus taking possession of the heart of darkness himself. In the end, Willard is reborn and goes out of the camp, having gained possession of the heart of darkness. At the last minute he makes a decision – to give in to the evil and stay in the camp, to become the savages’ new chief or to abandon them. By saving Ned and the savages and not exterminating the whole tribe, he has travelled his own personal journey and reached the ultimate end of his own soul. Through the eerie music of Carmine Coppola, the hypnotic images and the terrifying scenes, we enter the ultimate hell of the human soul, and this is where the film is at its most effective. The directing by Martin Scorsese is astonishing, as is the cinematography of Vittorio Storaro. The whole film is shot as if in a trance, and the hallucinations are terrifying. The faces of the madmen, bathed in perspiration, the dark figures of the savages, the dark shores of the river – all are captured so that the hellish visions can take your breath away. With the exception of Kurtz’s first appearance, which is too over-simplified, the direction is outstanding, especially the use of light and darkness. The troubled production obviously did not harm the film, but probably contributed to its dark tone. Apocalypse Now is haunting, hellish, terrifyingly intelligent and magnificently crafted. It slowly takes us through the horror and absurdity of war and the meaning and beauty of it. Not only is it one of the best films ever made, but it is also a journey through psychoanalysis into the innermost recesses of the human soul that none of us would ever dare to travel to on our own. It is Francis Ford Coppola’s masterpiece, the film for which he sacrificed everything. It is immortal, a true masterpiece of filmmaking, unforgettable.

I see many films, and I do not remember that I was more absorbed than by this one. Not only were the characters so vividly and brilliantly drawn by an excellent cast, but their intimate interplay was depicted with inspired understatement and nuance. The scenery of the film, which is magnificent, deserves to have been given an Oscar. The central theme of the film is the conflict between Ludlow’s militantly antiwar and pacifistic position and his sons’ desire to do their duty, while their father is antigovernment and antiwar. But the conflict is not the main focus, but the fracture that comes between these three devoted brothers when they all fall in love with the same woman. A tragic story, yes, a painful one at times, but never dull. Every time I thought I knew what would happen next, the plot took a new unexpected turn, and I sat there riveted to the seat, mouthing “Wow” into the darkness. This film immediately became one of my all-time favorites. Since then I have seen it half a dozen times and I am still moved by its power and scope.

From his comedy in Usual Suspects to Get Out, Jordan Peele has proved that he has grown into a director. Get Out is one of the best and most original horror films of the last decade. Instead of having jump-scares and cheesy music, Get Out relies on the mystery and the fear of the unknown, subtly giving us a message about racism and how it feels to be black in America. As I mentioned, the best thing about Get Out is the writing. The characters are smart, they behave like reasonable people instead of the clichés of horror movies. Everything has a reason and everything has a meaning. Unlike other horror clichés, Get Out doesn't feign scares or replace them with unrelated humour. Besides, the humour (especially the character of Lil Rel Howery) is perfectly balanced with the story and comes at the right time. Unnerving, bleak and with brilliant performances (mainly from Daniel Kaluuya) and excellent writing, Get Out is a perfect portrayal of US society during the current era.

Awesome!! Blade II is a vampire superhero action horror sequel to the 1998 film, Blade. A sequel to a kickass film with an R-rating, and a mix of Daryl, still the same, and a Hellboy with a round head... Not only did it take four years for this sequel to come out after the first, but we see Wesley Snipes returning as Blade, and he's still awesome! I love this movie, but I love the first one way more. This is the second of the three Blade movies. In this one, he's looking for the Whistler, who is a vampire now. He finds him, and then he meets up with a group of vampires called the Blood Pack, who want his help to track down a vampire named Nomak (Luke Goss). The vampire basically has the power to turn vampires into reapers, who can hunt both vampires and humans. Anyway, that's the basic plot. There are some twists and turns from here and there, but it's still kickass. Because Wesley Snipes is so good at martial arts, and because it's a movie from 2002, the fight scenes are awesome. The choreographer basically says something like, "Aww, come on!" and the whole movie is all bloody and violent, and you can see the characters suddenly turn into CGI characters and it's like really bad. Especially when the old guy does the spinning kick and kicks Blade in the face, and turns into a CGI character, you can see it's a bit weak, but does it ruin the movie? No, it doesn't ruin it! This movie is awesome!!! The first ten minutes of the movie, in that time, Blade kills about 25 people. Like the first movie! There are like 50 or 60 people killed in the first ten minutes, it's awesome!!! Kris Kristofferson is an amazing badass! And like I said before, Norman Reedus still looks like a twelve-year-old, he's still Daryl. He has the same hair, the same stubborn face and he just looks like he doesn't get any older, damn it! They're all getting older, in the eyes of society, but they don't look it! Ron Perlman is awesome, he wants you to hate him, but you can't hate him because he's Ron Perlman, and you just laugh at him because he's so funny and so nasty, and so funny and so nasty, he's so nasty! And he is so nasty! He's awesome!!! Where's Hellboy 3? It's an amazing guy! He even had a special role in Alien: Resurrection, I mean, he is a phenomenal man! The effects are pretty good in this movie, too, except for the fight scenes when the characters suddenly turn into CGI characters, but it's okay, you can still forget that because the same thing happens in Spider-Man (2002), where they also use CGI characters, oh, it's like you had to back then, now they're doing better now, I'm sure of that. So this movie is directed by Guillermo del Toro, the fight choreography is also by him, the movie is written by David S. Goyer. I'm not a fan of him, but it's a good writer! How do you make a badass even more badass than Blade already is? I think it's possible, it's possible! It's possible and it's amazing! Wesley Snipes has that charm again, he has that badass, but he also has that comedy in him like in the second movie, in the lap dance place or whatever it was. Ron Perlman was going to shoot him and he shot at his gun and he sat there, all smiles, it's like he was laughing at you. It's so badass! You actually feel sorry for one of the characters, even though she was cute, just saying, but the end of the day is that this movie is one of the best sequels ever, and you should definitely see it!!!!! The story doesn't have many character developments, but it has enough to keep you interested and entertained. And like I said, if you're looking for a movie with brains, you'll find them here, and if you're looking for muscle, this will blow you away. Also, the new characters that they created are really cool, they are so funny and they make the movie better! So 9/10, my second favorite of the Blade trilogy, my favorite will always be the first Blade!

– a movie premiere with Mother, where we laughed and cried and clapped together with all the other spectators. I mean, really, we all clapped and jumped up. A real pleasure! The premise is a simple one: you take an ambitious businessman, a man chasing his own success, and then you put him together with three hungry, talented, and basically hungry-and-hungry young ballplayers and, in the end, they all end up changing each other. And the cast is superb, too! You've got Alan Arkin, Bill Paxton, and Suraj Sharma, Madhur Mittal, the real-life counterparts of the originals. We, my family, like sports films, and my mother loves them especially when it comes to ball games, so it was absolutely perfect to go to the movie with her on Mother's Day. If you like ball movies or know kids who love ball games, or any other sport for that matter, then you just have to see this movie! It's The Rookie meets Hoop Dreams!

I’ve just come back from the first showing we could find a babysitter for. I can now safely say that all my fears about this movie were groundless and I now have the highest regard for Guy Ritchie and his co-writers. Without going into spoilers, here are the three things that I was most afraid of seeing in the trailer: 1) the use of bullet-time in a period film. I thought it was completely anachronistic and pointless. But what they had established in the last movie and this one is that Holmes has an unusually keen sense of his surroundings, and the use of bullet-time is to suggest how painful a few scenes are to someone with that hyper-sensitivity, and it works beautifully. 2) Jared Harris looks so tame and non-threatening in the trailer and in the stills that I couldn’t imagine him as a fearsome adversary for Sherlock Holmes. But he is so devious and sly, and at times so sadistic, that I think they could not have chosen a better actor. There were a few times when I thought he was channeling his father (the wonderful Richard Harris) but without any of the warmth and sympathy that the late actor lent to his performances. Can you imagine Richard Harris playing a calculating perfectionist who had no regard for human life? You don’t have to after seeing his son. And he sings! 3) The relationship between Holmes and Watson, and in a small way with Irene Adler, is fantastically developed. Saying anything more would be too much of a spoiler. Seeing this with my husband (who is a devoted fan of the series and read the stories to me every rainy night, complete with character voices) was a fantastic experience. We can’t wait to see it again, and to own it.

I’m a South African, and having seen the film on Friday morning, I can say that this entertaining, uplifting and thoroughly entertaining film, which is also factually very accurate, completely surpassed my expectations. It’s a true story, but one told in intimate terms, and based on actual events. It covers all the major issues, and a whole host of the smaller ones, but without exaggerating. The way that the director lets the story unfold with the minimum of fuss, he allows the story to tell itself. I remember watching the 1995 World Cup on television, and the wonderful sight of a beaming Madiba as he came out with the Springbok jersey. And when in the last minutes, when the ball had barely touched the ground, Joel Stransky sent the ball flying over the bar, and the Springboks won, I cheered and cried at the same time. Then afterwards millions of South Africans, of all races, celebrated. It was a memorable occasion. It was the birth of the Rainbow Nation. Nelson Mandela is the greatest and most beloved of all South Africans. The man is a living legend, but at the same time he is so human and so real. When he was president he brought hope to all South Africans, both black and white. We’ll never stop loving that extraordinary man. I felt that Clint Eastwood and Morgan Freeman did South Africa and our beloved Madiba proud. Francois Pienaar is also an amazing South African, an intelligent, caring and finely tuned rugby player, who has always led by example. And Matt Damon does Pienaar the full justice of his abilities. I was glued to the screen from start to finish – I didn’t even move until the end credits had finished rolling and the lights came up – and I cried a few times, the last scene being especially moving. I was especially impressed by Morgan Freeman, and I wouldn’t be surprised if he received a nomination for an Oscar. If you think that his portrayal of Mandela is too laid-back to be true, then think again. I’ve known the real-life Madiba, and he is indeed that cool, that laid-back, a courageous and intelligent man, whose strength of character and courage are an example to the whole world. After being unjustly imprisoned for nearly thirty years by a repressive and cruel regime, he came out to run a country and to teach its people about the meaning of reconciliation. I thoroughly recommend this authentic and historically accurate film to film lovers, to Eastwood fans, to fans of Nelson Mandela and to all sports fans. Viva South Africa, viva Madiba. P.S. I’m a great fan of Clint Eastwood as an actor and as a director, and my favourite Eastwood-directed films, in no particular order, are: The Forgotten, Unforgiven, Gran Torino, The Outlaw Josey Wales, Letters from Iwo Jima, The Bridges of Madi-da- ison County, Bird, and Invictus. This one is another of his triumphs. He’s getting better with age. What a streak of creativity he has right now. P.P.S. Invictus is one of the best sports films I have ever seen. But it is much more than just a sports film.

The great catastrophe of the Indian Ocean was one of the most terrifying disasters in human history. It was the Christmas season and the beaches were crowded with vacationers. The death toll of nearly 250,000 was high because it did not respect national boundaries. It affected everyone. My relatives who were living in the South of Thailand were going to be on the beach that day, but a sudden illness forced them to change their plans. From some of my Thai acquaintances I heard how children rushed to the shore to see the amazing sight of the ocean receding only to be overwhelmed by the rushing waves. And later, when I flew over the coast of Indonesia, I saw with my own eyes the degree of destruction the rushing waves had left. How do you tell a story like this and do justice to both the victims and the survivors, many of whom suffered a personal tragedy, and many more who felt guilty for surviving? How does one tell some of the many stories of that day? These were the questions that faced the director Juan Antonio Bayona and the writer Sergio G. Sanchez when they decided to make a film about the Tsunami of 2004. They chose to focus on a Japanese-British family on vacation in Thailand, but they use this family as a springboard to show the horrible effects of the Tsunami, not only on the tourists, but also on the local population, which suffered even more. They have stated that this is a “true story” and have made every effort to achieve the greatest degree of realism possible. They have interviewed both members of the family and survivors, some of whom appear in the film. For example, the people who tell Ewan McGregor their stories in the bus station are almost all real survivors. He chose the places of the filming very carefully, using the real hotels and the real hospital. The filming of the actual destruction of the Orchid Beach Hotel and the hospital on Koh Tao Island took place in Spain, in a studio in Alicante. However, most of the film was shot on location in Thailand. This makes the film very realistic, and the many Thai actors and actresses give it a realism that the actors hired for the film could not have achieved. The director chose not to focus on the rushing waves, but to concentrate on the terror and the sense of disorientation that they must have caused. And yet, his depiction of the oncoming wave is horrifying enough to give a sense of the immensity of the destruction. Nor did he spare us the grisly scenes that follow. The climax of the film is as impressive as the approach of the waves. The lead roles are played by Ewan MacGregor as Henry and Naomi Watts as Maria, his wife, a doctor. The only other famous face in the cast is the elderly Geraldine Chaplin, who plays a woman who helps one of the boys at the hospital, but does not survive. MacGregor and Watts do seem to suit their roles, but they are really just acting out a scripted part: that of a couple that is separated from each other, of a father who is searching for his family among the wreckage and of a mother who is close to death for much of the time. The roles of the three sons are played by Tom Holland (Lucas), Samuel Joslin (Thomas) and Oaklee Pendergast (Simon). The two younger boys are sweet, but Tom Holland, in particular, has a great maturity, and he acts with a wonderful sense of restraint. I found it to be very touching, especially when he tries to convince his mother that his brother has drowned. Despite the other actors, it is Holland who plays the main role, since it is his story, the family’s story, that takes centre stage in the film, with its different narratives unfolding. No single story can give us a sense of the enormity of what happened on that day and the days after it. And one story set in one place can only give us a limited idea of the widespread impact of the disaster. How can we depict a story that occurred almost simultaneously in several places: in India and in Sumatra, for instance, and that reached as far as the African coast? Fortunately, Bayona does not attempt to do this, but focuses on a few individuals, so that the audience can understand the story of the many through them. It is a story in which The Impossible title is entirely appropriate, but the film does work and gives us a moving view of events. It was first shown in Spain on 11 October and in North America during the last week of December, and I would recommend it.

Anne Fletcher, a dancer and now a director, gives us this dazzling dance film. Having watched several similar teen dance films in the past (Take the Lead, Save the Last Dance, etc.), this film, not only by having its vigor and originality, but by being enjoyable, does justice to the genre. Fletcher does not spare the lyrical sequences; but she does not abuse them, either. She interweaves them into the plot without forcing them into it. The two leads (Jenna Dewan and Channing Tatum) are a pleasure to watch. Dewan has an excellent body, not that of an anorexic ballerina, and she has a remarkable talent for her dances. Tatum is deadpan with his delivery, which is sometimes unexpectedly funny. The rest of the cast is able to hold its own. Step Up has so many good moments that one forgives its awkwardly intertwined subplots and its scene-stealing extras.

On his first day at his new school, Cameron Stratford falls in love with Bianca Stratford, but not only is she a beautiful and popular girl, but her father has forbidden her to go out with a boy until her sister Kat has also started dating. The only problem is that Kat is a bad-tempered, nasty, unfriendly girl who can’t go anywhere with anyone. The solution: a friend of Cameron’s, Pat, who, for a fee, is to start dating Kat and thus enable him to go out with Bianca. But nothing ever goes according to plan in the matter of love. I’m not a great fan of teen comedies. They’re usually just lame, they fall back on the same old clichés that we’ve been subjected to since Animal House and The Fang, and the latest trend of adapting classic texts has given us a lot of rubbish, like She’s All That. The basic plot of this film is The Taming of the Shrew in modern dress, but it bears almost no resemblance to Shakespeare’s play, but that’s all right – the central idea is sufficiently interesting to stand alone. It may not surprise you at the end as to which of the two young lovers is going to get the girl, but it’s not about that. The film is funny, witty and pretty entertaining, with a host of little touches, funny characters, like the inept teacher Mr Morgan and the headmistress writing erotic plays. This is not a dirty film, and the jokes, which never descend to gross scatology, are what give it a lively, fresh feel rather than just mindlessly banging away at the same old. Compared with the abomination that was Prince and Lillard in She’s All That, this was a dream cast. Ledger is a rising star and does a good job here – he doesn’t overplay his role as a bad boy, and his falling in love is believable. For a change, she doesn’t revert to the self-effacing schoolgirl type, and her character is again well portrayed and quite sympathetic. Gordon-Levitt is okay, but hasn’t much to do, and neither has Oleynik. The best roles are those that don’t concern the central ones, and three of the supporting actors – Janney, Stacy Lynette Mitchell and, especially, Lara Miller – do really well. Sadly, Gabrielle Union is wasted in a small role again. I like her and would like to see her in more leading roles, but here, as in She’s All That, she is the token black girl in a predominantly white film – maybe I’m being a bit paranoid about that, but that’s how it feels. I was pleasantly surprised at the comedy, which, unlike the farces so often seen in films about teenagers, never descends to the gross jokes, and has characters and actors who have real wit and energy. Despite its predictability, it works, and the humour and side-characters just add to the feel of a well-made film. It’s not great art, but it’s better than most other teen-coms you could watch.

...And he got a... 7.3? Honestly, many mediocre Marvel movies get better ratings than that. This movie is on a level with The Dark Knight, the best superhero movie ever. People praised it when it came out, and now it’s cool to hate the trilogy. The second one improves on all of the first one’s features. Peter’s fight with being Spider-Man is the most important theme in the movie, and it’s done brilliantly. The action is even better than in many modern films, and there’s a fight scene on the subway, with music by Danny Elfman. This movie and the whole trilogy shouldn’t be dismissed as just a bunch of old, bad ’00s movies. It was the beginning of the MCU as we know it.

I wouldn't say it's an underrated film, but it's been a little buried by the reputation of other "popular" Nolan movies. Once again, Nolan demonstrates his ability to make metafilms. It's obviously my favorite Christopher Nolan film, next to Memento. Just as in Memento you can draw a parallel between the memories and the interpretations we see in the story, so we can relate the three acts of the magic trick told in this film with the film itself. As the film says, the revelation in a magic trick is the most exciting experience. So does this film. Indeed, the whole film can be weirdly related to a trick. It's one of those movies that, without any major event, seem to be ordinary and become great. Cinematically, it's a typical Nolan film. Breaks in time in the narrative are used here, but unlike most of his films, it's done more artistically than just to get the shock of the revelation. It is perhaps the movie where Nolan's broken times have been the most brilliant. As in most of his films, he delves into a single theme, here it's obsession. Obsession with Robert Angier is the motor of the film, is so well built that it does not even seem forced. There is a hero and an enemy in this film. Character development is so gradual that we see the hero turn into an enemy, while the villain still remains somewhat the same. Although we do not have a complete switch between the antagonist and the hero, as the movie progresses, the hero seems more "bad" than the villain. It's pretty hard to get that. Alfred Bordon is one of the most complex characters I've ever seen. We always have the impression that he is a little creepy, and many scenes are enough to prove this. Until the third act, when we see the man, we can not forgive his evil, but we can respect his determination as a magician. It might seem that the line between him and Nikola Tesla is a little funny, but Nikola Tesla is a scientist who has been rumored to travel through time. So it's justifiable. Hugh Jackman's role is also quite satisfactory. The most surprising thing is that he is completely detached from his Wolverine public persona. He is the best choice for Wolverine, in my opinion, but when he enters the screen, Wolverine's memory is always there. He is not even a little bit of Wolverine in this film. But the main focus is Christian Bale. It is a wonderful job. You don't get a clue about the complexity of the character he's playing. It's only after the revelation, and even after the second screening, that you start to notice the stuff and the real meaning of each scene. All in all, it's a wonderful movie. It is not just how obsession is shown as the main theme, nor how the twisted time is used in storytelling, nor how the end is twisted - everything is excellent. I give him a special 10/10 and A+.

While I was doing research for this article, I was amazed to find that this was the first time since a film from a Stephen King story had been shown on the big screen since The Bullet in 2004. 1408 was therefore a kind of comeback to the big screen for the author, who has worked with television for a couple of years. It is by far the most eerie and intense thriller I have seen so far this year. The premise is perhaps not the most solid and it does not always make sense, but it's effective. John Cusack plays a writer who used to be very promising, but who, since the tragic death of his daughter Katya (Jasmine Jessica Anthony), has started writing mediocre novels about the world's most haunted places. Traveling the world, he does his research and sleeps at supposedly haunted places and gets some colorful material that he can use in his next novel, and then moves on to the next project. He gets a letter from an old friend, who recommends a certain hotel room in New York City, the Dolphin Hotel, which is said to have quite a reputation. He does some research and learns that the Dolphin has a long and sad history of deaths, all of which involve the people who have lived in the 1408 room. He orders the room despite the warnings of hotel manager Gerald Olin (Samuel L. Jackson). Entering the room, nothing seems strange at first, but then the room itself begins to live and begins to torment him with various ghostly apparitions, mind games and even a very painful past. There is also a lot of personal psychological drama in the film. 1408 is the second film in the same genre that was released in less than two months (the other being April's vacancy) and is by far the better of the two. The film is surprisingly subdued and eerie, which is a welcome change from the recent Hostel 2; rather than bombarding the audience with ghosts and effects of torture, it sneaks into the skin and takes a more psychological approach. The film by Matt Greenberg, Scott Alexander and Larry Karaszewski fortunately does not explain room 1408 at all. It is just a very sinister being that somehow knows how to look into the troubled souls and then kill them with their own demons. In the wrong hands, this could have been a joke. But despite the fact that the film sometimes flies into the unbelievable, it is still well supported. It is partly due to the fact that the film does not lose its course and does not try to make as many special effects and jumps as possible. The fact that the more Enslin stays in the room, the more he is forced to confront his own demons and to keep his mind under control, is the center of the story and the horror. It is much more effective than the typical super-evil figures that have become a norm in supernatural horrors lately (usually gray-skinned people with hair over their faces), and it does not become moralizing. It is a difficult balance to find. When the room begins to show Enslin his own painful past, I was a bit worried that the film would then hit the audience with a morale. Of course, it does not happen and the film is appropriately frightening throughout. John Cusack is the main character and must carry the film alone, as it is basically a one-man show throughout the film, where the ghosts that haunt him are the main company. I have long been a fan of Cusack and think this is one of his stronger roles of recent times. He not only has to endure for the most part alone, but also to act as if he slowly goes mad without huffing and puffing, without becoming stupid and monotonous. Any actor will tell you that it is not an easy role to play madness. Cusack balances it very well and remains believable throughout. Sam L. Jackson is also outstanding in his small but not less important role as the man who tries to talk Enslin out of staying in the room. But the room itself is a character and creates the right atmosphere by constantly changing itself, even in the pictures on the walls, and thus creating an effective sense of horror that is always unusual but never so unusual that you can not still believe. 1408 succeeds where many others have failed because it is not about ghosts that jump out at the actors or that squander in the dark. Rather, it reaches much deeper than mere surface horror and is a very effective horror film. It may be argued that the whole thing falls apart when one applies logic to the story. But seriously, do you want to apply logic to a film about an evil hotel room that can read your mind? Well, you don't, and 1408 shows that horror can do more than just scare us. It can make us laugh and capture us. Interestingly, perhaps, is that it can achieve all this and yet so few horrors can.

Thor is a film that dares - and it works wonderfully. It is a film that, while keeping its mythological and fantastical tone, remains grounded in reality, and this, I think, raises the film above the general superheroism.

It is a strangely powerful and moving experience to see “The English Patient” again after Anthony Minghella’s death. His filmography was devoted to a single, intractable issue—the endless moral struggle of those who are consciously treading a very thin line. “The Talented Mr. Ripley” departed from the amoral Tom Ripley novel by Patricia Highsmith by giving the murderer a conscience. In “The Insider” he infused into the character of Jude Law a need to confess, and the emotional effect is powerful. And here, in “The English Patient,” the characters in love are never far from their corrosive sense of guilt. Ralph Fiennes and Kristin Scott Thomas are extraordinary. They strip their characters of every pretense, in an utterly compelling complicity with the audience. Juliette Binoche is simply brilliant, and her scenes with the magnificent Naveen Andrews are filled with an Minghella-like, sensually innocent, almost childlike naiveté. Minghella’s films were always, one way or another, the elusive combination of art and commerce. He was true to himself, yet considerate of the audience; he knew how to push our buttons without giving up his own. There is something luminous, honest, and striking about Minghella’s filmography. I already miss him, but I am grateful for the reflection of his soul he has left behind.

I have seen How to Train Your Dragon five times now, and it never gets boring. It only gets better and better every time. It is a big success for DreamWorks, perhaps their best feature film yet. The 3D is amazing, and it is sometimes breathtaking. I may have had the most fun in a movie theater watching How to Train Your Dragon. The script is really good and it has a lot of drama. This movie is for everyone. Adults and children can enjoy it equally and love it. It will probably become a series like Shrek. But I hope it doesn’t get bad sequels like Shrek 3 and Shrek Forever After. In any case, this movie will be remembered for its beautiful animation. 10/10 Highly Recommended.

I graduated from Texas Western in 1966 and attended the university all four years that Don Haskins (known as the Bear) coached the college basketball team. It should be noted that Haskins came to TWU in 1961 and built his team over five years, not in one year as the movie shows. I attended every home game in the winter of 1965-66 and remember every minute of it as if it were yesterday. I watched every away game that was on television, including every game the Miners played in the NCAA tournament. The producers of Glory Road did not leave out many facts, but their treatment of the story is a bit slanted. Here are some of the facts: The Miners defeated fourth-ranked Iowa in a holiday tournament in 1966. The game was not as close as the movie depicts. The comeback was against New Mexico in the Pit. The team was down 20 points when David Palacio entered the game in the second half. Then the team pulled together and came back in overtime. The game that was probably the best between the two best teams in the nation was the regional game between third-ranked TWU and fourth-ranked Kansas, not the final game between first-ranked Kentucky and second-ranked Duke in the tournament. Then the Miners played Utah in the first game of the tournament. If white player Jerry Armstrong had not defended against black Utah player Jerry Chambers, the Miners would not have made it to the finals to face Kentucky. Until Armstrong was put on Chambers, all defenders, including Lattin, Shed and Flournoy, were beaten by him. Chambers scored 38 points, most of them in the first half. He was the tournament's most valuable player. Haskins is beloved by all El Pasoans, whether they live here or not. It is wonderful that the rest of the nation and the world finally can learn about the great coach and his great 1966 team, which has been beloved by El Pasoans for 40 years. The acting in the movie was excellent, especially by Joshua Lucas as Haskins. He was very true to life. The actors who played the players were excellent. The movie depicts racial tensions between the black and white players that were not there on the real team. The book Glory Road is a must read because it is the true story, written by Don Haskins. Also, read David Lattin's book, "Slam Dunk to Glory." During the credits of the movie, the real life players, Don Haskins, Pat Riley and some of the players from 1966 should have been introduced before the rest of the cast was shown. Most people left the theater without learning who they were. I thought that was the best part of the movie. The movie and the story are a 10 and deserve an academy award.

However, one could easily wonder if he would not have taken his own life without being killed, because each scene, each image, almost every moment of this film, so heavy with despair, anger, and disgust for humankind, it could only be that Pasolini was about to slam himself into the ground. Although on the surface it is an adaptation of one of Desade’s most indecent works, brought to life during the horrific excesses of the second world war and with the authentically squalid rapes of the Fascist upper classes, it also contains many contemporary critical elements: Pasolini hated the modern world and explained that the abominable “salad banquet” scene as a not so subtle attack on the world dominance of fast-food outlets. (The scenes of obscenity can also be read as despairing attacks on the free world of sexual eroticism, and those who come to Salot as a kind of sexual picture, and as a cinema de provocation, will be greatly disappointed.) In addition to its nihilistic content, which has been well described elsewhere, Salot has an overall atmosphere that is somehow designed to make the viewer as depressed as possible. Add to this the eerie overtones of the big-band music, the mournful piano music and the deliberately (or not) badly dubbed lines, and the effect on the viewer is complete. Salot is a long primal scream, which is intended to shake the viewer out of his complacency, and the film is a clear success in this regard. Whether you can watch it again or “entertain yourself” is a different question. But Salot is an important film that must be carefully considered, and it must only be carefully considered by those who are prepared for it.

Saw II is a pure, tense and tight thriller. The best thrillers, shockers and horror movies have many unexpected twists and turns, and it is this that marks Saw II as one of the better entries in its genre. This is not a movie where people are walking backwards into dark rooms. That would be too predictable for Saw II. No, this is a movie where you can’t say there is one thing you can predict. Few movies make me sit on the edge of my seat, and this was one of them. There were no dozer-offers in the theater, and I witnessed the lowest number of cell phone interruptions. Like the original Saw, the sequel is a bit bloody in some parts, but that is to be expected. After all, this wasn’t sold as a comedy. If you are looking for a thriller that keeps you on the edge of your seat, then you should give this one a chance. And even more people in the audience were waiting for a third sequel.

Never having played the game, I did not know much about the story, but I heard that it was a hit, so I finally saw it and was very surprised, the story is very faithful to the games as far as I have seen, the action is also good and the effects are very good, I don't like the choice of the actors, but they do their best, Compared to other game adaptations, it's probably one of the better ones, even though it won't survive (again, no pun intended), Compared to other games-to-movies, it is probably one of the better ones, and even though it may not survive (again, no pun intended), it's one of the better ones, and although it will probably not be a timeless classic, at least it's a good family film to watch that is not so difficult to enjoy, even if you haven't played the game.

I know there's a spoiler warning at the top, but I'm warning you again. Don't read this because I'm going to give everything away. I had this movie all wrong. I admit that at first I didn't get it and was annoyed, but after talking to my friend who came with me we both gasped when we saw what happened. The twist is that the intervention actually worked. He was cured, but he was pretending to relapse because he didn't want to live with the memory of what had happened to his family. He felt guilty for ignoring that his wife was clearly mentally ill. The line "Would you rather die a good man or live a monster?" shows that he would rather die as a good man (by being lobotomized) than live with the memories. The symbolism of the fire and water show when he's hallucinating (fire) and when he's in reality (water trickling). The delusion he has arranged for himself to save himself from the truth is that his wife died in a fire. All the people he talks to in the fire, ie the woman in the cave, the madman in the cell, the scarred face who supposedly killed his wife, the car that exploded, etc., are all delusions. Water symbolizes reality. He is afraid of water (which is right, his children were drowned and all died in front of the water ) , and then at the beginning he says he suffers from seasickness. He is mortally afraid of water. To get the full impact of this movie you have to watch it a few times (I have only seen it once, but I swear I'll see it again). I think the Wall Street Journal reviewer John Anderson had it right when he said that "it requires several viewings to understand fully as art". Its concept is more important than the story, the structure more important than the largely unnecessary twists. It is a thriller, a crime film, and a psychological thriller on collective guilt.

I don't think I've ever been more surprised by how much I enjoyed a film. I had very low expectations when I decided to watch "The Village," because I knew how much the critics had criticized it. I don't mean to say that I'm a man who respects criticism as a sacrosanct. However, since the films I love are usually the least controversial ones, I had little hope that "The Village" would be any good. And besides, I'd noticed that since "The Sixth Sense," M. Night Shyamalan's films had been getting steadily worse, so it seemed that the harsher reaction to "The Village" was merely the continuation of a pattern I'd recognized in the first place. So I didn't see the film, and only recently decided to watch it on cable, out of curiosity more than anything. Alas, the first fifteen minutes were a little boring. The film has a lot of characters, and it takes a while to figure out who is most important. All we know is that the villagers live in a primitive hamlet near a forest in the nineteenth century. They believe that the forest is haunted by evil, sentient creatures who will not harm them as long as they stay out of the forest. The villagers have a lot of rules for protection, like avoiding the color red (why does Shyamalan keep going back to red?) and wearing yellow hoods. Rules are made to be broken, and so a quiet, mysterious young man (Joaquin Phoenix) wants to go into the forest and visit the "big cities" where the medical care is better. Among other things, he hopes to find a cure for his friend, who has a mental disorder (Adrien Brody). Meanwhile, he's falling in love with the blind girl (Bryce Dallas Howard), whose role will become increasingly important as the film progresses. The love story between Phoenix and Bryce Dallas Howard is both believable and convincing, and it transcends the usual cliches. Their words are not very many, but they're quite memorable. My favorite line is: "We don't do the things we want to do, so that others don't know we want to do them." The villagers speak in an old-fashioned manner, without contractions, using big words. Their accents are American, but their language resembles a nineteenth-century English novel. Finally, the acting is surprisingly natural. The cast is quite good: William Hurt, Sigourney Weaver, Joaquin Phoenix, Adrien Brody, and Bryce Dallas Howard. The film is primarily about the relationship between the villagers, but the relationship with the evil creatures is also important. This is a more "Twilight Zone"-style horror movie than an out-and-out horror film. But as in his earlier works, Shyamalan has a final message of hope and optimism. However, when the creatures show up, Shyamalan is excellent at showing us how terrified the villagers are. Like all great horror directors, he knows not to show the monsters directly, but to focus on the horror and terror of the villagers. Although the theme of blindness is not a new one, Shyamalan uses the blind girl Bryce Dallas Howard's role very effectively. Instead of showing us the blind girl's blind spots, he leads the camera behind her and only shows us what she sees. Then we soon realize that we only see what she can see. In some cases, it seems that we are just as blind as she is. However, I don't want to talk too much about the story, because the film has a lot of surprises. Some critics have dismissed this as a crudely written story, but I don't agree at all. Some of the criticisms of the plot are a little short-sighted. Shyamalan's films always follow the same structure: we are swept up in the events, and it is only when we reach the end that we understand what the film was about. Only then can we understand the deep meaning of the film. I've already seen the film three times, and I've found something new each time. Besides, the social themes suggest that Shyamalan is well versed in Joseph Campbell's theory of primitive society and the origins of drama. The film's plot is much more complex than the average thriller, and I'm surprised that not many people have understood it. That is what is so wonderful and amazing about this film.

I had been wondering since the film was released, why Martin Scorsese had made it. I knew very little about it, only that it was an adventure story about an orphan living in the walls of a railway station in Paris. It sounded like nothing Scorsese would do. However, that's just the framework of a tribute to the dawn of cinema, and in particular to one of its great pioneers, Georges Méliès. ktov Station, one of the first films in the world by the Lumière brothers, A Trip to the Moon by Méliès, and many others are reminiscent of this, a real treat for film lovers. Yes, it is a children's film, but really adults have more to enjoy. In his most technically advanced film to date, Scorsese brilliantly shows how far filmmaking has come. As for the performances, the children of the young stars, Ben Kingsley as Georges Méliès, Sasha Baron Cohen as a stubborn and obsessed train station director, and Helen McCrory as the wife of Méliès, it was all excellent. I did not see Hugo in 3D, but the Blu-ray looks absolutely spectacular and is full of beautiful images of early twentieth-century Paris. The film is much better than the end, where Scorsese seems to be unsure what to do with the final act when the children have found the secret. But before it is really magic, and I recommend this film with two thumbs up.

Chris, the father of a child, a single father, is forced to struggle in the harsh environment of the iek bank, which he represents as a Will Smith actor. Chris, the father, seeks to give his son a good home, to pursue happiness. Not only is the hardship of a single parent revealed, but the fact that when you fall, you will get up and you will go. HEATH LEEGER IN A CAREER-BOOSTING PERFORMANCE. Dark, brooding, with incredible action and a complex storyline, THE DARK KNIGHT contains a career-defining performance from Heath Ledger, as well as other Oscar-worthy performances, and it remains the best film, not only about the Bat-family, but also about any superhero ever.

"I thought this was the beginning of your story... We are so limited by time," said Doctor Banks in the first thirty seconds of the film. Little did I know at first that this was the theme of the whole film. At the heart of the film lies the question of the power of language and how much it has influenced our way of thinking, of seeing the world around us, etc. When the alien race arrives on earth, Doctor Banks must find out what language they use and how to communicate with them in order to understand why they are here. The further she goes, the more she learns, the more she discovers that they don't think like we do, that they don't communicate like we do, and that they are not bound by time like we are. From the moment her daughter speaks to her, to the very spelling of her daughter's name, this theme permeates the whole film, from her daughter's thoughts to the big revelation at the end. We see the beginning of the film and think it's the beginning of a story, like everyone does, but as we become more and more involved and learn what Doctor Banks learns, we are also freed from the limits of time. The question is, if you knew your life from beginning to end, would you change anything? This film is more than just another alien invasion, a story we've seen a thousand times before; it's deeper than that, and we should appreciate it for what it is. The art of storytelling. Easily a 10/10.

The film is an insult to the memory of Fatih Sultan Mehmet, to Ottoman history, and to the intelligence of any spectator. It is a perfect example of how western Orientalists will project themselves. The reasons why the conquest of Constantinople was essential for the Turks’ survival — the economic and political reasons — are totally omitted. Mehmet II, a highly educated man, is nothing but a fanatic in this film. Emperor Constantine XI Palaeologis, whom the Turks respected, is shown as a buffoon. Suicide bombing, a phenomenon of the late 20th century, is a recurrent theme in the film. All Ottoman soldiers are depicted as suicide bombers! What is the point of this? It is one of the most crass and shallow productions in a long series of recent films and serials that aim at de-educating Turkey, keep on undermining its intelligence, and prey on the Turks’ feelings of being the object of western scorn, Orientalist fancies, and the memory of the First World War. All the sub-plots fail as miserably as the main theme: an absurd love affair, a wife without dialogue, Vardar Pazhia’s unexplained actions and motives, etc., etc. This film has been subject to severe criticism in Turkey. I cannot understand why it is so warmly defended on IMDB. It even fails to awaken any sense of national pride in its spectators. No character study, no historical context, no wit, even no propaganda, only the first, and a relatively large-scale, representation of the conquest. And that is the only reason why people flock to watch it. One cannot deny that filming war scenes is an improvement on Turkish cinema. Unfortunately, that is all.

"Cheerleader" is a song by Jamaican singer and songwriter OMI. The song was written and produced by OMI, along with Clifton Dillon, Mark Bradford, and Ryan Dillon. It was first written in 2008 by OMI, when he composed the melody. Over the course of the next several years, he refined the song with the help of the famed Jamaican producer Clifton Dillon. First recorded with the help of veteran session musicians Sly and Robbie and Dean Frazer, it was released as a single by the independent label Oufah Records, where it topped the Jamaican charts and also saw airplay in other places like Hawaii and the United Arab Emirates. The single was later picked up by the U.S. dance music label Ultra Records, who reached out to two young German producers to remix the track. One of the producers, a German dj and producer named Felix Jaehn, who incorporated a tropical sound with conga drums and trumpets, was favored by the label and the producers, and his version was released in May 2015. "Cheerleader" saw great success that year, topping the charts in twenty countries, including the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, France, Ireland, Sweden, and Germany.

Michael Peter Malone (April 18, 1940 – December 21, 1999) was an American historian and educator who was president of Montana State University from 1991 to 1999. One of the foremost historians and writers of the century, he was named by the Missoulian and the Great Falls Tribune as one of the one hundred most influential people of the twentieth century in the state of Montana. In his childhood, Malone was born in Pomeroy, Washington, to John and Delores Cheyne Malone. His father, a farmer, and his two brothers owned farms in Garfield, Walla Walla, and Whitman counties. Malones were Irish and Michael was very proud of his heritage. His mother, Delores, was born in Zillah, Washington, and his parents were married on November 14, 1936. His father managed a hardware store and was active in the Holy Rosary Catholic Church in Pomeroy.

Bookchin is an artist based in Brooklyn, New York, whose work in the field of new media has gained her wide recognition. She was awarded a Guggenheim grant in 2002. Her work has been shown at the PS1 Contemporary Art Center, the Massachusetts Museum of Contemporary Art, the Museum of Contemporary Art in Barcelona, the Museum of Contemporary Art in Vienna, the Kunstwerke, Berlin, the Walker Art Center, the Whitney Museum of American Art, and the Shedhalle in Zurich. Her works take many forms, ranging from on-line games to collaborations, “hacktivist” actions, texts, and manifestos. They all explore the consequences of the digital revolution and the Internet for aesthetics, work, leisure, and politics. Most of her recent works have consisted of a compilation of fragments of webcasts, often from the popular blogging site YouTube. She was a member of the RT Mark art collective from 1998 to 2000, and was a collaborator on the “spontaneous act of public disempowerment” that the group organized in 1999 against the “GATT” (General Agreement on Trade and Tariffs). She received her B.A. from Purchase College in New York in 1984 and her M.A. in photography from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago in 1990.

Constans Rodko (August 24, 1908 – September 30, 1995) was a Latvian painter who settled in the United States. His parents were of Estonian and Belarusian origin. He was married to his first wife in Riga and had four children. They lived in Germany during World War II, but were able to travel to New York City on August 25, 1950, on the General Harry Taylor from Bremerhaven, Germany. His artistic talent was appreciated only in the United States. He lived with his children in Brooklyn, New York, and divorced his first wife and married a second, a woman named Catherine Dennison. She was also a painter, and the couple exhibited and sold their works together. They moved to Sea Cliff, on Long Island, near Glen Cove. He lived on the second floor of a Russian school. His second wife produced many miniatures, and he produced some of his best paintings. He sold some and gave others as gifts to his four children. He liked to play and listen to Russian gypsy and folk music, and paint Russian scenes, and spoke Russian, so that many people thought he was Russian. He was a multi-instrumentalist, and his wife was a tailor and loved cats. She considered them her children, since she had no children with Rodko. She adopted his four children from his first marriage. He had seven grandchildren and two great-grandchildren. Around the end of the 1970s, Rodko moved to Brentwood, Long Island, where Catherine died of a stroke in 1984.

Syed Mahmood Naqvi (28 August 1941 – 4 September 2009) was an Indian scientist, working at the National Geophysical Research Institute, in Hyderabad. During his four-decade career he was the recipient of many prestigious and humanitarian awards, was a Fellow of the Indian Geophysical Union, the Andhra Science Academy, the Indian National Science Academy and the Indian Academy of Sciences. He also served as a Vice President of the Geological Society of India, the Geological Mining and Metallurgical Society and the Indian Society of Applied Geochemistry. Born in Amroha, and his education completed in Aligarh, he was appointed a scientist at the National Geophysical Research Institute, Hyderabad, on 9 November, 1964. He did his doctorate on the petrology, structure, petrology, geochemistry and tectonics of the central part of the Chitradurga schist belt of the Dharwar craton.

This hurricane, which was called in popular parlance the Cyclone of Five Days, and which made havoc in Cuba and the United States in October, 1910, sprang up on the 9th of that month in the southern part of the Antilles and gradually increased its force and range of motion, and at last, on the 12th, was ranked as a hurricane. It was afterward, by crossing the tip of Cuba, that it reached its maximum intensity, that is, a four on the Saffir–Simpson scale. The same day, describing a spiral movement to the right, the hurricane again struck Cuba, then turned toward Florida and landed at Cape Romano. It passed over the state, and then skirted the coast of the United States south of the Gulf of Mexico. By the unusual curve of its course, which led at first to think that it was two hurricanes which struck land in quick succession, the course of this hurricane was subject to much controversy at the time; at last, it was recognized to be one. Upon analyzing this case, we have come to a better understanding of the eddies which follow similar paths.

Moskvitch 2138-M2140 is a large family automobile produced by the AZLK from January 1976 to 1988. The production model was presented in 1975. From 1981 the improved version of the export model M2140 was designed and marked as 2140 SL in the socialist countries and as 1500 SL outside. The main differences between these two models were a completely new design of the dashboard and the installation of headrests on the front seats. From the beginning of 1982, the M2138 models were removed from the assembly line and the M2140 became the only Moskvitch automobiles available in all markets. The same year, the bodywork was slightly improved: the shield emblem was changed for the emblem with the inscription "AZLK" in a metal frame, the filling was changed from metal to plastic, the side mirrors were slightly redesigned. The last generation of the M2137 estate car was the last of the Soviet automobiles with flaps in the taillights, until the end of the model in 1985.

Domenico di Zanobi, previously known as the Master of the Nativity of St. John the Baptist, was an Italian painter of the Renaissance. His birth and death dates are unknown. He is known to have been active as a mature artist from 1467 to 1481. His paintings were first grouped together in 1966 by the American art historian Everett Fahy, who recognized about twenty works in a similar style. Since none of the works were signed, Fahy called their author the Master of the Nativity of St. John the Baptist, in reference to a painting in the collection of the Philadelphia Museum of Art. In 1996 the Florentine scholar Annamaria Bernacchioni identified the artist as Domenico di Zanobi, who had been an apprentice of Filippino Lippi in Florence and Prato. The Nativity, originally attributed by Fahy to the Master of the Nativity of St. John the Baptist, was said to have been commissioned by the Chellini family of Florence in 1476 from a painter named Domenico. Since the painting was clearly not by Domenico di Michelino, who also worked for the Chellini family, Bernacchioni concluded that it must be by Domenico di Zanobi, who had worked in a workshop with Domenico di Michelino in Florence by 1467.

“Harmony Part” is a Japanese animated film, produced by the Signal.MD studio and directed by Kenji Kamiyama, with a script by Mitsuki Takahata, distributed in Japan by Warner Brothers Pictures on March 18, 2017. A dubbed version was released in the United Kingdom on August 16, 2017 and in the United States one month later. The title song is a remake of the Monkees song "Daydream Believer" performed by the actress in the title role, Mitsuki Takahata. While taking a nap, Kokone Morikawa dreams of the Kingdom of Heartland. It is a world where everything is centered on cars: the king's castle is a car factory, where the inhabitants of the kingdom come to work tirelessly to produce new cars. Its daughter Ancien (in the dream a young Kokone), has a tablet called "Magic", thanks to which she gives life to various machines, in particular to a blue toy dog named Joy and to a motorcycle called Heart. The king does not like the fact that the machine called Heart came to life, he takes away the magic and Heart from Ancien, and confines the princess to a tower. Moreover, the kingdom is threatened by a giant molten metal monster, called "Colossus", against which the king and the inhabitants of Heartland are building giant robots. Ancien meets a servant of the king, Peach, who is a motorcyclist. Together with him, Ancien decides to defeat Colossus, but the king's adviser Bewan is planning to overthrow both the king and Ancien.

Jack Shaftoe, also known as the King of Vagrants, the Half-Cocked Jack, the Sword of Divine Fire, Ali Zaybak, and Jack the Coiner, is one of the three leading characters in the 2,686-page epic The Baroque Cycle by Neal Stephenson. Born in 1660 to a poor London family, Jack, the youngest of three half-brothers, became a mudlark at the age of five, but soon gave it up, when his elder brother, Dick, was drowned in an abortive raid on a Dutch galley. After a few years spent in serving as an impromptu assistant to the men who were to be hanged from the Deaf Tree at Tyburn, Jack left England to roam the European continent. Jack’s travels are the subject of most of The Baroque Cycle, which covers his adventures in many parts of the world between 1683 and 1714.

“JOHN NZAU MWANGANGI (born 1 November 1990) is a Kenyan long-distance runner who has competed in distances from 5,000 metres to the half-marathon. He won the African Cross Country Championships in Tunisia in 2011. In Europe he has won the Dam-to-Dam race, the 20-kilometres Paris race, the Greifenseelauf, the Valencia half-marathon and the Valencia marathon. Born in Mwingi, a town in Eastern Province of Kenya, he was a winner in the Morat-Fribourg race and the Greifenseelauf in Switzerland in 2008. In 2009, after finishing second in the cross country and 5,000 metres in the prison service in his country, he won the 20-kilometres de Lausanne and the Grand Prix de Berne. In August, he won the silver medal at the African Junior Athletics Championships in Niger over 5,000 metres. He returned to Europe to renew his Greifenseelauf and Morat-Fribourg wins, won the half-marathon in a personal best of one hour and three minutes, and the shorter distances of La Corrida, the Basel city race and the Dam-to-Dam.

The Canadian singer and songwriter, born in Montreal on May 23, 1956, who has had numerous Juno nominations, is now lead singer for the Chicago rock band, replacing Peter Cetera, Jason Scheff and Jeff Coffey. He is from Montreal, but in the mid-80s moved to Toronto, where he currently lives. His voice is four-note and has sung more than 10,000 session vocals in his career. He has also had a few minor roles in the film, including the song "Bright Time" with Maren Ord for Thomas and the Magic Railroad, a children's film released in 2000. Donell is to perform a new version of this song in the upcoming anniversary film of Rainbow Sun Productions, which will premiere on YouTube on July 19, 2020. During the spring of 2018, after the departure of Coffey and the drummer Tris Imboden, Donell was invited by the founding members of Chicago (Walter Parazaider, James Pankow, Lee Loughnane and Robert Lamm) to become a new vocalist.

Rebecca Scown, née Boyd, born on 10 August 1983, is a New Zealander who competes in rowing. Rowing with Juliette Haigh, they won bronze in the women's coxless pair at the 2012 Summer Olympic games. Before this they had won gold in the pair in the World Cup in Lucerne, at the World Rowing Championships at Karapiro in New Zealand, and at the World Rowing Championships at Bled in 2011. After winning bronze in the New Zealand women's eight at the 2017 World Rowing Championships, she is currently taking a break from rowing. She was born in Hawera in 1983, and her cousin Sonia Waddell, née Scown, is also a rower. Her uncle, Alistair Scown, who is the father of Sonia Waddell, is a former All Black. Rebecca Scown was educated at Wanganui Collegiate School. Her teachers saw that she had the potential to become a good rower, and so in her final year at school they allowed her to represent Wanganui in the New Zealand Secondary Schools’ Rowing Champs.

Hazardous Mutation is the second album by the American cross-over thrash band Municipal Waste, and their first album for Earache Records. The central theme of the album is based around a party with zombies, monsters and ghouls and the lyrics are quite funny and violent. This was the first album produced by Nick Poulos. Hazardous Mutation was released in a special edition with a bonus live DVD.
