After the release of their debut album Waste ‘Em All!, Municipal Waste, whose name is taken from a garbage truck, were dubbed “Party Thrashers.” On the Hazardous Mutation bonus DVD, the band were asked about this. “We don’t really thrash, but we do like to party,” said bassist and vocalist Ryan Waste. “Someone else combined the two.” Also on the bonus DVD, the band were asked about their thrashy style, and what they brought to the genre, in a new way. “We’re trying to rejuvenate the scene,” said guitarist Garret “Tank” Smith. “We’re taking things bands did in six-minute songs and fitting them into two.”

Henry Clay Merriam (13 November 1837 – 12 November 1902) was a general of the United States army. He received the medal of honor for his services as an officer in command of a brigade of colored troops in the American Civil War. Later he served in the Indian wars of the West, and commanded the 7th regiment of infantry. After his promotion to brigadier general he was employed in the training and supply of troops in the Philippine–American War. He was born at Houlton, Maine, the son of Lewis and Mary Foss Merriam. He attended Colby College at Waterville, but left college in 1862 to become a captain in the twentyth regiment of Maine volunteers. He took part in the battle of Antietam, on 17 September, and for his services received a brevet to the rank of colonel. In 1863 he was sent to Louisiana to recruit troops, and was given command of the first regiment of native-born troops of the state. He commanded this regiment at the Siege of Port Hudson, and took part in the Battle of Champion Hill. In 1865, as the colonel of the 73rd United States Colored Troops, he commanded the assault on Fort Blakely, in Baldwin County, Alabama. For this action he was brevetted colonel, and was some years later, on 28 June 1894, awarded the medal of honor. His medal of honor citation reads:

David Francis MacCalman (born September 30, 1958) is a New Zealand Paralympic athlete, mainly in the pentathlon, in class P53. He lost the use of his legs when he broke his spinal cord diving into a river. He participated in the 1992 Summer Paralympics in Barcelona, Spain. There he came fourth in the men's shot put, fifth in the men's javelin throw, thirteenth in the men's discus throw, seventh in the men's 200 m T52 and eliminated in the men's 800 m T52. He also participated in the 1996 Summer Paralympics in Atlanta, United States. There he won a silver medal in the men's javelin throw, F51, and was sixth in the men's shot put, F51. He also participated in the 2000 Summer Paralympics in Sydney, Australia. There he won a gold medal in the men's pentathlon, P53, a gold medal in the men's javelin throw, F52, and was fifth in the men's shot put, F52. He also participated in the 2004 Summer Paralympics in Athens, Greece. There he was twelfth in the men's javelin throw, F52-53, and was ninth in the men's shot put, F52. In the New Year honors of 2001, he was appointed a Member of the New Zealand Order of Merit for services to sport. In 2011, he was the first New Zealander to buy the Rex bionic exoskeleton to aid him in walking.

John Robinson Jeffers (1887–1962), American poet and conservationist, was born in San Francisco on 10 January 1887, and died on 20 January 1962. A great part of his poems are narrative or epic; but he is also known for his short lyrics and is regarded as a founding father of the American conservation movement. His "inhumanism" made him a much-esteemed writer in some circles, in spite of or because of his reluctance to occupy a position that only human beings could occupy. It was because of this reluctance that he opposed American involvement in World War II, and was therefore ostracized by the press. He was born on 10 January 1887 in Allegheny, Pennsylvania, now part of the city of Pittsburgh, the son of the Rev. Dr. William Hamilton Jeffers, a Presbyterian minister, biblical scholar and researcher, and Annie Robinson Tuttle. His brother was the astronomer and director of the Lick Observatory, the famous astronomer William Hamilton – later known as "Hamilton" – who later became John Robinson's biographer. In his youth he traveled through Europe and studied in Germany, France and Switzerland; an outstanding student, he was taught the classics, Greek and Latin literature. He was fluent in German, French and English at the age of twelve and took a bachelor's degree at the age of eighteen from Occidental College in Los Angeles. As a student, he was involved in hunting, fishing and all the literary circles of the college.

He was a graduate of Moscow State University and at the present time he is the director of the Sternberg Institute of State Astronomical Station, the International Astronomical Union. He was the chairman of the IAU commission on planetary nomenclature from 1978 to 1989 and now he is the deputy chairman of the IAU Commission on Planetary System Nomenclature. He was the chairman of the group on the study of the planets from 1978 to 1997 in the Astronomical Council of the Russian Academy of Sciences. From 1991 to 1995 he was a member of the Lunar Base Structural Committee of the American Society of Civil Engineers. He was a member of the International Extreme Environments Association from 1989 to 1994. He was a member of the editorial board of the journal Planetary Science from 1993 to 1997 and from 1990 to 1997 he was a member of the editorial board of Earth and Universe. He is a member of the International Astronomical Union, Commission No. 16 and has published over 230 scientific papers. He is a member of the International Union of Geodesy and Geophysics, the International Astronomical Union, the International Geographical Union, and the International Academy of Astronautics.

John Sampson Merrick (born March 20, 1982) is an American golfer who plays on the PGA Tour. Early life and amateur career. Merrick was born and grew up in Long Beach, California, and learned to play golf at the municipal course of the Recreation Park, a masterpiece of William F. Bell. He was a student at Wilson High School and won the Moore League high school golf tournament. At the age of nineteen he won the Southern California Golf Association Amateur, the first title he had won at the age of nineteen since Tiger Woods in 1994. He was the medalist at the Pac-10 Men's Golf Championship in 2003, leading the UCLA Bruins to their first Pac-10 title since 1985. At the 2003 NCAA Intercollegiate in Glendale, he set a course record of 63 with three eagles, the only collegiate player who had done so that year. At the 2002 US Amateur in Oakland Hills, he tied for second in the stroke play with a two-under-par 137 (71-66) and reached the second round, where he lost 2: 1 to the finalist Hunter Mahan.

Václav Hlavat (27 January 1894 - 11 January 1969) was a Czechoslovak American mathematician, who wrote about the theory of general realism and even discussed it with Albert Einstein. It was precisely his work on a difficult, but interesting equation from Einstein's unified field theory, which was reported as one of the great achievements of the year 1953. Einstein himself said that if anyone could solve these equations, it would be professor Hlavaty, and so it turned out. He was born in Louny in Bohemia (in the Czech Republic today) and died in Bloomington, Indiana. He received his doctorate from Charles University in Prague in 1921, participated in the Velvet Revolution in the 40s, and in 1948 he joined the University of Indiana, where he became a professor of mathematics and then professor emeritus.. In his memory, a special mathematical essay was published. He was the first president of the Czechoslovak Academy of Sciences in Washington, D.C., which was established by Czechoslovak and Slovak intellectuals.

The Udhauli () festival is celebrated by the Kirat community of the Rai people. The yearly festival signifies the return to lower, warmer regions when winter approaches. The return from lower to higher regions is called Ubhauli, and it too is an annual festival. On the Udhauli day, the Kirats thank the Goddess of the Earth for a good harvest. It is said that winter begins from that day, and that birds and animals flee from the cold regions to warmer climes. In the eastern part of Nepal, the festival is celebrated with the dance of the sakali (also called chandi, see below) to the accompaniment of psalms. The sakali dance is a popular custom in many parts of the country, and is performed in a ring to the beat of drums, cymbals, and other instruments. The major destinations for the dancers are Dhankuta, Pathari, Kane Pokhari, and Kerabari. This annual festival is recorded in the Kirat holy book, the Mundhum.

The bishop of the island of Bermuda is the ordinary of the Anglican Church of the Island of Bermuda, which is one of the six ecclesiastical jurisdictions under the Archbishop of Canterbury. The present Bishop is N. W. Dill. From the year 1612, the year of the settlement of the island by the wreck of the Sea Venture, which had lost on its first voyage Richard Buck, a cleric of the Church of England, until 1825, the nine parishes of the Church of England had not sufficient preachers, and no bishop had been installed, and indeed there had not been any colonial bishop until 1787, when Charles Inglis was appointed the first bishop of the Diocese of Nova Scotia, embracing present-day New Brunswick, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and Quebec. From 1825 to 1839, the island was included in the diocese of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. In 1839, Newfoundland and Bermuda were separated as a new diocese, with Aubrey George Spencer as first bishop.

NELSON EDWARDS was born in 1917 in the hamlet of Fenwick, Alabama. He was the son of farmers and moved to Detroit in 1937, where he began work at the Chrysler factory and was a member of the union. After his brother John had been inspired to join the union, he himself began his career during the great era of unionism in the 1930s, and was elected to be a union steward in the plant where the castings were made. In 1941 he was dismissed from his job at the Chrysler plant and later secured a job at the Ford Lincoln plant on the west side of Detroit. Later he became active in his new union, Local 900, which had been a free-recognition union. He served on the educational and citizenship committee, and in 1944 was elected chairman of this committee. For many years Jack was active in the social and political life of the city, the state and the nation.

The School is in all its parts for boys and girls; the boys' house is situated in the  b d. of the building. The school buildings were erected in 1768. The school was founded in 1951 by the Augustinian Friars, and is a member of the network of Augustinian schools around the world, and it admits students of all denominations. History The property was originally occupied by the Sisters of the Sacred Heart, who had a school there until 1904, when they transferred to Newcastle, where they founded the Sacred Heart College, and by the Poor Sisters of Nazareth, who conducted an orphanage. The Augustinians acquired the property in 1951, and the school has been run from there since that time. Girls were admitted in 1986. Boarding was discontinued in 1998 due to falling numbers.

The Ojibwa, like the other Algonquin tribes, are a people organized according to the principle of the patrilineal clan or the totem. The Ojibwa word for totem was borrowed into English. The totems, most often animal, were responsible for the occupations of the members, their inter-tribal relations, and marriages. In this way, the clan still remains an important part of the identity of the Ojibwa. In tradition, the Ojibwa people are divided into a number of clans or totems, which are mainly animal (or as the Ojibwa would say it, in English: heart). Translated literally, the heart would be the “expression of one’s heart” or, in other words, the tribe. According to their oral tradition, the Anishinaabe lived along the Atlantic Ocean when the Great Spirits appeared to them from the sea and taught them the sacred way of life; six of the seven Great Spirits that remained to teach established the tribes of the east. The five original Anishinaabe totems were (Bull-Head), (the Spirit who makes the sound, the crane), (pintail duck), (the tender, i.e., bear), and (little) moose.

Yunalis Mat Zara’ai (Jawi:   , born November 14, 1986) is a Malaysian singer-songwriter. She first gained popularity when her song was played over a million times on Myspace, which caught the attention of an indie pop record label and management company. In early 2011, she signed with the Fader Label. Known for her collaboration with Usher in her debut single “Crush” in the US, which peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard Adult R&B chart. She began writing songs at the age of fourteen and then taught herself to play the guitar. At the age of eighteen, while still pursuing a law degree, she performed for the first time in front of a live audience. At the end of the year, she published her first album, “Yuna”, and was nominated for five Malaysian Music Awards (the Malaysian equivalent of the Grammy). She won four awards, including Best New Artist and Best Song for her breakthrough hit “Dan Sebenarnya”.

The second episode of the fourth season of Bob's burgers, Fort-Night, is the second episode of the series and is the second Halloween special, written by Mike Olsen, featuring the voice of Aziz Ansari and the voice of Molly Shannon. The episode follows the story of the Belcher family, Tina, Gene and Louise, stuck in a fort on Halloween night, with their friends Darryl (Ansari), Andy (Laura Silverman) and Ollie (Sarah Silverman) in it, and being frightened by the psychotic Millie (Shannon), a classmate of Louise who doesn't want to help them. The children have to get out of the fort before the night falls. The Fort-Night episode was first broadcast on October 6, 2013 on Fox and had an audience of 4.21 million. After the broadcast, the series went into a month-long break to give the network a chance to promote the major leagues. The episode received a positive critical response, especially from the character.

For Slouching Toward Gomorrah: Modern Liberalism and the Decline of America is a book by Robert Bork, a former federal judge. Bork's thesis is that American and Western civilization is in decline, and that this decline is caused by modern liberalism and the rise of the New Left. The title is a play on the last lines of the poem The Second Coming by W. B. Yeats: "What wild beast, its hour come round at last, slinks to Bethlehem to be born? " But the title is more directly inspired by Joan Didion's Slouching Toward Bethlehem. Bork first documents the rapid expansion of modern liberalism in the United States during the 1960s, and argues that the radical nature of modern liberalism is not in keeping with the American political tradition. He then attacks a variety of social, cultural, and political developments as signs of the decline and degeneration of American culture. Among these developments are affirmative action, the sexualization and violence in the mass media, legalization of abortion, support for assisted suicide and euthanasia, feminism, and the decline of religion. As a former judicial nominee of President Ronald Reagan, Bork attacks the judicial system, and argues that judicial activist judges and activist liberal judges are the main culprits in the corruption of American culture.

Klamath County was a county of California from 1851 to 1874. During its existence the county seat changed twice and some of its former territory was broken up and added to other counties. It was created out of the western portion of Trinity County and included all the northwest of the state, from the northern Mad River to the border of Oregon on the north, from the Pacific on the west to the center of Siskiyou County on the east. It was the only county in California to be abolished. Its first county seat was Trinidad, on the southwestern coast. It was moved to Crescent City in 1854, because of its larger population. But the county seat of the west was not in favor of the interests of the mines in the east, and in 1856 it was moved to Orleans. The year 1857 saw the founding of Del Norte County, which included Crescent City.

Philippe Sautet is a French chemist born on 8 May 1961 in Salon-de-Provence. He was elected to the Académie française on 30 November 2010. He is research director at the CNRS, and is attached to the chemistry laboratory at the ENS de Lyon, where he has devoted a great deal of his professional activity to molecular modelling. He is also a professor at the University of California at Los Angeles. He is a graduate of the École polytechnique in Paris, and did his doctorate at the University of Paris Orsay between 1985 and 1988, under the supervision of Odile Eisenstein. He then worked as a CNRS researcher at the Institut de recherche sur le catalyse in Villeurbanne from 1988 to 1995, and was a visiting researcher at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California between 1991 and 1992. After his return from the United States, he was a teacher at the École polytechnique between 1993 and 2005, and then served as director of UMR 5182 (the Chemistry laboratory at the ENS de Lyon, France) between 2003 and 2010. This laboratory has an 80-strong research staff. He has also been the director of the Institut de Chimie de Lyon, UMR 3023 (with a staff of 1,000), since 2007.

Peebles Rovers F.C., a Scottish association football club based in Peebles in the Scottish Borders, was founded in 1893 and plays its home games at Whitestone Park. It is affiliated to the East of Scotland District Association, which is in the seventh division of the Scottish league system. They were members of the Scottish League for a short period between 1923 and 1926, where they performed modestly, finishing 14th and 8th in the two full seasons they played and 14th in the shortened 1925–26 season. They played a total of 86 Scottish league matches, winning 28, drawing 15, and losing 43. They scored 159 goals and conceded 190. Their best win at home was 7–1 against Beith on 18 April 1925; their best away was 5–2 against Galston on the previous Saturday, 11 April 1925. In 1937 Peebles moved from their Victoria Park home to Whitestone Park. The new owner had bought the rights to develop the eastern end of Victoria Park for residential development, but his plans were thwarted by the outbreak of World War II.

Colonel Sir John Edmond Hugh Boustead, DSO, MC & Bar, GCB (14 April 1895 – 3 April 1980) was a British military officer, modern penta-hlete, and diplomat who served in a variety of Middle East countries, including the ambassadorship to Abidjan from 1961 to 1965. The son of a Ceylonese tea-planter, he began his career in the navy, but soon afterwards entered the army, where he fought in the trenches of World War I, where he was decorated with his first of two MCs. He played in the Olympic games of 1920, and was a mountaineer and explorer, until he was appointed by the Sudan Government as commander of the Camel Corps. He was a diplomat until his retirement in 1965, and wrote an autobiography, "The Wind of the Morning," in 1971, nine years before his death in  ud. He was born on 14 April 1895 at Nuwara Eliya, Ceylon, and educated at Cheam and the Britannia Royal Naval College (subsequently the Royal Agricultural College, Dartmouth). At the outbreak of World War I, he entered the Navy as a midshipman. On 15 May 1915 he was promoted to acting- lieutenant, but a month later he deserted from the Navy while on leave at Simon’s Town, South Africa, to go to the front as an officer in the Transvaal Scottish. He was later decorated for bravery at the Battle of Arras, for which he was named in the citation of 26 July 1917.

Joseph Henry Haywood (born in Wednesbury in April 1893) was an English association footballer who played as a wing half-back and an English rugby league footballer who played as a prop forward. Born in Wednesbury, he was brought up at Hindley and later played at right-half for Man U. and at the start of the 1914 season was given £50 as a player on the reserve list. He played in 14 matches in the first season and appeared at both left and right-half back. In the 1914–15 season he did not appear until February 6, but played 12 times, being about equally at right-half and left-half. His career was interrupted by the First World War, and he left at the end of the 1919–20 season when he began to play in the northern league and Man U. asked £20 to transfer his registration. He played at Warrington and Widnes. His debut for Warrington was on September 6, 1919, and he played his last match for them on April 24, 1920.

Katherine (Kay) Walsh was an English actress, dancer and film director. She was born on November 15, 1911, in London. Her film career prospered when she met her future husband, the film director David Lean, with whom she worked on prestige productions such as In Which We Serve and Oliver! She was brought up in Pimlico by her grandmother, and as a child danced in the West End theatres. When she was seventeen she went out with Pownall Pellew, later the 9th Viscount Exmouth, and they were passionate about racing cars. Her film debut was in the 1941 film 'How's the Punctuality'. She appeared in a small role in the film Mystery of Stambul in 1934 and in the film Get your man in the same year. She played in many short films during the next few years. Then she met the film director David Lean and was involved in a romance, and Pownall Pellew was dismissed. They married on November 23, 1940. She appeared in In Which We Serve and This Happy Breed, both directed by Lean and written by Noel Coward. It was she who fought for Lean to be given a co-director's credit for In Which We Serve.

Mattia Busche (born on 9 May 1985) is an American former professional road cyclist who rode between 2009 and 2016 for teams,, and. In 2009 he was famous for his fast rise from an amateur team from Wisconsin to a pro team in one season. He was twice winner of the American national road race championship. Busche is the son of and grew up in Wauwatosa, Wisconsin, and studied at Luther College in Decorah, Iowa. He began running at a young age and became a cyclist in 2005 while recovering from a running injury. He was a two-time NCAA All-American in cross-country and the 2007 Iowa Conference champion. After his graduation in 2007, Busche turned to road racing and joined the ISCorp amateur team. In his second year of competition, he tested the professional Continental team Kelly Benefit Strategies, and he was then offered a contract by the UCI Pro Tour team. Busche spent two years with and moved with a number of riders to the American team, which then merged with the Canadian team, in the 2012 season.

Franklinton is a neighborhood of Columbus, Ohio, to the west of the downtown area. Founded in 1797, it is the first settlement of Americans in Franklin County, and was the county seat until 1824. As the city of Columbus grew, it annexed and incorporated the town in 1859. This neighborhood is bordered by the Scioto River on the north and east, Harmon Avenue on the east, Stimmel Road and Greenlawn Avenue on the south, and Interstate 70 on the west. The main road is West Broad Street, one of the two major streets in Columbus. Parts of the neighborhood are sometimes called the bottoms, because much of the area is susceptible to flooding by the Scioto and Olentangy Rivers, and floodwalls are required to prevent the flooding of the city. The low-lying bottoms are conducive to agriculture, and the river is a direct connection to the Ohio River. The completion of the floodwall in 2004 spurred new development in eastern Franklinton, destroying three public housing projects and displacing residents. Developments are mostly high-end mixed-use buildings, resulting in significant gentrification in the area.

This object, whose planetary designation is 136108 Haumea, is a dwarf planet located in the outer planets, beyond the orbit of Neptune. It was discovered in 2004 by a team of astronomers led by Mike Brown at the Palomar Observatory in the United States and possibly in 2005 by a team led by Jose Luis Ortiz Moreno at the Sierra-Negra Observatory in Spain, a claim disputed by its opponents. It was named Haumea on September 17, 2008, in expectation of its discovery as a dwarf planet. Its estimated size would make it the third largest known trans-Neptunian object, after Eris and Pluto, but the uncertainty in this estimate overlaps somewhat with the larger estimates of the size of Makemake. Haumea's mass is about one-third that of Pluto and a thousandth that of Earth. Although it has not been directly observed, its light curve can be calculated as an ellipsoid of Jacobi (which it would have to be if it were a planet), of which the major axis is twice the diameter of the minor. In October of the year, the discovery of a ring system around Haumea was announced, the first of its kind in a TNO. The elongated shape of Haumea, its fast rotation and its rings, its high albedo, which would be due to the crystallization of the water ice of its surface, would indicate that it is the result of a collision that left it the most important member of a collisional family whose members are the large TNOs and the two known moons of Haumea, Hna and Namaka.

The definition of a corporation is the action of a company or group acting as one unit. The theory of the corporation defines the ethical strategies of the company and determines the image of the company. The roles of the corporation play various roles in the different parts of the company. They help the company to solve any problem that may arise. For example, with the onset of globalization, the language barriers of companies will increase, causing many problems and preventing the company from operating. Management is used to overcome this problem by making the company more flexible. Competition has also intensified, and many companies are finding it difficult to compete in terms of quality and productivity. However, the management of the corporation can solve this problem by allowing employees to be empowered. Positive corporation is when employees feel happy and satisfied at work and produce the best results. This is good for the company, because it can create an efficient team that can be very beneficial for the company. It also helps to reduce the turnover of the workforce, allowing the organization to retain the best employees.

KBJR-TV, virtual channel 6, UHF channel 19 is an NBC and CBS affiliate licensed to Superior, Wisconsin, serving Duluth, Superior, northernmost Michigan, and northwestern Wisconsin. Owned by Gray Television of Atlanta, it is a duopoly with KDLH (Channel 3), a CW affiliate with its studios in Duluth. Both stations share studios in Canal Park, Duluth, and KBJR-TV's transmitter is in Hilltop Park, west of downtown Duluth. Its sister station, KRII (Channel 11/UH-41), in Chisholm, serves the northern end of the market, including the Iron Range, Grand Rapids, and International Falls. This station, except for commercials and IDs, carries a feed of KBJR's programs. It also serves as a full-power translator of all the various KBJR channels and subchannels.

The Sancak of Rhodes, or Rhodes Province, [Ottoman Turkish Sancak-i / Liva-i Rodos; tr. Rodos sancak], also known as the Livadia of Rhodes, [15] was a secondary Ottoman administrative district, comprising the Dodecanese islands or southern amotas, of which Rhodes was the centre. After the conquest of Rhodes in 1522 by the Ottomans, it remained under the control of a beylerbey and did not become part of the island province of the Archipelagos until 1546. During the next two and a half centuries the Dodecanese, with the exception of Samos, were almost independent, and they were not administered by the general vilayet until the 1860s. Rhodes did not enjoy this independence and ceased to be a major commercial centre and a place of strategic importance under the Ottomans, once the eastern Mediterranean became an Ottoman lake. Only from the 18th century onwards does the island seem to have become a major tourist resort.

The Lennox Bridge, in the Glenbrook suburb of the Blue Mountains, is a heritage-listed bridge on Mitchell's Pass over Brookside Creek, also known as Lapstone Creek. Across this stream, which is known locally as Lapstone Creek, passes the railway line. It was designed by David Lennox, and was built in 1832-3 by convicts led by James Randall. The property is owned by the Blue Mountains City Council, and was added to the State Register of Significant Places on 2 April 1999. The stone-arched bridge has a single span, is 21 metres long, and is about seven metres above water level, with a road width of 18 metres. The first road up the eastern slopes of the Blue Mountains was built by William Cox in 1814–15. It was "very steep and sharp" and it was subject to frequent landslips, which meant that it was quickly replaced in 1824 by the Bathurst Road (now Old Bathurst Road), which avoided the waterways but was so steep that it was difficult for travel and dangerous. When Thomas Mitchell was appointed Surveyor-General in 1828, one of the first matters he addressed was the improvement of the Great Western Road. One of his first tasks was to establish a road halfway between the existing two, in preference to the governor's suggestion of establishing a permanent road-building team on the old Bathurst Road.

Munkerup is a township on the seashore of Hornbaek-Dronningmlle, in the north of Zealand, about 2 versts west of Dronningmlle and 3 versts east of Gilleleje. The population in 1910 was 791. The name of the place is first mentioned as Munnckerup in 1582, and in the market-list of 1681 Munkerup is said to consist of two half-farms and two scats in Tornbakke and three scats in Hule-ad. In about the year 1920, Munkerup began to develop as a fashionable bathing place, when the artists Carl Loher and Holger Drachmann began to resort to it. The first villas began to spout forth on the Grandahl road about the year 1936, but it was not until the 50s and 60s that the place really took on a resort look. The fashionable bathing-hotel Hulead Badehotel attracted many guests from Copenhagen. Some, like the architect Poul Henningsen, built their own villas. The Munkerup child-sanatorium, or Munkerup Borg-nes-sanatorium, was founded in the middle of the thirties, for the treatment of children suffering from the bilious ailment.

A head-on engagement is a situation where a surface-to-air missile or a fighter plane attacks another aircraft while the target is flying toward it. This makes the engagement of IR homing missiles more difficult, because the target's hot engine exhaust nozzles are facing away from the attacker. Usually, only all-aspect IR missiles are capable of head-on attacks. Generally, most radar guided missiles can engage targets from head-on, but aircraft tend to have smaller cross-sections at this angle, and a missile's radar may not have the range to acquire the target at maximum range in this situation. Missiles are usually less likely to hit their target in a head-on attack because of the speed of the closing. If the missile is going at Mach 2, and the target at Mach 1, the combined speed of Mach 3, gives the missile little time to react to the sudden maneuvers the target may perform or to countermeasures. Moreover, the target can evade the missile, then come at it again just before impact, which means the missile has to turn in a much smaller arc than the target. Although missiles are faster than airplanes, that advantage often suffices to keep the missile out of the lethal range of the aircraft.

Diamonds and Rain is the third album and the second full-length album by the Canadian Christian rock band The Choir, released in 1986. It was the first release of the band without the word Youth. After the release of Shades of Gray, Shadow Records closed, and the Youth Choir was once again without a record company. At the same time, Myrrh Records was looking for artists in the rock genre and sent the record industry consultant Tom Willett from Nashville to Los Angeles to establish Myrrh-LA. After six months of looking for new talent, Tom Willett was dragged by a local promoter to a Youth Choir concert and found it to be "creatively advanced and musically prophesying. " They were recruited in June of the same year, just after their third appearance at Cornerstone, and they were the first Myrrh artist to play an alternative rock. However, Willett was not satisfied with the name of the band and suggested dropping the word Youth to reflect the musical maturity of the band. Daugherty and Steve Hindalong, the drummer and lyricist, had already considered such a change and agreed. So the band would now be called The Choir and start recording.

Jackson Heights is a neighborhood in northwest Queens, New York City. It is bordered by North Corona on the east, Elmhurst on the south, Woodside on the west, northwestern Astoria (Ditmars–Steinway) on the northwest, and East Elmhurst on the northeast. In the last decade, nearly half the population of the neighborhood was born abroad. In the 2010 United States Census, the population of the neighborhood was 108,152. The neighborhood was built on a vast wetland called “Trains Meadow” until 1909, when Edward A. MacDougall’s Queensboro Development Corp. purchased all the unused land and farms and named it Jackson Heights after John C. Jackson, a respected local entrepreneur and a descendant of one of Queens’s founding families. As public transportation developed, the neighborhood became increasingly residential, and apartments and townhouses were built. Starting in the 1960s, the middle-class white residents began to leave for the suburbs, and non-whites began to arrive.

Pranas Vaitkus, 10 February, 1876 - 21 September, 1901, was a Lithuanian poet. After graduating from the Gymnasium in Marijampol, he studied law at St. Petersburg University. For infringing the press ban he was imprisoned for a month in 1899, and he was not given any official employment. Eduards Volters helped him to get a position in the library of the Russian Academy of Sciences, but tuberculosis broke out and he was forced to return to his homeland. He died at the age of twenty-five and left only about a hundred poems. His first poems appeared in 1896 in Varpas, but the greater part of his verses appeared in Vienyb lietuvnink, the Lithuanian newspaper published in Palestine, Pennsylvania. His first collection was issued posthumously in the United States in 1903. His verses, especially those on Lithuanian nature, are popular and have been adopted as folk songs. His verses are eloquent, tender, deprived of more elaborate metaphors and poetics, and show a depth of feeling that stands it apart from other poetry of the period. Biography:

Vice Admiral Sir William Charles Fahie KCB, D.D., a distinguished officer of the British Navy, was a native of Jamaica, and was one of the most distinguished naval officers of the American War of Independence, the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars. Unlike many of his contemporaries, he spent almost his entire career in the West Indies, where he was born and where he spent the periods of his reserve and retirement. During the American War of Independence, which lasted from 1775 to 1783, he was able to take advantage of his knowledge of the country; and between 1783 and 1793 he was in reserve, after which he was recalled to take part in the expedition of Sir John Jervis against the French West Indies. However, Fahie remained in the West Indies during the next 20 years of war, and served as captain in the invasion of Martinique and in the subsequent battle of 14–17 April 1809, in which he captured the French ship Haupoult. In 1810 he participated in the invasion of Guadeloupe, and was transferred to European waters for the first time since 1780. At the end of the war, Fahie remained in the service and was appointed commander-in-chief of the Leeward Islands station. In 1824 he retired and was appointed a Knight Commander, subsequently settling in the British West Indies with his second wife.

Isabella Macdonald (née Clark) was the first wife of John A. Macdonald, one of the founding fathers of the Dominion of Canada and the first Prime Minister of Canada. She married him in 1843 in Kingston, Ontario. She lived for two years in perfect happiness with her husband, when she fell seriously ill. Her first son died at thirteen months old; but her second, Hugh John Macdonald, became premier of Manitoba. After several recovery periods, she died at the age of forty-eight, without having recovered from her illness. Early life and family Isabella was born in Dalnavert, Invernessshire, Scotland, daughter of Alexander and Margaret Clark. She met her husband, John Alexander Macdonald, a cousin, in Great Britain in 1842. On this trip, he went to the Isle of Man, to see his cousin, Margaret Greene, née Clark, who lived in a small farmhouse near Douglas, with her sister, Isabella. Macdonald took an immediate liking to her, and suggested that she visit the following year, supposedly to see another sister, Maria, who had married John Alexander Macpherson. Then, in 1843, she sailed for Canada to visit the Macphersons and the Macdonalds in Ontario. It was during this trip that, after a few months of courtship, they became engaged, and on September 1, 1843, they were married in the home of her sister, Maria, and her husband, John Alexander Macpherson, by the Rev. Mr. Machar, minister of St. Andrew's Presbyterian Church in Kingston. The bride and groom were related through their grandmother, and cousin marriages were not uncommon in those days. They settled in Kingston. Although their marriage started out well, Isabella soon realized that her husband was only interested in two things: business and the human anatomy.

Clive D. L. Wynne (born in London, 1961) is a British-Australian ethologist, specializing in the behaviour of dogs and their wild relatives. He was born and bred on the Isle of Wight, and studied at University College London and at the University of Edinburgh. He has studied a wide range of species, from pigeons to antechinuses, but from around 2006, he has combined his childhood interest in dogs with his professional interests and now studies and teaches about the behavior of dogs and their wild relatives. - Wynne was educated on the Isle of Wight at Sandown High School, then studied Human Sciences at University College London, where he was influenced by the evolutionary psychologist Henry Plotkin. It was in Edinburgh that he earned his doctorate in psychology, with a dissertation on the behavior of the Barbary pigeon. After doing postdoctoral research at Ruhr-University Bochum, Duke University and the University of Konstanz, where he worked under the guidance of John Staddon and Juan Delius, he became a professor at the University of Western Australia. From there he moved to the University of Florida in 2002 and then to the University of Arizona in 2013. He was founding director of the Canine Science Collaboratory in 2014.

Alexei Alexandrovich Surkov (13 October 1899 in the village of Serednevo, province of Yaroslavl — 14 June 1983 in Moscow, Soviet Union) was a Russian poet, editor and literary critic. He was a member of the St Petersburg Writers' Union and the St Petersburg Writers' Union. After the February Revolution he served in the Red Army, and later he worked for the Komsomol. In the late 1920s he published poems. He was a member of the Russian Association of Proletarian Poets and of the group of the Russian Association of Proletarian Poets, whose slogan was: "Soviet art should be political and pro-Communist. " In April 1932, after the fact that Stalin forbade the dissolution of the Russian Association of Proletarian Poets and other associations of writers and poets, Surkov attacked Boris Pasternak at the Writers' meeting and called him a subjective idealist. For him, the world is not outside, but inside.

Murra is a city of the General Lopez Department of the province of Santa Fe, Argentina, and takes its name from an Irishman, John James Murra, who was born in 1822 in Haysland, in Kilrane, County Wexford, close to the port of Rosslare, and who, having found a good job as a tenant farmer, decided to emigrate. He went to Buenos Aires and went to the pampas to look for farming. At first he worked as a border maker between two farms, became a sheep tenant farmer, then got his own ranch in Salto, bought more land in the vicinity of Rojas and in the province of Santa Fe. At his death in 1909 he was rich. In 1911, as the railway was being extended, land belonging to Murra's heirs near Rosario was acquired, and the station was established, and in 1966 the town, which arose around it, was called Murra.

'A Billion Lights' is a song by British boy band JLS. It is the only single (other than the charity single "Proud" ) to be released from their fifth studio album, Goodbye - The Greatest Hits, released on November 17, 2013., the day before the album's release. On December 15, 2012, Marvin Humes announced on his radio show JAM that JLS would be releasing a fifth album in 2013. "Every boy band will be a five-album thing, and usually they do greatest hits albums, but we don't know if we're ready for that yet. " There will be an album next year, for sure. We've got a lot of competition, and not just boy bands. We have to stay ahead of the game, keep coming up with new hits. " - On February 1, 2013, the album was officially announced. On March 26, 2013, Marvin Humes revealed that the band would be in Los Angeles to record the album. "We're going to LA and we're going to work with Rodney Jerkins and we're looking at some new people as well."

Mark Ellingson, born in 1905, was the fifth president of the RIT, succeeding John A. Randall, and he served until 1969. He had started as a teacher at RIT and was promoted to president, a position he held longer than any before or since, and he was responsible for the establishment of the school’s present modern shape. During his twenty-three-year term, the student population increased from 2,250 day and night pupils to 16,000, with more than $200 million in funds under management. Ellingson presided over a great expansion of the school’s endowment, a merger in 1937 with the Empire State School of Printing, a change of name to the present RIT in 1944, and the building and transfer to the new campus in Henrietta. In addition, he was responsible for establishing the National Institute for the Deaf, which opened in 1968, and the tallest building on the Henrietta campus, a dormitory called Tower A, is named for him.

"Coming to Homerica" is the twenty-first and last episode of the twentieth season of the American animated series The Simpsons. It was originally aired on May 17, 2009 on the Fox network. The plot is a parody of illegal aliens in the United States, complete with vigilantes and border fences. The first airing in the United States coincided with Norwegian Constitution Day. Plot Krusty is informed that Krustyburgers are the most unhealthy fast food in the world, so he decides to open his own Krustyburger, which is completely vegetarian. The inhabitants like the new burgers, but soon they are poisoned by a rat in the mill, which eats spoiled barley from the neighboring town of Ogdenville. The resulting boycott destroys the local barley industry, and the residents of Ogdenville, who are portrayed as overly stereotypical Norwegians, are forced to leave the city (to the sad waltz "Aasen's Death" by Edvard Grieg and a part of the Finlandia hymn by his Finnish counterpart Jean Sibelius).

Holdhus Church (historically called Holdhus Sjakre) is a former parish church of the Church of Norway in Bjrnafjorden municipality, Vestland, Norway. It is situated in the village of Holdhus, and although it is not in use now, it is a church of the parish of Fusa, which belongs to the presbytery of Fana, in the diocese of Bjrgvin. The brown-colored wooden church was built in 1726 according to the long-church design, but parts of the building go back to 1618. It seats about 90 people. The church is known for its art inside. Its walls are painted in rosemaling, a type of Norwegian folk art. The earliest historical records of the church go back to 1306, but that was not when it was built. The first church in Hlandsdal valley was a wooden stave church, and was called... It was probably built during the 13th century. In 1618, the old choir of the church was demolished, and a new wooden choir was built in its place. In 1726, the old nave was demolished, and a new timbered nave was built, which seats about 90 people. This new nave was joined to the choir that was built in 1618. After that, there were no more medieval parts left in the church. In 1890, a new church was built about one mile to the southeast, which was the new Hlandsdal Church. This meant that the old church would no longer be needed as a parish church. In 1889, it was sold to the merchant Hans H. Holdhus, with the intention of demolishing it within two years. However, in 1890, he sold it to the Norwegian Association for the Preservation of Ancient Monuments. Since then, it has been used as a museum, and is still used by the presbytery on special occasions. The new owners undertook a major restoration and repair project of the building in 1905–1906, which was led by the architect Schak Bull.

The first inroads of Islam in Chad are to be traced to Uqba ibn Nafi, whose descendants are still living in the Lake Chad region. When in the 14th century Arab emigrants began to arrive from the East in large numbers, the conversion had already taken place. The christening of Chad was gradual, and due to the slow progress of the extension of the Islamic civilization outside its political limits. To the Chadian Muslims, forty-eight per cent are orthodox, twenty-one per cent are schismatics, twenty-three per cent are simple Muslims, and four per cent are professed Muslims. The religion of the Chadians has been little influenced by the great mystic and reformatory movements of the epoch of the Islamic Middle Ages, nor by the reactionary upheavals which have affected other countries. As for the clergy, Chad had not been much influenced by the schisms and reformations which characterized the later periods of Islamic history. On the other hand, the Sanusi brotherhood, founded in the middle of the last century in Libya, possessed considerable political and commercial influence in the region of Lake Chad at the beginning of the century. An ecclesiastical and religious reform movement, the influence of which was feared by the French, and headed by the fanatical Sanusi, the adherents of which, restricted as they were to the tribes of the uul, and the toubou of the Eastern Tibesti, were not numerous.

Malayalam scholar, teacher and scholar. He was born in 1866, and lived until 1919. He is well known for his reformist approach towards Muslims and the Muslims of his time. He is regarded as the father of the new madrasahs in the state of Kerela. He was born in 1866 (Hijrah) in the village of Adyar, in the state of the south of India. His father was Kalamuhyadhi Kutti, a close friend of Sayyid Alaith, a poet. He was abandoned in his childhood by his father. His mother and his uncles brought him up with a strict religious ethos. They later added the name of his mother's family to his name, and he became known as Kulilath Muhammad Musaliar. He is known by three abbreviations, "C. H. ", "M. C. C." and "C. A." The abbreviations have stuck to him and to his sons as well. His sons, later on, came to be known as "M. C. C. Brothers".

Joy Dietrich is a Korean-born American journalist, writer, film-maker and producer. Her documentary film Tie a Yellow Ribbon, which was shown in 2007, has won several awards. She was born in Korea, but was adopted and brought up in the United States. In her early life she was the only Asian American in her American neighbourhood, and her family life was not a happy one. She experienced racial prejudice, and finally left her hometown, not planning to return. She described her upbringing in an interview in 2007: You know, the racial tension in my community was at one time unbearable. I was the only Asian American in the town. I think just leaving the town helped me to see that there was another life, that there was an alternative life. I came from a very dysfunctional family, and between the family and the community, it was a very, very bleak and depressing existence. So I left my hometown. I haven't been back since.

Anglicans are followers of a Western Christian tradition, the fruits of the English Reformation and the Protestant Reformation in Europe. It is one of the largest Christian denominations, with about 110 million adherents worldwide. The followers of Anglicanism are called Anglicans, and in some countries they are also called Episcopalians. Anglicans are mainly the members of the national or regional ecclesiastical provinces of the world Anglican Communion, which is the third largest Christian communion in the world after the Roman Catholic Church and the Orthodox Church. These provinces are in full communion with the Archbishop of Canterbury, whom the British monarch elects personally, and who is the primus inter pares of the communion, the “first among equals”, calls the Lambeth Conference, leads the primatial conference, and is the president of the Anglican Consultative Council. Some churches that are not part of the Anglican Communion or are not recognized by it also call themselves Anglican, such as those that form the Continuing Anglican Movement and the Anglican Renewal Movement.

The World Triathlon Cup is an annual international series of triathlon races. The Cup is organized by World Triathlon, the international organization of the sport. Inaugurated in 1991, the World Triathlon Cup was an attempt to establish a series of competitions under its direction, parallel to the ITU Triathlon World Championships. Consequently, a World Cup winner was crowned in addition to the World Champion. However, after the conclusion of the 2008 series, the ITU reorganized its competitions and introduced the World Triathlon Series as a new and more important series, relegating the World Triathlon Cup to a second tier of the competition, and as a result the number of races in the World Cup was reduced. Points from the World Triathlon Cup races are now only used to determine an athlete’s world ranking. Originally, the top twenty athletes in each race would be given points corresponding to their positions, and the athlete with the most points at the end of the season would be declared the World Triathlon Cup Champion.

An American actor, a martial artist, a boxing coach, a boxing cornerman, a boxing doctor, an athlete who is also a cornerman in the ring. It was born in Pasadena on December 11, 1956. It was raised in San Jose, California and in Brooklyn, New York. His father was a boxer in the United States Marine Corps and later he taught boxing to young Eastman. When he was 13, he was a member of the Police Athletic League, where he was an amateur boxer under Gus Spencer. He also trained at the Garden City Boxing Club and at the Bath Beach Health Club in Brooklyn, New York. Besides boxing, he was trained in martial arts as a young man. He practiced taekwondo under the leadership of Dan Kyu Choi and was the captain of the taekwondo team of the Choi Institute of Sports and later became the California State Tae Kwon Do Champion. He received a black belt from the teacher byung-hun. He was the first and original member of the world-famous Ernie Reyes West Coast Demo Team and was the first to add gymnastics and acrobatics to martial arts demonstrations. It has been passed on to this day, and the same West Coast Demo Team is doing a martial arts show all over the world.

The Arabic term in question is nisbah, a name for the system of nominal, adjectival, and verbal terminations employed in Classical Arabic to mark grammatical case. In fully vocalized Arabic, and especially in books written for children or beginners in Arabic, the written forms are pronounced, but in the spoken dialects of Arabic they are not preserved; often they are omitted in a protracted pause. A further exception is made in poetry, where they are preserved only at the end of a line; but the rule of terminations is not universal. At the end of a sentence or line of verse the termination n is invariably omitted (except in the case of nun, which is preserved) as well as the vowel ending, which may be retained or not as required by the metre. According to the knowledge of nisbah which each speaker possesses, he may omit the terminations in reading the standard language, thus rendering it more like the spoken dialects. Many Arabic textbooks for foreigners omit or give only a cursory introduction to the subject of nisbah. Arabic without nisbah requires a different, a more regular word order, which is akin to that found in the spoken dialects. Etymology: The term literally means 'to make Arabic'. It is the stem masdar of the root rb, 'to pour forth', and it means 'to render eloquent, to express, to disclose'. The term is related to the word 'Arab' itself.

Gary Lewis North was born on April 15, 1954, in Chattanooga, Tennessee. He is a retired four-star General of the United States Air Force, who served as Commander of Pacific Air Forces and as the executive director of the Pacific Air Combat Forces at Hickam Air Force Base, Hawai'i, from August 19, 2009, until August 9, 2012. North was commissioned in 1976, having graduated from the Air Force Reserve Officer Training Corps program at East Carolina University. He served in a large number of commands and positions on the staff, including four long and four short overseas tours. North served twice on the staff of the unified military headquarters as executive officer to the director of the joint staff, and as director of political-military affairs for the Asia-Pacific region. He was on the staff of the air force as chief of the joint requirements division and deputy director of joint matters, and as the director of operations at the Pacific Air Forces at Camp H.M. Smith, Hawai'i. Before his current position, North was Commander of the 9th Air Force and the United States Air Forces in the Middle East, with a staff of two wings in the 9th Air Force and eight air expeditionary wings in the Central Command. He served as Commander of the Combined Air Forces of the Central Command and as the Combined Air Forces of the U.S. Central Command.

Steven Spooner is an American pianist and currently a professor at the Peabody Institute in Baltimore, Maryland. As a performer, Spooner has appeared in recitals at Carnegie Hall, the Vredenburg Music Centre in Utrecht, the Salle Cortot in Paris, Budapest’s Liszt Academy of Music, the Festival de Musique in Geneva, and countless other concert halls in Europe, South America, Asia and the United States. Recently, Spooner concluded a series of recitals in the manner of those historic performances by Anton Rubinstein in the concert halls of Paris in 1885. These concerts featured a program of 17 recitals of the standard piano repertoire from the baroque to the twenty-first century. He is also a sought-after collaborator and has performed with an eclectic list of singers and instrumentalists, including bassist Daxun Zhang of the Silk Road Ensemble, former trombonist of the Philadelphia Orchestra M. Dee Stewart, and Israeli-born violinist Leor Maltinsky. Spooner’s orchestral appearances have included the Danubia Symphony Orchestra, the Brevard Symphony Orchestra, the New Orleans Civic Symphony, the Ozark Chamber Orchestra, and, most recently, the Chamber Orchestra of the Kremlin, which toured North America. Spooner is a Steinway Artist.

High-Angle Control System (HACS) is a British system of anti-aircraft gunfire control introduced into the British Royal Navy in 1931 and used extensively during World War II. HACS determined the deviation necessary to hit a flying target of known height, bearing and speed. The first HACS was developed in the 1920s and was first used in January 1930, when HACS I was put into service on board the battleship HMS Ile of Wight. HACS I had no automatic stabilization or mechanical assistance for the aiming of the turrets. HACS III, introduced in 1935, was provided with automatic stabilization, worked hydraulically, had much improved data transmission and introduced the HACS III table. HACS III was a vastly improved computer that featured several improvements such as a faster maximum speed of 350 knots, automatic fuze predictions, improved geometry in the deflection screen, and automatic gyro stabilization of the data received from the director. HACS was a control system, based on an efficient data transmission between the outside gun director, the firing control room and the ship's large anti-aircraft guns.

Dyllan W. M. is a documentary film maker and the founder of the media company, The Makers, Inc. With Peter Kunhardt, she produced 'Gloria: In Her Own Words' (HBO), 'Finding Your Roots with Henry Louis Gates Jr.' (PBS), 'Makers: Women Who Make America' (AOL) and many others. Her films include 'Gloria: In Her Own Words' (HBO), 'The African Americans: Many Rivers to Cross' (PBS), 'Teddy: In His Own Words' (HBO), 'Faces of America with Henry Louis Gates Jr.' (PBS), 'This Emotional Life' (PBS), 'Afro-American Lives' (PBS), 'Oprah's Roots' (PBS), 'In Memoriam - 9/11' (HBO) and 'In Memoriam' (HBO) and from 2003-2005 she served as director of content and operations for the Freedom Center at Ground Zero, a cultural institution proposed as part of the Lower Manhattan Development Corp.'s plans for the World Trade Center site. [1][2]

According to the historians, there were three different castles, built by the Teutonic Order on the bank of the Neman River in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. Their exact location is not known, and historians have disputed on this. The first fortress was built in 1337 by the crusaders, among them Henry IV, Duke of Bavaria, in whose honour it was named after him. Emperor Louis IV proclaimed it the capital of conquered Lithuania. The newly built castle withstood a 22-day siege of Grand Duke Gediminas, but the Order abandoned it in 1344. Then the Order set fire to the first Bavaria castle and rebuilt a new one closer to Prussia. The second Bavaria castle endured a six-day siege by Lithuanians in 1381, but was destroyed in 1384 by Vytautas, who slandered the Teutonic Order after the end of the Lithuanian civil war. The third Bavaria castle was built in the spring of 1387 where the old castle of George was, but it didn’t get to keep its name and was called George. It was destroyed and burned by Vytautas in April 1403 during the first Samogitian revolt. The history of the third Bavaria castle is uncertain, and it is disputed by the historians.

In the field of collecting stamps, the value of a stamp is determined by the condition in which it is found. The three most important features are the centering, the margins and the gum. Superb is sometimes used for a stamp in perfect condition. Extremely fine or extra fine means a perfectly centered stamp with wide margins. Very fine (or fine) is a well-centered stamp with ample margins. Fine is a stamp with four or more close margins. Average is a stamp that has been cut or trimmed on one side, or that has a part of the design cut off by the perforations. This is generally not collected or sold, except in the case of rare or very old stamps, unless as an insert or a study copy. A stamp in poor condition is one that is dirty, soiled or cut to shape. The only stamps worth having in this condition are the great rarities, such as the British Guiana one-penny carmine.

The USS Illinois (BB-7) was a pre-dreadnought battleship built for the United States Navy. She was the first of a series of battleships and the second ship of the United States Navy to be named after the state of Illinois. Her keel was laid down in February 1897 at the Newport News Shipbuilding and Drydock Company, and she was launched in October 1898. The Illinois was armed with four six-inch guns in her main battery and could steam at a maximum speed of 25 knots. From 1902 to 1907, she served in the North Atlantic Squadron, later renamed the Atlantic Fleet. During this time, she was involved in two accidental collisions with other battleships. From December 1907 to February 1909, she sailed around the world with the Great White Fleet. Beginning in November 1912, the ship was used as a training ship. In 1919, she was transferred to the state of New York to be used as a training ship for the New York Naval Militia. In 1924, as a result of the Washington Naval Treaty, the ship was converted into a floating armory, and served as a floating armory, barracks, and school for the next thirty years. In January 1941, the ship was renamed the USS Prairie State, in order to free up her name for a new battleship. In the end, the ship was sold for scrap in 1956.

Joseph Henry Reason (23 March 1905 – 26 July 1997) was an American librarian. For twenty-five years he was the director of the library of Howard University. He was the first African-American to be nominated for president of the American Library Association and was elected to that office. In 1999, American Library Association selected him as one of the 100 most important leaders of the twentieth century. Early life and education Reason was born in Franklin, Louisiana, the first child of Joseph and Bertha Peoples Reason. His son, J. Paul Reason, was the first African-American to hold the rank of Admiral of the United States Navy. In 1928 he received a BA degree from the University of New Orleans in history. In 1929–30 he taught languages at the private Gilbert Academy for black students in New Orleans. In 1931 he married Bernice Chism, and they had two children: Barbara Reason Butler and Joseph Paul Reason. In 1932 he earned a second BA in French from Howard University, and in 1936 a master's degree in French from the University of Pennsylvania. His first article appeared in the Quarterly World in the spring of 1934 on the subject of Tacna-Arica.

The Death Valley Symphony is a small work written in 1949 by Ferde Grofé, depicting the journey of the pioneers through the harsh desert of Death Valley in California. The work was commissioned by the Death Valley 49ers, a non-profit association dedicated to the preservation of pioneer and mining history in the area of Death Valley, which includes Death Valley National Park and its surroundings. The music was part of the commemoration of the centenary of the death of the pioneers who came through Death Valley in search of gold and other riches, and also the centennial of the State of California. Grofé conducted the work himself with the Hollywood Bowl Orchestra on December 3, 1949, in the Desolation Canyon area of Death Valley National Monument (now Death Valley National Park). A procession of wagons accompanied the music into the area, and actor James Stewart narrated the event. The concert was attended by a crowd of 50,000 people.

Vladimir Mikhailovich Bekhterev [Bekhterey] (January 20, 1857 - December 24, 1921) was a Russian neurologist and the founder of objective psychology. He is best known for his discoveries on the role of the hippocampus in memory, for his study of reflexes, and for the illness known as Bekhterev's disease. In addition, he is known for his rivalry with Ivan Pavlov on the study of conditioned reflexes. Early life. Vladimir Mikhailovich Bekhterev was born in Soraly, a village in the Russian Empire in the Vyatka province, between the Volga and the Ural mountains. Mikhail Pavlovich, the father of Vladimir Mikhailovich, was a police inspector in the district. Marya Mikhailovna, the mother of Vladimir Mikhailovich, was a daughter of a titular councilor and studied in a boarding school, where she was also taught music and French. Bekhterev was the youngest of three brothers: after him were Nikolai and Alexander, older by six and three years. In 1864 the family moved to Vyatka province, and a year later, the father died of tuberculosis, while Bekhterev was still a very young child. Although childhood was not easy, Bekhterev had the opportunity to enter the gymnasium of Vyatka, one of the oldest in Russia, in 1867, and in 1873 entered the medical academy of St. Petersburg.. Then he entered the surgical medical academy of St. Petersburg, where he worked under Professor Jan Lucjan Mierzejewski [ljm]. He developed his interest in neurology and psychiatry here.

A diaper, cloth diaper, or'real diaper' (British English), is a reusable diaper made of natural fibers, synthetic materials, or a combination of both. Often, it is made of industrial cotton, bleached white or left natural, or wool, bamboo or hemp. Artificial fibers, like a towel or a microfibre layer inside the diaper or a polyurethane laminate (PUL) as a waterproof layer on the outside, are also used. Synthetic fabrics such as microfleece or suedecloth are also often used inside the diaper as a "stay-dry" liner, because of the non-absorbent properties of this type of fabric. Modern diapers come in many shapes: they are preformed cloth diapers, all-in-one diapers, fitted diapers with covers, pocket diapers or'stuffable' diapers consisting of a waterproof outer shell into which absorbent materials can be inserted. There are many features of modern diapers that are borrowed from disposable diapers, such as the hourglass form, materials that separate moisture from the skin, double gussets and an inner elastic for better fit and retention of the liquid.

Young Perspective is a concept advanced by youth movements, which aim to make visible the obstacles they encounter in trying to participate, be taken into account and exercise their rights, because of the system of adultcentric oppression that has been the basis of societies throughout history. Young Perspective attempts to ingrain the realities, needs, problems and opinions of youth onto the public agenda, through the voices of youth, in order to bring about intergenerational articulation and destroy the discourses that legitimately limit rights. It defines adultcentrism as a system of oppression which oppresses young people, generating stigmatization of who they are and the role they play in society, a form of ageism that generates asymmetrical power relations between the generations, affecting children, adolescents and young people, subjecting them to the adults who systematically make their problems, needs and experiences invisible, impose their plans, lifestyles and deny the possibility of forming bonds of intergenerational solidarity.

Automobile Internet is the term used for the Internet in a car. The connection is usually via tethering to a mobile phone or via a mobile hotspot that can be built into or carried by the car. Among those which have been built into cars are: General Motors OnStar, which is a subscription-based communication service which offers telecommunication, security, a free number of telephone services, a navigation system, and an automatic diagnostic system. BMW Assist, which is a telematics system that helps the car find help if it gets into trouble. Mercedes-Benz mbrace, which can connect the car to a smart phone or a personal computer. The data subscription-based system Cadillac CUE. Ford Sync, which can be connected to a personal computer via the O2 network. The Chrysler Uconnect Web, which has a hotspot with a range of up to 150 feet via the 3G EV-DO network of Autonet. The hotspot includes Bluetooth for cell phones, a hard drive, Sirius XM satellite radio, and GPS. It is a subscription-based service, which is free for the first year. The Toyota Safety Connect, a telematics system introduced in 2009, which provides telecommunication, assistance, safety, remote diagnostics, and other services. On the Entune system, it is integrated with the Entune App. On the Lexus, it is part of the Enform system, which adds telecommunications and destination services. The subscription is free for the first year, after which it can be renewed annually. The dangers of connecting a car to a cellular network are that it may expose the vehicle's control system to hacking.

Bhola was born on August 8, 1927, and died on January 21, 2019. He was a great hockey player, who had represented India in the 1956 and 1960 Olympic games and won gold and silver medals for the country, respectively. Born in a middle-class family in Multan (Pakistan), his forefathers belonged to the Dadan Sikhs and had settled in Multan near the end of the eighteenth century. He had studied at the Government Model School in Khanewal, where there was no electricity and only one community pump for the whole town to fetch water. His father woke the family at dawn every day to go to the pump, fill a jerrycan with water and then go back home to do chores. After completing his schooling, he came to New Delhi for higher education and took up a course in electrical engineering at the then Government College of Engineering, now known as the Delhi Technological University. After graduating from the GCE in February 1952, he joined the Indian Air Force. In 1962, he was selected by the Indian Air Force for a two-year master’s degree course in electrical engineering at the College of Aeronautics, Cranfield University, in the United Kingdom, where he graduated with distinction.

Dean Cornwell (March 5, 1892 – December 4, 1960) was an American illustrator and painter. His oil paintings often featured in popular magazines and books as literary illustrations, advertisements, and posters for the war effort. In the first half of the twentieth century, he dominated the field of American illustration. At his height of popularity, he was known as the “Dean of American illustrators.” Cornwell was born in Louisville, Kentucky. His father, Charles L. Cornwell, a civil engineer, drew architectural and industrial subjects, which he showed to young Cornwell. His first job was a cartoonist on the Louisville Herald. In 1912 he moved to Chicago and worked for the Chicago Trib. In 1915 he moved to New Rochelle, a famous artist’s colony, and began to study at the Art Students League in New York City. At the end of 1919 he went to London to study under Frank Brangwyn.

The Swiss ePrix (in full: the Julius Baer Swiss E-Prix) was a Formula E car race that took place in the streets of Bern on June 22, 1902. It was the eleventh round of the season, the first and only Swiss ePrix, and the second race to be held in Switzerland after the Zurich ePrix. The race was won by Jean-Eric Vergne, who, after starting from pole, led the race from the first to the last lap. A close second was scored by Mitch Evans in a Jaguar, and third was the Swiss driver Sébastien Buemi in a car from the Nissan e.Dams team. On the first lap, a red flag was thrown, as several cars were involved in a collision and blocked the track. After a 40-minute break, the race was resumed, and the starting positions were given again. These changes caused complaints from several drivers who had moved up during the first lap. The only driver who couldn't start the race was the e.dams driver Robin Frijns, whose car was badly damaged in the first collision.
